\section{Other Graphical Representations of
Data}\label{other-graphical-representations-of-data}

There are many other types of graphs. Some of the more common ones are
the scatterplot, and a time series plot. There are also many different
graphs that have emerged lately for categorical and numerical data. Many
are found in publications and websites.

\textbf{Boxplots} are another graphical display for numerical data that
allow us to compare the distributions of two or more groups. They
summarize important features of the data, such as the median,
variability, and potential outliers. Because boxplots are based on
specific numerical summaries, we will develop those ideas in the next
chapter before constructing and interpreting boxplots.

\subsection{Scatterplots}\label{scatterplots}

Sometimes you have two numerical variables, and you want to see if they
are related. A scatterplot helps you visualize the relationship between
the two variables. A scatterplot displays ordered pairs on a coordinate
system, with one variable plotted on the horizontal (x) axis and the
other on the vertical (y) axis.

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-scatter-plot}{}\label{exm-scatter-plot}

A study was conducted on tire rubber and recorded the abrasion loss, the
hardness of the rubber, and tensile strength. Suppose you are interested
in visualizing the relationship of the rubber abrasion loss versus the
hardness of the rubber. Create a scatterplot of the variables \Var{loss}
and \Var{hard}. Describe the relationship, if any exists.

\includegraphics{Rguroo_Icons/Rguroo_repo_logo.png} The dataset for this
example is available in the Rguroo dataset repository \Repo{MASS}, with
the dataset name \Data{Rubber}. Table~\ref{tbl-rubber} displays the
first five rows of the dataset. A complete description of the variables
is provided in the \hyperref[code-book-rubber]{dataset code book} that
follows.

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Code book for Rubber Dataset}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\textbf{Description:} This dataset recorded data from accelerated
testing of tire rubber.

Format

This dataset contains the following columns:

\Var{loss}: the abrasion loss in gm/hr.

\Var{hard}: the hardness in Shore units.

\Var{tens}: tensile strength in kg/sq m.

Source O.L. Davies (1947) Statistical Methods in Research and
Production. Oliver and Boyd, Table 6.1 p.~119.

O.L. Davies and P.L. Goldsmith (1972) Statistical Methods in Research
and Production. 4th edition, Longmans, Table 8.1 p.~239.

References Venables, W. N. and Ripley, B. D. (1999) Modern Applied
Statistics with S-PLUS. Third Edition. Springer.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

In order to create a scatterplot, we need to determine which variable
will be placed on the x-axis and which on the y-axis. Since tire
hardness could influence abrasion loss, we will use \Var{hardness} in
Shore units on the x-axis and \Var{loss} in grams per hour on the
y-axis.

Note: A Shore unit is a numerical measure of the hardness of materials
such as rubber and plastics. It indicates how resistant a material is to
being indented, with higher numbers representing harder materials and
lower numbers representing softer ones.

Click to expand the box below see how to create a scatterplot of
\Var{loss} versus \Var{hardness}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]
\begin{minipage}[t]{5.5mm}
\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{minipage}[t]{\textwidth - 5.5mm}

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{\includegraphics[width=0.22917in,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_Icons/R_circle_logo.pdf}
Creating Scatterplot in Rguroo}\vspace{3mm}

\textbf{Before you begin:} Make sure you have already imported the
\Data{Rubber} dataset into your Rguroo account, as was shown
\hyperref[Importing-Data-to-Rguroo-Chapter-2]{here}.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Open the \textbf{Plots} toolbox in Rguroo.\\
\item
  Open the \Dpd{Create Plot} dropdown, and select \Fun{Scatterplot}.
  This opens the Scatterplot dialog.\\
\item
  In the Scatterplot dialog, choose the \Data{Rubber} dataset from the
  \Dpd{Dataset} dropdown.\\
\item
  Choose the \Var{hardness} variable from the \Dpd{Predictor (x)}
  dropdown.
\item

\includegraphics{index_files/mediabag/Rguroo_outputs/Graphical_Description_of_Data/scatterplot_rubber.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-rubber}Loss versus Hardness}

\end{figure}%

Figure~\ref{fig-rubber} shows the relationship between hardness (in
Shore units) on the horizontal axis and abrasion loss (in grams per
hour) on the vertical axis. The points are spread across hardness values
from about 45 to 88 and loss values from roughly 30 to 370. As hardness
increases, the abrasion loss generally decreases, forming a clear
downward trend.

This downward trend indicates a negative relationship between hardness
and loss. Softer rubber (lower Shore values) tends to have higher loss,
while harder rubber (higher Shore values) tends to have lower loss.
Although the points are somewhat scattered and not perfectly aligned,
the overall pattern is fairly consistent, suggesting a moderately strong
negative relationship.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{\textbf{Time-Series
Plot}}{Time-Series Plot}}\label{time-series-plot}

A time series plot is a graph showing numerical data in chronological
order. The horizontal axis represents time, and the vertical axis
represents the measured variable. For example, a time series plot could
be used to show housing prices over the last five years.

The purpose of a time-series plot is to look for patterns or trends over
time. However, we must be cautious when interpreting trends. For
example, just because you observe an increase does not mean the increase
will continue indefinitely. As an example, prior to 2007, many people
noticed that housing prices were increasing. The belief at the time was
that housing prices would continue to increase. However, the housing
bubble burst in 2007, and many houses lost value.

\begin{example}[Creating a Time Series
Plot]\protect\hypertarget{exm-time-series}{}\label{exm-time-series}

Data was collected from a simulation study of motorcycle accidents
designed to test crash helmets. The study recorded the acceleration of
the rider's head immediately after impact. Head acceleration measures
how quickly the speed of the head changes during the crash and is
measured in \(g\) units where \(1g = 9.8 m/s^2\) meters per second
squared. Create a time series plot of the head acceleration versus time.

\includegraphics{Rguroo_Icons/Rguroo_repo_logo.png} The dataset for this
example is available in the Rguroo dataset repository \Repo{MASS}, with
the dataset name \Data{mcycle}. Table~\ref{tbl-mcycle} displays the
first five rows of the dataset. A complete description of the variables
is provided in the \hyperref[code-book-mcycle]{dataset code book} that
follows.

\end{example}

because it moves forward in time and helps us see how things change.

use the scatterplot graph to create the time series plot.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics{index_files/mediabag/Rguroo_outputs/Graphical_Description_of_Data/scatterplot_mcycle.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-mcycle}Time versus Head Acceleration}

\end{figure}%

Figure~\ref{fig-mcycle} shows how head acceleration changes after an
impact. At first, the acceleration stays close to zero, meaning the head
hasn't begun to move yet. Around 20 milliseconds, there is a sudden and
dramatic drop to about --120 g, indicating a rapid backward motion
caused by the initial force of the impact. Immediately afterward, the
acceleration rebounds sharply upward to more than +60 g, showing the
head snapping forward. Following this, the acceleration values fluctuate
between negative and positive g's, but gradually settle toward zero.
This suggests that the head's motion is slowing down and returning to a
stable state. Overall, the pattern reflects a typical impact response:
an initial delay, a strong backward acceleration, a forward rebound, and
then diminishing movement over time.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Code book for Fertility Prenatal Dataset}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\textbf{Description} Data is from the World Bank on money spent on
expenditure of countries and the percentage of women receiving prenatal
care in those countries.

Format

This dataset contains the following columns:

\Var{Country.Name}: Countries around the world

\Var{Country.Code}: Three letter country code for countries around the
world

\Var{Region}: Location of a country around the world as classified by
the World Bank

\Var{IncomeGroup}: The income level of a country as classified by the
World Bank

\Var{f1960-f2017}: Fertility rate of a country from 1960-2017

\Var{p1986-p2018}: Percentage of women receiving prenatal care in the
country in 1986-2018

\Var{e200-2016}: Expenditure amounts of the countries for medical care
in 2000-2016 (\% of GDP)

Source Fertility rate, total (births per woman). (n.d.). Retrieved July
8, 2019, from https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.DYN.TFRT.IN

Chapter 1 discussed what a population, sample, parameter, and statistic
are, as well as how to take different types of samples. Chapter 2
discussed ways to graphically display data. There was also a discussion
of important characteristics: center, variations, distribution,
outliers, and changing characteristics of the data over time.
Distributions and outliers can be identified using graphical means.
Finding the center and variation can be done using numerical methods
that will be discussed in this chapter. Both graphical and numerical
methods are part of a branch of statistics known as \textbf{descriptive
statistics}. Later, descriptive statistics will be used to make
decisions and/or estimate population parameters using methods that are
part of the branch called \textbf{inferential statistics}.

\section{Measures of Center}\label{measures-of-center}

This section focuses on measures of central tendency. Many times you are
asking what to expect on average. For example, when you pick a major,
you would probably ask how much you can expect to earn in that field. If
you are thinking of relocating to a new town, you might ask how much you
can expect to pay for housing. If you are planting vegetables in the
spring, you might want to know how long it will be until you can
harvest. These questions, and many more, can be answered by knowing the
center of the data. There are three measures of the ``center'' of the
data: the mode, median, and mean. Any of the values can be referred to
as an ``average.''

The \textbf{mode} is the data value that occurs most frequently in the
data. To find it, you count how often each data value occurs, and then
determine which value occurs most often. If there is a tie between two
values for the most number of times, then both values are the mode and
the data are called bimodal (two modes). If every data value occurs the
same number of times, there is no mode. If there are more than two
values that appear the most times, then usually there is no mode. The
mode is not always a useful measure of center, especially when a dataset
has more than one mode.

The \textbf{median} is the data value in the middle of a sorted list of
data. To find the median, you arrange the data in order and then
determine which value is in the middle of the data values.

The \textbf{mean} is the arithmetic average of the numbers. The mean,
median, and mode are all measures of center, although the word
``average'' is most commonly used to refer to the mean.

In this course, we work primarily with numerical data, so our focus will
be on the mean and median as measures of center. The mode is more
commonly used with categorical data, where it identifies the most
frequently occurring category. While the mean and median both require
numerical values, the key difference is that the mean uses every data
value in its calculation, making it sensitive to extreme values, whereas
the median depends only on the position of the middle value.

\subsection{Population Mean and Sample
Mean}\label{population-mean-and-sample-mean}

Because the mean is used extensively in statistics, it has special
notation that distinguishes between a population and a sample. The
\textbf{population mean}, denoted by the Greek letter \(\mu\)
(pronounced ``mu''), represents the true average of an entire
population. It is calculated using the formula
\(\mu=\frac{\sum{x}}{N}\), where \(N\) is the total number of values in
the population, \(x\) represents each individual data value, and
\(\sum{x}\) means to add up all the data values. In practice, we rarely
know the population mean because we typically cannot collect data from
every member of a population.

Instead, we work with samples and calculate the \textbf{sample mean},
denoted by \(\bar{x}\) (pronounced ``x-bar''). The sample mean uses the
same calculation process as the population mean but with different
notation: \(\bar{x}=\frac{\sum{x}}{n}\), where \(n\) is the number of
values in the sample. Notice that we use a lowercase \(n\) for sample
size and an uppercase \(N\) for population size. The sample mean
\(\bar{x}\) serves as our best estimate of the unknown population mean
\(\mu\). This relationship between sample statistics and population
parameters is fundamental to inferential statistics -- we use what we
observe in a sample to make informed conclusions about the larger
population.

The mean without the minimum value is 2.75 kg, and the median is 2.7 kg.

The mean of the \Data{cats} dataset with all the values is 2.72 kg,
while the median is 2.7 kg. Notice that when the maximum value was
excluded from the dataset, the mean decreased slightly but the median
did not change, and when the minimum value was excluded from the

shows that the mean is affected by extreme values, while the median is
not. We say the median is a resistant measure of center because it is
not affected by extreme values as much.

\end{tcolorbox}

An \textbf{extreme value} is a data value that is much higher or much
lower than the rest of the data. When extreme values are present, the
median is generally a better measure of center than the mean because the
median is not pulled by those values. When there are no extreme values,
the mean and median tend to be similar, and the mean is commonly used.
This is because the mean is \textbf{not resistant} to outliers --- it is
affected by extreme values, which can pull it higher or lower. The
median, on the other hand, is \textbf{resistant} --- it remains stable
even when extreme values are present in the data.

Later in this chapter, you will learn a formal method for determining
whether an extreme value qualifies as an \textbf{outlier} --- a data
point that falls far enough from the rest of the data to be flagged as
unusual.

You need to be aware that people generally choose the measure of center
that best supports their claim. When you read an article in the
newspaper and it talks about the ``average'' it usually means the mean
but sometimes it refers to the median. Some articles will use the word
``median'' instead of ``average'' to be more specific. If you need to
make an important decision and the information says ``average'', it
would be wise to ask if the ``average'' is the mean or the median before
you decide.

As an example, suppose that a company wants to report the mean salary as
the average salary for the company. The high salaries of the
administrators will pull the mean upward, making the average appear
higher. The company can then say that employees are paid well because
the average is high. However, the employees would prefer to use the
median since it is not affected as much by the extreme administrative
salaries and gives a lower measure of center. This makes the salaries
appear lower and suggests that a raise is in order.

Why use the mean instead of the median? Imagine repeatedly taking
different samples from the same population. Some samples may include
many large values, while others may include many small values. When we
calculate the mean for each sample, some sample means will overestimate
the true center of the population and others will underestimate it. Over
many samples, these overestimates and underestimates tend to balance
out. The median, however, can tend to underestimate or overestimate the
center more often in one direction, depending on how the middle values
fall in the samples. For this reason, the mean does not systematically
overestimate or underestimate the center of the population, making it a
reliable measure of center.

To understand how different measures of center relate to skewed or
symmetric distributions, see Figure~\ref{fig-centers-dist}. For a
left-skewed distribution, the mean is smaller than the median. For a
right-skewed distribution, the mean is larger than the median. For a
symmetric distribution, the mean and the median are the same.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{images/centers_distribution_new.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-centers-dist}Mean, median, mode as related to
distribution}

\end{figure}%

\subsection{Weighted Average}\label{weighted-average}

Another type of average is a weighted average. Weighted averages are
commonly used in situations where some components matter more than
others. For example, a teacher may use a weighted average when
calculating a student's final course grade. Homework, quizzes, and exams
may all contribute to the final grade, but exams might count more
because they measure overall understanding more directly. In this case,
exams are given more weight than homework, so they have a larger impact
on the final grade. Similarly, employers may use weighted averages in
performance evaluations when some aspects of a job are more important
than others.

As an example, a full-time teacher at a community college may be
evaluated on their service to the college, their service to the
community, whether their paperwork is turned in on time, and their
teaching. However, teaching is much more important than whether their
paperwork is turned in on time. When the evaluation is completed, more
weight needs to be given to the teaching and less to the paperwork. This
is a weighted average.

To calculate a weighted average, each data value is multiplied by its
weight (the number representing its importance), then these products are
added together. Finally, this sum is divided by the total of all the
weights. The formula captures this process:

\(\text{weighted average}=\frac{\sum{x \cdot w}}{\sum{w}}\)

where \(x\) represents each data value and \(w\) represents the weight
(or importance) assigned to that value.

\begin{example}[Calculating Weighted
Average]\protect\hypertarget{exm-weighted-average}{}\label{exm-weighted-average}

In your biology class, your final grade is based on several components:
a lab score, scores on two major tests, and your score on the final
exam. Each component is graded out of 100 points. The lab score is worth
15\% of the course grade, the two exams are worth 25\% each, and the
final exam is worth 35\% of the course. Suppose you earned scores of 95
on the labs, 83 and 76 on the two exams, and 84 on the final exam.
Compute your weighted average for the course.

\end{example}

\begin{example}[Calculating Weighted
Averages]\protect\hypertarget{exm-weighted-average-faculty-ratings}{}\label{exm-weighted-average-faculty-ratings}

The faculty evaluation process at John Jingle University rates a faculty
member on the following activities: teaching, publishing, committee
service, community service, and submitting paperwork in a timely manner.
The process involves reviewing student evaluations, peer evaluations,
and supervisor evaluation for each teacher and awarding him/her a score
on a scale from 1 to 10 (with 10 being the best). The weights for each
activity are 20 for teaching, 18 for publishing, 6 for committee
service, 4 for community service, and 2 for paperwork.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  One faculty member had the following ratings: 8 for teaching, 9 for
  publishing, 2 for committee work, 1 for community service, and 8 for
  paperwork. Compute the weighted average of the evaluation.
\item
  Another faculty member had ratings of 6 for teaching, 8 for
  publishing, 9 for committee work, 10 for community service, and 10 for
  paperwork. Compute the weighted average of the evaluation.
\item
  Which faculty member had the higher average evaluation?
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  Variable: \(x\) = rating, \(w\) = weight

\section{Measures of Spread}\label{measures-of-spread}

Variability is a fundamental concept in statistics that describes how
spread out data values are from each other. Consider measuring the
height of everyone in your classroom -- you'll quickly notice that not
everyone has the same height. Some students are taller, some are
shorter, and there's a range of heights in between. This spread in the
data is what we call variability. The same principle applies to other
measurements. If you sampled the income levels of people in a town,
you'd find that incomes vary widely from person to person.

Understanding variability helps us describe datasets more completely.
When data values are clustered closely together, we say there is low
variability. When data values are spread far apart, we say there is high
variability. To quantify this spread, we need numerical measures that
capture how dispersed the data are. This section introduces several
measures of variability, also known as measures of variation or spread.

Recall the \hyperref[exm-mean-median-cats]{example} where we calculated
the average weight of a cat to be 2.72 kg. While this tells us the
center of the data, it doesn't tell us the whole story. Were most cats
close to this weight, or did weights vary dramatically? We know the
highest and lowest weights, but what about everything in between?
Understanding only the center leaves important questions unanswered.

To fully describe a dataset, we need measures of both center and spread.
The measures of variability discussed in this section provide that
additional information.

The \textbf{range} of a set of data is the difference between the
highest and lowest data values (the maximum and minimum values). The
\textbf{interval} refers to the lowest and highest values themselves.
The range is a single value while the interval consists of two values.

\begin{example}[Calculating the
Range]\protect\hypertarget{exm-range}{}\label{exm-range}

Calculate the range of the body weight of cats.

\includegraphics{Rguroo_Icons/Rguroo_repo_logo.png} The dataset for this
example is available in the Rguroo dataset repository \Repo{Kozak}, with
the dataset name \Data{cats}. Table~\ref{tbl-Cats} displays the first
six rows of the dataset. A complete description of the variables is
provided in the \hyperref[code-book-cats]{dataset code book} that
follows.

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

From the effect of extreme values
\hyperref[exm-effect-extreme-values]{example}, the maximum weight of a
cat was 3.9 kg and the minimum was 2 kg. So the range is \(3.9-2=1.9\)
kg. But what does that tell you? You don't know if the weights are
really spread out, or if they are close together.

\end{tcolorbox}

Unfortunately, the range does not provide a very accurate picture of
variability because it only considers two values: the highest and
lowest. A better approach is to examine how far each data value is from
the mean. This distance from the mean is called a \textbf{deviation}. By
looking at all the deviations together, we get a much more complete
picture of how spread out the data are.

\subsection{Variance and Standard
Deviation}\label{variance-and-standard-deviation}

To measure the overall spread of data, statisticians calculate the
average of the squared deviations from the mean, which is called the
\textbf{variance}. The variance gives us a single number that captures
how dispersed the data values are from the mean. For a population, the
variance is denoted by \(\sigma^2\) (where \(\sigma\) is the Greek
letter sigma).

The \textbf{population variance} is calculated using the formula:

\[\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum\left(x-\mu \right)^2}{N}\]

where \(\mu\) is the population mean, \(N\) is the population size, and
\(\sum\) means to sum all the squared deviations.

While variance is mathematically useful, it has one drawback: it's
measured in squared units. For example, if your data are heights
measured in centimeters, the variance would be in square centimeters (cm
\(^2\)), which is difficult to interpret. To solve this problem, we take
the square root of the variance to get the \textbf{standard deviation},
denoted by \(\sigma\) for a population.

The \textbf{population standard deviation} is:

\[\sigma =\sqrt{ \frac{\sum\left(x-\mu \right)^2}{N}}\]

The standard deviation is measured in the same units as the original
data, making it much easier to understand and communicate. If your data
are in kilograms, the standard deviation is also in kilograms.

\subsection{Sample Variance and Sample Standard
Deviation}\label{sample-variance-and-sample-standard-deviation}

Since we typically work with samples rather than entire populations, we
need sample versions of these measures. The \textbf{sample variance},
denoted by \(s^2\), is calculated similarly to the population variance
but with one important difference: we divide by \(n-1\) instead of
\(n\).

The \textbf{sample variance} is:

\[s^2=\frac{\sum\left(x-\bar{x}\right)^2}{n-1}\]

where \(\bar{x}\) is the sample mean and \(n\) is the sample size.

The reason we use \(n-1\) instead of \(n\) relates to a statistical
concept called degrees of freedom. Using \(n-1\) makes the sample
variance a better estimate of the population variance. While the
mathematical reasoning is complex, the practical result is that dividing
by \(n-1\) corrects for the bias that would occur if we divided by
\(n\).

The \textbf{sample standard deviation} is simply the square root of the
sample variance:

\[s=\sqrt{ \frac{\sum\left(x-\bar{x}\right)^2}{n-1}}\]

Like the population standard deviation, the sample standard deviation is
measured in the same units as the original data.

In most real-world situations, we work with samples rather than entire
populations, so the \textbf{sample variance} (\(s^2\)) and
\textbf{sample standard deviation} (\(s\)) are the measures we use most
often in this course. Although we have provided the formulas for the
population variance (\(\sigma^2\)) and population standard deviation
(\(\sigma\)) for reference, our examples and Rguroo instructions will
focus on the sample versions. If you ever need to compute population
variance or standard deviation, they can be calculated using the
\Fun{Numerical Summaries} function in Rguroo under the
\textbf{Analytics} toolbox.

\subsection{Computing Variance and Standard
Deviation}\label{computing-variance-and-standard-deviation}

While understanding these formulas is important, in practice you'll
typically use technology (such as Rguroo or statistical software) to
calculate variance and standard deviation. These tools handle the
computations quickly and accurately, allowing you to focus on
interpreting the results.

\subsection{Interpreting Variance and Standard
Deviation}\label{interpreting-variance-and-standard-deviation}

In general, a ``small'' variance and standard deviation indicate that
data values are close together and more consistent, while a ``large''
variance and standard deviation indicate that data values are spread out
and less consistent. Whether you want high or low variability depends on
the context.

For example, if you're manufacturing bolts, you want the lengths to be
very consistent. A small standard deviation means the bolts are nearly
identical, which is ideal. On the other hand, if you're administering a
test to evaluate pilot ability, you want the test scores to show enough
variability to distinguish strong candidates from weaker ones. If nearly
everyone scores about the same, the standard deviation will be small and
it will be difficult to identify the best pilots. A larger standard
deviation indicates that scores are more spread out, making it easier to
differentiate between high-performing and low-performing candidates.

\subsection{What Makes a Standard Deviation ``Small'' or
``Large''?}\label{what-makes-a-standard-deviation-small-or-large}

The meaning of ``small'' and ``large'' depends on the context and scale
of your data. To a bicyclist whose average speed is 20 mph, a standard
deviation of \(s = 20\) mph is huge -- it would mean speeds vary wildly
from nearly stopped to 40 mph. To an airplane whose average speed is 500
mph, a standard deviation of \(s = 20\) mph is quite small, representing
only minor variations in cruising speed. The ``size'' of the standard
deviation must always be interpreted relative to the mean and the nature
of what you're measuring.

Standard deviations are also meaningful when comparing two samples
measured on the same scale. For instance, in the previous
\hyperref[exm-standard-deviation]{example}, female cats had a standard
deviation of 0.27 kg while male cats had a standard deviation of 0.47
kg. Because both groups are measured in kilograms, we can directly
compare these values and conclude that female cat weights are more
consistent (less spread out) than male cat weights.

\subsection{Using the Standard
Deviation}\label{using-the-standard-deviation}

The standard deviation helps describe where the data tend to lie
relative to the mean. When the data are symmetric and have most values
clustered around a typical center, the empirical rule provides a helpful
guideline. The Empirical Rule says that about 68\% of the data fall
within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95\% fall within two
standard deviations, and about 99.7\% fall within three standard
deviations. These percentages are not exact, but they often give a
reasonable picture of where most of the data lie.
Figure~\ref{fig-empirical-rule} shows how data is distributed according
to the empirical rule for a symmetric, bell-shaped distribution.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics{images/empirical_rule.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-empirical-rule}The Empirical Rule (68-95-99.7 Rule)
showing the percentage of data within standard deviations of the mean
for symmetric distributions}

\end{figure}%

For data that are not symmetric, other rules can still be used.
Chebyshev's rule gives a minimum proportion of the data that must lie
within a certain number of standard deviations of the mean, regardless
of the overall shape of the distribution. The results from this rule are
usually less precise than those from the empirical rule, but they apply
to a much wider range of situations. Figure~\ref{fig-chebyshev-rule}
illustrates Chebyshev's rule, which guarantees at least 75\% of data
within 2 standard deviations and at least 89\% within 3 standard
deviations, regardless of distribution shape.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics{images/chebyshev_rule.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-chebyshev-rule}Chebyshev's Rule showing minimum
percentages of data within k standard deviations of the mean for any
distribution}

\end{figure}%

\subsection{Identifying Unusual Values with Standard
Deviation}\label{identifying-unusual-values-with-standard-deviation}

The empirical rule tells us that about 95\% of data in a symmetric
distribution falls within two standard deviations of the mean. This
means that data values outside this range are relatively rare -- they
occur in only about 5\% of cases. We can use this insight to classify
data values as common or unusual:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Common values}: Data values within two standard deviations of
  the mean (the middle 95\%)
\item
  \textbf{Unusual values}: Data values more than two standard deviations
  away from the mean (the outer 5\%)
\end{itemize}

To determine whether a specific data value is common or unusual, we need
to measure how many standard deviations it is from the mean. This
standardized distance is called a \textbf{z-score} (or \(z\)-value), and
it is calculated using the formula:

\[z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\]

where \(x\) is the data value, \(\mu\) is the population mean, and
\(\sigma\) is the population standard deviation.

The \(z\)-score tells us how many standard deviations a data value is
from the mean. For example, a \(z\)-score of 2.5 means the data value is
2.5 standard deviations above the mean, while a \(z\)-score of -1.8
means the data value is 1.8 standard deviations below the mean. Using
our rule of thumb:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  If \(|z| \leq 2\) (\(z\)-score is between -2 and 2), the value is
  \textbf{common}
\item
  If \(|z| > 2\) (\(z\)-score is less than -2 or greater than 2), the
  value is \textbf{unusual}
\end{itemize}

In practice, we rarely know the true population parameters \(\mu\) and
\(\sigma\). Instead, we use the sample mean \(\bar{x}\) and sample
standard deviation \(s\) to estimate them:

\[z=\frac{x-\bar{x}}{s}\]

While this sample-based \(z\)-score provides a good approximation, keep
in mind that it is an estimate and may be less accurate when working
with small samples.

\begin{example}[Determining If a Value Is
Unusual]\protect\hypertarget{exm-unusual-value}{}\label{exm-unusual-value}

Using the tornado dataset from the previous
\hyperref[exm-empirical-rule]{example}, where the mean number of annual
tornadoes in Oklahoma is 56 and the standard deviation is 27.6,
determine whether each of the following values is unusual by calculating
its \(z\)-score.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  In 1974, there were 45 tornadoes in Oklahoma. Is this value unusual?
  Why or why not?
\item
  In 1999, there were 145 tornadoes in the Oklahoma. Is this value
  unusual? Why or why not?
\end{enumerate}

\includegraphics{Rguroo_Icons/Rguroo_repo_logo.png} The dataset for this
example is available in the Rguroo dataset repository \Repo{Kozak}, with
the dataset name \Data{Tornado_OK}. Table~\ref{tbl-Tornado} displays the
first six rows of the dataset. A complete description of the variables
is provided in the \hyperref[code-book-tornado]{dataset code book} that
follows.

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Variable: \(x\) = number of tornadoes in Oklahoma
\end{enumerate}

To answer this question, first find how many standard deviations 45 is
from the mean. From the previous \hyperref[exm-empirical-rule]{example},
we know \(\bar{x}=56\) and \(s=27.6\). For \(x=45\),
\(z=\frac{45-56}{27.6}=-0.399\)

Since this value is between -2 and 2, then it is not unusual to have 45
tornadoes in a year in Oklahoma. The \(z\) value is negative, so that
means that 45 is less than the mean number of tornadoes.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  Variable: \(x\) = number of tornadoes in Oklahoma
\end{enumerate}

For this question the \(x = 145\), \(z=\frac{145-56}{27.6}=3.22\)

Since the \(z\) value is more than 2, then it would be considered
unusual to have 145 tornadoes in a year in Oklahoma.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Comparing Values Using
z-Scores}\label{comparing-values-using-z-scores}

A \(z\)-score does more than tell you whether a single value is common
or unusual. Because a \(z\)-score measures distance from the mean in
\textbf{standard deviations} rather than in the original units, it
allows you to compare values that come from different groups or are
measured on completely different scales.

Suppose you want to know whether you did better on a statistics exam or
a history exam. Comparing the raw scores does not tell you much, because
the two exams may have had different class averages and different
amounts of spread. A score of 80 might be excellent on a difficult exam
where most students scored in the 60s, but only average on an easy exam
where most students scored in the 80s. Converting each score to a
\(z\)-score puts both values on the same scale so they can be compared
fairly.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\textbf{Key Concept.} To compare values from different groups or
different scales, convert each value to a \(z\)-score using the mean and
standard deviation of its own group.

\end{tcolorbox}

When comparing values with \(z\)-scores, follow these steps:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Identify the mean and standard deviation for each group separately.
\item
  Calculate the \(z\)-score for each value using its own group's mean
  and standard deviation.
\item
  Compare the \(z\)-scores, paying attention to whether higher or lower
  values are better in the context.
\item
  State your conclusion in the context of the problem.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{example}[Comparing Performances on Different
Scales]\protect\hypertarget{exm-compare-z-race}{}\label{exm-compare-z-race}

Jordan ran a 5K race in 22 minutes. The mean finishing time for runners
in Jordan's age group was 28 minutes with a standard deviation of 4
minutes. Priya swam a 400-meter race in 6.5 minutes. The mean finishing
time for swimmers in Priya's age group was 8 minutes with a standard
deviation of 1.2 minutes. Relative to their own events, who had the
better performance?

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

Variable: \(x_1\) = 5K running time (minutes)

Variable: \(x_2\) = 400-meter swimming time (minutes)

Jordan's and Priya's times cannot be compared directly because running
5K and swimming 400 meters are very different events. Instead, find how
many standard deviations each time is from the mean of its own event.

For Jordan: \(z=\frac{22-28}{4}=\frac{-6}{4}=-1.50\)

For Priya: \(z=\frac{6.5-8}{1.2}=\frac{-1.5}{1.2}=-1.25\)

Both \(z\)-scores are negative, which means both athletes finished
faster than the average for their event. In a race, a \emph{lower} time
is better, so the more negative \(z\)-score represents the better
performance. Jordan's time is 1.50 standard deviations below the mean,
while Priya's time is 1.25 standard deviations below the mean. Relative
to their own events, Jordan had the better performance.

Notice that neither \(z\)-score is less than \(-2\), so neither time is
unusual. Both athletes performed well, but not unusually well.

\end{tcolorbox}

The next example shows how comparing \(z\)-scores can lead to a
different conclusion than comparing the raw values.

\begin{example}[Comparing Values from Different
Groups]\protect\hypertarget{exm-compare-z-cats}{}\label{exm-compare-z-cats}

In the \hyperref[exm-standard-deviation]{example} on calculating the
standard deviation, you used Rguroo to find the mean and standard
deviation of cat body weights separated by sex
(Figure~\ref{fig-spread-sex}). The heaviest female cat in the dataset
weighs 3.0 kg. Consider a male cat that weighs 3.5 kg.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Which cat weighs more?
\item
  Which cat is heavier relative to other cats of the same sex?
\item
  Is either cat's weight unusual for its sex?
\end{enumerate}

\includegraphics{Rguroo_Icons/Rguroo_repo_logo.png} The dataset for this
example is available in the Rguroo dataset repository \Repo{Kozak}, with
the dataset name \Data{cats}. Table~\ref{tbl-Cats} displays the first
six rows of the dataset. A complete description of the variables is
provided in the \hyperref[code-book-cats]{dataset code book}.

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

Variable: \(x_1\) = body weight of a female cat (kg)

Variable: \(x_2\) = body weight of a male cat (kg)

From the Rguroo output in Figure~\ref{fig-spread-sex}, female cats have
a mean weight of \(\bar{x}=2.36\) kg with a standard deviation of
\(s=0.27\) kg, and male cats have a mean weight of \(\bar{x}=2.9\) kg
with a standard deviation of \(s=0.47\) kg.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\item
  The male cat weighs more, since 3.5 kg is greater than 3.0 kg.
\item
  Find the \(z\)-score for each cat using the mean and standard
  deviation of its own sex.

  Female cat: \(z=\frac{3.0-2.36}{0.27}=\frac{0.64}{0.27}\approx 2.37\)

  Male cat: \(z=\frac{3.5-2.9}{0.47}=\frac{0.6}{0.47}\approx 1.28\)

  The female cat's weight is 2.37 standard deviations above the mean for
  female cats, while the male cat's weight is only 1.28 standard
  deviations above the mean for male cats. Even though the male cat
  weighs more, the female cat is heavier relative to other cats of her
  sex.
\item
  The female cat's \(z\)-score of 2.37 is greater than 2, so her weight
  is unusual for a female cat. The male cat's \(z\)-score of 1.28 is
  between \(-2\) and 2, so his weight is common for a male cat.
\end{enumerate}

This example shows why \(z\)-scores are useful. Comparing the raw
weights suggests the male cat stands out more, but comparing the
\(z\)-scores shows that the female cat is the one who is unusually heavy
for her group.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Homework for Measures of Spread
Section}\label{homework-for-measures-of-spread-section}

\textbf{Use Rguroo on all problems. State the variable on all problems.}

\begin{enumerate}

  Cholesterol levels were collected from patients certain days after
  they had a heart attack and are in Table~\ref{tbl-Cholesterol}. Find
  the mean, median, range, variance, and standard deviation for
  cholesterol levels 2 days after the heart attack.

\textbf{Description:} Students in an introductory statistics class
(MS212 taught by Professor John Eccleston and Dr Richard Wilson at The
University of Queensland) participated in a simple experiment. The
students took their own pulse rate. They were then asked to flip a coin.
If the coin came up heads, they were to run in place for one minute.
Otherwise they sat for one minute. Then everyone took their pulse again.
The pulse rates and other physiological and lifestyle data are given in
the data.

Five class groups between 1993 and 1998 participated in the experiment.
The lecturer, Richard Wilson, was concerned that some students would
choose the less strenuous option of sitting rather than running even if
their coin came up heads, In the years 1995-1998 a different method of
random assignment was used. In these years, data forms were handed out
to the class before the experiment. The forms were pre-assigned to
either running or non-running and there were an equal number of each. In
1995 and 1998 not all of the forms were returned so the numbers running
and sitting was still not entirely controlled.

This dataset contains the following columns:

\Var{height}: height of subject in cm

\Var{weight}: weight of subject in kg

\Var{age}: age of subject in years

\Var{gender}: male or female

\Var{Smokes}: whether a subject regularly smokes, yes means does smoke,
no means does not smoke

\Var{alcohol}: whether a subject regularly drinks alcohol, yes means the
person does, no means the person does not

\Var{exercise}: whether a subject exercises, low, moderate, high

\Var{ran}: whether a subject ran one minute between pulse measurements
(ran) or sat between pulse measurement (sat)

\Var{pulse_before}: the pulse rate before a subject either ran or sat
(bpm)

\Var{pulse_after}: the pulse rate after a subject either ran or sat
(bpm)

\Var{year}: what year the data was collected (93-98)

\href{https://gksmyth.github.io/ozdasl/oz/ms212.html}{Source} Pulse
rates before and after exercise. (2013, September 25).

References The data was supplied by Dr Richard J. Wilson, Department of
Mathematics, University of Queensland.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Ranking}\label{ranking}

Along with the center and the variability, another useful numerical
measure is the ranking of a number. A \textbf{percentile} is a measure
of ranking. It represents a location measurement of a data value to the
rest of the values. Many standardized tests give the results as a
percentile. Doctors also use percentiles to track a child's growth.

The \(k^{th}\) \textbf{percentile} is the data value that has \(k\%\) of
the data at or below that value.

For instance, a score at the \(90^{th}\) percentile means that 90\% of
the scores were at or below this score --- in other words, the person
did the same as or better than 90\% of the test takers. A score at the
\(70^{th}\) percentile means that 70\% of the scores were at or below
this score.

It is important to understand that a percentile is a ranking, not a
score. If a test was out of 100 points and you scored at the \(80^{th}\)
percentile, that does not mean you earned 80 points. It means you scored
the same as or better than 80\% of the people who took the test. If all
the scores were really low, you could have still failed the test. On the
other hand, if many of the scores were high you could have gotten a 95\%
or more. The percentile tells you how you compared to others, not what
your actual score was.

\subsection{Quartiles: Dividing Data into
Fourths}\label{quartiles-dividing-data-into-fourths}

While the median divides a dataset into two equal halves, we can also
divide data into four equal parts using \textbf{quartiles}. Quartiles
are special percentiles that split the data into fourths, with one
quarter (25\%) of the data falling between each consecutive quartile.
Just as the median helps us understand the center of the data, quartiles
help us understand how the data is distributed across its entire range.

There are three quartiles that divide the data into four equal groups:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{First quartile (Q1)}: At least 25\% of the data values are
  less than or equal to \(Q1\)
\item
  \textbf{Second quartile (Q2)}: At least 50\% of the data values are
  less than or equal to \(Q2\) (this is the median)
\item
  \textbf{Third quartile (Q3)}: At least 75\% of the data values are
  less than or equal to \(Q3\)
\end{itemize}

Together, these quartiles give us a more complete picture of the data's
distribution than the median alone.

\textbf{Finding Quartiles in Rguroo}

To find the quartiles in Rguroo, you use the same steps as finding the
mean, standard deviation, and variation in Summary Statistic as
described \hyperref[Calculating-summary-stats-in-Rguroo]{here}. In the
Statistics section of the dialog, simply select the checkboxes for
Quartile 1, Median (Q2), and Quartile 3.

}

\subsection{The Five-Number Summary}\label{the-five-number-summary}

To get a comprehensive picture of how data is distributed, statisticians
often use the \textbf{five-number summary}, which consists of five key
values arranged in order:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Minimum}: The smallest value in the dataset
\item
  \textbf{First quartile (Q1)}: The value at or below which at least
  25\% of the data falls
\item
  \textbf{Median (Q2)}: The value at or below which at least 50\% of the
  data falls
\item
  \textbf{Third quartile (Q3)}: The value at or below which at least
  75\% of the data falls
\item
  \textbf{Maximum}: The largest value in the dataset
\end{enumerate}

Together, these five numbers give us a complete snapshot of the data's
spread from lowest to highest.

\subsection{Interquartile Range (IQR)}\label{interquartile-range-iqr}

The \textbf{interquartile range (IQR)} measures the spread of the middle
50\% of the data. It is calculated as:

\[IQR = Q_3 - Q_1\]

The IQR tells us how spread out the central portion of the data is. A
large IQR indicates that the middle half of the data is widely spread,
while a small IQR suggests the data is more tightly clustered around the
median. Because the IQR focuses on the middle 50\% of the data, it is
not affected by extreme values, making it a robust measure of spread.

\subsection{Identifying Outliers Using the
IQR}\label{identifying-outliers-using-the-iqr}

The IQR can also help us identify \textbf{outliers} -- data values that
are unusually far from the rest of the data. To do identify potential
outliers using the IQR, we create boundaries called \textbf{fences}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Lower fence} = \(Q_1 - 1.5 \times IQR\)
\item
  \textbf{Upper fence} = \(Q_3 + 1.5 \times IQR\)
\end{itemize}

Any data value below the lower fence or above the upper fence is
considered a potential outlier. These values are far enough from the
bulk of the data that they warrant special attention, as they may
represent unusual observations, measurement errors, or genuinely
exceptional cases.

\subsection{Boxplots: Visualizing the Five-Number
Summary}\label{boxplots-visualizing-the-five-number-summary}

A \textbf{boxplot} (also called a box-and-whisker plot) provides a
visual representation of the five-number summary and makes it easy to
see the distribution of data at a glance. Here's how to read a boxplot:

\textbf{Basic boxplot structure:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  A rectangular \textbf{box} extends from Q1 to Q3, containing the
  middle 50\% of the data
\item
  A line inside the box marks the \textbf{median}
\item
  \textbf{Whiskers} (lines) extend from the box to the minimum and
  maximum values
\item
  The horizontal axis shows the scale of the variable being measured
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Modified boxplot (more common):} In a modified boxplot, the
whiskers are shortened to show only the data within the fences:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The left whisker extends to the smallest value that is still above the
  lower fence
\item
  The right whisker extends to the largest value that is still below the
  upper fence
\item
  \textbf{Outliers} beyond the fences are shown as individual points
  (dots, circles, or asterisks)
\end{itemize}

This modified version makes it easier to spot outliers and see the
typical range of the data.

\subsection{Interpreting Shape from
Boxplots}\label{interpreting-shape-from-boxplots}

Boxplots also reveal information about the shape of the distribution.
Figure~\ref{fig-boxplot-comparison} illustrates how different
distribution shapes appear in boxplots.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{images/boxplot_comparison.png}

}

\subcaption{\label{fig-boxplot-comparison-1}Boxplots showing three
distribution shapes}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{images/boxplot_histogram_comparison.png}

}

\subcaption{\label{fig-boxplot-comparison-2}Corresponding histograms for
comparison}

}

\caption{\label{fig-boxplot-comparison}Comparing Shapes of Boxplots}

\end{figure}%

\textbf{Symmetric distribution:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The box appears balanced around the median
\item
  Both whiskers are approximately the same length
\item
  The median line is near the center of the box
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Skewed left:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The left whisker is noticeably longer than the right
\item
  The median is shifted toward the right side of the box (toward Q3)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Skewed right:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The right whisker is noticeably longer than the left
\item
  The median is shifted toward the left side of the box (toward Q1)
\end{itemize}

If a boxplot is symmetric with long whiskers relative to the size of the
box, the distribution may have a bell shape with data concentrated near
the center and thin tails. However, a symmetric boxplot alone is not
sufficient to confirm a bell-shaped distribution.

\textbf{Part (b):} Using the summary statistics from Rguroo
(Figure~\ref{fig-Pulse-summary}):

\begin{figure}[H]

}

\caption{\label{fig-Pulse-summary}Numerical Summary of Time Between

The mean is 11 (1/50 seconds), the median is 7.5 (1/50 seconds), and the
standard deviation is 10.5 (1/50 seconds). The five-number summary is:
minimum = 0.5, Q1 = 3.5, median = 7.5, Q3 = 15, and maximum = 69 (1/50
seconds).

\textbf{Part (c):} Because the distribution is skewed right, the median
(7.5) is a more appropriate measure of center than the mean (11). The
mean is pulled to the right by the long tail of high values, making it
larger than the median. Since the median is resistant to extreme values,
it better represents the typical time between nerve pulses.

IQR is Q3 − Q1 = 15 − 3.5 = 11.5 (1/50 seconds), indicating substantial
variability. The outliers and the right skew visible in both the density
plot and the boxplot confirm that the median is the better measure of
center for this dataset --- the extreme values pull the mean higher but

  From the \Dpd{Data Import} dropdown, select
  \Fun{Dataset Repository}.\\
\item
  In the top search box, type \TypeIn{kozak}, then select the
  \Repo{Statistics Using Technology – Kozak} repository.\\
\item
  In the middle search box, type the first few letters of the dataset
  name, and choose your desired dataset name that appears in the lower
  panel.\\
\item
  Click \Button{Import}. The dataset will be imported to your Rguroo
  account.
\item
  Click \Button{Close} to exit the dialog.\\
\item
  To view the dataset, double-click the dataset name under the
  \textbf{Data} toolbox list.
\end{enumerate}

\end{minipage}%
\end{tcolorbox}

Every day you encounter uncertainty. Will it rain during your commute?
Is a new medication likely to help a patient? Does a positive test
result mean someone actually has a disease? Should a business stock more
inventory before a holiday weekend? Although these questions cannot be
answered with certainty, probability gives us a mathematical framework
for measuring uncertainty and making informed decisions.

Probability is not just an abstract mathematical topic. It is the
foundation of all statistics. When we collect data and draw conclusions,
we are always asking: \emph{How likely is it that what we observed
happened by chance alone?} Without understanding probability, we cannot
answer that question in a meaningful way.

Probability is the ``language'' that connects data to decisions. The
ideas in this chapter form the foundation for everything that comes next
in this course. Taking the time to build a solid foundation here will
make the rest of the course much more meaningful.

The ideas in this chapter appear across every discipline. A
criminologist asks: what is the likelihood that an eyewitness
identification is correct? A nurse asks: if I screen 100 patients, how
many will test positive by chance alone? An economist asks: what is the
probability that a recession will occur in the next two years? A
political scientist asks: what is the chance that a polling reflects the
true opinions of voters? These are all probability questions.

This chapter begins with the fundamental vocabulary and rules of
probability, then develops two major approaches to calculating
probabilities, and introduces how technology --- specifically
\textbf{Rguroo} --- can be used to simulate random processes and explore
probability hands-on.

\section{Fundamentals of Probability}\label{fundamentals-of-probability}

\subsection{Random Processes and
Experiments}\label{random-processes-and-experiments}

Some things in life are \textbf{deterministic}. For example, if you drop
a ball, you can calculate exactly where it will land (assuming you know
all the relevant conditions). But many things are \textbf{random},
meaning the outcome is not fully predictable in advance no matter how
much information you have.

A \textbf{random process} is any process or phenomenon in which
individual outcomes are unpredictable, even though a pattern of outcomes
tends to emerge over a large number of repetitions.

Random processes appear everywhere in daily life. A coin flip, a card
drawn from a shuffled deck, and a product coming off an assembly line
all have outcomes you cannot predict in advance. The same is true in
higher-stakes situations such as whether a patient responds to a
treatment, whether it rains on a given day, or which candidate a
randomly selected voter supports.

A \textbf{probability experiment} is any process whose outcome is
determined by chance. This is different from an experiment in everyday
language, which usually means a planned scientific test. In statistics,
we use the word experiment more broadly, to describe situations in which
chance is involved. From this point on, we will simply say
\textbf{experiment}. The experiment must be well-defined. That means you
must be able to describe all possible outcomes in advance, and you must
observe exactly one outcome each time the experiment is performed.

\subsection{Outcomes, Sample Spaces, and
Events}\label{outcomes-sample-spaces-and-events}

Every probability experiment produces a result. An \textbf{outcome} is a
single possible result of a probability experiment. When you roll a die,
getting a 3 is one outcome; when you flip a coin, getting heads is one
outcome. Outcomes must cover every possibility and cannot overlap --- no
two outcomes can occur at the same time in a single trial.

The \textbf{sample space} is the complete list of all possible outcomes.
If outcomes are the individual items, the sample space is the entire
collection. We write it using set notation with curly braces and label
it \(S\). For a fair six-sided die, the sample space is
\(S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\) --- all six faces, nothing more.

An \textbf{event} is any group of outcomes of interest. Events are
subsets of the sample space and are usually named with capital letters
like \(A\), \(B\), or \(C\). A \textbf{simple event} contains exactly
one outcome, such as \(B = \{5\}\) --- rolling a 5. A \textbf{compound
event} contains more than one outcome, such as \(A = \{2, 4, 6\}\) ---
rolling an even number --- or \(C = \{5, 6\}\) --- rolling a number
greater than 4. Notice that \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) are all built from
the same six outcomes in \(S\); the sample space does not change, only
the event of interest does.

Two special events come up often. A \textbf{certain event} contains
every outcome in the sample space and will always occur. For example,
rolling a number between 1 and 6 (inclusive) on a standard die is a
certain event because every possible outcome (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6)
satisfies this condition. An \textbf{impossible event} contains no
outcomes at all and is written as the empty set, \(\emptyset\). For
example, rolling a 9 on a standard die is an impossible event because no
outcome in the sample space \(\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\) equals 9.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Key Terms}\vspace{3mm}

An \textbf{outcome} is a single possible result of a probability
experiment. Outcomes must cover every possibility and cannot overlap,
which means no two outcomes can occur at the same time in a single
trial.

The \textbf{sample space} is the complete list of all possible outcomes.
We write the sample space using set notation with curly braces and label
it \(S\).

An \textbf{event} is any group of outcomes of interest. Events are
subsets of the sample space and are usually named with capital letters
like \(A\), \(B\), or \(C\).

A \textbf{simple event} contains exactly one outcome.

A \textbf{compound event} contains more than one outcome.

A \textbf{certain event} contains every outcome in the sample space and
will always occur.

An \textbf{impossible event} contains no outcomes at all and is written
as the empty set, \(\emptyset\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Probability: Definition and
Rules}\label{probability-definition-and-rules}

Now that we know what outcomes, sample spaces, and events are, we can
define probability itself, establish the rules every probability must
follow, and understand how probabilities behave when an experiment is
repeated many times.

The \textbf{probability} of an event \(A\), written \(P(A)\) (read
``probability of A''), is a number between 0 and 1 (inclusive) that
represents how likely A is to occur.
\[0 \leq P(A) \leq 1   \text{ for any event } A\]

Probabilities can be expressed as fractions, decimals, or percentages.
For example, \[P(A) = 1/4 = 0.25 = 25\%\].

When we say an event has a probability of 0.30, we mean that if we were
to repeat this experiment a very large number of times under the same
conditions, about 30\% of those repetitions would result in that event
occurring. Probability does not tell us what will happen on any single
trial; it tells us about long-run patterns.

Before we can calculate a probability, we need to ask a key question:
are the outcomes in our sample space equally likely? This matters
because it determines how we find probabilities.

Outcomes are \textbf{equally likely} when every outcome in the sample
space has the same probability of occurring; no outcome is favored over
any other. When rolling a fair six-sided die, for instance, each face
has the same chance of occurring. In contrast, outcomes are \textbf{not
equally likely} when some results are more probable than others. In a
lottery, the outcome ``you win'' is far less likely than ``you do not
win,'' so the outcomes are clearly unequal.

To see this distinction more concretely, consider three quick examples.
First, selecting a ball from a bag containing 4 red balls and 4 blue
balls (all the same size) produces equally likely outcomes, since each
individual ball has the same chance of being chosen. Second, if that
same bag instead holds 4 red balls and 8 blue balls, the outcomes are no
longer equally likely because blue is more likely to be drawn simply due
to having more balls. Third, flipping a weighted coin where heads is
twice as likely as tails also fails the equally likely condition, since
the two faces do not share the same probability.

A \textbf{probability model} lists the possible outcomes of a
probability experiment and each outcome's probability. Every valid
probability model must satisfy two rules. These are not optional; they
are requirements that any set of numbers must meet in order to qualify
as probabilities.

\textbf{Rule 1: Probability is always between 0 and 1 (inclusive)}
\[0 \leq P(A) \leq 1   \text{ for every event } A\]

No probability can be negative. No probability can be greater than 1. If
you calculate a probability outside this range, you have made an error.

\textbf{Rule 2: The probabilities of all outcomes in the sample space
must sum to 1} \[\sum P(\text{all outcomes}) = 1\]

This means that one of the outcomes in the sample space must occur when
the experiment is performed. When you list all possible outcomes of an
experiment, their probabilities must add up to exactly 1, or 100\%.

\begin{example}[Verifying Probability
Rules]\protect\hypertarget{exm-equally-likely}{}\label{exm-equally-likely}

A psychology researcher studies the types of social media platforms used
most frequently by college students. Based on survey data, she estimates
the following probabilities:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\caption{Estimated probabilities for most-used social media
platform}\label{tbl-socialmedia}\tabularnewline
\toprule\noalign{}
Platform & Estimated Probability \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endfirsthead
\toprule\noalign{}
Platform & Estimated Probability \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Instagram & 0.34 \\
TikTok & 0.28 \\
Snapchat & 0.18 \\
X (Twitter) & 0.11 \\
Other / None & 0.09 \\
\end{longtable}

Verify this model satisifies the rules of probability model.

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

Verify Rule 1: Each probability is between 0 and 1.

Verify Rule 2: \(0.34 + 0.28 + 0.18 + 0.11 + 0.09 = 1.00\)

Both rules are satisfied, so this is a valid probability model.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Finding a Missing
Probability]\protect\hypertarget{exm-missing-prob}{}\label{exm-missing-prob}

A weather forecasting model gives the following probabilities for
tomorrow's weather in a coastal city:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\caption{Weather probability model with missing
value}\label{tbl-weather}\tabularnewline
\toprule\noalign{}
Weather & Probability \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endfirsthead
\toprule\noalign{}
Weather & Probability \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Sunny & 0.45 \\
Partly Cloudy & 0.30 \\
Overcast & ? \\
Rain & 0.12 \\
\end{longtable}

Assuming that the four listed outcomes are all the possibilities for
tomorrow's weather, what is the probability of overcast so the
probability values define a probability model?

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

Since all probabilities must sum to 1:

\[P(\text{Overcast}) = 1 - 0.45 - 0.30 - 0.12 = 0.13\]

There is a 13\% chance of overcast skies tomorrow.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Two Approaches to Calculating
Probability}\label{two-approaches-to-calculating-probability}

There are two fundamental ways to determine the probability of an event.

\textbf{Relative Frequency (Empirical) Probability}

The first approach is based on observation and data. We either conduct
the experiment many times, or use existing data, and measure how often
the event occurs. The resulting probability estimate is called the
\textbf{relative frequency} or \textbf{empirical probability}.

Recall from Chapter 2 that the \textbf{relative frequency} of an event
is the number of times it occurs out of the total number of trials:
\[\text{Relative Frequency of A} = \dfrac{\text{Number of times A occurred}}{\text{Total number of trials}}\]

This is the \textbf{empirical approach} to probability. It is based on
observed data rather than assumptions. The relative frequency gives an
estimate of the true probability, and that estimate improves as the
number of trials increases.

\begin{example}[Empirical Probability from Survey
Data]\protect\hypertarget{exm-empirical-prob}{}\label{exm-empirical-prob}

The General Social Survey (GSS) is a national survey conducted regularly
in the United States. In a recent survey, 1,832 out of 2,867 respondents
reported that they use social media daily. What is the probability a
randomly selected U.S. adult uses social media?

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

This estimate is based on observed data, so it is an empirical
probability and we would use relative frequency to find the probability

\[ P(\text{uses social media daily}) \approx \dfrac{1832}{2867} \approx 0.639\]

We estimate there is about a 63.9\% chance that a randomly selected U.S.
adult uses social media daily.

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{When Would You Use Empirical Probability}

Empirical probability (based on observed data) is most appropriate when:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Outcomes are not equally likely and you cannot determine the
  probabilities theoretically. For example, the probability that a
  randomly selected person prefers chocolate ice cream over vanilla
  cannot be calculated theoretically---it must be measured through
  observation or surveys.
\item
  The outcomes depend on real-world behavior or complex systems with too
  many factors to model theoretically. Examples include the probability
  that a patient responds to a treatment, the probability that a
  customer returns a product, or the probability of rain tomorrow. These
  involve too many unknown factors to calculate theoretically.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Theoretical Probability}

The second approach is used when we know the structure of the experiment
and can assume that all outcomes in a sample space are equally likely.
Rather than collecting data, we count outcomes.

If all outcomes in the sample space, \(S\), are \emph{equally likely},
the probability of event \(A\) is:
\[P(A) = \dfrac{\text{Number of outcomes in } A}{\text{Total number of outcomes in }S}\]

This is called the \textbf{classical} or \textbf{theoretical}
probability. It is calculated by reasoning about the structure of the
experiment; no data collection is required.

We use theoretical (classical) probability when:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The outcomes are equally likely and the sample space is well-defined,
  as in rolling a fair die or drawing cards from a well-shuffled deck.
\item
  The probability can be determined through logic and counting methods
  rather than observation.
\end{itemize}

The key difference: Empirical probability requires data collection and
observation, while theoretical probability requires only logical
analysis of equally likely outcomes.

\begin{example}[Theoretical
Probability]\protect\hypertarget{exm-theoretical-prob}{}\label{exm-theoretical-prob}

A fair six-sided die is rolled. Sample space:
\(S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\), with 6 equally likely outcomes. Find the
following probabilities.

\textbf{(a)} P(rolling a 4)

\textbf{(b)} P(rolling an even number)

\textbf{(c)} P(rolling a number \textgreater{} 4)

\textbf{(d)} P(rolling a number \textless{} 10)

\textbf{(e)} P(rolling a 7)

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\textbf{(a)} The event space for the event ``rolling a 4'' is
\(A= \{4\}\). Using the theoretical probability formula,
\[P(\text{rolling a }4) = P(A) = \frac{1}{6} \approx 0.167\]

\textbf{(b)} The event space for the event ``rolling an even number'' is
\(B = \{2,4,6\}\). Then, the probability is
\[ P(\text{rolling an even number}) = P(B) = \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5\]

\textbf{(c)} The event space for the event ``rolling a number
\textgreater{} 4'' is \(C = \{5,6\}\). The probability of event \(C\) is

\[P(\text{rolling a number }> 4) = P(C) = \frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3} \approx 0.333\]

\textbf{(d)} The event space for the event ``rolling a number
\textless{} 10'' is \(D = \{1,2,3,4,5,6\} = S\). The probability of
event \(D\) is

\[ P(\text{rolling a number }< 10)=P(D) = \frac{6}{6} = 1\]

which makes this a certain event.

\textbf{(e)} The event space for the event ``rolling a 7'' is
\(E = \{\emptyset\}\). Therefore, the probability of event \(E\) is

\[P(\text{rolling a }7) = P(E) = \frac{0}{6} = 0\]

which makes this an impossible event.

\end{tcolorbox}

You might wonder: if I flip a coin just 10 times and get 7 heads, does
that mean the probability of heads is 0.70? The \textbf{Law of Large
Numbers} answers this question.

The \textbf{Law of Large Numbers} states that as the number of trials,
\(n\), of an experiment increases, the relative frequency of an event
gets closer and closer to the true probability of that event. In other
words, as we perform more and more trials, the ratio
\(\left(\dfrac{\text{frequency of A}}{n}\right)\) approaches \(P(A)\).

For example, if you flip a fair coin:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  After 10 flips, you might get 7 heads (70\%) which is quite far from
  the true probability of 50\%
\item
  After 100 flips, you might get 57 heads (57\%) becoming closer to 50\%
\item
  After 1,000 flips, you might get 493 heads (49.3\%) very close to 50\%
\item
  After 10,000 flips, you'll get even closer to exactly 50\%
\end{itemize}

This does not mean you are ``due'' for tails after a streak of heads.
The coin has no memory. What actually happens is that early imbalances
become less and less important as trials accumulate --- 2 extra heads
out of 10 flips is 70\%, but 2 extra heads out of 1,000 flips is only
50.2\%.

\subsection{Simulation: Exploring Probability with
Rguroo}\label{simulation-exploring-probability-with-rguroo}

One of the most powerful ways to build intuition about probability is
through \textbf{simulation}: using technology to imitate a random
process thousands of times and observing the results. Instead of
flipping an actual coin 10,000 times by hand, Rguroo can simulate those
flips in seconds and display the results. Simulation makes the Law of
Large Numbers visible and concrete.

Simulations are especially useful when:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Theoretical probabilities are difficult to calculate. For example,
  determining the probability of winning a complex card game might
  involve complicated counting, but you can simulate 10,000 games and
  see how often you win.
\item
  We want to see how relative frequencies converge over many trials. For
  example, you can watch in real-time as the percentage of heads gets
  closer and closer to 50\% as the number of coin flips increases.
\item
  We want to explore what random variation really looks like.
  Simulations help us understand that getting 7 heads in 10 flips is not
  unusual for a fair coin, because we can see how much natural variation
  occurs in repeated experiments.
\end{itemize}

The key advantage of simulation is that it allows us to perform
thousands or even millions of trials instantly, revealing patterns that
would be impossible to observe through physical experiments alone.

\begin{example}[Simulating a Die
Roll]\protect\hypertarget{exm-simulation-die-roll}{}\label{exm-simulation-die-roll}

Suppose you want to explore whether a fair six-sided die actually
produces each face with equal frequency. The theoretical probability of
rolling any single face is \(1/6 \approx 0.167\). But does that hold up
when you actually simulate rolls? And how many trials do you need before
the results start to look balanced?

You can investigate this using Rguroo's simulation tool.

\end{example}

rolls of a fair die}

\end{figure}%

This is the \textbf{Law of Large Numbers} in action. With a small number
of trials, random variation produces noticeable differences between the
outcomes. With a large number of trials, those differences smooth out
and the relative frequencies converge toward the theoretical probability
of \(1/6 \approx 0.167\).

\end{tcolorbox}
