\subsection{Why the Boundary Value
Matters}\label{sec-foundations-boundary}

As noted earlier, a hypothesis test begins by assuming the null
hypothesis is true and asking how the sample statistic would behave
under that assumption. For this we need to work with one specific value
of the parameter. In the two-sided Case 3 the answer is immediate: the
null hypothesis \(H_0: p = p_0\) (or \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\)) names a
single value, so ``\(H_0\) is true'' means the parameter equals that one
value, so there is no question about which value to use. In the
one-sided Cases 1 and 2, however, the null hypothesis is not a single
value but a whole range --- for example, \(H_0: p \leq 0.70\) allows any
proportion at or below 0.70. In principle, we can assume any value in
this range as the true population proportion. Fortunately, there is a
natural choice that serves as the basis for the hypothesis test. So what
is this choice?

The choice is the \textbf{boundary value} --- the value \(p_0\) or
\(\mu_0\) that separates the null hypothesis from the alternative
hypothesis. The reason comes from the need to control errors in
hypothesis testing, which we discuss in
Section~\ref{sec-foundations-errors}. Every hypothesis test must keep
the probability of incorrectly rejecting the null hypothesis \(H_0\) at
or below a chosen level. To do this, we use the value of the parameter
that is hardest to distinguish from the alternative hypothesis. That
value is the boundary value. A claim like \(p \leq 0.70\) is most easily
mistaken for the alternative ``\(p > 0.70\)'' when the truth sits right
at \(0.70\); a true proportion well below 0.70 would rarely provide
evidence suggesting \(p > 0.70\). Using the boundary value therefore
gives the most \textbf{conservative hypothesis test}: if the error rate
is controlled at the boundary, it is automatically controlled for every
other value in the null region. You will see a more detailed explanation
of why the maximum error probability occurs at the boundary in
Section~\ref{sec-boundary-value} in the next chapter.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Evaluating \(H_0\) at the Boundary Value}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

From this point on, whenever we speak of ``the null hypothesis being
true'' for the purpose of computing probabilities, we take the parameter
equal to the \textbf{boundary value} (\(p_0\) for a proportion,
\(\mu_0\) for a mean). This is the value within the null hypothesis that
is hardest to distinguish from the alternative hypothesis. Using the
boundary value gives a conservative test.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Is the Parameter a Mean or a
Proportion?}\label{sec-foundations-mean-vs-prop}

Before working through specific examples, it is worth pausing to address
a question that often causes some confusion: in a given real-world
problem, how do you tell whether the parameter of interest is a
population proportion \(p\) or a population mean \(\mu\)? The
distinction is important because it determines everything that follows
--- the notation, the hypotheses, the sampling distribution, and the
computations. Fortunately, the diagnostic is simple.

The key is to identify the \textbf{variable measured on each individual}
in the population and ask whether that variable is \textbf{categorical}
or \textbf{numerical}.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  If the variable is \textbf{categorical} with two outcomes
  (success/failure, yes/no, agree/disagree, has/does not have), the
  parameter is a \textbf{proportion} \(p\) --- the fraction of the
  population that is a success.
\item
  If the variable is \textbf{numerical} (a score, a quantity, a
  measurement), the parameter is a \textbf{mean} \(\mu\) --- the average
  value of that variable in the population.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Quick Check: Mean or Proportion?}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

Identify the variable measured on each individual.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Categorical} (yes/no, success/failure) → \textbf{proportion}
  \(p\)
\item
  \textbf{Numerical} (a quantity, a score, a measurement) →
  \textbf{mean} \(\mu\)
\end{itemize}

A useful test: does the problem ask what \emph{fraction} or
\emph{percentage} of the population has some characteristic, or what
\emph{average value} a measurement takes?

\end{tcolorbox}

Two common sources of confusion are the words \textbf{percentage} and
\textbf{average}.

The word \textbf{percentage} can describe either type of parameter. For
example, \emph{``What percentage of voters support the candidate?''} is
a proportion question because each voter either supports the candidate
or does not. In contrast, \emph{``What is the average exam percentage
among students?''} is a mean question because each student has a
numerical percentage score, and we are averaging those scores.

The word \textbf{average} usually signals a mean, but not always. A
question such as \emph{``What is the average number of hours students
sleep each night?''} is clearly about a mean. However, a statement such
as \emph{``On average, 60\% of voters support the candidate''} is really
describing a proportion. Rather than relying on keywords, focus on the
variable measured on each individual: is it categorical or numerical?

In the examples that follow, the first three concern a population
proportion \(p\) --- the YouTube example, the physical inactivity
example, and the social media news example. The next three concern a
population mean \(\mu\) --- the SAT example, the sleep example, and the
commute time example. As you read each setup, try to identify the
variable measured on each individual before reading the parameter. The
categorical-versus-numerical diagnostic should quickly tell you whether
the problem is about a proportion or a mean.

\begin{example}[Writing Hypotheses:
Proportions]\protect\hypertarget{exm-foundations-hypotheses-prop}{}\label{exm-foundations-hypotheses-prop}

For each scenario, identify the boundary value and write the null and
alternative hypotheses for the population proportion \(p\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  A school district claims that \textbf{more than 70\%} of its students
  use YouTube daily.
\item
  A health agency hopes that \textbf{fewer than 35\%} of adults in its
  country are physically inactive.
\item
  A university administration wants to know whether the proportion of
  students who get most of their news from social media \textbf{differs
  from 36\%}.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\item
  The phrase ``more than'' gives a one-sided alternative in the upper
  direction, with boundary value \(p_0 = 0.70\): \[
  \begin{cases}
  H_0: p \leq 0.70 \\
  H_a: p > 0.70
  \end{cases}
  \]
\item
  The phrase ``fewer than'' gives a one-sided alternative in the lower
  direction, with boundary value \(p_0 = 0.35\): \[
  \begin{cases}
  H_0: p \geq 0.35 \\
  H_a: p < 0.35
  \end{cases}
  \]
\item
  The phrase ``differs from'' gives a two-sided alternative, with
  boundary value \(p_0 = 0.36\): \[
  \begin{cases}
  H_0: p = 0.36 \\
  H_a: p \neq 0.36
  \end{cases}
  \]
\end{enumerate}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Writing Hypotheses:
Means]\protect\hypertarget{exm-foundations-hypotheses-mean}{}\label{exm-foundations-hypotheses-mean}

For each scenario, identify the boundary value and write the null and
alternative hypotheses for the population mean \(\mu\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  We wish to investigate whether the mean math SAT score of incoming
  freshmen at a university is \textbf{higher than} the national mean of
  508 points.
\item
  We wish to investigate whether the mean nightly sleep among students
  at a university is \textbf{less than} 7 hours.
\item
  We wish to investigate whether the mean one-way commute time among
  workers in a metropolitan area \textbf{differs from} the national mean
  of 26.8 minutes.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\item
  The phrase ``higher than'' gives a one-sided alternative in the upper
  direction, with boundary value \(\mu_0 = 508\): \[
  \begin{cases}
  H_0: \mu \leq 508 \\
  H_a: \mu > 508
  \end{cases}
  \]
\item
  The phrase ``less than'' gives a one-sided alternative in the lower
  direction, with boundary value \(\mu_0 = 7\): \[
  \begin{cases}
  H_0: \mu \geq 7 \\
  H_a: \mu < 7
  \end{cases}
  \]
\item
  The phrase ``differs from'' gives a two-sided alternative, with
  boundary value \(\mu_0 = 26.8\): \[
  \begin{cases}
  H_0: \mu = 26.8 \\
  H_a: \mu \neq 26.8
  \end{cases}
  \]
\end{enumerate}

\end{tcolorbox}

Notice that the two examples are structurally identical. Only the symbol
for the parameter and the units of the boundary value differ; the logic
of translating a research question into a pair of hypotheses is the
same.

\section{Making a Decision in a Hypothesis
Test}\label{sec-foundations-decision}

Once we have stated the null and alternative hypotheses, the next step
is to determine whether the observed data provide sufficient evidence
against the null hypothesis and in favor of the alternative hypothesis.
Although six logical combinations of decisions and hypotheses can be
imagined, a hypothesis test leads to only two conclusions: either we
\textbf{reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_a\)} or we \textbf{fail to reject
\(H_0\)}. These possibilities are summarized in
Figure~\ref{fig-hypothesis_decision_matrix}.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Foundations_of_Inference/hypothesis_decision_matrix.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-hypothesis_decision_matrix}The six logical
combinations of decisions and hypotheses.}

\end{figure}%

First, let's clarify the distinction between \textbf{accepting} \(H_0\)
and \textbf{failing to reject} \(H_0\). This distinction is easier to
understand by considering a criminal trial. In our judicial system, a
defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable
doubt. The hypotheses can therefore be written as

\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \text{The defendant is innocent} \\
H_a: \text{The defendant is guilty.}
\end{cases}
\]

If there is not sufficient evidence to conclude that the defendant is
guilty beyond a reasonable doubt, we \textbf{fail to reject} \(H_0\);
that is, we fail to reject the claim that the defendant is innocent.
However, this does not mean that we have proved the defendant is
innocent. A verdict of \emph{not guilty} simply means that the evidence
was not strong enough to establish guilt. The trial is designed to look
for convincing evidence of guilt, not to prove innocence.

Hypothesis tests follow the same logic. They are designed to look for
evidence against the null hypothesis and in favor of the alternative
hypothesis, not to prove that the null hypothesis is true. If the
observed data provide sufficiently strong evidence against \(H_0\), we
\textbf{reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_a\)}. Otherwise, we \textbf{fail
to reject \(H_0\)}.

Although our goal is to find evidence in favor of the alternative
hypothesis, we do so by evaluating the null hypothesis. We begin by
assuming \(H_0\) is true and ask whether the observed data are
inconsistent with that assumption. Consequently, the conclusion of a
hypothesis test is always expressed in terms of the null hypothesis: we
either \textbf{reject \(H_0\)} or \textbf{fail to reject \(H_0\)}.

\subsection{The Two Types of Error}\label{sec-foundations-errors}

Because a hypothesis test reaches a decision from a sample rather than
from the whole population, our conclusion can be wrong. There are
exactly two ways to be wrong, and distinguishing them is essential to
understanding how tests are designed.

A \textbf{Type I error} occurs when we \textbf{reject \(H_0\) even
though \(H_0\) is actually true}. We have declared an effect that does
not exist --- a false alarm.

A \textbf{Type II error} occurs when we \textbf{fail to reject \(H_0\)
even though \(H_a\) is actually true}. We have missed an effect that is
genuinely present --- a missed discovery.

These outcomes, together with the two ways of being right, are
summarized below. The truth (which we never actually know) runs across
the top; our decision runs down the side.

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& \(H_0\) is true & \(H_a\) is true \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{Reject \(H_0\)} & Type I error & Correct decision \\
\textbf{Fail to reject \(H_0\)} & Correct decision & Type II error \\
\end{longtable}

Figure~\ref{fig-types-of-error} traces the same four outcomes as a flow
from the unknown truth, through our decision, to the result. The truth
about \(H_0\) is unknown to us (left). For each possibility we may
either reject or fail to reject \(H_0\) (middle), leading to a correct
decision or to one of the two errors (right): a Type I error rejects a
true \(H_0\), and a Type II error fails to reject when \(H_a\) is true.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Foundations_of_Inference/types_of_error.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-types-of-error}The four possible outcomes of a
hypothesis test.}

\end{figure}%

We measure these errors using probabilities. Specifically, \(\alpha\)
(the Greek letter alpha) denotes the probability of a Type I error, and
\(\beta\) (the Greek letter beta) denotes the probability of a Type II
error.

The meaning of each error is always tied to the context of the problem.
The next two examples translate the abstract definitions into plain
language, once for a proportion and once for a mean.

\begin{example}[Interpreting Errors: YouTube Use
(Proportion)]\protect\hypertarget{exm-foundations-error-prop}{}\label{exm-foundations-error-prop}

Recall the claim that more than 70\% of a district's students use
YouTube daily, with hypotheses \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p \leq 0.70 \\
H_a: p > 0.70
\end{cases}
\] Describe what a Type I error and a Type II error would mean in this
context.

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

A \textbf{Type I error} occurs if we reject \(H_0\) and conclude that
more than 70\% of students use YouTube daily, when in fact the true
proportion is 70\% or less (\(H_0\) is true). We would be claiming a
higher usage rate than really exists.

A \textbf{Type II error} occurs if we fail to reject \(H_0\) and
therefore do not conclude that more than 70\% use YouTube daily, when in
fact the true proportion does exceed 70\% (\(H_a\) is true). We would be
missing a real difference.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Interpreting Errors: SAT Scores
(Mean)]\protect\hypertarget{exm-foundations-error-mean}{}\label{exm-foundations-error-mean}

Recall the claim that the mean math SAT score of incoming freshmen is
higher than the national mean of 508, with hypotheses \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu \leq 508 \\
H_a: \mu > 508
\end{cases}
\] Describe what a Type I error and a Type II error would mean in this
context.

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

A \textbf{Type I error} occurs if we reject \(H_0\) and conclude that
the mean SAT score exceeds 508, when in fact the true mean is 508 or
less (\(H_0\) is true). We would be claiming the freshmen score higher
than they really do.

A \textbf{Type II error} occurs if we fail to reject \(H_0\) and
therefore do not conclude that the mean exceeds 508, when in fact the
true mean is greater than 508 (\(H_a\) is true). We would be missing a
genuine difference.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{The Trade-Off Between the Two
Errors}\label{sec-foundations-tradeoff}

We would like to make both kinds of error, Type I and Type II, as rarely
as possible. Unfortunately, for a fixed sample size, the two are
connected: reducing the chance of one error increases the chance of the
other.

Let's look at a smoke detector example to clarify this trade-off. Let
\(H_0\) be ``there is no fire'' and \(H_a\) be ``there is a fire.'' If
we make the detector less sensitive to avoid false alarms from burnt
toast or steam, we reduce Type I errors but increase the risk that the
detector stays silent during a real fire, creating more Type II errors.
If we make the detector more sensitive so it rarely misses a real fire,
we reduce Type II errors but increase false alarms, creating more Type I
errors. The same trade-off appears in every hypothesis test. Making it
harder to reject \(H_0\) reduces the chance of a Type I error but
increases the chance of a Type II error. Making it easier to reject
\(H_0\) has the opposite effect. For a fixed sample size, the two types
of errors cannot both be minimized at the same time---every hypothesis
test must strike a balance between them.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Foundations_of_Inference/tradeoff-seesaw.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-tradeoff-seesaw}The trade-off between Type I and
Type II errors.}

\end{figure}%

Faced with this trade-off, statisticians choose to focus first on
controlling Type I errors: \emph{we keep the maximum probability of a
Type I error at a small prespecified level called \textbf{significance
level}, and then try to make the probability of a Type II error as small
as possible within that constraint.} One reason for focusing on Type I
errors is that falsely claiming an effect exists --- for example, saying
a new drug works when it does not --- can have serious consequences.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Type I and Type II error possibilities}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

If we reject \(H_0\), a Type I error is possible, but a Type II error is
not.

If we fail to reject \(H_0\), a Type II error is possible, but a Type I
error is not.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{The Significance Level}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

The largest probability of a Type I error that we are willing to
tolerate is called the \textbf{significance level} of the test, denoted
by \(\alpha\) (the Greek letter alpha). It is chosen \emph{before}
looking at the data. The most common choice is \(\alpha = 0.05\),
meaning we accept at most a 5\% chance of rejecting a true null
hypothesis; values of \(\alpha = 0.10\) and \(\alpha = 0.01\) are also
used. A smaller \(\alpha\) makes the test more conservative --- less
willing to reject \(H_0\), and therefore less prone to a Type I error
but more prone to a Type II error.

\end{tcolorbox}

With the significance level fixed, every test must answer the same
practical question: given the data, do we reject \(H_0\) or not? There
are two standard ways to answer it, the \textbf{p-value approach} and
the \textbf{critical region approach}, and they always lead to the same
conclusion. We present the p-value approach first, because it is the
most widely reported in practice and the most directly interpretable,
and then the critical region approach.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Homework for
Section~\ref{sec-foundations-hypotheses} and
Section~\ref{sec-foundations-errors}}{Homework for Section~ and Section~}}\label{sec-foundations-hyp-error-hw}

For each of the following scenarios, do the following:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Identify the population of interest and the parameter (\(p\) for a
  proportion, \(\mu\) for a mean).
\item
  State the null and alternative hypotheses in words.
\item
  Write the null and alternative hypotheses using mathematical notation,
  and identify the boundary value.
\item
  State whether the test is one-sided or two-sided.
\item
  Describe what happens if a Type I error occurs in the context of the
  problem.
\item
  Describe what happens if a Type II error occurs in the context of the
  problem.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{YouTube Use Among Teens.} A school district claims that more
  than 70\% of its students use YouTube daily.
\item
  \textbf{Physical Inactivity Among Adults.} A national health agency
  hopes that fewer than 35\% of adults in its country are physically
  inactive.
\item
  \textbf{Social Media as a News Source.} A university administration
  wants to know whether the proportion of its students who get most of
  their news from social media differs from 36\%.
\item
  \textbf{SAT Math Scores.} A researcher wishes to investigate whether
  the mean math SAT score of incoming freshmen at a university is higher
  than the national mean of 508 points.
\item
  \textbf{Nightly Sleep.} A researcher wishes to investigate whether the
  mean nightly sleep among students at a university is less than 7
  hours.
\item
  \textbf{Commute Time.} A researcher wishes to investigate whether the
  mean one-way commute time among workers in a metropolitan area differs
  from the national mean of 26.8 minutes.
\item
  \textbf{Battery Life.} A manufacturer advertises that its rechargeable
  batteries last 12 hours on average. A consumer group suspects the true
  mean is less than 12 hours and tests a random sample of batteries.
\item
  \textbf{Defect Rate.} A factory's quality-control standard requires
  that no more than 2\% of its parts be defective. An inspector wants to
  determine whether the true defect rate exceeds 2\%.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Making a Decision: The p-Value
Approach}\label{sec-foundations-pvalue}

The p-value approach measures \emph{how consistent} the observed data
are with the null hypothesis, and rejects \(H_0\) when the data are
sufficiently inconsistent with it.

To make the idea of ``consistent'' more precise, we tentatively assume
that \(H_0\) is true. This means assuming the boundary value of the null
hypothesis: \(p = p_0\) for a proportion or \(\mu = \mu_0\) for a mean.
Under this assumption, each of the statistics --- the count \(X\), the
sample proportion \(\hat{p}\), and the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) --- has a
known sampling distribution describing how it varies from sample to
sample. Using this distribution, we then ask the central question:
assuming \(H_0\) is true, what is the probability that the statistic
(\(X\), \(\hat{p}\), or \(\bar{X}\)) takes a value at least as far in
favor of \(H_a\) as the value we actually observed (\(x_{\text{obs}}\),
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\), or \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\))?

Intuitively, the p-value tells us how surprising the data we observed
would be if the null hypothesis were actually true. Even when \(H_0\)
holds exactly, we don't expect a sample statistic to land precisely on
\(p_0\) or \(\mu_0\) every time --- sample-to-sample variation is
normal. The p-value asks a sharper question: among all the outcomes that
could occur by random sampling under \(H_0\), how extreme is the one we
actually got? A value near 0 says our data would be a rare, surprising
result if \(H_0\) were true; a value near 1 says our data look like an
unremarkable draw from a world where \(H_0\) holds. The box below states
this precisely.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{The p-Value}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

The \textbf{p-value} is the probability, computed \emph{assuming the
null hypothesis is true}, of obtaining a value of the statistic at least
as \textbf{favorable to} the alternative hypothesis \(H_a\) as the
observed value.

A small p-value means the observed data are inconsistent with \(H_0\),
and therefore count as evidence \emph{against} \(H_0\). A large p-value
means the data are consistent with \(H_0\), and therefore do not provide
strong evidence against it.

\end{tcolorbox}

To compute the probability that defines the p-value, we need a sampling
distribution. The specific sampling distribution depends on the
statistic and is taken up in the next two chapters; here we only need to
know that such a distribution exists.

What counts as ``at least as supportive of \(H_a\)'' depends on the
direction of the alternative. We call the collection of such values the
\textbf{\(H_a\) support}, and the p-value is the probability of the
statistic landing in this region when \(H_0\) is true. The crucial point
is that the \(H_a\) support is anchored at the \emph{observed value} ---
it is defined by which outcomes are as convincing as, or more convincing
than, what we actually observe. We illustrate all three cases with the
SAT example, where the boundary value is \(\mu_0 = 508\).

\textbf{Case 1: upper-tail alternative (\(H_a: \mu > 508\)).} Here
larger values of the sample mean are more supportive of \(H_a\), so the
\(H_a\) support consists of the observed value and everything above it.
If the observed mean is \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\), the support is
every value at or above 542, and the p-value is the probability of a
sample mean at least as large as 542. As
Figure~\ref{fig-ha-support-case1} shows, the support begins at the
observed value, not at the boundary; the boundary \(508\) is marked only
for reference.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{index_files/mediabag/Rguroo_outputs/Foundations_of_Inference/ha-support-case1.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-ha-support-case1}Case 1, \(H_a: \mu > 508\). The
\(H_a\) support (teal) is every value at or above the observed mean
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\).}

\end{figure}%

\textbf{Case 2: lower-tail alternative (\(H_a: \mu < 508\)).} Now
smaller values are more supportive of \(H_a\), so the \(H_a\) support
consists of the observed value and everything below it. If the observed
mean is \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 478\), the support is every value at or
below 478, and the p-value is the probability of a sample mean at least
as small as 478 (Figure~\ref{fig-ha-support-case2}).

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{index_files/mediabag/Rguroo_outputs/Foundations_of_Inference/ha-support-case2.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-ha-support-case2}Case 2, \(H_a: \mu < 508\). The
\(H_a\) support (teal) is every value at or below the observed mean
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 478\).}

\end{figure}%

\textbf{Case 3: two-sided alternative (\(H_a: \mu \neq 508\)).}
Describing the \(H_a\) support is a bit more involved here because
values on \emph{both} sides of the boundary can support \(H_a\). The
support still includes the observed value and everything beyond it, but
it also includes a \emph{mirror-image} region on the opposite side of
the boundary --- the values that are just as far from the boundary as
the observed value, and farther. The picture depends on which side of
the boundary the observed value falls on:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{If the observed value lies above the boundary} (say
  \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\), which is 34 above the boundary), the
  support is every value at or above 542, together with every value at
  or below the mirror value \(508 - 34 = 474\)
  (Figure~\ref{fig-ha-support-case3a}).
\item
  \emph{If the observed value lies below the boundary} (say
  \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 478\), which is 30 below the boundary), the
  support is every value at or below 478, together with every value at
  or above the mirror value \(508 + 30 = 538\)
  (Figure~\ref{fig-ha-support-case3b}).
\end{itemize}

Either way, the p-value collects probability from both tails: the tail
containing the observed value, plus the symmetric mirror tail on the
opposite side.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{index_files/mediabag/Rguroo_outputs/Foundations_of_Inference/ha-support-case3a.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-ha-support-case3a}Case 3a, \(H_a: \mu \neq 508\)
with the observed mean above the boundary. The \(H_a\) support (teal) is
every value at or above \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\), together with
every value at or below its mirror value \(474\).}

\end{figure}%

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{index_files/mediabag/Rguroo_outputs/Foundations_of_Inference/ha-support-case3b.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-ha-support-case3b}Case 3b, \(H_a: \mu \neq 508\)
with the observed mean below the boundary. The \(H_a\) support (teal) is
every value at or below \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 478\), together with
every value at or above its mirror value \(538\).}

\end{figure}%

To see all three cases in the running examples: the YouTube test
(\(H_a: p > 0.70\)) and the SAT test (\(H_a: \mu > 508\)) are both Case
1, so their p-values come from the upper tail. The physical inactivity
test (\(H_a: p < 0.35\)) and the sleep test (\(H_a: \mu < 7\)) are Case
2, drawing their p-values from the lower tail. The social media test
(\(H_a: p \neq 0.36\)) and the commute-time test
(\(H_a: \mu \neq 26.8\)) are two-sided Case 3, collecting probability
from both tails at once.

Once the p-value is in hand, the decision rule is the same in every case
and compares the p-value to the significance level \(\alpha\), chosen in
advance.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Decision Rule Using the p-Value}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\[
\text{If } \text{p-value} \leq \alpha, \text{ reject } H_0. 
\qquad 
\text{If } \text{p-value} > \alpha, \text{ fail to reject } H_0.
\]

\end{tcolorbox}

The logic is direct. If the observed result, and results even more
extreme, would be unlikely to occur under \(H_0\) --- unlikely enough
that their combined probability falls at or below \(\alpha\) --- we
treat that as sufficient evidence to reject \(H_0\). If instead the
result is the sort of thing that happens fairly often under \(H_0\), we
have no strong reason to reject the null.
Figure~\ref{fig-pvalue-decision} summarizes this rule.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth,height=\textheight]{index_files/mediabag/Rguroo_outputs/Foundations_of_Inference/pvalue-decision-rule.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-pvalue-decision}The p-value decision rule.}

\end{figure}%

A useful feature of the p-value is that it conveys not just a yes-or-no
decision but the \emph{strength} of the evidence. A p-value far below
the significance level \(\alpha\) indicates very strong evidence against
\(H_0\); a p-value just barely below \(\alpha\) indicates evidence that
clears the bar only narrowly.

The following examples illustrate how a p-value is read once it has been
computed --- by software such as Rguroo in the later chapters ---
without our performing the computation here.

\begin{example}[Reading a p-Value: YouTube Use
(Proportion)]\protect\hypertarget{exm-foundations-pvalue-prop}{}\label{exm-foundations-pvalue-prop}

For the YouTube test with \(H_0: p \leq 0.70\) versus \(H_a: p > 0.70\),
suppose the analysis returns a p-value of \(0.107\). Using
\(\alpha = 0.05\), state the decision and interpret it.

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

The p-value of \(0.107\) means that \emph{if the true proportion were
exactly 0.70}, there would be about an 10.7\% chance of observing a
sample result at least as supportive of \(H_a\) as the one we obtained.
Because \(0.107 > 0.05\), we \textbf{fail to reject \(H_0\)}. The
observed result is not unusual enough under \(H_0\) to provide strong
evidence that more than 70\% of students use YouTube daily.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Reading a p-Value: SAT Scores
(Mean)]\protect\hypertarget{exm-foundations-pvalue-mean}{}\label{exm-foundations-pvalue-mean}

For the SAT test with \(H_0: \mu \leq 508\) versus \(H_a: \mu > 508\),
suppose the analysis returns a p-value of \(0.029\). Using
\(\alpha = 0.05\), state the decision and interpret it.

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

The p-value of \(0.029\) means that \emph{if the true mean were exactly
508}, there would be about a 3\% chance of observing a sample mean at
least as large as the one we obtained. Because \(0.029 \leq 0.05\), we
\textbf{reject \(H_0\)} in favor of \(H_a: \mu > 508\). A sample mean
this high would be unusual if the true mean were only 508, providing
evidence that the mean SAT score of incoming freshmen exceeds the
national figure.

\end{tcolorbox}

Once again the two examples differ only in their surface details. In
both, the p-value is a probability computed under \(H_0\), and in both
the decision comes from comparing that probability to the same
\(\alpha\).

\section{Making a Decision: The Critical Region
Approach}\label{sec-foundations-critical-region}

The critical region approach decides \emph{in advance} which values of
the statistic are extreme enough to warrant rejecting \(H_0\), and then
simply checks whether the observed value is among them. It needs no
probability computed from the observed value; the threshold is fixed
before the data are examined.

As with the p-value, we begin by tentatively assuming that \(H_0\) is
true, using the boundary value of the null hypothesis (\(p = p_0\) for a
proportion, \(\mu = \mu_0\) for a mean). Under this assumption each
statistic --- the count \(X\), the sample proportion \(\hat{p}\), or the
sample mean \(\bar{X}\) --- has a sampling distribution describing how
it varies from sample to sample. We use that distribution to mark off
the values that would be unusual under \(H_0\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{The Critical Region}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

The \textbf{critical region} (or \textbf{rejection region}) is the set
of values of the statistic for which we reject \(H_0\). The value or
values that separate ``reject'' from ``fail to reject'' are called
\textbf{critical values}. The critical values are chosen so that,
\emph{when \(H_0\) is true}, the probability that the statistic falls in
the critical region equals the significance level \(\alpha\).

Because the critical region is built to have probability \(\alpha\)
under \(H_0\), rejecting \(H_0\) whenever the statistic lands in it
guarantees that the probability of a Type I error is exactly \(\alpha\).
This is what controls the error rate.

\end{tcolorbox}

The shape of the critical region matches the direction of the
alternative hypothesis: we reject \(H_0\) when the statistic falls in
the direction that \(H_a\) predicts. We illustrate all three cases with
the SAT example, where the boundary value is \(\mu_0 = 508\). The
critical values shown are hypothetical, chosen only to illustrate; their
actual computation is taken up in the later chapters.

\textbf{Case 1: upper-tail alternative (\(H_a: \mu > 508\)).} Large
values of the sample mean support \(H_a\), so the critical region sits
in the \textbf{upper tail} --- reject \(H_0\) when the sample mean is at
or above an upper critical value. In Figure~\ref{fig-critical-case1} the
critical value is \(535\), so the rejection region is every value at or
above \(535\). The left panel shows an observed mean of \(542\), which
falls inside the rejection region, so we reject \(H_0\); the right panel
shows an observed mean of \(521\), which falls outside, so we fail to
reject \(H_0\).

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{index_files/mediabag/Rguroo_outputs/Foundations_of_Inference/critical-case1.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-critical-case1}Case 1, \(H_a: \mu > 508\), with a
critical value of \(535\). The rejection region (coral) is every value
at or above \(535\). \emph{Left:} observed mean \(542\) is inside the
region --- reject \(H_0\). \emph{Right:} observed mean \(521\) is
outside --- fail to reject \(H_0\).}

\end{figure}%

\textbf{Case 2: lower-tail alternative (\(H_a: \mu < 508\)).} Small
values support \(H_a\), so the critical region sits in the \textbf{lower
tail} --- reject \(H_0\) when the sample mean is at or below a lower
critical value. In Figure~\ref{fig-critical-case2} the critical value is
\(481\), so the rejection region is every value at or below \(481\). The
left panel shows an observed mean of \(474\) (inside --- reject
\(H_0\)); the right panel shows an observed mean of \(495\) (outside ---
fail to reject \(H_0\)).

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{index_files/mediabag/Rguroo_outputs/Foundations_of_Inference/critical-case2.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-critical-case2}Case 2, \(H_a: \mu < 508\), with a
critical value of \(481\). The rejection region (coral) is every value
at or below \(481\). \emph{Left:} observed mean \(474\) is inside the
region --- reject \(H_0\). \emph{Right:} observed mean \(495\) is
outside --- fail to reject \(H_0\).}

\end{figure}%

\textbf{Case 3: two-sided alternative (\(H_a: \mu \neq 508\)).} Extreme
values in \emph{either} direction support \(H_a\), so the critical
region occupies \textbf{both tails} --- reject \(H_0\) when the sample
mean is at or below a lower critical value or at or above an upper
critical value. Because rejection can happen on either side, the
significance level is split evenly between the two tails, with
probability \(\alpha/2\) assigned to each. In
Figure~\ref{fig-critical-case3} the critical values are \(481\) and
\(535\), so the rejection region is every value at or below \(481\)
together with every value at or above \(535\). The left panel shows an
observed mean of \(542\), which falls in the upper tail (inside ---
reject \(H_0\)); the right panel shows an observed mean of \(515\),
which falls in the middle (outside --- fail to reject \(H_0\)).

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{index_files/mediabag/Rguroo_outputs/Foundations_of_Inference/critical-case3.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-critical-case3}Case 3, \(H_a: \mu \neq 508\), with
critical values \(481\) and \(535\). The rejection region (coral) is
both tails: at or below \(481\) or at or above \(535\). \emph{Left:}
observed mean \(542\) is in the upper tail --- reject \(H_0\).
\emph{Right:} observed mean \(515\) is in the middle --- fail to reject
\(H_0\).}

\end{figure}%

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Decision Rule Using the Critical Region}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

Construct the critical region so that, under \(H_0\), the probability
the statistic falls in it equals \(\alpha\). Then:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  If the observed statistic \textbf{falls in the critical region},
  reject \(H_0\).
\item
  If the observed statistic \textbf{falls outside the critical region},
  fail to reject \(H_0\).
\end{itemize}

\end{tcolorbox}

Locating the critical values requires a sampling distribution, just as
the p-value does, and the actual computation --- carried out with Rguroo
in the later chapters --- depends on the statistic. The conceptual point
that matters here is independent of those details: the critical region
is a fixed target set up before the data are examined, and the decision
is simply a matter of seeing whether the observed value lands inside it.

The two worked examples below show how a critical-region decision is
read once the critical value has been found, without our performing the
computation here.

\begin{example}[Using the Critical Region: YouTube Use
(Proportion)]\protect\hypertarget{exm-foundations-critical-prop}{}\label{exm-foundations-critical-prop}

For the YouTube test with \(H_0: p \leq 0.70\) versus \(H_a: p > 0.70\),
suppose that for a sample of \(n = 20\) students and \(\alpha = 0.05\)
the critical region is found to be \(X \geq 18\), where \(X\) is the
count of daily users. The observed count is \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\).
State the decision.

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

The critical region is \(X \geq 18\). The observed count
\(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\) does not reach \(18\), so it falls
\emph{outside} the critical region. We therefore \textbf{fail to reject
\(H_0\)}: the data do not provide strong enough evidence that more than
70\% of students use YouTube daily.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Foundations_of_Inference/cr_image_YouTube.png}

}

\caption{YouTube use example: observed count outside the critical
region; fail to reject \(H_0.\)}

\end{figure}%

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Using the Critical Region: SAT Scores
(Mean)]\protect\hypertarget{exm-foundations-critical-mean}{}\label{exm-foundations-critical-mean}

For the SAT test with \(H_0: \mu \leq 508\) versus \(H_a: \mu > 508\),
suppose that for \(\alpha = 0.05\) the critical region is found to be
\(\bar{X} \geq 535\). The observed sample mean is
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\). State the decision.

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

The critical region is \(\bar{X} \geq 535\). The observed mean
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\) exceeds \(535\), so it falls
\emph{inside} the critical region. We therefore \textbf{reject \(H_0\)}
in favor of \(H_a: \mu > 508\): the data provide evidence that the mean
SAT score of incoming freshmen exceeds the national figure.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Foundations_of_Inference/cr_image_SAT.png}

}

\caption{SAT scores example: observed mean inside the rejection region;
reject \(H_0.\)}

\end{figure}%

\end{tcolorbox}

As with the p-value examples, the two differ only in their surface
details. In both, the critical region is fixed in advance to have
probability \(\alpha\) under \(H_0\), and in both the decision comes
from checking whether the observed value lands inside it.

\subsection{The Two Approaches Always
Agree}\label{sec-foundations-equivalence}

The p-value approach and the critical region approach are two
descriptions of one and the same test. They are guaranteed to reach the
identical decision, because each is built from the same significance
level \(\alpha\) and the same sampling distribution under \(H_0\).

The connection is easiest to see by picturing the boundary of the
critical region. The observed statistic falls inside the critical region
precisely when it is at least as extreme as the critical value --- and
that is exactly the situation in which the probability of a result this
extreme or more so, the p-value, is at or below \(\alpha\). The two
statements

\[
\text{the observed value lies in the critical region} 
\qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad 
\text{p-value} \leq \alpha
\]

are therefore equivalent, and the corresponding decisions always match.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Two Routes, One Decision}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

The critical region approach answers the question ``for which values of
the statistic would we reject \(H_0\)?'' and checks whether the observed
value is among them. The p-value approach answers the question ``given
the value we observed, how strong is the evidence against \(H_0\)?'' and
compares that strength to \(\alpha\). Both control the Type I error
probability at \(\alpha\), and both always lead to the same conclusion.
The p-value approach has the added advantage of quantifying \emph{how}
strong the evidence is, not merely whether it crosses the threshold.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{From Hypothesis Tests to Confidence
Intervals}\label{sec-foundations-confidence-intervals}

A hypothesis test answers a yes-or-no question about a \emph{single}
candidate value of the parameter: is that value (call it the boundary
value, \(p_0\) or \(\mu_0\)) consistent with the data, or not? Often,
though, we want something more informative --- not a verdict on one
value, but a whole range of values that the data find plausible. This is
the role of a \textbf{confidence interval}. The two tools answer
different questions, but as we will see, they are built from exactly the
same sampling distributions.

Before explaining how confidence intervals are constructed, let's first
see what one looks like and how to interpret it. Suppose we survey
\(n = 400\) registered voters and find that
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.55\) support a proposed policy. Rather than
testing a single hypothesized value of \(p\), we might instead ask: what
range of values of \(p\) are plausible given our data? A method we will
construct later in this section might give us the interval
\((0.50, 0.60)\), along with a \textbf{confidence level} of 95\%. We
would report this as: ``we are 95\% confident that the true proportion
of voters who support the policy is between 0.50 and 0.60.''

The same reasoning applies to a population mean. Instead of estimating a
population proportion, suppose a sample of \(n = 50\) employees has an
average commute time of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 27.3\) minutes. A 95\%
confidence interval for the true mean commute time \(\mu\) might be
\((25.1, 29.5)\) minutes --- we are 95\% confident that the true average
commute time falls in this range.

Both examples report a 95\% confidence interval. But what does ``95\%
confident'' actually mean here? The answer is subtler than it first
appears, and we will make it precise shortly. For now, notice something
familiar in both examples: each interval consists of the observed
statistic (\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.55\),
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 27.3\)) and extends some distance in each
direction --- a structure that will turn out to be closely connected to
the hypothesis tests.

At first glance, confidence intervals and hypothesis tests may seem like
different inferential tools. In reality, they are two sides of the same
idea. The key realization is that we already possess everything needed
to build such a range. A two-sided hypothesis test is, in effect, a
\emph{consistency check} for a proposed value: test the parameter
against that single value, and if we fail to reject, the value is
consistent with our data; if we reject, it is not. Nothing stops us from
running that check not for one candidate value but for \emph{every}
candidate value. Collect all the values that survive --- all the values
we would fail to reject --- and the resulting set is a confidence
interval. This connection can be summarized in a simple rule, called
\textbf{inverting a test}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Confidence Interval by Inverting a Test}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

A \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%\) confidence interval for a parameter (a
proportion \(p\) or a mean \(\mu\)) consists of \textbf{all candidate
values that would \emph{not} be rejected} by a two-sided test of that
value at significance level \(\alpha\).

The confidence level and the significance level are complementary:
\(\alpha = 0.05\) corresponds to a 95\% confidence interval,
\(\alpha = 0.10\) to a 90\% interval, and so on.

\end{tcolorbox}

To picture the inversion, imagine sweeping a candidate value along the
number line and testing each one, as in Figure~\ref{fig-ci-inversion}.
Consider the SAT example, where a sample of math SAT scores has an
observed mean of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\). Each dot marks a
candidate value for the population mean \(\mu\). A two-sided test
rejects candidate values far from 542 (coral) and fails to reject those
close to it (teal). The stretch of non-rejected values between the two
switching points --- marked by the bracket --- is the confidence
interval: the band of mean values the data deem plausible. (No
computation is shown here; the figure simply records, for a grid of
candidate values, which ones a test would reject.)

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{index_files/mediabag/Rguroo_outputs/Foundations_of_Inference/ci-by-inversion-mean.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-ci-inversion}A confidence interval as an inverted
test, illustrated for the mean math SAT score.}

\end{figure}%

This construction also explains what the confidence level \emph{means}
--- and the idea is easy to misstate, so it's worth stating carefully.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Interpreting the Confidence Level}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

Imagine repeating the whole study many times: each time we draw a fresh
random sample and build an interval by this method. Because of sampling
variability, the intervals shift from sample to sample, and some capture
the true parameter while others miss it. The \textbf{confidence level}
is the long-run percentage of intervals that capture the true value. A
95\% confidence interval comes from a method that succeeds in 95\% of
such repetitions.

In practice we collect a single sample and build a single interval. That
one interval either contains the true parameter or it does not --- we
cannot know which. What we \emph{can} say is that it was produced by a
method with a known, high success rate over the long run.

\end{tcolorbox}

Two consequences of this relationship between tests and intervals are
worth highlighting, because they will reappear in both later chapters.

First, a confidence interval can stand in for a two-sided test. To test
whether a particular value (say \(p_0\) or \(\mu_0\)) is consistent with
the data at level \(\alpha\), simply check whether that value lies
inside the \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%\) confidence interval. If the value
falls \emph{outside} the interval, it would have been rejected, so we
reject \(H_0\). If it falls \emph{inside} the interval, we fail to
reject \(H_0\).

Second, the interval is generally more informative than the test alone.
A test tells us only whether a single value is or is not consistent with
the data. The interval reports the entire collection of consistent
values, and so conveys both the likely magnitude and the direction of
the effect --- not merely whether an effect is present.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Homework for
Section~\ref{sec-foundations-pvalue},
Section~\ref{sec-foundations-critical-region}, and
Section~\ref{sec-foundations-confidence-intervals}}{Homework for Section~, Section~, and Section~}}\label{sec-foundations-decision-hw}

No computations are required for these problems; they ask you to reason
with the concepts of this chapter.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  In your own words, explain what a p-value measures. Why is a
  \emph{small} p-value considered evidence \emph{against} the null
  hypothesis?
\item
  A test of \(H_0: p = 0.50\) versus \(H_a: p \neq 0.50\) produces a
  p-value of \(0.21\). Using \(\alpha = 0.05\), state the decision and
  explain what it does and does not tell us about \(H_0\).
\item
  Two researchers test the same hypotheses on the same data at the same
  significance level. One uses the p-value approach and the other uses
  the critical region approach. Explain why they must reach the same
  decision.
\item
  For the SAT example (\(H_a: \mu > 508\)), describe in which tail the
  critical region lies and explain why. Do the same for the sleep
  example (\(H_a: \mu < 7\)) and the commute-time example
  (\(H_a: \mu \neq 26.8\)).
\item
  Explain the difference between a Type I error and a Type II error in
  terms of the decision rule ``reject \(H_0\) when the p-value is at

  likely?
\item

  as \((508, 576)\). Without doing any computation, state whether a

  or fail to reject. Explain your reasoning. What about

\item

  Why is it incorrect to say that a particular 95\% confidence interval

\item
  Describe, in words and without formulas, how you could build a

\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Looking Ahead}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

This chapter has laid out the logic that every inference procedure
shares: a research question expressed as null and alternative
hypotheses, the two types of error and the strategy of controlling the
Type I error at a significance level \(\alpha\), the two equivalent
decision rules based on the p-value and the critical region, and the
construction of a confidence interval by inverting a test. None of this
reasoning depends on the parameter being studied.

What remains is to fill in the parameter-specific machinery --- the
sampling distribution of the statistic under \(H_0\), the formulas for
the p-value and the critical region, and the software steps to compute
them. The next chapter does this for a population proportion \(p\),
using the sampling distribution of the count \(X\), and the chapter
after that does the same for a population mean \(\mu\), using the
sampling distribution of the sample mean \(\bar{X}\). In each case the
computations are new, but the framework is the one you have just
learned.

\end{tcolorbox}

Proportions}\label{inference-for-population-proportions}

In the foundations chapter, we developed the \emph{logic} of statistical
inference --- null and alternative hypotheses, the two types of error,
the significance level, the p-value and critical region approaches to
making a decision, and the idea of a confidence interval --- without
performing any computations. That development and reasoning do not
depend on which parameter we study. In this chapter we put it to work
for a \textbf{population proportion} \(p,\) filling in the
parameter-specific machinery the foundations chapter deferred: the
statistics and their sampling distribution, the calculations that
produce a p-value and a critical region, and the software steps to carry
them out in Rguroo. We consider both one-population and two-population
settings for proportions.

Because the conceptual framework is already in place, this chapter
focuses on computation. We will recall each idea briefly as we use it,
with a pointer back to the foundations chapter for the full discussion,
and spend our effort on how the ideas are actually carried out for a
proportion. The same pattern will repeat in the next chapter for a
population mean: new computations, the same framework.

We begin with hypothesis testing for one population proportion.

\section{Hypothesis Testing: Concepts and
Setup}\label{sec-concept-setup}

In many real situations, we encounter numerical claims about population
proportions: the proportion of teenagers who use a particular app, the
proportion of adults who meet health guidelines, or the proportion of
students who rely on social media for news. But how can we determine
whether such claims are reasonable? When does sample evidence support a
claim, and when should we question it?

To see how we might answer such questions, we will work through examples
and develop the reasoning needed to evaluate claims and reach
conclusions. We begin by establishing the framework and notation we will
use throughout this chapter.

\subsection{Setting the Stage: A Running Example}\label{sec-stage}

Suppose we want to know what proportion of students at our university
prefer online classes. The \textbf{population} is all students at our
university. The \textbf{response variable} is \emph{class mode
preference}, a categorical variable (also called a \textbf{factor}) that
classifies each student into one of two categories: prefers online
classes or does not prefer online classes. We define ``prefers online
classes'' as a \textbf{success} and the other category as a
\textbf{failure}.

In statistics, the terms success and failure do not imply that one
outcome is good and the other is bad. A success simply refers to the
outcome we are interested in studying, while a failure refers to the
other outcome. For example, if we are studying the proportion of
manufactured parts that are defective, we might define a defective part
as a success. Similarly, if we are studying the proportion of patients
who experience a side effect from a medication, experiencing the side
effect could be defined as a success. In both cases, ``success''
identifies the outcome of interest, not a desirable outcome.

The parameter of interest is the \textbf{population proportion}, denoted
by \(p\)---the fraction of all students at our university who prefer
online classes. Since we cannot survey every student, we collect data
from a random \textbf{sample} and use it to learn about \(p.\)

This example illustrates the key elements of proportion inference:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  A population with a characteristic we want to measure
\item
  A categorical response variable with two outcomes (success/failure)
\item
  A parameter \(p\) representing the true population proportion of
  successes
\item
  A sample from which we compute a \textbf{statistic} to estimate \(p\)
\end{itemize}

Let's develop this framework more formally.

\subsection{From Samples to Statistics}\label{sec-samples-to-stats}

When we collect a sample of size \(n,\) we count how many individuals
have a success outcome. Before the sample is collected, this count is
unknown, so we treat it as a \textbf{random variable} and denote it by
\(X.\) The corresponding \textbf{sample proportion} is also a random
variable, given by \(\hat{p}=X/n\) (read ``p-hat'').

After the data are collected, we observe the count of successes in our
sample, which we denote by \(x_{\text{obs}}\) (read ``x-observed''). The
corresponding \textbf{observed sample proportion} is
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}=\frac{x_{\text{obs}}}{n}\) (read
``p-hat-observed'') which provides an estimate of the population
proportion \(p.\)

In our example of students who prefer online classes, suppose we
randomly select \(n = 100\) students. Before we collect the sample,
\(X\) represents the number of students who will say they prefer online
classes in a random sample of \(n=100\) students. The value of \(X\)
could be anywhere from 0 to 100. Correspondingly, \(\hat{p}\) represents
the proportion of students in the sample who say that they prefer online
classes. After we survey the students, suppose 62 say they prefer online
classes. Then, the observed count is \(x_{\text{obs}} = 62\) and the
observed proportion is \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 62/100 = 0.62\) or 62\%.
.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\(X\) is a random variable representing the number of successes across
all possible samples; \(x_{\text{obs}}\) is the specific count from our
actual sample. Similarly, \(\hat{p}=X/n\) is a random variable
representing the sample proportion across all possible samples, while
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}=x_{\text{obs}}/n\) is the observed sample
proportion from our actual sample. We use \(x_{\text{obs}},\) or
equivalently \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}},\) to make decisions about \(p.\)

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Notation Summary}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

As we work through the examples in this chapter, it may be helpful to
keep the following symbols and their meanings in mind.

\begin{example}[Daily YouTube Use Among
Teens]\protect\hypertarget{exm-youtube-ppss}{}\label{exm-youtube-ppss}

According to a
\href{https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2023/12/11/teens-social-media-and-technology-2023/}{Pew
Research Center report}, about 71\% of U.S. teenagers say they visit
YouTube every day (Pew Research Center, \emph{Teens, Social Media and
Technology}, 2023).

Suppose a school district claims that more than 70\% of students in its
district use YouTube daily. To examine this claim, a random sample of
\(n=20\) students is selected, and 17 of them report that they use
YouTube daily.

Describe or compute the following related to the claim:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The response variable and its possible categories
\item
  The success category of the response variable
\item
  The population of interest\\
\item
  The parameter of interest \(p\)
\item
  The sample
\item
  The statistic \(X\) and its observed value \(x_{\text{obs}}\)
\item
  The observed sample proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) that is an
  estimate of \(p\)
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\item
  The response variable is \emph{Daily Use of YouTube} with two possible
  response categories ``Yes'' and ``No''.
\item
  The success category is ``Yes'', that is if the student uses YouTube
  daily.
\item
  The population of interest is all students in the district.
\item
  The parameter of interest \(p\) is the proportion of students in the
  district who use YouTube daily.
\item
  The sample is the 20 students who were randomly selected and
  questioned about their YouTube use.
\item
  The statistic \(X\) is the number of students in a sample of size
  \(n = 20\) who use YouTube daily. From our sample, the observed value
  is \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17.\)
\item
  The observed sample proportion (an estimate of \(p\)) is
\end{enumerate}

\[\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = \frac{x_{\text{obs}}}{n}=\frac{17}{20} = 0.85.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Physical Inactivity Among
Adults]\protect\hypertarget{exm-physical-inactivity-ppss}{}\label{exm-physical-inactivity-ppss}

The
\href{https://www.who.int/news/item/26-06-2024-nearly-1.8-billion-adults-at-risk-of-disease-from-not-doing-enough-physical-activity}{World
Health Organization reports} that approximately 31\% of adults worldwide
do not meet recommended levels of physical activity (World Health
Organization, 2024).

Suppose a national health agency hopes that fewer than 35\% of adults in
its country are physically inactive. To examine this claim, a random
sample of \(n=50\) adults is selected, and 10 of them are found to be
physically inactive.

Describe, and when relevant compute, the following related to the claim:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The response variable and its possible categories
\item
  The success category of the response variable
\item
  The population of interest\\
\item
  The parameter of interest \(p\)
\item
  The sample
\item
  The statistic \(X\) and its observed value \(x_{\text{obs}}\)
\item
  The observed sample proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) that is an
  estimate of \(p\)
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\item
  The variable of interest is \emph{Physical Activity}, with possible
  categories of ``Inactive'' and ``Active''.
\item
  The success category is ``Inactive'', since we want to make inference
  about those who are physically inactive.
\item
  The population of interest is all adults in the country.
\item
  The parameter of interest \(p\) is the proportion of adults in the
  country who are physically inactive.
\item
  The sample is the 50 adults who were randomly selected and their
  physical activity levels were recorded.
\item
  The statistic \(X\) is the number of individuals in a sample of size
  \(n=50\) who are inactive, and its observed value is
  \(x_{\text{obs}} = 10.\)
\item
  The observed sample proportion (an estimate of \(p\)) is
\end{enumerate}

\[\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = \frac{x_{\text{obs}}}{n}=\frac{10}{50} = 0.20.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Social Media as a Primary News
Source]\protect\hypertarget{exm-social-media-news-ppss}{}\label{exm-social-media-news-ppss}

According to a
\href{https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/fact-sheet/social-media-and-news-fact-sheet/}{Pew
Research Center report}, 36\% of U.S. adults ages 18--29 say they
regularly get news from social media (Shearer, 2023).

Suppose the university administration is unsure whether the same
percentage applies to students at their university and wants to
determine whether the true proportion of students who get most of their
news from social media differs from 36\%.

To investigate this question, a random sample of \(n=15\) students is
selected, and 9 of them report that they get most of their news from
social media.

Describe, and when relevant compute, the following related to the claim:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The response variable and its possible categories
\item
  The success category of the response variable
\item
  The population of interest\\
\item
  The parameter of interest \(p\)
\item
  The sample
\item
  The statistic \(X\) and its observed value \(x_{\text{obs}}\)
\item
  The observed sample proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) that is an
  estimate of \(p\)
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\item
  The response variable is regarding how students get their news, We
  call the variable ``\emph{Use Social Media}'', and the possible
  categories are ``Yes'', and ``No''.
\item
  The success category is ``Yes''.
\item
  The population of interest is all students at the university.
\item
  The parameter of interest \(p\) is the proportion of students at the
  university who get most of their news from social media.
\item
  The sample is the 15 students who were randomly selected and surveyed
  about their primary news source.
\item
  The statistic \(X\) is the number of students in a sample of size
  \(n=15\) who get most of their news from social media, and its
  observed value is \(x_{\text{obs}} = 9.\)
\item
  The observed sample proportion (an estimate of \(p\)) is
\end{enumerate}

\[\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = \frac{x_{\text{obs}}}{n}=\frac{9}{15} = 0.60.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

To use sample evidence to evaluate a claim about a population
proportion, we first need to state clearly the claims we are
considering. Because our decision is based on a sample rather than the
entire population, there is always a possibility of reaching the wrong
conclusion. As we saw in Chapter 8, we might reject a claim that is
actually true, or we might fail to reject a claim that is actually
false. These two possibilities correspond to Type I and Type II errors,
which we will now consider in the context of inference for a population
proportion.

\subsection{Null and Alternative Hypotheses and Errors for a
Proportion}\label{sec-null-alternative}

The foundations chapter (Section~\ref{sec-foundations-hypotheses})
developed the null and alternative hypotheses, the three forms they
take, and the two types of error in full. Here, we briefly review the
notation for hypothesis tests involving a population proportion and then
apply these ideas to our examples.

For a population proportion, the \textbf{alternative hypothesis} \(H_a\)
is the claim we seek evidence for, and the \textbf{null hypothesis}
\(H_0\) is its complement, the value or range we assume true unless the
data force us to abandon it. Both are statements about the population
proportion \(p,\) not about the sample, so they are written using \(p\)
and not \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}.\) Writing \(p_0\) for the
\textbf{boundary value} that separates the null from the alternative,
the three forms are:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Case 1: } 
&\begin{cases} H_0: p \leq p_0 \\ H_a: p > p_0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\text{Case 2: } 
&\begin{cases} H_0: p \geq p_0 \\ H_a: p < p_0 \end{cases}
\\[1em]
\text{Case 3: } 
&\begin{cases} H_0: p = p_0 \\ H_a: p \neq p_0 \end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\] Cases 1 and 2 are \textbf{one-sided} and Case 3 is
\textbf{two-sided}, exactly as in
Section~\ref{sec-foundations-three-forms}.

Recall too the two ways a test can be wrong: a \textbf{Type I error}
rejects \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is in fact true, and a \textbf{Type II
error} fails to reject \(H_0\) when \(H_a\) is in fact true (see
Section~\ref{sec-foundations-errors}). The following examples write the
hypotheses and interpret both errors for our three proportion scenarios.

\begin{example}[Daily YouTube Use Among Teens
(continued)]\protect\hypertarget{exm-youtube-error}{}\label{exm-youtube-error}

Recall Example~\ref{exm-youtube-ppss} where a school district was
interested to test the claim that more than 70\% of students in its
district use YouTube daily.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  State the null and alternative hypotheses in words.
\item
  Write the null and alternative hypotheses using mathematical notation.
\item
  Describe what happens if a Type I error occurs in the context of the
  problem.
\item
  Describe what happens if a Type II error occurs in the context of the
  problem.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\item
  The null hypothesis states that 70\% or fewer students in the district
  use YouTube daily. The alternative hypothesis states that more than
  70\% of students in the district use YouTube daily.
\item
  \[
  \begin{cases}
  H_0: p \leq 0.70 \\
  H_a: p > 0.70
  \end{cases}
  \]
\item
  A Type I error occurs if we reject \(H_0\) and conclude that more than
  70\% of students in the district use YouTube daily when, in fact, the
  true proportion is 70\% or less (\(H_0\) is true).
\item
  A Type II error occurs if we fail to reject \(H_0\) and therefore do
  not conclude that more than 70\% of students in the district use
  YouTube daily when, in fact, the true proportion is greater than 70\%
  (\(H_a\) is true).
\end{enumerate}

\end{tcolorbox}
