\section{Making a Decision about a Population
Proportion}\label{making-a-decision-about-a-population-proportion}

For a two-sided test, an observed sample proportion either above or
below the null value can provide evidence against \(H_0.\) For example,
in the social media example with \(H_0: p = 0.36\) versus
\(H_a: p \neq 0.36,\) a sample proportion that differs from \(0.36\) in
either direction could provide evidence in favor of \(H_a.\) However,
simply observing that \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) differs from \(0.36\) is
not enough to reject \(H_0.\) Some difference is expected because of
random sampling variation. We need to perform a hypothesis test to
determine whether the observed difference is large enough to provide
sufficient evidence against \(H_0.\)

For a one-sided test, there is an additional consideration: the observed
sample proportion must first be in the direction specified by \(H_a\) to
provide evidence against \(H_0.\) For instance, in
Example~\ref{exm-youtube-ppss}, the Daily YouTube Use Among Teens
example, the hypotheses are \(H_0: p \leq 0.70\) versus
\(H_a: p > 0.70.\) If a sample of \(n = 20\) students resulted in only
\(x_{\text{obs}} = 12\) students reporting daily use, then
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = \frac{12}{20} = 0.60.\) Since \(0.60\) falls
within the values specified by \(H_0\) rather than in the direction of
\(H_a,\) this sample result clearly does not provide evidence against
\(H_0\) in favor of \(H_a.\)

On the other hand, if \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) were greater than
\(0.70,\) being in the direction of \(H_a\) would not by itself be
enough to reject \(H_0.\) We would still need to perform the hypothesis
test to determine whether the observed result is sufficiently far from
the null value to be unlikely to occur by random chance, assuming
\(H_0\) is true.

Now consider sample results that point in the direction of \(H_a.\) For
the YouTube example (\(H_a: p > 0.70\)), \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\) out of
\(n = 20\) gives \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.85,\) which is greater than
\(0.70.\) For the physical inactivity example (\(H_a: p < 0.35\)),
\(x_{\text{obs}} = 10\) out of \(n = 50\) gives
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.20,\) which is less than \(0.35.\) For the
social media example (\(H_a: p \neq 0.36\)), \(x_{\text{obs}} = 9\) out
of \(n = 15\) gives \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.60,\) which is noticeably
different from \(0.36.\) Each of these results points in the direction
of \(H_a.\) But is that enough to reject \(H_0\)?

Not necessarily!

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Consistency With \(H_a\) Is Not the Same as Strong Evidence in Favor of
\(H_a\)}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

A sample result that points in the direction of \(H_a\) does not by
itself constitute strong evidence in favor of \(H_a.\) Because of
sampling variability, such a result can occur by chance even when
\(H_0\) is true. The key question is whether the sample result would be
\textbf{unlikely to occur by chance} if \(H_0\) were true. If so, we
have strong evidence against \(H_0\) and in favor of \(H_a.\)

\end{tcolorbox}

We now turn to actually carrying out a hypothesis test for a proportion.
Recall from Section~\ref{sec-foundations-tradeoff} that, because
reducing one type of error tends to increase the other, we control the
probability of a Type I error by holding it to a small, prespecified
\textbf{significance level} \(\alpha.\) Recall also that there are two
equivalent ways to reach a decision: the \textbf{p-value approach} and
the \textbf{critical region approach}. These approaches always lead to
the same decision.

There are two methods we will use to carry out a hypothesis test for one
population proportion: a \textbf{large-sample approach} based on the
normal distribution and an \textbf{exact approach} based on the binomial
distribution. We begin with the large-sample approach in
Section~\ref{sec-large-sample-one-prop}, which relies on the central
limit theorem and requires a sufficiently large sample for the normal
approximation to work well. We then consider the exact binomial approach
in Section~\ref{sec-making-decision-binomial}, which uses the binomial
distribution directly and does not require a large sample.

It is important to distinguish these two methods from the p-value and
critical region approaches. The large-sample and exact binomial methods
determine how we calculate the probabilities for the test. The p-value
and critical region approaches determine how we use those probabilities
to make a decision about \(H_0.\)

The exact binomial method is an ideal choice when we want to avoid
relying on a large-sample approximation because it uses the binomial
distribution directly to calculate exact probabilities. It does not
require a large sample for the normal approximation to be valid.
Nevertheless, there are good reasons to begin with the large-sample
approach. Most importantly, the basic ideas generalize naturally to
other inference problems, such as comparing two population proportions
and drawing inferences about population means. In addition, large-sample
methods have historically been widely used, so you will frequently
encounter them in published research. Finally, because the large-sample
approach builds on the familiar normal distribution, it provides an
accessible starting point for learning how hypothesis tests are carried
out.

\section{Large Sample Hypothesis
Testing}\label{sec-large-sample-one-prop}

The large sample approach rests on the \textbf{Central Limit Theorem
(CLT)}, which you have already seen in Chapter 7. Recall that the CLT
tells us that, for a sufficiently large sample, the sampling
distribution of a sample mean is approximately normal, even when the
population distribution itself is not normal. At first, this may seem
unrelated to proportions: the CLT concerns sample means, while our
interest here is in a sample proportion. However, as we will see next, a
sample proportion can itself be viewed as a sample mean. This connection
allows us to apply the CLT directly to sample proportions and provides
the foundation for the large-sample approach.

\subsection{A Sample Proportion Is a Mean}\label{sec-prop-is-mean}

Suppose we record whether each individual in our sample has the
characteristic of interest by assigning a value of 1 to each success and
a value of 0 to each failure. For example, in the YouTube study
(Example~\ref{exm-youtube-ppss}), a student who uses YouTube daily
receives a 1, and a student who does not receives a 0. If our sample of
\(n = 20\) students produced 17 daily users, the data would consist of
17 ones and 3 zeros. The sum of these 20 values is 17, and their average
is

\[
\frac{17}{20} = 0.85,
\]

which is exactly the observed sample proportion,
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}.\)

More generally, if a sample of size \(n\) produces some number of
successes, then

\[
\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = \frac{\text{number of successes}}{n} = \frac{\text{sum of the 0/1 values}}{n}.
\]

Thus, when successes and failures are coded as 1 and 0, the observed
sample proportion is simply the \textbf{mean of the zeros and ones} in
the sample.

The same idea applies to any random sample of size \(n.\) For each
possible sample, the sample proportion \(\hat{p}\) is the mean of its
0/1 values. Thus, a sample proportion is a special case of a sample
mean: it is the mean of observations that can take only the values 0 and
1.

This connection allows us to apply the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) to
sample proportions. Recall that the CLT tells us that, for a
sufficiently large sample size, the sampling distribution of a sample
mean is approximately normal. Since a sample proportion is a sample mean
based on 0/1 observations, its sampling distribution is also
approximately normal for a sufficiently large sample.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Applying the Central Limit Theorem to
\(\hat p\)}{Applying the Central Limit Theorem to \textbackslash hat p}}\label{applying-the-central-limit-theorem-to-hat-p}

Since \(\hat{p}\) is a sample mean of 0s and 1s, its sampling
distribution follows the same general pattern as other sample means. For
a population with proportion of successes \(p,\) the sampling
distribution of \(\hat{p}\) has:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Mean: \(\mu_{\hat{p}}=p\)
\item
  Standard deviation: \(\sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}}\)
\end{itemize}

This standard deviation is often called the \textbf{standard error} of
\(\hat{p}.\) It measures how much we expect \(\hat{p}\) to vary from
sample to sample. By the CLT, when \(n\) is sufficiently large,
\(\hat{p}\) follows approximately a normal distribution:

\[
\hat{p} \sim N\!\left(p,\; \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\right).
\]

Since \(p\) is unknown, we need to specify a value for it to use this
result for inference. Recall that in hypothesis testing we assume the
null hypothesis is true, and that the maximum Type I error occurs at the
boundary value \(p_0\) of \(H_0\) (see
Section~\ref{sec-foundations-boundary}). We therefore evaluate the
sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\) at \(p = p_0,\) giving:

\[
\hat{p} \sim N\!\left(p_0,\; \sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}\right).
\]

We call this the \textbf{null distribution} of \(\hat{p},\) since it
describes the behavior of \(\hat{p}\) at the boundary value \(p_0\) of
the null hypothesis \(H_0,\) where the Type I error is at its maximum.
This normal null distribution of \(\hat{p}\) is the foundation for
decisions in hypothesis testing in the large sample method.

An option is to use a standardized statistic called the \(z\)-score,
obtained by subtracting \(p_0\) from \(\hat{p}\) and dividing by the
standard error:

\[
z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{\dfrac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}}.
\]

This unit-less quantity is then compared to a standard normal
distribution. In this textbook, we instead work directly with
\(\hat{p}\) and compare it to its null distribution. This requires fewer
computational steps and, more importantly, keeps our decisions on the
original scale --- conclusions are about a sample proportion rather than
an abstract standardized value.

\subsection{What is Considered a Large Sample
Size?}\label{what-is-considered-a-large-sample-size}

What constitutes a large sample size for the normal approximation to
hold? A common rule of thumb is to check the expected numbers of
successes and failures. In particular, the approximation is typically
considered reliable when \(np_0 \geq 10\) and \(n(1 - p_0) \geq 10.\)
When both of these conditions are satisfied, the binomial distribution
tends to be reasonably symmetric, and the normal model provides a good
fit.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Large Sample Condition: The 10-10 Rule}\vspace{3mm}

The normal approximation for \(\hat{p}\) is considered reliable when
both of the following hold:

\[np_0 \geq 10 \qquad \text{and} \qquad n(1-p_0) \geq 10.\]

These conditions ensure that the sample is large enough for the CLT to
provide a good approximation. If either condition fails, the exact
binomial method (see Section~\ref{sec-pvalue} and
Section~\ref{sec-critical-region}) is the appropriate choice.

\end{tcolorbox}

To illustrate the 10--10 rule, consider the YouTube Daily Use example,
where \(n=20\) and \(p_0=0.70\):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Expected successes: \(np_0 = 20\times 0.70 = 14\)
\item
  Expected failures: \(n(1-p_0) = 20\times 0.30 = 6\)
\end{itemize}

Since the expected number of failures is less than 10, the 10--10 rule
is not satisfied. Therefore, the normal approximation may not be
reliable for this example.

In contrast, for the Physical Inactivity example, where \(n=50\) and
\(p_0=0.35\):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Expected successes: \(np_0 = 50\times 0.35 = 17.5\)
\item
  Expected failures: \(n(1-p_0) = 50\times 0.65 = 32.5\)
\end{itemize}

Since both values exceed 10, the 10--10 rule is satisfied. Therefore,
the normal approximation is appropriate for the Physical Inactivity
example.

\subsection{Decision Based on a p-value}\label{sec-large-sample-pvalue}

We explained the idea behind the p-value approach in
Section~\ref{sec-foundations-pvalue}. In this section we show how
p-values are computed using the \textbf{large sample} method for a
population proportion.

To compute a p-value, we first need to identify which possible sample
results provide at least as much support for \(H_a\) as the result we
actually observed. For this purpose, we define what we call the \(H_a\)
support.

The \textbf{\(H_a\) support} is the set of all possible values of the
sample proportion \(\hat{p}\) that are \textbf{at least as favorable} to
\(H_a\) as the observed sample proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}.\)

For one-sided tests, this is straightforward: as shown in
Figure~\ref{fig-onetailed-pvalue}, if \(H_a: p > p_0,\) larger values of
\(\hat{p}\) are more favorable to \(H_a,\) so the \(H_a\) support
consists of \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) and all values above it.
Symmetrically, for \(H_a: p < p_0,\) the \(H_a\) support consists of
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) and all values below it.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth,height=\textheight]{index_files/mediabag/Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/onetailed_pvalue.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-onetailed-pvalue}One-tailed p-value regions. Top:
right-tailed test, p-value is the area where p-hat is greater than or
equal to the observed value. Bottom: left-tailed test, p-value is the
area where p-hat is less than or equal to the observed value}

\end{figure}%

For the two-sided test \(H_a: p \neq p_0,\) the \(H_a\) support consists
of values in both tails of the null distribution that are at least the
same distance \(d\) from \(p_0\) as \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) (see
Figure~\ref{fig-ha-support}). Because the normal null distribution is
symmetric about \(p_0,\) these values are symmetrically positioned about
\(p_0\) . If \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} > p_0,\) the \(H_a\) support is the
set of values \(\hat{p} \geq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) together with their
mirror image relative to \(p_0\) in the left tail. If
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} < p_0,\) the \(H_a\) support is the set of values
\(\hat{p} \leq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) together with their mirror image
relative to \(p_0\) in the right tail.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth,height=\textheight]{index_files/mediabag/Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/ha_support_number_line.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-ha-support}The \(H_a\) support for a two-sided test.
The shaded segments show the values of \(\hat{p}\) that are as favorable
or more favorable to \(H_a\) than \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}.\) The dashed
tick marks the mirror image of \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) relative to
\(p_0,\) each being a distance \(d\) from \(p_0.\)}

\end{figure}%

Once the \(H_a\) support has been identified, the p-value is the
probability, assuming \(H_0\) is true, that \(\hat{p}\) falls in the
\(H_a\) support. For the large-sample method, we compute this
probability using the normal null distribution at the boundary value
\(p=p_0.\) Thus, \[
\text{p-value} = P(\hat{p} \text{ is in the } H_a \text{ support}), \text{ assuming that } p=p_0.
\] Recall from Section~\ref{sec-foundations-boundary} why we use the
boundary value \(p=p_0.\) A more detailed explanation is provided in the
optional Section~\ref{sec-closer-look-cr-pvalue}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{p-value for the Large Sample Test}\vspace{3mm}

All probabilities are computed using the null distribution
\(\hat{p} \sim N\!\left(p_0,\, \sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}\right).\)

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Alternative Hypothesis
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\(H_a\) Support
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
p-value
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(H_a: p > p_0\) & \(\hat{p} \geq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) &
\(P(\hat{p} \geq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}})\) \\
\(H_a: p < p_0\) & \(\hat{p} \leq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) &
\(P(\hat{p} \leq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}})\) \\
\(H_a: p \neq p_0,\) if \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} > p_0\) &
\(\hat{p} \geq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) and its mirror relative to \(p_0\)
& \(2 \times P(\hat{p} \geq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}})\) \\
\(H_a: p \neq p_0,\) if \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} < p_0\) &
\(\hat{p} \leq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) and its mirror relative to \(p_0\)
& \(2 \times P(\hat{p} \leq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}})\) \\
\end{longtable}

\end{tcolorbox}

As explained in Section~\ref{sec-foundations-pvalue}, we compare the
p-value to the significance level \(\alpha\) to make our decision: \[
\text{If p-value} \leq \alpha, \text{ reject } H_0. \qquad \text{If p-value} > \alpha, \text{ fail to reject } H_0.
\] Recall that a small p-value means that \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) and
values at least as supportive of \(H_a\) would be unlikely to occur if
\(H_0\) were true. Thus, a small p-value provides evidence against
\(H_0\) and in favor of \(H_a.\)

The p-value approach also indicates the strength of the evidence: a very
small p-value indicates strong evidence against \(H_0,\) while a p-value
just below \(\alpha\) indicates weaker evidence.

\begin{example}[Physical Inactivity Among Adults - p-value
Approach]\protect\hypertarget{exm-inactivity-large-sample}{}\label{exm-inactivity-large-sample}

Recall Example~\ref{exm-physical-inactivity-ppss}. A national health
agency hopes that fewer than 35\% of adults in its country are
physically inactive. A random sample of \(n = 50\) adults was selected
and \(x_{\text{obs}} = 10\) were found to be physically inactive. The
hypotheses are: \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p \geq 0.35 \\
H_a: p < 0.35
\end{cases}
\]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Check the 10-10 rule to see whether the conditions for the normal
  approximation hold.
\item
  Determine the \(H_a\) support.
\item
  Write a probability statement that describes the p-value.
\item
  Use Rguroo's \Fun{Proportion Inference} function to obtain the
  p-value, and state your conclusion in the context of the problem using
  significance level of \(\alpha=0.05.\)
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. To check the large sample condition, we compute the expected number
of successes and failures under \(H_0.\) Using the boundary value
\(p_0 = 0.35\):

\[np_0 = 50 \times 0.35 = 17.5 \geq 10\]

\[n(1 - p_0) = 50 \times 0.65 = 32.5 \geq 10.\]

Both conditions are satisfied, so the large sample normal approximation
is appropriate for this example.

b. We have \(x_{\text{obs}}=10\) and \(n=50,\) which gives \[
\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}=\frac{10}{50}=0.20.
\] Since the alternative hypothesis is \(H_a: p<0.35,\) smaller values
of \(\hat{p}\) provide stronger evidence in favor of \(H_a.\) Therefore,
the \(H_a\) support consists of all sample proportions less than or
equal to the observed value:

\[
\textbf{H}_a\ \textbf{Support:}\;\; \hat{p} \le 0.20.
\]

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth,height=\textheight]{index_files/mediabag/Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/ha_support_number_line_onesided_left.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-ha-support-onesided-left}One-sided \(H_a\) support
for \(p_0=0.35\) and \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.20.\)}

\end{figure}%

c. The p-value is computed as \[
\text{p-value} = P\left(\hat{p} \le 0.2),\; \text{ assuming }  p=0.35\right.
\]

\begin{example}[Social Media as a Primary News Source - p-value
Approach]\protect\hypertarget{exm-social-media-pvalue-large-sample}{}\label{exm-social-media-pvalue-large-sample}

Recall Example~\ref{exm-social-media-news-ppss}, where a Pew Research
Center report stated that 36\% of U.S. adults ages 18--29 say they
regularly get news from social media. A university administration was
unsure whether the same percentage applied to students at their
university. Thus, they set out to test the hypotheses \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p = 0.36 \\
H_a: p \neq 0.36.
\end{cases}
\] To investigate this claim, the university initially took a sample of
\(n=15\) students. However, they realized that this sample was too small
to apply the large-sample test. So, they increased their sample to
\(n=35\) students. In their sample of \(n=35\) students, they found that
21 students stated that they regularly get news from social media.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Check the 10-10 rule to determine whether the conditions for the
  normal approximation hold.
\item
  Determine the \(H_a\) support.
\item
  Write a probability statement that describes the p-value.
\item
  Use Rguroo's \Fun{Proportion Inference} function to obtain the
  p-value, and state your conclusion in the context of the problem using
  significance level of \(\alpha=0.01.\)
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. To check the large sample condition, we compute the expected number
of successes and expected number of failures under \(H_0.\) Using the
boundary value \(p_0 = 0.36\):

\[np_0 = 35 \times 0.36 = 12.6 \geq 10\]

\[n(1 - p_0) = 35 \times 0.64 = 22.4 \geq 10.\]

Both conditions are satisfied, so the large sample normal approximation
is appropriate for this example.

b. We have \(x_{\text{obs}}=21\) and \(n=35,\) which gives \[
\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}=\frac{21}{35}=0.60.
\] Since this is a two-sided alternative, values of \(\hat{p}\) far from
\(p_0\) in \emph{either} direction count as evidence against \(H_0.\)
The observed proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}=0.60\) lies
\(0.60-0.36=0.24\) above \(p_0,\) so a value equally far \emph{below}
\(p_0\) --- namely \(0.36-0.24=0.12\) --- provides just as much evidence
against \(H_0.\) Since \(p_0=0.36,\) and \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}=0.60,\)
the \(H_a\) support is given by

\[
\textbf{H}_a\ \textbf{Support:}\;\; \hat{p} \geq 0.60 \text{ or } \hat{p} \leq 0.12.\]

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth,height=\textheight]{index_files/mediabag/Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/ha_support_number_line_example.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-ha-support-example}Two-sided \(H_a\) support for
\(p_0=0.36\) and \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.60.\)}

\end{figure}%

c. The p-value is computed as \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{p-value}
&= P\left(\hat{p} \le 0.12\right) + P\left(\hat{p} \ge 0.60\right) \\
&= 2\times P\left(\hat{p} \ge 0.60\right), \qquad \text{assuming } p=0.36.
\end{aligned}\] The last equalty holds, since the normal distribution is
symmetric about \(p_0=0.36,\)

d. Click to expand the box below to see how to use the
\Fun{Proportion Inference} function to obtain the p-value.

\textbf{Using Raw Data}

So far, we have performed proportion inference using a summary of the
sample, namely the sample size \(n\) and the observed count
\(x_{\text{obs}}.\) In practice, however, we often work directly with a
raw dataset rather than a pre-computed summary. Now, we show how to
perform proportion inference from raw data using Rguroo.

We illustrate this using data from the General Social Survey (GSS), one
of the longest-running and most widely used surveys in the United
States. Conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago, the GSS has
collected data on the attitudes, behaviors, and characteristics of
American adults since 1972, covering topics such as social values,
political views, religion, and lifestyle. The dataset that we use here,
\Data{GSS2024}, is a subset of the 2024 GSS data. After removing
observations with missing values, the dataset contains \(n = 388\)
respondents.

\begin{example}[Marijuana Legalization: p-Value Approach Using Raw
Data]\protect\hypertarget{exm-gss-marijuana-pvalue}{}\label{exm-gss-marijuana-pvalue}

The \Data{GSS2024} dataset contains responses from \(n = 388\) adults in
the United States. The variable \Var{Grass} records whether each
respondent supports the legalization of marijuana, with possible
responses of \emph{Yes} (supports legalization) or \emph{No} (does not
support legalization). A researcher claims that more than 70\% of
American adults support the legalization of marijuana.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Write the null and alternative hypotheses.
\item
  Check the 10-10 rule to determine whether the conditions for the
  normal approximation hold.
\item
  Determine the \(H_a\) support.
\item
  Write a probability statement that describes the p-value.
\item
  Use Rguroo's \Fun{Proportion Inference} function to obtain the
  p-value, and state your conclusion in the context of the problem using
  significance level of \(\alpha=0.05.\)
\end{enumerate}

Dataset Name: \Data{GSS2024}

This dataset is a subset of the 2024 General Social Survey (GSS) data,
obtained from NORC at the University of Chicago. After removing
observations with missing values, the dataset contains \(n = 388\)
individuals.

The variables included in this dataset are described below.

\Var{Age}: Age of the respondent (in years).

\Var{Sex}: Sex of the respondent

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Male\\
\item
  Female
\end{itemize}

\Var{Degree}: Highest degree earned by the respondent.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  No HS (Less than high school)
\item
  HS (High school)\\
\item
  JC (Junior college)
\item
  Bachelor (Bachelor's degree)
\item
  Graduate (Graduate degree)
\end{itemize}

\Var{Race}: Race of the respondent

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  White\\
\item
  Black\\
\item
  Other
\end{itemize}

\Var{Grass}: Respondent's opinion on whether marijuana should be made
legal

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Yes (supports legalization)\\
\item
  No (does not support legalization)
\end{itemize}

\Var{Life}: Respondent's general satisfaction with life

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Very satisfied\\
\item
  Pretty satisfied\\
\item
  Not too satisfied
\end{itemize}

\Var{Tax}: Respondent's opinion on whether taxes are too high

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  High (Too high)
\item
  OK (About right)
\item
  Low (Too low)
\end{itemize}

\Var{Mode}: Mode of data collection

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  In-person\\
\item
  Phone\\
\item
  Web
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Source}

Smith, T. W., Davern, M., Freese, J., \& Morgan, S. L. \emph{General
Social Survey, 1972--2024}. NORC at the University of Chicago.
\url{https://gss.norc.org}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. The null and alternative hypotheses are \(H_0: p \leq 0.70.\) and
\(H_a: p > 0.70.\)

b. To check the large sample condition, we compute the expected number
of successes and expected number of failures under \(H_0.\) Using the
boundary value \(p_0 = 0.70\):

\[np_0 = 388 \times 0.70 = 271.6 \geq 10\]

\[n(1 - p_0) = 388 \times 0.30 = 116.4 \geq 10.\]

Both conditions are satisfied, so the normal approximation is
appropriate for this example.

c. From the Rguroo output, we have \(x_{\text{obs}}=282\) and \(n=388,\)
which gives \[
\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}=\frac{282}{388}\approx 0.727.
\] Since the alternative hypothesis is \(H_a: p>0.70,\) larger values of
\(\hat{p}\) provide stronger evidence in favor of \(H_a.\) Therefore,
the \(H_a\) support consists of all sample proportions greater than or
equal to the observed value: \[
\textbf{H}_a\ \textbf{Support:}\;\; \hat{p} \ge 0.727.
\]

d. The p-value is computed as \[
\text{p-value} = P\left(\hat{p} \ge 0.727\right), \text{assuming } p=0.70.
\]

\centering{

}

\caption{\label{fig-ha-support-onesided-right}One-sided \(H_a\) support
for \(p_0=0.70\) and \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \approx 0.727.\)}

\end{figure}%

\Fun{Proportion Inference} function to obtain the p-value.

\subsection{Decision Based on a Critical
Region}\label{sec-large-sample-cr}

We now turn to the \textbf{critical region approach}, the other standard
way to reach a decision. Recall from
Section~\ref{sec-foundations-critical-region} that the critical region
is the set of values of the statistic for which we reject \(H_0\) in
favor of \(H_a.\) Whereas the p-value approach summarizes the evidence
with a probability computed from the observed proportion
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}},\) the critical region approach decides \emph{in
advance} which values of \(\hat{p}\) are extreme enough to reject
\(H_0,\) and then simply checks whether \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) falls
in the critical region.

The decision is governed by a decision rule: a rule that specifies which
values of \(\hat{p}\) lead to rejecting \(H_0.\) For a one-sided test
with \(H_a: p > p_0,\) large values of \(\hat{p}\) favor the alternative
hypothesis, so the critical region lies in the right tail of the null
distribution. To determine the critical region, we use the distribution
of \(\hat{p}\) under the null hypothesis \(p=p_0,\) namely \[
\hat{p}\sim N\left(p_0, \sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}\right).
\] We choose the critical value so that the probability of falling in
the critical region when \(H_0\) is true equals the significance level
\(\alpha.\) The shape of the critical region --- right tail, left tail,
or both --- depends on the alternative hypothesis, as shown in
Figure~\ref{fig-critical-regions}.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.95\textwidth,height=\textheight]{index_files/mediabag/Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/critical_regions_row.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-critical-regions}Critical regions for right-tailed,
left-tailed, and two-tailed tests on the null distribution of
\(\hat{p}.\)}

\end{figure}%

For the right-tailed test, we find the critical value \(c\) so that
there is probability \(\alpha\) in the right tail: \[
P(\hat{p} \geq c)=\alpha.
\] We then reject \(H_0\) if the observed sample proportion satisfies
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \geq c.\)

Similarly, for a one-sided test with \(H_a: p < p_0,\) small values of
\(\hat{p}\) favor the alternative hypothesis, so the critical region
lies in the left tail. We find \(c\) such that \[
P(\hat{p} \leq c)=\alpha,
\] and reject \(H_0\) if \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \leq c.\)

For a two-sided test with \(H_a: p \neq p_0,\) both unusually small and
unusually large values of \(\hat{p}\) favor the alternative hypothesis.
The critical region therefore lies in both tails. We find lower and
upper critical values, \(c_1\) and \(c_2,\) that leave probability
\(\alpha/2\) in each tail: \[
P\left(\hat{p} \leq c_1 \right)=\frac{\alpha}{2}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
P\left(\hat{p} \geq c_2 \right)=\frac{\alpha}{2}.
\] We reject \(H_0\) if \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \leq c_1\) or
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \geq c_2.\)

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Critical Region for the Large Sample Test}\vspace{3mm}

All critical values are found using the null distribution
\(\hat{p} \sim N\!\left(p_0,\, \sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}\right).\)

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Alternative Hypothesis
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Critical Region
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Critical Value Condition
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(H_a: p > p_0\) & \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \geq c\) &
\(P(\hat{p} \geq c) = \alpha\) \\
\(H_a: p < p_0\) & \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \leq c\) &
\(P(\hat{p} \leq c) = \alpha\) \\
\(H_a: p \neq p_0\) & \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \leq c_1\) or
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \geq c_2\) &
\(P(\hat{p} \leq c_1) = P(\hat{p} \geq c_2) = \alpha/2\) \\
\end{longtable}

\end{tcolorbox}

In practice, we will use Rguroo's \Fun{One-Population Proportion}
inference function to find the critical region, as shown in the
following examples.

\begin{example}[Physical Inactivity Among Adults - Critical Region

physically inactive. A random sample of \(n = 50\) adults was selected

\begin{cases}

H_a: p < 0.35
\end{cases}
\]

region, and state your conclusion in the context of the problem.

Features dialog with Critical Region Graph selected}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo output: One-Population Proportion Inference - Marijuana
Legalization}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\end{tcolorbox}

The left panel of Figure~\ref{fig-GSS2024-cr} from the Rguroo output
shows the critical region graph on the scale of the data. The red shaded
region corresponds to the critical region and consists of all sample
proportions \(\hat{p} \ge 0.73827.\)

The probability associated with this region is the significance level,
\(\alpha = 0.05.\) Since the observed sample proportion,
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}=0.7268\) (displayed by the green triangle), does
not fall within the critical region, we fail to reject \(H_0\) and
conclude that there is not sufficient evidence to support that more than
70\% of American adults support the legalization of marijuana.

\section{Exact Binomial Hypothesis
Testing}\label{sec-making-decision-binomial}

In the previous section, we used the large-sample method to carry out a
hypothesis test for a population proportion. This method uses the normal
distribution to approximate the sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\) and
works well when the sample is sufficiently large. We now consider the
exact binomial method, which uses the binomial distribution directly and
therefore does not require a large-sample approximation. The basic
reasoning of the hypothesis test remains the same: we determine how
unusual the observed sample result would be if \(H_0\) were true and use
either the p-value or critical region approach to make a decision. The
main difference is the statistic we use. With the large-sample method,
we worked with the sample proportion \(\hat{p}.\) With the exact
binomial method, we work directly with \(X,\) the number of successes in
the sample. Since \(\hat{p}=X/n,\) these two statistics contain the same
information; we are simply expressing the sample result in a different
way.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{The Distribution of
\(X\)}{The Distribution of X}}\label{sec-distribution-x}

To use \(X\) for inference, we need to know its probability
distribution. Since we are sampling from a population and counting
successes, the binomial distribution provides the appropriate model.
Recall from \textbf{?@sec-binomial-probability-distribution} that a
random variable follows a \textbf{binomial distribution} when:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The number of trials \(n\) is fixed
\item
  Each trial results in one of two outcomes: success or failure
\item
  The probability of success \(p\) is the same for every trial
\item
  The trials are independent of one another
\end{itemize}

In our sampling context, each individual in the sample either has the
characteristic of interest (success) or does not (failure). Since the
sample is selected randomly, the trials are practically independent. The
probability of success \(p\) is constant---it equals the population
proportion. (Strictly speaking, sampling without replacement causes
\(p\) to change slightly with each draw, but when the sample is small
relative to the population, this change is negligible and we treat \(p\)
as constant.)

Therefore, \[
X \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p).
\]

This distribution will be the foundation for computing probabilities and
making decisions about \(p.\)

\subsection{Decision Based on a p-Value}\label{sec-pvalue}

The p-value approach measures \emph{how unusual} the observed count
\(x_{\text{obs}}\) would be if the null hypothesis were true, and
rejects \(H_0\) when the data are sufficiently unusual under \(H_0.\) To
make this concrete for a proportion, we evaluate probabilities at the
boundary value \(p_0\) (see Section~\ref{sec-foundations-boundary}),
using the binomial distribution of the count \(X.\)

Using the definition of \textbf{\(H_a\) support} from
Section~\ref{sec-foundations-pvalue}, the \textbf{\(H_a\) support} for
the exact binomial method consists of the values of \(X\) that are at
least as supportive of \(H_a\) as the observed value \(x_{\text{obs}}.\)
The p-value then is the probability, assuming \(p=p_0,\) that \(X\)
takes a value in the \(H_a\) support:

\[
\text{p-value} = P(X \text{ is a value in the } H_a \text{ support),  assuming }  p = p_0.
\]

A small p-value is evidence against \(H_0.\)

What counts as ``the \(H_a\) support'' depends on the form of the
alternative hypothesis.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]
\begin{minipage}[t]{5.5mm}
\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{minipage}[t]{\textwidth - 5.5mm}

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Case 1: \(H_a: p > p_0\) (e.g., \(H_a: p > 0.70\))}\vspace{3mm}

Larger values of \(X\) are more supportive of \(H_a.\) The \(H_a\)
support consists of \(x_{\text{obs}}\) and all values larger than
\(x_{\text{obs}},\) so the p-value is \[
\text{p-value} = P(X \geq x_{\text{obs}}), \text{ assuming } p = p_0.
\]

\end{minipage}%
\end{tcolorbox}

To understand Case 1, note that a larger value of \(X\) means more
successes in the sample, which corresponds to a higher sample proportion
\(\hat{p}.\) A higher sample proportion is less consistent with \(H_0\)
and more supportive of the claim that the true population proportion
exceeds \(p_0.\) For example, in the YouTube example where
\(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\) out of \(n = 20,\) the \(H_a\) support consists
of the values \(\{17, 18, 19, 20\}\) --- the observed count and every
larger possibility.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]
\begin{minipage}[t]{5.5mm}
\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{minipage}[t]{\textwidth - 5.5mm}

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Case 2: \(H_a: p < p_0\) (e.g., \(H_a: p < 0.35\))}\vspace{3mm}

Smaller values of \(X\) are more supportive of \(H_a.\) The \(H_a\)
support consists of \(x_{\text{obs}}\) and all values smaller than
\(x_{\text{obs}},\) so the p-value is \[
\text{p-value} = P(X \leq x_{\text{obs}}), \text{ assuming } p = p_0.
\]

\end{minipage}%
\end{tcolorbox}

Case 2 is the mirror image of Case 1: a smaller value of \(X\) means
fewer successes in the sample, which corresponds to a lower sample
proportion \(\hat{p}.\) A lower sample proportion is less consistent
with \(H_0\) and more supportive of the claim that the true population
proportion is less than \(p_0.\) For example, in the Physical Inactivity
example where \(x_{\text{obs}} = 10\) out of \(n = 50,\) the \(H_a\)
support is \(\{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9, 10\}\) --- the observed count and
every smaller possibility.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]
\begin{minipage}[t]{5.5mm}
\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{minipage}[t]{\textwidth - 5.5mm}

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Case 3: \(H_a: p \neq p_0\) (e.g., \(H_a: p \neq 0.36\))}\vspace{3mm}

A value \(x\) is in the \(H_a\) support if it is at least as unlikely as
the observed value \(x_{\text{obs}}\) under \(H_0,\) that is, \[
P(X = x) \leq P(X = x_{\text{obs}}), \text{ assuming } p = p_0.
\]

Such values can occur in either tail of the distribution.

\end{minipage}%
\end{tcolorbox}

The two-sided case is easiest to see in a picture. For the Social Media
News example with \(x_{\text{obs}} = 9\) out of \(n = 15\) and
\(p_0 = 0.36,\) Figure~\ref{fig-social-media-pvalue} shows the binomial
distribution of \(X\) under \(H_0,\) where
\(X \sim \text{Binomial}(15, 0.36).\)

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.6\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/social-media-pvalue.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-social-media-pvalue}Two-sided p-value for the Social
Media example; shaded regions represent outcomes at least as unlikely as
x\_obs = 9 under H0, when p = 0.36.}

\end{figure}%

The \(X\) values corresponding to the orange bars are the values of
\(X\) whose probability under \(H_0\) is at most equal to \(P(X = 9).\)
Therefore, the \(H_a\) support appears in both tails: large values
\(9, 10, 11, \ldots\) on the right and small values \(0, 1\) on the
left. The p-value is the total probability of the orange bars.

The decision rule using the p-value is the same as the one introduced in
Section~\ref{sec-foundations-pvalue} and used with the large-sample
method: we reject \(H_0\) when the p-value is less than or equal to the
significance level \(\alpha.\) The interpretation is also the same. A
small p-value means that the observed result and results at least as
supportive of \(H_a\) would be unlikely if \(H_0\) were true. The
difference is that with the exact binomial method, we express the
observed result as the number of successes \(x_{\text{obs}}\) and
calculate the p-value directly from the binomial distribution of \(X.\)

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Decision Rule Using the p-Value}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

When testing at significance level \(\alpha,\) \[
\text{If p-value} \leq \alpha, \text{ reject } H_0. \qquad \text{If p-value} > \alpha, \text{ fail to reject } H_0.
\]

\end{tcolorbox}

In practice, we use statistical software such as Rguroo to compute
p-values. Rguroo's \Fun{One-Population Proportion} inference function
carries out a complete hypothesis test from the inputs \(n,\)
\(x_{\text{obs}},\) and the form of \(H_a\) (including \(p_0\)). The
next four examples illustrate how to obtain the p-value and reach a
decision, using our three running examples plus the raw-dataset example
from the GSS.

\begin{example}[Daily YouTube Use Among Teens
(continued)]\protect\hypertarget{exm-youtube-pvalue}{}\label{exm-youtube-pvalue}

Recall Example~\ref{exm-youtube-ppss}. A school district claims that
more than 70\% of students in its district use YouTube daily, that is,
\(H_a: p > 0.70.\) A random sample of \(n = 20\) students is selected,
and \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\) of them report daily YouTube use. The
hypotheses are \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p \leq 0.70 \\
H_a: p > 0.70
\end{cases}
\]

Use Rguroo's One-Population Proportion inference function to obtain the
p-value, and use it to make a decision at significance level
\(\alpha = 0.05.\)

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

Our sample of \(n = 20\) students yielded \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\) daily
users, giving \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 17/20 = 0.85.\) We use Rguroo to
compute the p-value and decide whether this result is statistically
significant.

\begin{example}[ESP Card-Guessing Experiment - Exact Binomial
(P-value)]\protect\hypertarget{exm-esp-pvalue}{}\label{exm-esp-pvalue}

In a classic test of extrasensory perception (ESP), a participant tries
to identify which of five symbols (a star, a circle, a square, a cross,
or wavy lines) appears on a hidden card, without seeing it. If the
participant has no real ability to sense the symbol and is simply
guessing, the probability of a correct guess on any single trial is
\(p = 0.20\).

A researcher wants to test whether a particular participant performs
worse than random guessing, a phenomenon some parapsychology researchers
have called ``psi-missing'' and attributed to an unconscious avoidance
of the correct answer. The participant completes \(n = 20\) trials, and
\(x_{\text{obs}} = 1\) of the guesses is correct. Test, at the
\(\alpha = 0.05\) level, whether these results provide evidence that the
participant's true probability of a correct guess is below \(0.20\).

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

The null and alternative hypotheses are \[
H_0: p \ge 0.20 \quad \text{vs.} \quad H_a: p < 0.20.
\]

Since \(np_0 = 20 \times 0.20 = 4 < 10\), the sample is too small to
rely on the normal approximation, so we use the exact binomial method.
Because we are only given the sample size and the number of successes
rather than raw data for each trial, we enter the information using
\textbf{summary statistics} rather than a raw dataset, following the
same instructions as in the
\hyperref[solution-pvalue-youtube-binomial]{solution} of
\hyperref[prop-inference-youtube]{the YouTube example}.

In the summary-statistics entry dialog, since there is no dataset to
select variables and levels from, we instead type in our own labels:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Factor label: \texttt{Guess\ Outcome}
\item
  Success label: \texttt{Correct}
\item
  Failure label: \texttt{Incorrect}
\end{itemize}

along with the sample size (\(n = 20\)), the number of successes
(\(x_{\text{obs}} = 1\)), the hypothesized proportion (\(p_0 = 0.20\)),
the direction of the alternative hypothesis (\(p < 0.20\)), and the
exact binomial method.

The Rguroo dialog for this example is shown below.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

}

\caption{\label{fig-esp-test}Rguroo dialog for the one-proportion exact
binomial test, entered using summary statistics for the ESP
card-guessing experiment.}

\end{figure}%

Click to expand the box below to see the Rguroo output.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo output: One-Population Proportion Inference --- ESP Test}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\end{tcolorbox}

The exact binomial p-value is \(0.069\). This is the probability,
computed under \(H_0\) (i.e., assuming \(p = 0.20\)), of observing a
result at least as favorable to \(H_a\) as the one obtained --- that is,
\(X \le 1\) success out of 20 trials.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_html_output/Proportion Inference/ESP_test_docx/G_pvalueTestPropBinomial.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-esp-test-pvalue}P-value graph for the exact binomial
test of the ESP card-guessing experiment.}

\end{figure}%

Since the p-value is greater than \(\alpha = 0.05\), we fail to reject
\(H_0\). There is not sufficient evidence at the 5\% significance level
that the participant's true probability of a correct guess is below
0.20, i.e., the results are not sufficient to conclude that psi-missing
occurred.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Social Media as a Primary News - Source Exact Binomial
(P-value)]\protect\hypertarget{exm-social-pvalue}{}\label{exm-social-pvalue}

Recall Example~\ref{exm-social-media-news-ppss}. A university
administration wants to determine whether the proportion of students who
get most of their news from social media differs from 36\%, that is,
\(H_a: p \neq 0.36.\) A random sample of \(n = 15\) students is
selected, and \(x_{\text{obs}} = 9\) report using social media as their
primary news source. The hypotheses are \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p = 0.36 \\
H_a: p \neq 0.36
\end{cases}
\]

Use Rguroo's One-Population Proportion inference function to obtain the
p-value, and use it to make a decision at significance level
\(\alpha = 0.10.\)

\end{example}

\Dialog{One Population Proportion Inference}.
Figure~\ref{fig-social-test} shows the completed Rguroo dialog for this
example. We input the \Des{Factor} label as \TypeIn{Use Social Media},
the \Des{Success} label as \TypeIn{Yes} (a student who uses social media
as their primary news source), and the \Des{Failure} label as
\TypeIn{No}. We enter a sample size of \TypeIn{15} and number of
successes of \TypeIn{9}. In the \textbf{Test of Hypothesis} section, we
select \TypeIn{!=} (not equal to) from the \Dpd{Alternative Hyp. p}
dropdown and enter \TypeIn{0.36}. We select the \Des{Binomial} checkbox
and leave the \Des{Significance Level} at the default value of
\TypeIn{0.05}.

\begin{example}[Heavy Chinstrap Penguins - Exact Binomial
(P-value)]\protect\hypertarget{exm-penguins-heavy-pvalue-binomial}{}\label{exm-penguins-heavy-pvalue-binomial}

The Palmer Station Antarctica LTER penguins data include body-mass
measurements for three penguin species. Here we restrict attention to a
sample of \(n = 34\) Chinstrap penguins, given in the
\Data{palmer_penguins_Chinstrap} dataset. A Chinstrap penguin is
classified as \emph{heavy} if its body mass is 4400 grams or more. The
variable \Var{Heavy} records this classification, with possible values
\emph{Yes} (heavy) or \emph{No} (not heavy).

We wish to test the claim that more than 10\% of Chinstrap penguins in
the island are heavy. That is, test the hypotheses \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p \leq 0.10 \\
H_a: p > 0.10
\end{cases}
\]

Because the sample size is small --- under \(H_0\) we would expect only
\(34 \times 0.10 = 3.4\) heavy penguins, well below the usual guideline
of at least 10 --- the normal approximation is not appropriate here, and
we instead use the exact binomial method.

Use Rguroo's One-Population Proportion inference function, with the
binomial method, to obtain the p-value, and make a decision at
\(\alpha = 0.05\) significance level.

The dataset for this example is available in the Rguroo dataset
repository \Repo{Kozak}, with the dataset name
\Data{palmer_penguins_Chinstrap}. Table
Table~\ref{tbl-PalmerPenguinsChinstrap} displays the first six rows of
the dataset. A complete description of the variables is provided in the
\hyperref[code-book-palmer-penguins-chinstrap]{dataset code book} that
follows.

\end{example}

\Var{species}: Penguin species. All penguins in this dataset are
Chinstrap penguins.

\Var{bill_length_mm}: Length of the penguin's bill, in millimeters (mm).

\Var{bill_depth_mm}: Depth of the penguin's bill, in millimeters (mm).

\Var{flipper_length_mm}: Length of the penguin's flipper, in millimeters

\subsection{Decision Based on a Critical
Region}\label{sec-critical-region}

Recall from Section~\ref{sec-foundations-critical-region} that the
critical region approach identifies, in advance, the values of the
statistic that lead us to reject \(H_0.\) We used this same approach
with the large-sample method. For the exact binomial method, the
reasoning is unchanged; the difference is that the critical region is
now defined in terms of the possible values of \(X,\) the number of
successes. As before, the location of the critical region is determined
by the direction of the alternative hypothesis \(H_a\):

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\[\text{Reject } H_0 \text{ if } 
\begin{cases}
X \geq c & \text{when } H_a: p > p_0 \\
X \leq c & \text{when } H_a: p < p_0 \\
X \leq c_1 \text{ or } X \geq c_2 & \text{when } H_a: p \neq p_0
\end{cases}\] The values \(c,\) \(c_1,\) and \(c_2\) are called
\textbf{critical values}, and the corresponding values of \(X\) form the
\textbf{critical region} (also called the \textbf{rejection region}).

\end{tcolorbox}

To find the critical values, we use the null distribution \[
X\sim\text{Binomial}(n,p_0).
\] We choose the largest critical region for which the probability of a
Type I error does not exceed the significance level \(\alpha.\)

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]
\begin{minipage}[t]{5.5mm}
\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{minipage}[t]{\textwidth - 5.5mm}

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Sometimes the Actual Significance Level Is Less Than \(\alpha\)}\vspace{3mm}

Because the binomial distribution is discrete, \(X\) takes only
whole-number values. As a result, changing a critical value causes the
probability of the critical region to change in steps rather than
continuously. Therefore, we often cannot find a critical region with a
probability exactly equal to \(\alpha.\)

Rguroo returns the \textbf{largest} critical region whose probability
under \(H_0\) is at or below \(\alpha.\) The probability of this
critical region is the actual significance level of the test and is
reported as the \textbf{Exact Significance Level} in the Rguroo output.

For example, if we choose \(\alpha = 0.05,\) Rguroo might return a
critical region with an actual significance level \(0.0476\) or
\(0.0342.\) In either case, the probability of a Type I error is below
the chosen significance level of \(0.05.\)

\end{minipage}%
\end{tcolorbox}

In practice, we use Rguroo's \Fun{One-Population Proportion} inference
function to find this critical region.

\begin{example}[Daily YouTube Use Among Teens - Exact Binomial (Critical
Region)]\protect\hypertarget{exm-youtube-rejection}{}\label{exm-youtube-rejection}

Recall Example~\ref{exm-youtube-ppss} and
Example~\ref{exm-youtube-pvalue}. We test \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p \leq 0.70 \\
H_a: p > 0.70
\end{cases}
\] with \(n = 20\) and \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17.\)

Use Rguroo's One-Population Proportion inference function to obtain the
critical region, and use it to make a decision at significance level
\(\alpha = 0.05.\)

\end{example}

\begin{example}[ESP Card-Guessing Experiment - Exact Binomial (Critical

Recall Example~\ref{exm-esp-pvalue}. We test \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p \geq 0.20 \\

\] with \(n = 20\) and \(x_{\text{obs}} = 1.\)

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

The filled-out dialog is shown in Figure~\ref{fig-esp-test-cr}. We input

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  the \Des{Factor} label as \TypeIn{Guess Outcome},
\item
  \Des{Success} as \TypeIn{Correct} (since we are counting correct
  guesses), and
\item
  \Des{Failure} as \TypeIn{Incorrect}.
\end{itemize}

We also input the sample size, number of successes, the alternative
hypothesis, and select the method \Des{Binomial}.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Homework for
Section~\ref{sec-making-decision-binomial}}{Homework for Section~}}\label{homework-for-sec-making-decision-binomial}

For each of the scenarios described below, use Rguroo's
\Fun{One-Population Proportion} inference function with the
\Des{Binomial} option to carry out the hypothesis test at the given
significance level.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Before running the analysis, identify the following inputs for the
  Rguroo dialog:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \Des{Factor Label}: A descriptive name for the variable being
  studied\\
\item
  \Des{Success}: The outcome that counts as a success\\
\item
  \Des{Failure}: The outcome that counts as a failure\\
\item
  \Des{Sample Size}: The value of \(n\)\\
\item
  \Des{# of Successes}: The value of \(x_{\text{obs}}\)\\
\item
  \Des{Proportion of …}: A descriptive label for what the population
  proportion represents
\end{itemize}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\item
  State the null and alternative hypotheses.
\item
  Carry out the test using the \textbf{p-value approach} and the
  \textbf{Binomial Exact} method:\\
  \strut ~~~~(i) Specify the \(H_a\) support.\\
  \strut ~~~~(ii) State the p-value and determine whether you reject or
  fail to reject \(H_0.\)
\item
  Carry out the test using the \textbf{critical region (rejection
  region) approach} and the \textbf{Binomial Exact} method:\\
  \strut ~~~~(i) Specify the critical region.\\
  \strut ~~~~(ii) Identify \(x_{\text{obs}}\) and determine whether you
  reject or fail to reject \(H_0.\)
\item
  State your conclusion in the context of the problem.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Airport Security Screening}: An airport reports that 5\% of
  randomly selected passengers require additional security screening. In
  a random sample of \(n = 40\) passengers at a particular terminal,
  \(x_{\text{obs}} = 5\) required additional screening. Is there
  evidence that the proportion of passengers requiring additional
  screening at this terminal is greater than 5\%? Use \(\alpha = 0.05.\)
\item
  \textbf{Defective Computer Chips}: A manufacturer claims that 4\% of
  the computer chips it produces are defective. A quality-control
  inspector randomly selects \(n = 50\) chips and finds that
  \(x_{\text{obs}} = 5\) are defective. Is there evidence that the true
  proportion of defective chips is greater than 4\%? Use
  \(\alpha = 0.10.\)
\item
  \textbf{Seed Germination Rate}: A seed company states that 90\% of a
  particular variety of seeds will germinate under specified growing
  conditions. A gardener randomly selects \(n = 20\) seeds and finds
  that \(x_{\text{obs}} = 15\) germinate. Is there evidence that the
  true germination rate is less than 90\%? Use \(\alpha = 0.05.\)
\item
  \textbf{Online Order Returns}: A small online retailer has
  historically had 8\% of its orders returned. After changing its
  product descriptions, the retailer randomly examines \(n = 30\) recent
  orders and finds that \(x_{\text{obs}} = 1\) was returned. Is there
  evidence that the proportion of orders being returned has decreased
  from 8\%? Use \(\alpha = 0.05.\)
\item
  \textbf{Free-Throw Shooting}: A basketball player has historically
  made 85\% of her free throws. During a randomly selected set of
  \(n = 20\) free throws, she makes \(x_{\text{obs}} = 14\). Is there
  evidence that her true free-throw success rate differs from 85\%? Use
  \(\alpha = 0.05.\)
\item
  \textbf{Rare Side Effect}: A commonly used medication is known to
  produce a particular side effect in 2\% of patients. Among a random
  sample of \(n = 60\) patients receiving the medication at a clinic,
  \(x_{\text{obs}} = 4\) experience the side effect. Is there evidence
  that the proportion of patients experiencing the side effect at this
  clinic differs from 2\%? Use \(\alpha = 0.05.\)
\end{enumerate}

\section{A Closer Look at Critical Regions and p-values
(Optional)}\label{sec-closer-look-cr-pvalue}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Note}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

This section is optional. The material here is not required for
performing hypothesis tests, but it is highly recommended for readers
who want a firmer conceptual grasp of what is happening behind the
procedures.

\end{tcolorbox}

In the previous sections, you learned two equivalent approaches for
testing a hypothesis about a population proportion: the \textbf{critical
region approach} and the \textbf{p-value approach}. In both approaches,
we computed probabilities for our decisions using the boundary value of
the null hypothesis, and we relied on Rguroo's \Fun{Proportion Infrence}
function to produce the critical region or the p-value automatically.

This section is intended to deepen your understanding of \emph{why}
these procedures work the way they do. Specifically, we address two
questions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Why do we use the boundary value of \(H_0\) when computing
  probabilities required for our decisions?} The null hypothesis in many
  tests is a statement such as \(H_0: p \leq p_0\) or
  \(H_0: p \geq p_0,\) which encompasses many possible values of \(p.\)
  Yet we always use the single boundary value \(p_0\) in our
  calculations. There is a principled reason for this, and understanding
  it clarifies what a hypothesis test is really doing.
\item
  \textbf{How are critical regions and p-values actually obtained from a
  probability distribution?} Rguroo's \Fun{Proportion Inference}
  function returns these quantities directly, but doing so hides the
  underlying probability calculation. By using Rguroo's
  \textbf{probability calculator} instead, we can see exactly which area
  under a sampling distribution corresponds to the critical region or
  the p-value.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Why Use the Boundary Value in \(H_0\)?
**}{Why Use the Boundary Value in H\_0? **}}\label{sec-boundary-value}

In this section we explain \emph{why} we use the boundary value of
\(H_0\) when computing the probability of a Type I error. The front-half
discussion stated this as a fact: for a composite \(H_0\) such as
\(H_0: p \leq p_0,\) the maximum Type I error probability over the
values allowed by \(H_0\) occurs at the boundary \(p_0,\) so controlling
the error there automatically controls it everywhere in \(H_0.\) Here we
\emph{demonstrate} this empirically: we compute the probability of a
Type I error for several specific values of \(p\) within \(H_0,\) for
one decision rule, and observe that the maximum occurs at the boundary.
A formal account, including worked examples and the underlying
mathematics, is given in
\href{https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/26939169.2025.2610942}{Jamshidian
and Jamshidian (2026)}.

\begin{example}[Daily YouTube Use Among Teens
(continued)]\protect\hypertarget{exm-youtube-type1}{}\label{exm-youtube-type1}

Recall Example~\ref{exm-youtube-ppss} where a school district claimed
that more than 70\% of students in its district use YouTube daily, and a
random sample of \(n = 20\) students was selected. The null and
alternative hypotheses are: \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p \leq 0.70 \\
H_a: p > 0.70
\end{cases}
\]

Consider the critical region: Reject \(H_0\) if \(X \geq 17.\)

For this critical region, compute \(P(\text{Type I error})\) when

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(p = 0.60\)
\item
  \(p = 0.65\)
\item
  \(p = 0.70.\)
\end{enumerate}

In each case, interpret the probability in the context of the problem.

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. Since the sample size is \(n = 20\) and \(p = 0.60,\) we have
\(X \sim \text{Binomial}(20, 0.60).\) Using Rguroo's probability
calculator, we compute
\[P(\text{Type I error}) = P(\text{Reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ is true})\]
\[= P(X \geq 17 \mid p = 0.60).\]

Click to expand the box below to see how to calculate the probability of
Type I error.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]
\begin{minipage}[t]{5.5mm}
\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{minipage}[t]{\textwidth - 5.5mm}

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{\includegraphics[width=0.22917in,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_Icons/R_circle_logo.pdf}
Calculating Type I Error Probability}\vspace{3mm}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Open the \textbf{Probability-Simulation} toolbox in Rguroo.\\
\item
  From the \Dpd{Probability} dropdown, select
  \Fun{Probability Calculator –> Discrete}.
\item
  (Optional) In the \texttt{Calculation} textbox, type a name for the
  calculation (e.g., \texttt{Type\ I\ error}).\\
\item
  In the \Dpd{Distribution} dropdown, select \Fun{Binomial}.
\item
  In the \Des{No. of Trials} textbox, enter \TypeIn{20}.
\item
  In the \Des{Prob. of Success} textbox, enter \TypeIn{0.60}.
\item
  In the next dropdown menu, select \Dpd{Above}, and in the textbox next
  to it, enter \TypeIn{17}.
\item
  (Optional) Select the \Des{Graph} checkbox to see a graph showing
  calculation details.
\item
  Click the preview icon
  \includegraphics{Rguroo_Icons/preview_inline.png} to see the result.
\item
  (Optional) In the \includegraphics{Rguroo_Icons/save_as.png} textbox,
  enter the name \TypeIn{TypeI_Error} to save this calculation to your
  Rguroo account.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]
\begin{minipage}[t]{5.5mm}
\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{minipage}[t]{\textwidth - 5.5mm}

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Click here to see the Rguroo dialog}\vspace{3mm}

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics[width=5.20833in,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_dialogs/Proportion_inference/Prob_Type_I_error_dialog.png}

}

\caption{Probability calculator dialog for computing Type I error
probability}

\end{figure}%

\end{minipage}%
\end{tcolorbox}

\end{minipage}%
\end{tcolorbox}

\end{tcolorbox}

Figure~\ref{fig-youtube-type1a} shows the Rguroo Probability Calculator
output for \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(20, 0.60),\) giving

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\[P(\text{Type I error}) = P(X \geq 17\mid p=0.60) \approx 0.016.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

That is, if the true proportion of students in the district who use
YouTube daily is \(p = 0.60,\) and our decision rule is to reject
\(H_0\) whenever \(X \geq 17\) in a sample of \(n = 20\) students, then
there is only a \(1.6\%\) chance of committing a Type I error; that is,
incorrectly concluding that more than 70\% of students in the district
use YouTube daily.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/Prob_Type_I_Error_graph.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-youtube-type1a}Binomial distribution for
\(X \sim \text{Binomial}(n = 20, p = 0.60)\) showing the Type I error
probability as the upper-tail area \(P(X \geq 17) = 0.016.\)}

\end{figure}%

b. To compute the probability of Type I error for the critical region
\(X \geq 17\) when \(p = 0.65,\) we follow the same steps as in the
\hyperref[calculating-typeI-error]{part (a)}, but enter \TypeIn{0.65} in
the \Des{Prob. of Success} box. The Rguroo output gives

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\[P(\text{Type I error}) = P(X \geq 17\mid p=0.65) \approx 0.044.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

That is, if the true proportion of students in the district who use
YouTube daily is \(p = 0.65,\) and our decision rule is to reject
\(H_0\) whenever \(X \geq 17\) in a sample of \(n = 20\) students, then
there is approximately a \(4.4\%\) chance of committing a Type I error;
that is, incorrectly concluding that more than 70\% of students in the
district use YouTube daily.

c. Entering \TypeIn{0.70} in the \Des{Prob. of Success} box gives

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\[P(\text{Type I error}) = P(X \geq 17\mid p=0.70) \approx 0.107.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

That is, if the true proportion of students in the district who use
YouTube daily is \(p = 0.70,\) and our decision rule is to reject
\(H_0\) whenever \(X \geq 17\) in a sample of \(n = 20\) students, then
there is approximately a \(10.7\%\) chance of committing a Type I error;
that is, incorrectly concluding that more than 70\% of students in the
district use YouTube daily.

\begin{example}[Physical Inactivity Among Adults
(continued)]\protect\hypertarget{exm-physical-inactivity-type1}{}\label{exm-physical-inactivity-type1}

Recall Example~\ref{exm-physical-inactivity-ppss} where a national
health agency claimed that fewer than 35\% of adults in its country are

\begin{cases}
H_0: p \geq 0.35 \\
H_a: p < 0.35
\end{cases}
\]

Consider the critical region: Reject \(H_0\) if \(X \leq 13.\)

For this critical region, compute \(P(\text{Type I error})\) when

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(p = 0.35\)
\item
  \(p = 0.40\)
\item
  \(p = 0.50.\)
\end{enumerate}

In each case, interpret the probability in the context of the problem.

\end{example}

That is, if the true proportion of inactive adults in the population is
\(p = 0.40,\) and our decision rule is to reject \(H_0\) whenever

c. Entering \TypeIn{0.50} in the \Des{Prob. of Success} box gives

\[P(\text{Type I error}) = P(X \leq 13\mid p=0.50) \approx 0.00046.\]
