That is, if the true proportion of inactive adults in the population is
\(p = 0.50,\) and our decision rule is to reject \(H_0\) whenever
\(X \leq 13\) in a sample of \(n = 50\) adults, then there is
approximately a \(0.046\%\) chance of committing a Type I error; that
is, incorrectly concluding that fewer than 35\% of adults in the
population are physically inactive.

\end{tcolorbox}

Now that we have computed the probability of a Type I error at various
values of \(p,\) let us look back at what we observed in our examples.

For the one-sided cases, there is a range of values of \(p\) in \(H_0,\)
and we computed the probability of a Type I error at several of them.
You may have noticed a pattern: in both the YouTube example and the
Physical Inactivity example, the probability of a Type I error was
largest at the value of \(p\) where \(H_0\) and \(H_a\) meet, the
\textbf{boundary value of \(p\) in \(H_0\)}. For the YouTube example,
this is \(p = 0.70,\) and for the Physical Inactivity example, this is
\(p = 0.35.\) Is this a coincidence that the probability of a Type I
error is largest at the boundary value?

The answer is, it is not a coincident. Figure~\ref{fig-type-range} shows
the probability of a Type I error across a range of values of \(p\) in
\(H_0,\) for the two examples that we considerd here and for three
different decision rules in each case.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/TypeI_error_range.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-type-range}Type I error probabilities for binomial
tests as a function of \(p.\) Panel (a) shows
\(X \sim \text{Binomial}(20, p)\) with \(P(X \geq 16, 17, 18)\); panel
(b) shows \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(50, p)\) with
\(P(X \leq 11, 12, 13).\) The red dashed line marks \(\alpha = 0.05.\)
The gray dotted line shows the boundary of \(H_0.\)}

\end{figure}%

In panel (a), for the YouTube example, the null hypothesis is
\(H_0: p \leq 0.70,\) so the boundary value is \(p = 0.70.\) The three
curves correspond to the decision rules \(X \geq 16,\) \(X \geq 17,\)
and \(X \geq 18.\) For all three rules, the probability of a Type I
error increases as \(p\) gets closer to the boundary value of \(0.70,\)
and reaches its maximum at \(p = 0.70.\)

In panel (b), for the Physical Inactivity example, the null hypothesis
is \(H_0: p \geq 0.35,\) so the boundary value is \(p = 0.35.\) The
three curves correspond to the decision rules \(X \leq 11,\)
\(X \leq 12,\) and \(X \leq 13.\) Again, for all three rules, the
probability of a Type I error is largest at the boundary value
\(p = 0.35\) and decreases as \(p\) moves away from it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Key Result: Maximum Type I Error Occurs at the Boundary Value}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

For the one-sided tests, the probability of a Type I error is largest at
the boundary value of \(H_0.\)

\end{tcolorbox}

Notice also that the horizontal dashed red line in each panel is drawn
at \(0.05.\) This represents a commonly chosen upper bound for the
probability of a Type I error --- that is, the significance level
\(\alpha = 0.05.\) As discussed in the previous sections, the decision
rule (critical region) that we use is chosen to satisfy two
requirements:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  At the boundary value of \(H_0,\) the probability of a Type I error
  does not exceed the desired significance level \(\alpha.\)
\item
  Among all critical regions satisfying (1), we choose the one
  containing the largest number of \(X\) values, so that the probability
  of a Type II error is as small as possible.
\end{enumerate}

Therefore, as shown in Figure~\ref{fig-type-range}, the critical region
corresponding to the significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\) for the
YouTube example is \(X\geq 18,\) and that for the Physical Inactivity
example is \(X\leq 11.\)

\subsection{Obtaining Critical Regions and p-values Using Rguroo's
Probability Calculator}\label{sec-prob-calculator}

In this subsection, we revisit examples from earlier in the chapter, but
instead of using Rguroo's \Fun{Proportion Inference} function, we
compute critical values and p-values directly from the sampling
distribution under \(H_0\) using Rguroo's \Fun{Probability Calculator}
function. This approach makes visible the area-under-the-curve
interpretation of both quantities.

\subsubsection{Using Inverse Probability to Find the Critical
Region}\label{using-inverse-probability-to-find-the-critical-region}

When using a probability calculator, we could find a critical region by
trying different candidate decision rules and checking their Type I
error probabilities one at a time, as illustrated in
Figure~\ref{fig-type-range}. For example, we might check whether the
rule ``\(X \ge 17\)'' has a Type I error probability close to 0.05, then
try ``\(X \ge 18,\)'' and so on. While this trial-and-error approach
works, there is a more direct method.

Many calculators provide an inverse probability function. A probability
function starts with a value of \(X\) and returns the corresponding
probability. An inverse probability function works in the opposite
direction: we provide a probability, such as \(\alpha=0.05,\) and it
returns the value of \(X\) that creates that probability. This allows us
to find the rejection-region boundary directly rather than testing
several possible decision rules one at a time.

To find the critical region, we use the binomial distribution with the
boundary value of \(p\) from \(H_0\) as the probability of success and
\(n\) as the number of trials. Instead of providing a value of \(X\) and
asking for a probability, we provide the significance level \(\alpha\)
as the probability. The inverse probability function then returns the
corresponding boundary value of \(X,\) which we use to determine the
critical region. Below, we show how this is done in Rguroo using its
built-in probability calculator.

\begin{example}[YouTube Use: Finding the Critical
Region]\protect\hypertarget{exm-youtube-rejection-calc}{}\label{exm-youtube-rejection-calc}

In the YouTube Use example (Example~\ref{exm-youtube-ppss}), we are
testing \(H_0: p \leq 0.70\) versus \(H_a: p > 0.70,\) where \(p\) is
the true proportion of students in the district who use YouTube daily.
Using a sample of \(n = 20\) students and a significance level of
\(\alpha = 0.05,\) find the critical region for this test.

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

Since the alternative hypothesis is \(H_a: p > 0.70,\) large values of
\(X\) provide evidence in favor of \(H_a.\) Therefore, we need a
critical region in the upper tail of the binomial distribution. We use
Rguroo's \Fun{Probability Calculator} and the significance level
\(\alpha\) to find the boundary value of \(X\) that defines this region.

Click to expand the box below to see how to use the
\Fun{Probability Calulator} function in Rguroo.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]
\begin{minipage}[t]{5.5mm}
\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{minipage}[t]{\textwidth - 5.5mm}

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{\includegraphics[width=0.22917in,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_Icons/R_circle_logo.pdf}
Critical Region Using Calculator --- YouTube example}\vspace{3mm}

\item

  \Des{Prob. of Success} to \TypeIn{0.70}.
\item
  From the dropdown, select \Dpd{Upper Tail} and enter \TypeIn{0.05} as
  the significance level \(\alpha.\)
\item
  Select the checkbox \Des{Graph} to see a detailed output.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo Discrete Probability Calculator dialog}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_dialogs/Proportion_inference/youtube-rejection-dialog.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-youtube-rejection-dialog}Rguroo Probability
Calculator Settings for the YouTube Critical Region Example}

The output, shown in Figure~\ref{fig-youtube-rejection}, gives \[
P(X \geq 17)=0.1071 > 0.05
\quad\text{and}\quad
P(X \geq 18)=0.03548 < 0.05.
\]

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/YouTube_rejection.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-youtube-rejection}Rguroo Probability Calculator
Output for the YouTube Critical Region Example}

\end{figure}%

Thus, the decision rule \(X \geq 17\) would produce a Type I error
probability greater than our significance level and cannot be used.
However, the decision rule \(X \geq 18\) has a Type I error probability
below 0.05 and therefore satisfies the significance-level requirement.

Therefore, the critical region at significance level \(\alpha=0.05\) is
\[
X \geq 18.
\] In other words, if 18 or more of the \(n=20\) students in the sample
report daily YouTube use, we reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_a: p>0.70.\)

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Physical Inactivity: Finding the Critical
Region]\protect\hypertarget{exm-inactivity-rejection-calc}{}\label{exm-inactivity-rejection-calc}

In the Physical Inactivity example
(Example~\ref{exm-physical-inactivity-error}), we are testing
\(H_0: p \geq 0.35\) versus \(H_a: p < 0.35,\) where \(p\) is the true
proportion of adults in the population who are physically inactive.
Using a sample of \(n = 50\) adults and a significance level of
\(\alpha = 0.05,\) find the critical region for this test.

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

Since the alternative hypothesis is \(H_a: p < 0.35,\) small values of
\(X\) provide evidence in favor of \(H_a.\) Therefore, we are looking
for a critical region in the lower tail of the binomial distribution. We
use Rguroo's Discrete Distributions Probability Calculator with the
settings shown in Figure~\ref{fig-inactivity-rejection-dialog}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Set the \Des{No. of Trials} to \TypeIn{50} and the
  \Des{Prob. of Success} to \TypeIn{0.35}, the boundary value of \(p\)
  in \(H_0.\)
\item
  From the dropdown, select \Dpd{Lower Tail} and enter \TypeIn{0.05} as
  the significance level \(\alpha.\)
\end{itemize}

Because we are using the inverse probability function, the calculator
returns the boundary value of \(X\) that leaves probability \(0.05\) in
the lower tail. We then use this value to determine the critical region.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_dialogs/Proportion_inference/inactive-rejection-dialog.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-inactivity-rejection-dialog}Rguroo Probability
Calculator Settings for the Physical Inactivity Critical Region Example}

\end{figure}%

The output, shown in Figure~\ref{fig-inactivity-rejection}, gives
\[P(X \leq 12) = 0.06613 \geq 0.05 \quad \text{and} \quad 
P(X \leq 11) = 0.03423 \leq 0.05.\]

we reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_a: p < 0.35.\)

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/inactive_rejection.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-inactivity-rejection}Rguroo Probability Calculator
Output for the Physical Inactivity Critical Region Example}

\end{figure}%

This means that the decision rule \(X \leq 12\) exceeds our significance
level, while the decision rule \(X \leq 11\) satisfies it. Therefore,
the rejection region at significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\) is
\[X \leq 11.\] That is, if we observe 11 or fewer inactive adults in our
sample of \(n = 50,\)

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Social Media as a Primary News Source: Finding the
Critical
Region]\protect\hypertarget{exm-social-rejection-calc}{}\label{exm-social-rejection-calc}

In the Social Media as a Primary News Source example
(Example~\ref{exm-social-media-news-error}), we are testing
\(H_0: p = 0.36\) versus \(H_a: p \neq 0.36,\) where \(p\) is the true
proportion of students who use social media as their primary news
source. Using a sample of \(n = 15\) students and a significance level
of \(\alpha = 0.05,\) find the critical region for this test.

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

Since the alternative hypothesis is \(H_a: p \neq 0.36,\) both unusually
small and unusually large values of \(X\) provide evidence in favor of
\(H_a.\) Therefore, we are looking for a two-sided critical region. For
a two-sided test at significance level \(\alpha = 0.05,\) we split the
significance level equally between the two tails, allocating \(0.025\)
to each tail so that the total Type I error probability is \(0.05.\)

We use Rguroo's Discrete Distributions Probability Calculator with the
settings shown in Figure~\ref{fig-social-rejection-dialog}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Set the \Des{No. of Trials} to \TypeIn{15} and the
  \Des{Prob. of Success} to \TypeIn{0.36}, the value of \(p\) specified
  by \(H_0.\)
\item
  From the dropdown, select \Dpd{Outside Tails} and enter \TypeIn{0.025}
  in each tail box.
\end{itemize}

Because we are using the inverse probability function, the calculator
returns the boundary values of \(X\) that leave probability \(0.025\) in
each tail. These boundaries determine the two-sided critical region.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_dialogs/Proportion_inference/social-rejection-dialog.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-social-rejection-dialog}Rguroo Probability
Calculator Settings for the Social Media Critical Region Example}

\end{figure}%

The output, shown in Figure~\ref{fig-social-rejection}, gives
\[P(X \leq 2) + P(X \geq 9) = 0.1032 \geq 0.05,\] with the additional
note that \[P(X \leq 2) = 0.05281, \quad P(X \geq 9) = 0.05038,\]
\[P(X \leq 1) = 0.01168, \quad P(X \geq 10) = 0.01545.\]

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/social_rejection.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-social-rejection}Rguroo Probability Calculator
Output for the Social Media Critical Region Example}

\end{figure}%

The decision rule \(X \leq 2\) or \(X \geq 9\) exceeds our significance
level of \(\alpha = 0.05.\) Moving one step further in each tail, the
decision rule \(X \leq 1\) or \(X \geq 10\) satisfies our significance
level since
\[P(X \leq 1) + P(X \geq 10) = 0.01168 + 0.01545 = 0.02713 \leq 0.05.$
 Therefore, the critical region at significance level $\alpha = 0.05$ is \]X
\leq 1 \quad \text{or} \quad X \geq 10.\$\$ That is, if we observe 1 or
fewer, or 10 or more students in our sample of \(n = 15\) who use social
media as their primary news source, we reject \(H_0\) in favor of
\(H_a: p \neq 0.36.\)

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsubsection{Using Probability Calculator to Compute the
p-Value}\label{using-probability-calculator-to-compute-the-p-value}

We now illustrate how to compute the p-value and use it to make a
decision, starting with the two one-sided examples that we have seen.

\begin{example}[YouTube Use: Computing the p-Value and Making a
Decision]\protect\hypertarget{exm-youtube-pvalue-calc}{}\label{exm-youtube-pvalue-calc}

In the YouTube Use example (Example~\ref{exm-youtube-ppss}), we are
testing \(H_0: p \leq 0.70\) versus \(H_a: p > 0.70,\) where \(p\) is
the true proportion of students in the district who use YouTube daily. A
random sample of \(n = 20\) students is selected and
\(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\) report daily YouTube use.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Obtain the \(H_a\) support.
\item
  Compute the p-value.
\item
  At significance level \(\alpha = 0.05,\) make a decision and state
  your conclusion in the context of the problem.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. \textbf{Obtain the \(H_a\) support.}

Since \(H_a: p > 0.70,\) values of \(X\) that are at least as supportive
of \(H_a\) as \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\) are values greater than or equal
to 17. Therefore the \(H_a\) support is \(\{17, 18, 19, 20\}.\)

b. \textbf{Compute the p-value.}

The p-value is computed at the boundary value \(p_0 = 0.70\):
\[\text{p-value} = P(X \geq 17 \mid p = 0.70).\]

We compute this probability using Rguroo's Discrete Distributions
Probability Calculator with \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(20, 0.70).\)

Figure~\ref{fig-youtube-pvalue-calc} shows the Rguroo dialog and the
output, giving

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\[\text{p-value} = P(X \geq 17 \mid p = 0.70) \approx 0.1071.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{figure}

\begin{minipage}{0.50\linewidth}

\includegraphics[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_dialogs/Proportion_inference/youtube_pvalue_dialog.png}

\subcaption{\label{}Rguroo dialog for computing the p-value}
\end{minipage}%
%
\begin{minipage}{0.50\linewidth}

\includegraphics[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/youtube_pvalue.png}

\subcaption{\label{}Rguroo output showing the p-value}
\end{minipage}%

\caption{\label{fig-youtube-pvalue-calc}Rguroo setup (left) and p-value
output (right) for the YouTube example.}

\end{figure}%

c. \textbf{Make a decision.}

Since the p-value \(0.1071 > \alpha = 0.05,\) we fail to reject \(H_0.\)
The data do not provide sufficient evidence at the 5\% significance
level to conclude that more than 70\% of students in the district use
YouTube daily. Note that this conclusion is consistent with the critical
region approach: \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\) does not fall in the critical
region \(X \geq 18\) determined in
Example~\ref{exm-youtube-rejection-calc}.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Physical Inactivity: Computing the p-Value and Making a
Decision]\protect\hypertarget{exm-inactivity-pvalue-calc}{}\label{exm-inactivity-pvalue-calc}

In the Physical Inactivity example
(Example~\ref{exm-physical-inactivity-ppss}), we are testing
\(H_0: p \geq 0.35\) versus \(H_a: p < 0.35,\) where \(p\) is the true
proportion of adults in the population who are physically inactive. A
random sample of \(n = 50\) adults is selected and
\(x_{\text{obs}} = 10\) are found to be physically inactive.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Obtain the \(H_a\) support.
\item
  Compute the p-value.
\item
  At significance level \(\alpha = 0.05,\) make a decision and state
  your conclusion in the context of the problem.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. \textbf{Obtain the \(H_a\) support.}

Since \(H_a: p < 0.35,\) values of \(X\) that are at least as supportive
of \(H_a\) as \(x_{\text{obs}} = 10\) are values less than or equal to
10. Therefore the \(H_a\) support is \(\{0, 1, \ldots, 10\}.\)

b. \textbf{Compute the p-value.}

The p-value is computed at the boundary value \(p_0 = 0.35\):
\[\text{p-value} = P(X \leq 10 \mid p = 0.35).\]

We compute this probability using Rguroo's Discrete Probability
Calculator with \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(50, 0.35).\)
Figure~\ref{fig-inactivity-pvalue-calc} shows the Rguroo dialog setup
(left panel) and the Rguroo output (right panel) giving

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\[\text{p-value} = P(X \leq 10 \mid p = 0.35) \approx 0.0160.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{figure}

\begin{minipage}{0.50\linewidth}

\includegraphics[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_dialogs/Proportion_inference/inactivity_pvalue_dialog.png}

\subcaption{\label{}Rguroo dialog for computing the p-value}
\end{minipage}%
%
\begin{minipage}{0.50\linewidth}

\includegraphics[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/inactivity_pvalue.png}

\subcaption{\label{}Rguroo output showing the p-value}
\end{minipage}%

\caption{\label{fig-inactivity-pvalue-calc}Rguroo setup (left) and
p-value output (right) for the Physical Inactivity example.}

\end{figure}%

c. \textbf{Make a decision.}

Since the p-value \(0.0160 < \alpha = 0.05,\) we reject \(H_0\) in favor
of \(H_a: p < 0.35.\) The data provide sufficient evidence at the 5\%
significance level to conclude that fewer than 35\% of adults in the
population are physically inactive. Note that this conclusion is
consistent with the critical region approach: \(x_{\text{obs}} = 10\)
falls in the critical region \(X \leq 11\) determined in
Example~\ref{exm-inactivity-rejection-calc}.

\end{tcolorbox}

The two-sided case requires a bit more care. Since \(H_a: p \neq p_0\)
does not specify a direction, evidence against \(H_0\) can come from
either tail of the distribution. Recall from Case 3 that a value \(x\)
is in the \(H_a\) support if
\(P(X = x \mid p = p_0) \leq P(X = x_{\text{obs}} \mid p = p_0),\) that
is, if it is at least as unlikely as \(x_{\text{obs}}\) under \(H_0.\)

\begin{example}[Social Media as a Primary News Source: Computing the
p-Value and Making a
Decision]\protect\hypertarget{exm-social-pvalue-calc}{}\label{exm-social-pvalue-calc}

In the Social Media as a Primary News Source example
(Example~\ref{exm-social-media-news-ppss}), we are testing
\(H_0: p = 0.36\) versus \(H_a: p \neq 0.36,\) where \(p\) is the true
proportion of students who use social media as their primary news
source. A random sample of \(n = 15\) students is selected and
\(x_{\text{obs}} = 9\) report using social media as their primary news
source.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Obtain the \(H_a\) support.
\item
  Compute the p-value.
\item
  At significance level \(\alpha = 0.05,\) make a decision and state
  your conclusion in the context of the problem.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. \textbf{Obtain the \(H_a\) support.}

Since \(H_a: p \neq 0.36,\) values of \(X\) that are at least as
supportive of \(H_a\) as the observed value \(x_{\text{obs}} = 9\) are
those that are at least as unlikely as \(x_{\text{obs}} = 9\) under
\(H_0.\) That is, the \(H_a\) support consists of \(x_{\text{obs}} = 9\)
and all values \(x\) for which \[
P(X = x \mid p = 0.36) \leq P(X = 9 \mid p = 0.36).
\]

Figure Figure~\ref{fig-social-pvalue-calc} shows the Rguroo dialog and
output used to compute \(P(X = x \mid p = 0.36).\) The probability of
the observed value is \(P(X = 9 \mid p = 0.36) \approx 0.0349.\)
Therefore, any value of \(x\) with probability less than or equal to
\(0.0349\) is included in the \(H_a\) support, in addition to
\(x_{\text{obs}} = 9.\)

From the graph, the \(H_a\) support consists of \(\{0, 1\}\) in the left
tail and \(\{9, 10, 11, \ldots, 15\}\) in the right tail.

Note that the graph is truncated at \(X = 12,\) since the probabilities
for values greater than 12 are extremely small.

\section{Confidence Interval for a Population
Proportion}\label{sec-confidence-interval-one-pop}

Recall from Section~\ref{sec-foundations-confidence-intervals} that a
confidence interval gives us a range of plausible values for a
population parameter. In this section, our parameter is the population
proportion \(p,\) and we use the sample proportion \(\hat{p}\) as our
estimate of it. Because \(\hat{p}\) varies from sample to sample, we do
not expect it to equal \(p\) exactly. Instead, we use the observed
sample proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) to construct an interval of
plausible values for \(p.\)

As discussed in Section~\ref{sec-foundations-confidence-intervals}, the
confidence level describes the long-run success rate of the method used
to construct the interval. For example, a 95\% confidence interval comes
from a method that captures the true value of \(p\) in about 95\% of
repeated samples. In practice, however, we collect one sample and
construct one interval.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Confidence Level}\vspace{3mm}

Imagine that we repeatedly take random samples from the same population
and construct a confidence interval for \(p\) using the same method each
time. Because the samples differ, the intervals will also differ. Some
intervals will contain the true population proportion \(p,\) while
others will not.

The confidence level tells us the percentage of these intervals that we
expect to contain the true value of \(p.\) For example, a 95\%
confidence level means that, over many repeated samples, about 95\% of
the intervals constructed using this method would contain the true
population proportion \(p.\)

\end{tcolorbox}

Recall from Section~\ref{sec-foundations-confidence-intervals} that we
can construct a confidence interval by inverting a two-sided hypothesis
test. For a population proportion, we consider different candidate
values \(p_0\) and test \(H_0: p=p_0\) versus \(H_a:p\neq p_0\).

If we fail to reject \(H_0,\) our data are consistent with \(p_0,\) so
we consider \(p_0\) a plausible value for \(p.\) If we reject \(H_0,\)
we do not consider \(p_0\) plausible. We repeat this process for
different values of \(p_0.\) The collection of all values for which we
fail to reject \(H_0\) forms our confidence interval.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Confidence Interval by Test Inversion}\vspace{3mm}

A \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(p\) consists of
all candidate values \(p_0\) for which we fail to reject

\[
H_0:p=p_0
\]

in a two-sided hypothesis test at significance level \(\alpha.\)

\end{tcolorbox}

The following example illustrates this idea by testing a grid of values
of \(p_0\) and identifying which ones are consistent with the observed
data.

\begin{example}[Daily YouTube Use Among Teens: Building a Confidence
Interval from a
Grid]\protect\hypertarget{exm-youtube-ci-grid}{}\label{exm-youtube-ci-grid}

Recall Example~\ref{exm-youtube-ppss}. A sample of \(n = 20\) students
produced \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\) daily YouTube users, giving an observed
sample proportion of \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 17/20 = 0.85.\)

For each candidate value of \(p_0\) shown in the grid below, carry out
the two-sided hypothesis test \(H_0: p = p_0\) versus
\(H_a: p \neq p_0\) at significance level \(\alpha = 0.05,\) using the
binomial distribution with \(n = 20\) and \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17.\) Based
on the results, identify the range of values of \(p_0\) for which we
fail to reject \(H_0.\)

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{index_files/mediabag/Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/confidence_interval_grid_number_line_simple.pdf}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

For each candidate value of \(p_0\) in the grid, we compute the
two-sided p-value using the binomial distribution
\(X \sim \text{Binomial}(20, p_0).\) The p-value is the probability of
observing values of \(X\) that are at least as supportive of \(H_a\) as
the observed value \(x_{\text{obs}}=17,\) assuming \(H_0\) is true. We
then compare each p-value to \(\alpha = 0.05\) to decide whether to
reject or fail to reject \(H_0.\)

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\(p_0\) & p-value & Decision \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0.55 & 0.006 & Reject \(H_0\) \\
0.60 & 0.022 & Reject \(H_0\) \\
0.65 & 0.064 & Fail to reject \(H_0\) \\
0.70 & 0.220 & Fail to reject \(H_0\) \\
0.75 & 0.439 & Fail to reject \(H_0\) \\
0.80 & 0.781 & Fail to reject \(H_0\) \\
0.85 & 1.000 & Fail to reject \(H_0\) \\
0.90 & 0.445 & Fail to reject \(H_0\) \\
0.95 & 0.075 & Fail to reject \(H_0\) \\
0.99 & 0.001 & Reject \(H_0\) \\
\end{longtable}

The graph below shows the result graphically:

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{index_files/mediabag/Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/confidence_interval_grid_number_line.pdf}

As shown in the table and the graph, we fail to reject \(H_0\) for
candidate values of \(p_0\) ranging from 0.65 to 0.95, and reject
\(H_0\) for the candidate values 0.55, 0.60 and 0.99. Based on this
grid, the range of plausible values for \(p\) is approximately \(0.65\)
to \(0.95.\)

This gives us an approximate 95\% confidence interval based on the
candidate values in our grid. If we tested more closely spaced values of
\(p_0,\) we could locate the endpoints of the confidence interval more
precisely.

\end{tcolorbox}

The confidence interval that we obtained in the example above is an
approximation to the collection of values of \(p_0\) that are consistent
with our observed data at significance level \(\alpha = 0.05.\) Notice
that the interval is not symmetric around
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.85\): it extends further below
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) (down to approximately 0.65) than above it (up
to approximately 0.95). This asymmetry is not surprising when the sample
proportion is close to 0 or 1. Recall the large-sample condition from
Section~\ref{sec-large-sample-one-prop}. Using
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.85\) as our estimate of \(p,\) we compute:
\[n\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 20 \times 0.85 = 17 \geq 10,\] but
\[n(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}) = 20 \times 0.15 = 3 < 10.
\]

The large-sample condition fails because there are 3 observed failures.
With a relatively small sample and a sample proportion close to 1, the
binomial distribution can be noticeably skewed rather than approximately
normal. As a result, an exact confidence interval need not be symmetric
around \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}.\) A method based on a symmetric normal
approximation may not work well in this situation.

This example illustrates that the choice of method for constructing a
confidence interval matters. In the subsections that follow, we study
two methods in detail. We begin in Section~\ref{sec-ci-large-sample}
with the large-sample method, which uses the normal approximation and
produces a confidence interval that is symmetric around
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}.\) We consider this method first because it is
widely used in practice and builds directly on the large-sample methods
we have already developed for hypothesis testing. When the large-sample
condition is satisfied, the normal approximation generally works well;
however, it may be misleading when the condition is not satisfied, as in
this example.

We then consider the exact binomial method in
Section~\ref{sec-ci-binomial}. This method does not rely on the normal
approximation and can produce an asymmetric confidence interval. It is
particularly useful when the large-sample condition is not satisfied.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Symmetry of the Normal-Approximation Interval}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

Because the normal distribution is symmetric, the large-sample
confidence interval we will construct is symmetric around
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}.\) In contrast, an exact binomial confidence
interval does not need to be symmetric. This difference can be
especially noticeable when the sample size is small or
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) is close to 0 or 1.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Confidence Interval Based on the Large Sample Normal
Approximation}\label{sec-ci-large-sample}

We begin with the large-sample method for constructing a confidence
interval for a population proportion. This method uses the normal
approximation to the sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\) and is one of
the most commonly used methods for confidence intervals for a
proportion. It also builds directly on the large-sample methods we used
earlier for hypothesis testing.

Recall from Section~\ref{sec-large-sample-one-prop} that when the large
sample condition is satisfied, the sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\)
is approximately normal. We can use this normal distribution to
determine how far we should extend on either side of the observed sample
proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) to obtain a range of plausible
values for \(p.\)

To construct the interval, we first need to estimate the variability of
\(\hat{p}.\) Recall that the standard deviation of the sampling
distribution of \(\hat{p}\) is \[\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}.\] Because the
population proportion \(p\) is unknown, we use the observed sample
proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) in its place. The resulting estimate
of the standard deviation is called the standard error of \(\hat{p}\):
\[\text{SE}(\hat{p}) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}(1 - \hat{p}_{\text{obs}})}{n}}.\]

For a confidence interval, we check the large sample condition using
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\):
\[n\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \geq 10 \qquad \text{and} \qquad
n(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}) \geq 10.\]

When this condition is satisfied, the \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\)
confidence interval for \(p\) takes the form

\[\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \pm z^* \times \text{SE}(\hat{p}),\]

where \(z^*\) is the \textbf{critical value} from the standard normal
distribution corresponding to the desired confidence level.

The quantity \(z^* \times \text{SE}(\hat{p})\) is called the
\textbf{margin of error}. It tells us how far we extend below and above
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) when constructing the interval. A larger margin
of error produces a wider interval and reflects greater uncertainty in
our estimate of \(p.\)

Common critical values are:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Confidence Level & \(\alpha\) & \(z^*\) \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
90\% & 0.10 & 1.645 \\
95\% & 0.05 & 1.960 \\
99\% & 0.01 & 2.576 \\
\end{longtable}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Large Sample Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

When the large sample condition \(n\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \geq 10\) and
\(n(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}) \geq 10\) is satisfied, an approximate
\((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(p\) is:

\[\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \pm \underbrace{z^* \times
\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}})}{n}}}_{\text{margin of error}},\]

which gives the interval

\[\left(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} - z^* \times
\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}})}{n}},\;
\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} + z^* \times
\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}})}{n}}\right).\]

This interval is always symmetric around \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}.\) When
the large sample condition is satisfied, the normal approximation
generally works well; when it is not, the resulting confidence interval
may be misleading.

\end{tcolorbox}

As we saw in the example above, increasing the confidence level resulted
in a wider confidence interval. This illustrates an important
relationship between confidence level and interval width.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Confidence Level and Interval Width}\vspace{3mm}

For the same sample size and observed sample proportion, a higher
confidence level produces a wider confidence interval. To be more
confident that the interval captures the true population proportion, we
must include a wider range of plausible values for \(p.\) This wider
interval reflects the tradeoff we make to be more confident that the
interval captures the true population proportion.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Social Media as a Primary News Source: Large Sample
Confidence
Interval]\protect\hypertarget{exm-social-ci-large-sample}{}\label{exm-social-ci-large-sample}

Recall Example~\ref{exm-social-media-pvalue-large-sample}. A sample of
\(n = 35\) students produced \(x_{\text{obs}} = 21\) who reported using
social media as their primary news source, giving an observed sample
proportion of \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 21/35 = 0.60.\)

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\item
  Check the 10-10 rule and determine whether the large sample normal
  approximation applies.
\item
  Use Rguroo's \Fun{One-Population Proportion} inference function to
  obtain a 95\% large sample normal approximation confidence interval
  for the true proportion of students at the university who get most of
  their news from social media.
\item
  What is the margin of error for this interval?
\item
  In Example~\ref{exm-social-media-pvalue-large-sample}, we tested the
  hypotheses \[
  \begin{cases}
  H_0: p = 0.36 \\
  H_a: p \neq 0.36.
  \end{cases}
  \]
\end{enumerate}

Based on the confidence interval that you obtained in part (b), is
\(p=0.36\) a plausible value for the true proportion of students at the
university who get most of their news from social media? How does your
conclusion here compare to the conclusion from the hypothesis test in
Example~\ref{exm-social-media-pvalue-large-sample}?

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. \[n\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 35 \times 0.6 = 21 \geq 10, \;
\text{and} \,
n(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}) = 35 \times 0.4 = 14 \geq 10.\]

Both quantities satisfy the 10-10 rule. Therefore, the large sample
normal approximation is appropriate.

b. The following is a screenshot of the
\Dialog{One Population Proportion Inference} dialog for obtaining the
large sample normal confidence interval for this example.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_dialogs/Proportion_inference/normal-ci-social_dialog.png}

}

\caption{Rguroo Basics dialog showing how to obtain large sample normal
CI}

\end{figure}%

Click to expand the box below to see the Rguroo output.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo output: One-Population Proportion Inference Output - Social Media}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\end{tcolorbox}

From the Rguroo output, the 95\% large sample confidence interval for
\(p\) is \((0.4377, 0.7623).\) We are 95\% confident that the true
proportion of students at the university who get most of their news from
social media is between 0.438 (43.8\%) and 0.762 (76.2\%).

c. From the Rguroo output, the standard error is \(0.0828079.\) For a
95\% confidence level, \(z^*= 1.96.\) Using these two values,

\[\text{Margin of Error} = 0.0828079\times 1.96 \approx 0.1623\] The
Rguroo output also reports the width of the interval as \(0.324601.\)
Using this value, you can also obtain the margin of error as
\[\text{Margin of Error}=\frac{\text{width of the interval}}{2} = \frac{0.324601}{2}\approx 0.1623.\]

Note that the confidence interval is symmetric around the observed
sample proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.60,\) and it extends below
and above \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) by the margin of error \(0.1623.\)
Therefore the width of the interval is
\(2 \times 0.1623 \approx 0.3246.\) In general, for confidence intervals
that use the large sample normal approximation, the width of the
interval is always twice the margin of error.

d. The interval \((0.4377, 0.7623)\) does not contain the null value of
0.36, so 0.36 is not a plausible value for \(p.\) This is consistent
with the result of the hypothesis test in
Example~\ref{exm-social-media-pvalue-large-sample}, where we rejected
the null hypothesis \(H_0:p=0.36.\)

\end{tcolorbox}

As we saw in Example~\ref{exm-social-ci-large-sample}, the 95\%
confidence interval did not contain the null value \(p_0=0.36,\) and the
corresponding two-sided hypothesis test at \(\alpha=0.05\) rejected
\(H_0:p=0.36.\) This is not a coincidence. Recall from
Section~\ref{sec-foundations-confidence-intervals} that a confidence
interval can be constructed by inverting a two-sided hypothesis test.

More generally, a \((1-\alpha)\times100\%\) confidence interval and a
two-sided hypothesis test at significance level \(\alpha\) lead to the
same decision. If the null value \(p_0\) is inside the confidence
interval, it is a plausible value for \(p\) based on the observed data,
and we fail to reject \(H_0.\) If \(p_0\) is outside the confidence
interval, it is not a plausible value for \(p,\) and we reject \(H_0.\)

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Using a Confidence Interval to Make a Decision}\vspace{3mm}

For a two-sided hypothesis test \[
H_0:p=p_0
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
H_a:p\neq p_0,
\] at significance level \(\alpha,\) use the corresponding
\((1-\alpha)\times100%
\) confidence interval: If \(p_0\) is inside the confidence interval,
fail to reject \(H_0.\) If \(p_0\) is outside the confidence interval,
reject \(H_0.\) For example, a two-sided test at \(\alpha=0.05\)
corresponds to a 95\% confidence interval.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Confidence Interval Based on the Exact Binomial
Method}\label{sec-ci-binomial}

As we saw in Example~\ref{exm-youtube-ci-grid}, we can construct a
confidence interval for the population proportion \(p\) by testing a
grid of null hypotheses \(H_0: p = p_0\) and collecting all values of
\(p_0\) for which we fail to reject \(H_0.\) When this approach uses the
exact binomial distribution to carry out each test, the resulting
interval is called the \textbf{exact binomial confidence interval}. As
we noted in that example, this method has an important advantage: it
correctly reflects any asymmetry in the data, which can occur when the
large sample condition fails and the binomial distribution is skewed.

Of course, testing every conceivable value of \(p_0\) between 0 and 1 is
not practical. Fortunately, efficient algorithms can locate the exact
endpoints of the interval directly, without testing each value one by
one. These algorithms are implemented in Rguroo, making it
straightforward to obtain the exact binomial confidence interval in
practice. The following example illustrates how.

\begin{example}[Daily YouTube Use Among Teens: Exact Binomial Confidence
Interval]\protect\hypertarget{exm-youtube-ci-binomial}{}\label{exm-youtube-ci-binomial}

Recall Example~\ref{exm-youtube-ppss}. A sample of \(n = 20\) students
produced \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\) daily YouTube users, giving a sample
proportion of \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 17/20 = 0.85.\)

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\item
  Check the 10-10 rule to determine whether we can use the large sample
  normal approximation for this problem?
\item
  Use Rguroo's \Fun{One-Population Proportion} inference function to
  construct a 95\% exact binomial confidence interval for the true
  proportion of students in the district who use YouTube daily, and
  interpret the interval in the context of the problem.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. To check whether the large sample normal approximation is
appropriate, we apply the 10-10 rule: \[
\begin{aligned}
n\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}
&=20(0.85)=17\geq10,\\
n(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}})
&=20(0.15)=3<10.
\end{aligned}
\] The second condition is not satisfied because there are only 3
observed failures. Therefore, the large sample normal approximation is
not appropriate for this example.

From the Rguroo output, the 95\% exact binomial confidence interval for
\(p\) is \((0.628, 0.958).\) The following is an interpretation of this
interval:

We are 95\% confident that the true proportion of students in the
district who use YouTube daily is between 0.628 (62.8\%) and 0.958
(95.8\%).

Notice that this interval is consistent with what we found using the
grid in Example~\ref{exm-youtube-ci-grid}, where we identified the range
of plausible values as approximately 0.65 to 0.95. The exact interval
extends the lower endpoint to 0.628, which lies between the grid values
0.60 and 0.65, where the p-value crossed the 0.05 threshold, just as we
anticipated. The upper endpoint, 0.958, also agrees with the grid
analysis, which placed the upper crossing between 0.95 (fail to reject)
and 0.99 (reject). Thus, the grid approach gave us a good approximation
to the range of plausible values, while the exact binomial method
determines the endpoints more precisely.

Notice that the exact binomial interval is not symmetric around
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}=0.85.\) Its midpoint, as reported in the Rguroo
output, is approximately 0.793. Unlike the normal-approximation
interval, the exact binomial interval does not need to be centered at
the observed sample proportion.

\end{tcolorbox}

From the Rguroo output, the 95\% exact binomial confidence interval for
\(p\) is \((0.3325, 0.8091).\) We are 95\% confident that the true
proportion of students at the university who get most of their news from
social media is between 0.3325 (33.25\%) and 0.8091 (80.91\%).

The midpoint of the interval is reported as 0.571, which is not equal to
the observed sample proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.60.\) This is
because the exact binomial confidence interval does not need to be
symmetric around the observed sample proportion, unlike the large sample
normal approximation confidence interval, especially when the 10-10 rule
is not satisfied, as is the case here. The 10-10 rule is not satisfied
because \(n\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 15(0.6) = 9 < 10\) and
\(n(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}) = 15(0.4) = 6 < 10.\)

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Hypothesis Testing for Two
Proportions}\label{sec-hyp-test-two-prop}

Many important research questions require comparing proportions between
two groups. In medical research, clinical trials compare treatment
outcomes between patients receiving a new therapy and those receiving a
placebo or standard care. In the social sciences, researchers
investigate differences between demographic groups. In educational
research, teachers evaluate whether new instructional methods outperform
traditional approaches. Understanding how to compare two population
proportions allows us to evaluate whether observed differences in sample
data reflect genuine population differences or are due to chance
variation.

Consider a few recent examples: A Phase 3 trial of the mRNA-1273 vaccine
(Moderna) with over 30,000 participants found that 0.4\% of the
vaccinated group developed symptomatic COVID-19 compared to 4.9\% in the
placebo group---a substantial difference. A 2022 study examining 1,166
articles in \emph{Political Psychology} found that 35.1\% of lead
authors were women compared to 64.9\% men, highlighting a gender gap in
academic publishing. In each case, researchers collected data from two
independent samples, observed different sample proportions, and found
statistical evidence that the population proportions differed.

While these large-scale studies demonstrate striking differences, many
research questions involve smaller samples and more subtle effects where
the statistical evidence is less clear-cut. In this section, we develop
the concepts and tools for comparing two population proportions by
working with examples where the answer is not immediately obvious and
careful statistical reasoning is required.

We extend the hypothesis testing framework from one proportion to two
proportions. The same core concepts---null and alternative hypotheses,
test statistics, p-values, Type I and Type II errors, and significance
levels---continue to apply. However, we now focus on the
\textbf{difference between two population proportions} rather than a
single proportion.

\subsection{The Null and Alternative
Hypotheses}\label{the-null-and-alternative-hypotheses}

To develop these concepts and tools, we'll work with four examples: an
educational intervention comparing instructional approaches for teaching
proportional reasoning, a health behavior study evaluating text message
reminders for medication adherence, a workplace wellness program
assessing nicotine patches for smoking cessation, and an analysis of
gender differences in attitudes toward marijuana legalization from the
General Social Survey.

When comparing two population proportions, we focus on the difference
between them. We have two populations---let's call one population 1 and
the other population 2. It does not matter which population you
designate as population 1 and which as population 2, as long as you
clearly define your choice. We denote the population proportion for
population 1 by \(p_1\) and the population proportion for population 2
by \(p_2.\) Our goal is to make inferences about the difference between
these proportions: \(p_1 - p_2.\) To do this, we begin by formulating
hypotheses about this difference.

Just as in the one-population case, we can formulate both one-sided and
two-sided tests. The three cases are:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Case 1: } 
&\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 \leq p_2 \\
H_a: p_1 > p_2
\end{cases}
\qquad
\text{Case 2: } 
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 \geq p_2 \\
H_a: p_1 < p_2
\end{cases} \\
\\
\text{Case 3: } 
&\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 = p_2 \\
H_a: p_1 \neq p_2
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]

We can equivalently write these hypotheses in terms of the difference
\(p_1 - p_2\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Case 1: } 
&\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 - p_2 \leq 0 \\
H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0
\end{cases}
\qquad
\text{Case 2: } 
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 - p_2 \geq 0 \\
H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0
\end{cases} \\
\\
\text{Case 3: } 
&\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0 \\
H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]

Cases 1 and 2 are one-sided tests, while Case 3 is a two-sided test. In
practice, the choice of case depends on the research
question---specifically, whether we are testing for an increase, a
decrease, or any difference. Let's see how to set up the hypotheses for
each of our examples.

\begin{example}[Schema-Based Instruction: Stating
Hypotheses]\protect\hypertarget{exm-schema-hypotheses}{}\label{exm-schema-hypotheses}

Researchers want to know whether a new schema-based instructional
approach improves seventh-grade students' mastery of proportional
reasoning compared to traditional instruction. They randomly assign
\(n_1=50\) students to the new approach and \(n_2=50\) students to
traditional instruction. Let \(p_1\) represent the proportion of all
students who would achieve mastery under the new approach, and \(p_2\)
represent the proportion who would achieve mastery under traditional
instruction. State the appropriate null and alternative hypotheses to
address the research question.

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

Since the researchers want to know whether the new approach
\emph{improves} mastery (that is, whether \(p_1 > p_2\)), this is a Case
1 situation. The hypotheses are:

\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 \leq p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_0: p_1 - p_2 \leq 0\\
H_a: p_1 > p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0
\end{cases}
\]

The null hypothesis states that the new approach is no better than (or
is worse than) traditional instruction. The alternative hypothesis
states that the new approach produces a higher mastery rate.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Text Message Reminders: Stating
Hypotheses]\protect\hypertarget{exm-text-hypotheses}{}\label{exm-text-hypotheses}

Researchers are piloting a text message reminder system for diabetes
patients. They want to know whether daily text reminders improve
medication adherence compared to standard care, but they're also open to
the possibility that the reminders might perform worse (perhaps by being
annoying or overwhelming). They randomly assign \(n_1=40\) patients to
receive text reminders and \(n_2=50\) patients to receive standard care.
Let \(p_1\) represent the proportion of all patients who would have good
adherence with text reminders, and \(p_2\) represent the proportion who
would have good adherence with standard care. State the appropriate null
and alternative hypotheses.

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

Since the researchers have no strong directional prediction and want to
detect a difference in either direction, this is a Case 3 situation. The
hypotheses are:

\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 = p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0\\
H_a: p_1 \neq p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0
\end{cases}
\]

The null hypothesis states that the difference between the two
population proportions, \(p_1\) and \(p_2,\) is zero. A difference of
zero means that the two population proportions are equal, so there is no
difference in adherence rates between the two approaches. The
alternative hypothesis states that the difference is not zero, meaning
that the adherence rates differ between the two approaches.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Smoking Cessation: Stating
Hypotheses]\protect\hypertarget{exm-smoking-hypotheses}{}\label{exm-smoking-hypotheses}

A workplace wellness program is comparing two approaches to smoking
cessation. Employees are randomly assigned to either receive free
nicotine patches (60 employees - Group 1) or participate in a
self-guided quitting program (60 employees - Group 2). However, the
researchers believe that the self-guided approach might actually be more
effective because it emphasizes personal commitment and doesn't rely on
external aids. Let \(p_1\) represent the proportion of all employees who
would quit smoking with nicotine patches, and \(p_2\) represent the
proportion who would quit with the self-guided approach. State the
appropriate null and alternative hypotheses to test whether the
self-guided approach is more effective.

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

Since the researchers want to test whether the self-guided approach is
\emph{more effective} than nicotine patches (that is, whether
\(p_2 > p_1,\) or equivalently \(p_1 < p_2\)), this is a Case 2
situation. The hypotheses are:

\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 \geq p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_0: p_1 - p_2 \geq 0\\
H_a: p_1 < p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0
\end{cases}
\]

The null hypothesis states that nicotine patches are at least as
effective as (or more effective than) the self-guided approach. The
alternative hypothesis states that the self-guided approach produces a
higher quit rate.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[GSS 2024: Gender and Marijuana
Legalization]\protect\hypertarget{exm-gss-hypotheses}{}\label{exm-gss-hypotheses}

The General Social Survey (GSS) is a long-running national survey that
monitors societal change and studies the growing complexity of American
society. In a representative sample from the GSS 2024 data, there are
\(n_1=204\) females and \(n_2=184\) males who were asked whether they
support the legalization of marijuana. Of the 204 females, 142 said they
support legalization. Of the 184 males, 140 said they support
legalization. Researchers want to know whether this sample provides
evidence that the proportion of females who support legalization differs
from the proportion of males who support legalization. Let \(p_1\)
represent the proportion of females in the population who support
legalization, and \(p_2\) represent the proportion of males who support
legalization. State the appropriate null and alternative hypotheses.

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

Since the researchers want to know whether the proportions \emph{differ}
(in either direction) without specifying which gender should have higher
support, this is a Case 3 situation. The hypotheses are:

\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 = p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0\\
H_a: p_1 \neq p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0
\end{cases}
\]

The null hypothesis states that females and males support marijuana
legalization at the same rate. The alternative hypothesis states that
the support rates differ between the two groups.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Data, Statistic, and Sampling
Distribution}\label{sec-data-stat-dist}

To make inferences about \(p_1 - p_2,\) we collect a sample of size
\(n_1\) from population 1 and a sample of size \(n_2\) from population
2. Note that these sample sizes don't have to be equal---researchers
often work with unequal group sizes due to practical constraints or
deliberate design choices.

Let \(X_1\) denote the number of successes (favorable outcomes) in our
sample from population 1, and let \(X_2\) denote the number of successes
in our sample from population 2. Although we could compare the counts
through \(X_1-X_2,\) differences in counts are difficult to analyze and
can be misleading when the sample sizes differ. Instead, we compare
sample proportions and rely on the Central Limit Theorem for large
samples.

The sample proportions are \(\hat{p}_1 = X_1/n_1\) and
\(\hat{p}_2 = X_2/n_2.\) These are our point estimates of \(p_1\) and
\(p_2,\) respectively. To make inferences about the difference
\(p_1 - p_2,\) we naturally use the difference in sample proportions:
\(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2.\)

\textbf{The Sampling Distribution of \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\)}

When the sample sizes \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) are both sufficiently large,
the Central Limit Theorem tells us that the sampling distribution of
\(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) is approximately normal. The rule of thumb for
``sufficiently large'' is that each group must have at least 10
successes and 10 failures: \(n_1\hat{p}_1 \geq 10,\)
\(n_1(1-\hat{p}_1) \geq 10,\) \(n_2\hat{p}_2 \geq 10,\) and
\(n_2(1-\hat{p}_2) \geq 10.\)

When these conditions are met, the sampling distribution of
\(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) is approximately normal with mean
\(p_1 - p_2\) and standard error

\[
\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \sim N\left(p_1 - p_2, \; \text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2)\right),
\] where \[
\text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}}.
\]

Notice that the variability depends on both sample sizes and population
proportions.

\textbf{Simplification Under the Null Hypothesis}

Recall that when testing hypotheses, we work at the boundary of the null
hypothesis, since the Type I error is maximized there. For all three
cases above, the boundary value is \(p_1 - p_2 = 0,\) which means
\(p_1 = p_2.\)

At this boundary, the two population proportions are equal. We denote
their common value by \(p,\) so that \(p_1=p_2=p.\) As a result, the
standard error simplifies to:

\[
\text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2)
= \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n_1} + \frac{p(1-p)}{n_2}}
= \sqrt{p(1-p)\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}.
\]

Therefore, under the null hypothesis, the sampling distribution of
\(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) is:

\[
\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \sim N\left(0, \; \sqrt{p(1-p)\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}\right).
\]

This is the distribution we will use for hypothesis testing.

\textbf{Estimating the Common Proportion}

There is one practical issue: we do not know \(p,\) the common
population proportion under \(H_0.\) Because \(H_0\) assumes that
\(p_1=p_2,\) we treat the two samples as coming from populations with
the same proportion. We therefore combine the number of successes from
both samples and divide by the combined sample size. This gives us an
estimate of the common population proportion called the \textbf{pooled
sample proportion}: \[\hat{p} = \frac{X_1 + X_2}{n_1 + n_2}.\]

Using \(\hat{p}\) in place of \(p\) gives the \textbf{estimated standard
error}:

\[
\widehat{\text{SE}}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) 
= \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}.
\]

This estimated standard error is used in our test statistic and in
determining critical regions and p-values, just as we did in the
one-population case.

The following example works through all of these computations for one of
our four studies. The remaining three are summarized in
Table~\ref{tbl-two-prop-summary}.

\begin{example}[Schema-Based Instruction: Computing the Key
Quantities]\protect\hypertarget{exm-schema-quantities}{}\label{exm-schema-quantities}

In the schema-based instruction study, \(n_1=50\) students were assigned
to the new approach and \(n_2=50\) to traditional instruction. After the
intervention, 34 students in the new approach group achieved mastery,
while 24 students in the traditional instruction group achieved mastery.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Compute the sample proportions \(\hat{p}_1\) and \(\hat{p}_2\) and
  their difference.
\item
  Verify the large sample conditions.
\item
  Compute the pooled sample proportion \(\hat{p}.\)
\item
  Compute the estimated standard error of \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2.\)
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. \textbf{Sample proportions.}

\[\hat{p}_1 = \frac{34}{50} = 0.68, \qquad \hat{p}_2 = \frac{24}{50} = 0.48, \qquad \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = 0.20.\]

The new approach shows a 20 percentage point higher mastery rate in the
sample. We will test whether this provides sufficient evidence that
\(p_1 > p_2\) or whether it could reasonably arise by chance when both
approaches are equally effective.

b. \textbf{Large sample conditions.}

We check whether each group has at least 10 successes and 10 failures.

For Group 1 (new approach):

\[n_1 \hat{p}_1 = 50 \times 0.68 = 34, \qquad n_1(1 - \hat{p}_1) = 50 \times 0.32 = 16.\]

For Group 2 (traditional instruction):

\[n_2 \hat{p}_2 = 50 \times 0.48 = 24, \qquad n_2(1 - \hat{p}_2) = 50 \times 0.52 = 26.\]

All four counts are at least 10, so the large-sample conditions are
satisfied and the Central Limit Theorem applies.

c. \textbf{Pooled sample proportion.}

\[\hat{p} = \frac{34 + 24}{50 + 50} = \frac{58}{100} = 0.58.\]

Under the null hypothesis, we estimate that 58\% of students would
achieve mastery if both approaches were equally effective.

d. \textbf{Estimated standard error.}

\[
\widehat{\text{SE}}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) 
= \sqrt{0.58 \times 0.42 \times \left(\frac{1}{50} + \frac{1}{50}\right)}
= \sqrt{0.009744}
\approx 0.0987.
\]

This is the typical sample-to-sample variability in
\(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) if the null hypothesis is true.

\end{tcolorbox}

The same computations for all four studies are summarized in
Table~\ref{tbl-two-prop-summary}. We will refer back to this table when
working through hypothesis tests in the next subsection.

The \textbf{pooled sample proportion}, used under \(H_0: p_1 = p_2,\) is
\[\hat{p} = \frac{X_1 + X_2}{n_1 + n_2}.\]

\textbf{Large Sample Conditions}

The normal approximation is appropriate when each sample has at least 10
successes and 10 failures:
\[n_1\hat{p}_1 \geq 10, \quad n_1(1-\hat{p}_1) \geq 10, \quad n_2\hat{p}_2 \geq 10, \quad n_2(1-\hat{p}_2) \geq 10.\]

\textbf{Null Distribution Under \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\)}

When \(H_0\) is true and the large-sample conditions hold,
\[\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \sim N\left(0, \; \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}\right).\]

The \textbf{estimated standard error} is
\[\widehat{\text{SE}}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) = \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}.\]

This distribution and its standard error are used to compute critical
regions and p-values for all three forms of \(H_a\) (right-tailed,
left-tailed, two-tailed).

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Hypothesis Testing: p-Value and Critical Region
Approaches}\label{hypothesis-testing-p-value-and-critical-region-approaches}

As we explained earlier, there are two equivalent approaches to making
decisions in hypothesis testing: the p-value approach and the critical
region approach. We now apply both approaches to testing hypotheses
about the difference between two population proportions, \(p_1-p_2,\)
and show how to carry them out using Rguroo.

Recall that we developed the sampling distribution of
\(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2\) at the null boundary \(p_1-p_2=0\) in the
previous section. When the large-sample conditions are satisfied, we use
this approximately normal distribution, together with the pooled sample
proportion, to carry out the test. Both the p-value and critical region
approaches use this same sampling distribution to determine whether the
observed difference \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) provides sufficient
evidence against \(H_0\) and favors \(H_a.\)

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{A Note on Notation}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

In the one-sample sections, we used \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) to
distinguish the observed sample proportion from the random variable
\(\hat{p}.\) For two proportions, that notation becomes cumbersome ---
we would need \(\hat{p}_{1,\text{obs}}\) and \(\hat{p}_{2,\text{obs}}.\)
To keep the notation simpler, we use \(\hat{p}_1\) and \(\hat{p}_2\) for
both meanings. The context will make the meaning clear: when discussing
sampling distributions or probabilities, they represent random
variables; when working with the observed data or making a decision,
they represent the observed sample proportions.

\end{tcolorbox}

The p-value approach asks: ``How much support does the observed
difference provide for \(H_a\)?'' The critical region approach asks:
``Does the observed difference fall in the critical region?'' Both
approaches lead to the same conclusion, and we will use Rguroo to carry
out both approaches.

Let's examine each case in detail.

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Case 1: Right-Tailed Test
(\(H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0\))}{Case 1: Right-Tailed Test (H\_a: p\_1 - p\_2 \textgreater{} 0)}}\label{case-1-right-tailed-test-h_a-p_1---p_2-0}

In this case, we want to test whether \(p_1 > p_2.\) The alternative
hypothesis \(H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0\) is supported when
\(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) is positive, with larger positive differences
providing stronger support for \(H_a.\) Values near zero or negative
provide little or no support for \(H_a.\)

\textbf{p-Value Approach:}

The p-value measures he strength of the evidence against \(H_0\) and in
favor of \(H_a.\) For a right-tailed test, the p-value is the
probability of observing a difference that provides at least as much
support for \(H_a\) as our observed difference, assuming \(p_1=p_2\):

\[\text{p-value}
=
P\left(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2
\geq \text{observed difference}\right),\;
\text{assuming } p_1=p_2.\]

This is the area to the right of the observed difference under the
\(N\left(0, \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}\right)\)
distribution. A small p-value indicates strong evidence against \(H_0\)
and in favor of \(H_a,\) while a large p-value indicates that the data
do not provide strong evidence against \(H_0.\)

Decision Rule:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Reject \(H_0\) if p-value \(< \alpha\) (observed difference strongly
  support \(H_a\)).
\item
  Fail to reject \(H_0\) if p-value \(\geq \alpha\) (data do not
  strongly support \(H_a\)).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Critical Region Approach:}

The critical region consists of values in the upper tail of the sampling
distribution. These are the values of \(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2\) that are
sufficiently large to lead us to reject \(H_0\) in favor of
\(H_a: p_1-p_2>0.\) We find the critical value \(c\) o that the
probability of falling in the critical region is equal to the
significant level \(\alpha,\) assuming \(p_1=p_2\):

\[P\left(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2 \geq c\right) = \alpha,\;
\text{assuming }p_1=p_2.\]

Using the sampling distribution under this assumption,

\[\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2\sim N\left(0, \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}\right)\]

we choose \(c\) so that the area to the right of \(c\) is \(\alpha.\) We
reject \(H_0\) if the observed difference \(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2\) falls
in this critical region.

Decision Rule:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Reject \(H_0\) if \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 > c\) (observed difference
  strongly supports \(H_a\)).
\item
  Fail to reject \(H_0\) if \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c\) (observed
  difference does not strongly support \(H_a\)).
\end{itemize}

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics{Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/right-tail-test.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-right-tail-critical-pvalue}Critical region and
p-value for a right-tailed test}

\end{figure}%

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Case 2: Left-Tailed Test
(\(H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0\))}{Case 2: Left-Tailed Test (H\_a: p\_1 - p\_2 \textless{} 0)}}\label{case-2-left-tailed-test-h_a-p_1---p_2-0}

Case 2 is the mirror of Case 1. Small (negative) values of
\(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) support \(H_a,\) so the p-value and critical
region lie in the \textbf{lower} tail of the null distribution.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\textbf{p-value:}
\(\quad \text{p-value} = P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq \text{observed difference} \mid p_1 = p_2)\)

\textbf{Critical value \(c\):}
\(\quad P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c \mid p_1 = p_2) = \alpha\)

Decision: Reject \(H_0\) if p-value \(< \alpha,\) equivalently if
\(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c.\)

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics{Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/left-tail-test.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-left-tail-critical-pvalue}Critical region and
p-value for a left-tailed test}

\end{figure}%

\textbf{Critical Region Approach:}

The critical region consists of values in the lower tail of the sampling
distribution---these are the values that strongly support
\(H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0.\) We find the critical value \(c\) such that at
the boundary where \(p_1 = p_2\):

\[P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 < c \mid p_1 = p_2) = \alpha\]

Using the sampling distribution at the boundary, we find \(c\) from
\(N\left(0, \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}\right)\)
such that the area to the left equals \(\alpha.\)

Decision Rule:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Reject \(H_0\) if \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 < c\) (observed difference
  strongly supports \(H_a\)).
\item
  Fail to reject \(H_0\) if \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \geq c\) (observed
  difference does not strongly support \(H_a\)).
\end{itemize}

\begin{example}[Smoking Cessation: Hypothesis Test - p-Value
Example]\protect\hypertarget{exm-smoking-test-pvalue}{}\label{exm-smoking-test-pvalue}

For the smoking cessation study, we want to test whether the self-guided
approach has a higher quit-smoking rate than the nicotine patch
approach. Recall:

\tightlist
\item
  \(n_1 = 60,\) \(X_1 = 24,\) \(\hat{p}_1 = 0.40\)
\item
  \(n_2 = 60,\) \(X_2 = 30,\) \(\hat{p}_2 = 0.50\)
\item
  \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = -0.10\)
\end{itemize}

Hypotheses: \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 - p_2 \geq 0\\
H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0.
\end{cases}
\]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Give a probability statement that describes the p-value.
\item
  Use Rguroo to obtain the p-value for the test and state your
  conclusion based on the significance level \(\alpha = 0.10.\)
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

this standard error is reported in the Rguroo output.

The \(p\)-value is the probability of observing a difference at least as
small as the observed difference of \(-0.10,\) assuming \(p_1 = p_2\):
\[
\text{p-value} = P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq -0.10)\;\text{assuming}\;p_1 = p_2.
\]

b. To perform this hypothesis test in Rguroo, follow the same steps
given in the \hyperref[schema-test-pvalue]{solution} of

\end{tcolorbox}

The p-value is depicted in the Rguroo output graph labeled
\textbf{P-Value Graph: Large Sample z, Pooled SE} (shown in
Figure~\ref{fig-pvalue-smoke}). In the left panel (labeled ``Observed
Data Scale''), the area corresponding to the \(p\)-value is shaded in
red, and its value is 0.13546. This value is also reported in the
results table.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includesvg[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_html_output/Proportion Inference/smoking_prop2_pvalue_docx/G_pvalueTestPropz12.svg}

}
