study.}

\end{figure}%

Since the p-value is \(0.13546 > 0.10,\) we fail to reject \(H_0\) at
the 10\% significance level. There is not sufficient evidence in favor
of \(H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0.\)

Although the observed difference of \(-0.10\) is in the direction of
\(H_a\) (the self-guided approach showed a 50\% quit rate compared to
40\% for nicotine patches), the p-value of 0.13546 indicates that a
difference at least this supportive of \(H_a\) is not particularly
unusual, assuming \(p_1=p_2.\) Therefore, the data do not provide
sufficient evidence that the self-guided approach has a higher
quit-smoking rate than the nicotine patch approach.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Smoking Cessation: Hypothesis Test - Critical Region
Example]\protect\hypertarget{exm-smoking-test-cr}{}\label{exm-smoking-test-cr}

For the smoking cessation study, we want to test whether the self-guided
approach has a higher quit-smoking rate than the nicotine patch
approach. Recall:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(n_1 = 60,\) \(X_1 = 24,\) \(\hat{p}_1 = 0.40\)
\item
  \(n_2 = 60,\) \(X_2 = 30,\) \(\hat{p}_2 = 0.50\)
\item
  \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = -0.10\)
\end{itemize}

Hypotheses: \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 - p_2 \geq 0\\
H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0.
\end{cases}
\]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Using Rguroo, obtain the critical region for a test at significance
  level \(\alpha =0.10.\)
\item
  Based on the observed difference and the critical region in part (a),
  state the conclusion of the hypothesis test.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. To perform this hypothesis test in Rguroo, follow the same steps
given in the \hyperref[exm-schema-test-cr]{solution} of
Example~\ref{exm-schema-test-cr}. One difference is that in the
\Tab{Test of Hypothesis} tab, for \Des{Alternative Hypothesis p1 − p2},
you should select the \TypeIn{<} (less than) option because this is a
left-tailed test, and set the \Des{Significance Level} to \TypeIn{0.10}.
In addition, the values in the Basics dialog of
\Dialog{Two Population Proportion Inference} and in the
\Tab{Data Summary} tab should match those shown in
Figure~\ref{fig-smoking-inputs1}.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics{Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/G_smoking_inputs.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-smoking-inputs1}Rguroo input setup comparing
quit-smoking success rates for nicotine patch and self-guided groups}

\end{figure}%

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo output: Two-Population Proportion Inference - Smoking Cessation
Example}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\end{tcolorbox}

As discussed in Section~\ref{sec-data-stat-dist}, assuming \(p_1=p_2,\)
the statistic \(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2\) is approximately normally
distributed with mean 0 and standard error 0.09083. We use this null
distribution to determine the critical region.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includesvg[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_html_output/Proportion Inference/smoking_prop2_cr_docx/G_crTestPropz12.svg}

}

\caption{\label{fig-cr-smoke}p-value for the Smoking Cessation study.}

\end{figure}%

From the Rguroo output graph labeled \textbf{Critical Region Graph:
Large Sample z, Pooled SE} (shown in Figure~\ref{fig-cr-smoke}), the
\textbf{critical value} is \(c=-0.1164,\) displayed at the bottom of the
left panel. Therefore, the critical region is

\[
\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2<-0.1164.
\]

Since the observed difference \(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2=-0.10\) is greater
than \textbf{\(-0.1164\)}, it does \emph{not} fall in the critical
region, as shown by the green triangle outside the red-shaded region.
Therefore, we fail to reject \(H_0\) at the 10\% significance level.

Although the observed difference of \(-0.10\) is in the direction of
\(H_a\) (the self-guided approach had a 50\% quit-smoking rate compared
with 40\% for the nicotine patch approach), the observed difference does
not fall in the critical region. Therefore, the data do not provide
sufficient evidence that the self-guided approach has a higher
quit-smoking rate than the nicotine patch approach.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{Case 3: Two-Tailed Test
(\(H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0\))}{Case 3: Two-Tailed Test (H\_a: p\_1 - p\_2 \textbackslash neq 0)}}\label{case-3-two-tailed-test-h_a-p_1---p_2-neq-0}

In Case 3, \(H_a\) is supported when \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) is far
from zero in \emph{either} direction. The p-value is therefore a
\emph{two-tail} probability, and the critical region occupies both tails
with \(\alpha/2\) in each.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\textbf{p-value:}
\(\quad \text{p-value} = P(|\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2| \geq |\text{observed difference}| \mid p_1 = p_2)\)

\textbf{Critical values \(c_1, c_2\):}
\(\quad P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c_1 \mid p_1 = p_2) = P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \geq c_2 \mid p_1 = p_2) = \alpha/2\)

Decision: Reject \(H_0\) if p-value \(< \alpha,\) equivalently if
\(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c_1\) or
\(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \geq c_2.\)

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics{Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/two-tail-test.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-two-tail-test-critical-pvalue}Critical region and
p-value for a two-tailed test}

\end{figure}%

\textbf{Critical Region Approach:}

The critical region consists of values in both tails of the sampling
distribution---these are the values that strongly support
\(H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0.\) We find two critical values, \(c_1\) and
\(c_2,\) such that at the boundary where \(p_1 = p_2\):

\[P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 < c_1 \text{ or } \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 > c_2 \mid p_1 = p_2) = \alpha\]

We split \(\alpha\) equally between the two tails (\(\alpha/2\) in each
tail). Using the sampling distribution at the boundary:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(c_1\) is the value with area \(\alpha/2\) to its left
\item
  \(c_2\) is the value with area \(\alpha/2\) to its right
\end{itemize}

Decision Rule:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Reject \(H_0\) if \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 < c_1\) or
  \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 > c_2\) (observed difference strongly supports
  \(H_a\)).
\item
  Fail to reject \(H_0\) if \(c_1 \leq \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c_2\)
  (observed difference does not strongly support \(H_a\)).
\end{itemize}

\begin{example}[Text Message Reminders: Hypothesis Test - p-Value
Example]\protect\hypertarget{exm-text-test-pvalue}{}\label{exm-text-test-pvalue}

For the text message reminder study, we want to test whether adherence
rates differ. Recall:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(n_1 = 40,\) \(X_1 = 32,\) \(\hat{p}_1 = 0.80\)
\item
  \(n_2 = 50,\) \(X_2 = 28,\) \(\hat{p}_2 = 0.56\)
\item
  \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = 0.24\)
\item
  \(\hat{p} = 0.667\)
\end{itemize}

Hypotheses: \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0\\
H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0
\end{cases}
\]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\item
  Give a probability statement that describes the p-value.
\item
  Use Rguroo to obtain the p-value for the test and state your
  conclusion based on the significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\) .
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. The \(p\)-value is the probability of observing an absolute
difference at least as large as the observed difference of \(0.24,\)
assuming \(p_1 = p_2\): \[
\text{p-value} = P(|\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2| \geq 0.24), \;\text{assuming}\;  p_1 = p_2.
\] See Figure~\ref{fig-pvalue-text}.

b. To perform this hypothesis test in Rguroo, follow the same steps
given in the \hyperref[schema-test-pvalue]{solution} of
Example~\ref{exm-schema-test-pvalue}. One difference is that in the
\Tab{Test of Hypothesis} tab, for \Des{Alternative Hypothesis p1 − p2},
you should select the \TypeIn{!=} (not equal to) option because this is
a two-tailed test, and set the \Des{Significance Level} to
\TypeIn{0.05}. In addition, the values in the Basics dialog of
\Dialog{Two Population Proportion Inference} and in the
\Tab{Data Summary} tab should match those shown in
Figure~\ref{fig-text-test-pvalue}.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics{Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/G_text_inputs.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-text-test-pvalue}Rguroo input setup comparing
success rates for text reminders and standard care}

\end{figure}%

Click to expand the box below to see the Rguroo output.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo output: Two-Population Proportion Inference - Text Message
Reminder Example}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\end{tcolorbox}

The p-value is shown in the Rguroo output graph labeled \textbf{P-Value
Graph: Large Sample z, Pooled SE} (see Figure~\ref{fig-pvalue-text}). In
the left panel, labeled ``Observed Data Scale'', the areas representing
the \(p\)-value are shaded in red, and the p-value is 0.016395. This
value is also reported in the results table.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includesvg[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_html_output/Proportion Inference/text_prop2_pvalue_docx/G_pvalueTestPropz12.svg}

}

\caption{\label{fig-pvalue-text}p-value for the Text Message study.}

\end{figure}%

Since the p-value is \(0.016 < 0.05,\) we reject \(H_0\) at the
significance level \(\alpha =0.05.\) There is sufficient evidence in
favor of \(H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0.\) Therefore, the data provide
sufficient evidence that adherence rates differ between the two
approaches. Since the observed adherence rate is higher for the text
message reminder group (80\%) than for the standard care group (56\%),
the results suggest that text message reminders are associated with
higher adherence.

\end{tcolorbox}

For the text message reminder study, we want to test whether adherence

Since this is a two-sided test, the 5\% cutoff values \(c_1\) and
\(c_2\) are determined so that \[
P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c_1 \text{ or }  \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \geq c_2) = 0.05, \; \text{assuming}\; p_1 = p_2.
\]

\qquad \text{or} \qquad

\] This means that observed differences falling in either tail are
sufficiently extreme to lead us to reject \(H_0\) at significance level
\(\alpha=0.05.\)

red-shaded region. Therefore, we reject \(H_0\) at significance level
\(\alpha=0.05\) and conclude that there is sufficient evidence in favor
of \(H_a:p_1-p_2\neq0.\)

The data therefore provide sufficient evidence that adherence rates
differ between the two approaches. Since the observed adherence rate is
higher for the text message reminder group (80\%) than for the standard
care group (56\%), the results suggest that text message reminders are
associated with higher adherence.

\end{tcolorbox}

So far, in the examples above, we have performed two-population
proportion inference using summarized data---namely, the sample sizes
and the number of successes for each group. In practice, however, we
often begin with raw data rather than pre-computed summaries. By raw
data, we mean datasets where each individual observation is recorded as
a separate row, with variables indicating group membership and the
outcome for each case. The following example demonstrates how we can
carry out two-population proportion inference directly from raw data
using Rguroo.

\begin{example}[GSS 2024: Hypothesis Test Using Raw
Data]\protect\hypertarget{exm-gss-test}{}\label{exm-gss-test}

Consider the GSS marijuana legalization study. Use the \Data{GSS2024} to
test whether the proportion of U.S. adults who support the legalization
of marijuana differs between females and males. Define \(p_1\) as the
proportion of females who support legalization and \(p_2\) as the
proportion of males who support legalization.

Use significance level \(\alpha=0.05.\)

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Write the null and alternative hypotheses.
\item
  Test using the p-value approach.
\item
  Test using the critical region approach.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. The null and alternative hypotheses are:

\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0\\
H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0,
\end{cases}
\]

\textbf{Before you begin:} Make sure you have already imported the
\Data{GSS2024} dataset into your Rguroo account, as shown

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Open the \textbf{Analytics} toolbox in Rguroo.\\
\item
  From the \Dpd{Analysis} dropdown, select \Fun{Proportion Inference} →
  \Fun{Two Populations}. This opens the
  \Dialog{Two Population Proportion Inference} dialog.
\item
  From the \Dpd{Dataset} dropdown, select the dataset \Data{GSS2024}.
\item
  Fill in the \textbf{Response/Success} section of the dialog as
  follows:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    From the \Dpd{Response} dropdown, select the factor \Var{Grass}, the
    variable that indicates whether the respondents support legalization
    of marijuana.
  \item
    From the \Dpd{Success} dropdown, select the success level
    \TypeIn{Yes}.
  \item
    In the \Dpd{Failure} textbox, enter \TypeIn{No} (this is the
    default).
  \item
    (Optional) In the \Des{Response Label} textbox, enter
    \TypeIn{Legalize Marijuana}. The label is usually a more descriptive
    version of the variable name.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  In the \textbf{Population} section of the dialog, from the
  \Dpd{Population} dropdown, select the variable \Var{Sex}. You can

\item
  In the \Tab{Data Summary} tab, select \TypeIn{Female} from the

  Click the \Tab{Test of Hypothesis} tab and enter the following:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist

    In the \Dpd{Alternative Hypothesis p1 - p2} dropdown, select
    \TypeIn{!=} (not equal to) and enter \TypeIn{0} in the textbox.
  \item
    In the \textbf{Methods} section, select \Des{Large Sample z}.
  \item
    Leave the \Des{Significance Level} textbox at the default value of

\item
  (Optional) Click the \includegraphics{Rguroo_Icons/details.png} button

\item
  Click the preview icon
  \includegraphics{Rguroo_Icons/preview_inline.png} to view the output.

  Click the \includegraphics{Rguroo_Icons/save_as.png} button and save

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo output: Two-Population Proportion Inference - Marijuana
Legalization Example}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\end{tcolorbox}

b. p-Value Approach:

The \(p\)-value measures the strength of evidence the data provide
against \(H_0\) and in favor of \(H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0.\) Because this
is a two-sided test, differences at least as far from 0 as the observed
difference of \(-0.064791,\) in either direction, are at least as
supportive of \(H_a.\) Therefore, the p-value is \[
\text{p-value}
=
P\left(|\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2|\geq0.064791\right),\;\text{assuming}\; p_1=p_2.
\]

This probability is shown in the Rguroo output graph labeled
\textbf{P-Value Graph: Large Sample z, Pooled SE} (also shown in
Figure~\ref{fig-pvalue2-GSS}). In the panel labeled ``Observed Data
Scale'', the areas representing to the \(p\)-value are shaded in red,
and the p-value is 0.15268. This value is also reported in the results
table.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.7\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/fig-pvalue2-GSS.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-pvalue2-GSS}p-value for the marijuana legalization
example.}

\end{figure}%

Since the p-value is \(0.15268 > 0.05,\) we fail to reject \(H_0\) at
significance level \(\alpha = 0.05.\) There is insufficient evidence in
favor of \(H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0.\) Therefore, the data do not provide
sufficient evidence that support for marijuana legalization differs
between females and males.

c. Critical Region Approach:

Since this is a two-sided test, the critical values values \(c_1\) and
\(c_2\) are determined so that \[
P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c_1 \text{ or }  \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \geq c_2)= 0.05, \;\text{assuming}\; p_1 = p_2 .
\]

From the Rguroo output graph labeled \textbf{Critical Region Graph:
Large Sample z, Pooled SE} (also shown in Figure~\ref{fig-cr-GSS}),
these cutoff values are \(c_1=-0.088794\) and \(c_2=0.088794.\) These
values are displayed at the bottom of the panel labeled Observed Data
Scale. Therefore, the critical region is \[
\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2\leq-0.088794
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2\geq0.088794.
\] An observed difference that falls in either of these regions leads us
to reject \(H_0\) at significance level \(\alpha=0.05.\)

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.7\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/fig-cr-GSS.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-cr-GSS}Critical region for the marijuana
legalization example, with \(lpha = 0.05.\)}

\end{figure}%

Since the observed difference \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = -0.064791\) lies
between the two critical values, it does not fall in the critical
region, as shown by the green triangle outside the red critical region.
Therefore, we fail to reject \(H_0\) at significance level
\(\alpha = 0.05\) and conclude that there is \textbf{not} sufficient
evidence in favor of \(H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0.\)

\textbf{Conclusion:}

Both approaches lead to the same decision. At significance level
\(\alpha = 0.05\) , the data do not provide sufficient evidence that the
proportion who support marijuana legalization differs between females
and males.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population
Proportions}\label{sec-confidence-interval-two-prop}

In Section~\ref{sec-hyp-test-two-prop}, we learned how to test whether
two population proportions differ. For example, in the schema-based
instruction study (Example~\ref{exm-schema-test-pvalue}), we found
strong evidence that the new instructional approach produced higher
mastery rates than traditional instruction. The hypothesis test told us
that a difference exists, but it didn't tell us how large that
difference might be. Does the new approach improve mastery by 5
percentage points? 20 percentage points? 35 percentage points? The
hypothesis test alone cannot answer this question.

This is where confidence intervals become valuable. A confidence
interval for \(p_1 - p_2\) provides a range of plausible values for the
true difference between the two proportions, addressing the question
``How large is the difference?'' It tells us not just that a difference
exists, but also gives us insight into the magnitude and direction of
that difference. For instance, a confidence interval might tell us: ``We
are 95\% confident that the new approach improves mastery rates by
somewhere between 4 and 36 percentage points compared to traditional
instruction.'' This additional information helps researchers, educators,
and policymakers make more informed decisions.

Just as in the one-population case
(Section~\ref{sec-confidence-interval-one-pop}), a confidence interval
for \(p_1 - p_2\) can be derived by inverting hypothesis tests: given
the observed difference \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2,\) the
\((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) interval consists of all values \(d\) for
which we would fail to reject \(H_0: p_1 - p_2 = d\) in a two-sided test
at significance level \(\alpha.\) And as in the one-population case, the
\textbf{confidence level} describes the long-run behavior of the
construction method, not any single interval --- a 95\% method captures
the true difference in 95\% of repeated samples. In practice we use a
direct formula based on the normal approximation rather than carrying
out the test inversion by hand, but the logic is the same.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Large Sample Confidence Interval for
\(p_1 - p_2\)}{Large Sample Confidence Interval for p\_1 - p\_2}}\label{sec-ci-two-prop-large-sample}

When the large sample conditions are satisfied, we can construct a
confidence interval for \(p_1 - p_2\) using the normal approximation.
Recall from Section~\ref{sec-data-stat-dist} that when both samples are
sufficiently large, the difference in sample proportions
\(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) follows an approximately normal distribution.

However, there is an important difference between constructing a
confidence interval and conducting a hypothesis test. In hypothesis
testing, we assumed \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\) was true, which allowed us to use
a pooled estimate \(\hat{p}\) for the common proportion. When
constructing a confidence interval, we do not assume the proportions are
equal---in fact, we're trying to estimate how different they are!
Therefore, we cannot use the pooled proportion.

Instead, for a confidence interval, we estimate the standard error using
the individual sample proportions \(\hat{p}_1\) and \(\hat{p}_2\):

\[\text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}.\]

This is called the \textbf{unpooled standard error}, or simply the
\textbf{standard error}, because we do not pool the two samples
together.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Pooled vs.~Unpooled Standard Error}\vspace{3mm}

The two-proportion confidence interval uses the \textbf{unpooled}
standard error, based on \(\hat{p}_1\) and \(\hat{p}_2\) separately:
\[\text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}.\]

The two-proportion \textbf{hypothesis test}, by contrast, uses the
\textbf{pooled} standard error, based on the common proportion
\(\hat{p}\) under \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\) (see
Section~\ref{sec-data-stat-dist}):
\[\widehat{\text{SE}}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) = \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}.\]

The reason is the assumption being made. The hypothesis test assumes
\(p_1 = p_2,\) so we pool. The confidence interval makes no such
assumption --- we're trying to estimate the difference, not assume it
away --- so we estimate each proportion's variance from its own sample.

\end{tcolorbox}

The large sample conditions for a confidence interval are the same as
those for hypothesis testing. We need at least 10 successes and at least
10 failures in each group:

\[n_1\hat{p}_1 \geq 10, \quad n_1(1-\hat{p}_1) \geq 10, \quad n_2\hat{p}_2 \geq 10, \quad n_2(1-\hat{p}_2) \geq 10.\]

When these conditions are satisfied, the \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\)
confidence interval for \(p_1 - p_2\) takes the form:

\[(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) \pm z^* \times \text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2),\]

where \(z^*\) is the critical value from the standard normal
distribution corresponding to the desired confidence level, just as in
the one-population case.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={Large Sample Confidence Interval for \(p_1 - p_2\)}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

When the large sample conditions are satisfied, an approximate
\((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(p_1 - p_2\) is:

\[(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) \pm \underbrace{z^* \times \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}}_{\text{margin of error}}.\]

That is, the lower endpoint is
\((\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) - z^* \cdot \text{SE}\) and the upper endpoint
is \((\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) + z^* \cdot \text{SE},\) where
\(\text{SE}\) is the unpooled standard error given above.

\end{tcolorbox}

Common critical values remain the same:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Confidence Level & \(\alpha\) & \(z^*\) \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
90\% & 0.10 & 1.645 \\
95\% & 0.05 & 1.960 \\
99\% & 0.01 & 2.576 \\
\end{longtable}

Let's see how to construct and interpret confidence intervals for the
difference between two proportions using our earlier examples.

\subsection{Relationship Between Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis
Tests}\label{relationship-between-confidence-intervals-and-hypothesis-tests}

There is an important connection between confidence intervals and
two-sided hypothesis tests. A \((1-\alpha)\times100%
\) confidence interval and a two-sided hypothesis test at significance
level \(\alpha\) lead to the same decisions about the null value
\(p_1-p_2=0\):

\begin{itemize}
\item
  If a \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(p_1 - p_2\)
  \textbf{does not contain 0}, then 0 is not a plausible value for
  \(p_1-p_2,\) and we \textbf{reject} \(H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0\) at
  significance level \(\alpha\) in a two-sided test.
\item
  If a \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(p_1 - p_2\)
  \textbf{contains 0}, 0 is a plausible value for \(p_1-p_2,\) and we
  \textbf{fail to reject} \(H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0\) at significance level
  \(\alpha\) in a two-sided test.
\end{itemize}

This relationship provides a quick way to connect the confidence
interval to the corresponding two-sided hypothesis test. As noted,
however, confidence intervals provide more information than hypothesis
tests alone. They tell us not just whether the data provide evidence of
a difference, but also which values are plausible for the size and
direction of the difference.

This direct relationship applies only to two-sided hypothesis tests. For
a one-sided hypothesis test, you should not use this confidence interval
rule to determine whether to reject \(H_0.\)

\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. We check the large sample conditions using the individual sample
proportions:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Group 1 (text reminders):
  \(n_1\hat{p}_1 = 40 \times 0.80 = 32 \geq 10\) and
  \(n_1(1-\hat{p}_1) = 40 \times 0.20 = 8 < 10\)
\item
  Group 2 (standard care):
  \(n_2\hat{p}_2 = 50 \times 0.56 = 28 \geq 10\) and
  \(n_2(1-\hat{p}_2) = 50 \times 0.44 = 22 \geq 10\)
\end{itemize}

The condition \(n_1(1-\hat{p}_1) \geq 10\) is not satisfied. We have
only 8 observed failures in the text reminder group. Therefore, the
10-10 rule is not fully satisfied, and we should use caution when
applying the large-sample normal approximation. We will proceed with the
large-sample method here so that we can examine the resulting interval.

b. Follow the same Rguroo instructions as shown in
Example~\ref{exm-schema-ci}. The following is a screenshot of the
\Dialog{Two Population Proportion Inference} dialog for obtaining the
large sample confidence interval for this example.

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_dialogs/Proportion_inference/text-ci-dialog.png}

}

\caption{Rguroo dialog for constructing a confidence interval for the
text message study}

\end{figure}%

Click to expand the box below to see the Rguroo output.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo output: Two-Population Proportion Confidence Interval - Text
Message Reminders}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\end{tcolorbox}

From the Rguroo output, the 95\% confidence interval for \(p_1 - p_2\)
is \((0.0548067, 0.425193).\)

\textbf{Interpretation:} We are 95\% confident that the true difference
in adherence rates (text message reminders minus standard care) is
between 0.0548067 (about 5.5 percentage points) and 0.425193 (about 42.5
percentage points).

c. Since the entire interval is positive, the data suggest that the
adherence rate is higher for the text message reminder group than for
the standard care group. This is consistent with the two-sided
hypothesis test in Example~\ref{exm-text-test-pvalue}, where we rejected
\(H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0\) at significance level \(\alpha=0.05.\) The value
0 lies outside the 95\% confidence interval.

As expected, the two-sided test at \(\alpha=0.05\) and the corresponding
95\% confidence interval lead to the same conclusion.

\end{tcolorbox}

Marijuana Legalization}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

From the Rguroo output, the 95\% confidence interval for \(p_1 - p_2\)
is \((-0.153008, 0.0234262).\)

\textbf{Interpretation:} We are 95\% confident that the true difference
in support for marijuana legalization (females minus males) is between
\(-0.1530\) (about \(-15.3\) percentage points) and \(0.0234\) (about
\(2.3\) percentage points). Negative values indicate lower support among
females than males, while positive values indicate higher support among
females. Since the interval includes 0, the data are consistent with no
difference in the population proportions who support marijuana
legalization between females and males.

Note that the observed difference was
\(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \approx -0.065,\) meaning the sample showed
about 6.5 percentage points lower support among females. However, the
confidence interval indicates that plausible values for the true
difference range from about 15 percentage points lower support among
females to about 2 percentage points higher support among females.

c. This confidence interval is consistent with our hypothesis test
result in Example~\ref{exm-gss-test}. In that test, we failed to reject
\(H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0\) at significance level \(\alpha=0.05,\) with a
p-value of 0.153. The value 0 lies inside the 95\% confidence interval,
which corresponds to failing to reject \(H_0\) in the corresponding
two-sided test. Both the hypothesis test and the confidence interval
lead us to the same conclusion: the data do not provide sufficient
evidence that support for marijuana legalization differs between females
and males.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Homework for
Section~\ref{sec-confidence-interval-two-prop}}{Homework for Section~}}\label{homework-for-sec-confidence-interval-two-prop}

For each of the scenarios described below, answer the following:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\item
  Check whether the large sample conditions are satisfied using the
  individual sample proportions. Based on your answer, determine whether
  the large sample normal approximationis appropriate for constructing
  the confidence interval.
\item
  Use Rguroo's \Fun{Two-Population Proportion} inference function with
  the \Des{Large Sample z} option to obtain a 95\% confidence interval
  for \(p_1 - p_2.\) Interpret the interval in the context of the
  problem.
\item
  Does the confidence interval contain 0? What does this tell you about
  whether \(p_1-p_2=0\) is a plausible value for the difference in
  population proportions? If the hypothesis test you conducted in the
  homework for Section~\ref{sec-hyp-test-two-prop} was two-sided,
  compare your confidence interval conclusion with the hypothesis test
  conclusion. Are they consistent?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{College Student Smoking Rates by Gender} Recall Problem 1 from
  Section~\ref{sec-hyp-test-two-prop}. In a survey of 120 male students,
  18 reported being regular smokers. Among 150 female students, 12
  reported being regular smokers. Construct a 95\% confidence interval
  for the difference in smoking rates between male and female college
  students.
\item
  \textbf{Reading Program Effectiveness by Prior Tutoring} Recall
  Problem 2 from Section~\ref{sec-hyp-test-two-prop}. Of 85 students
  with previous tutoring, 68 passed the reading assessment. Of 92
  students without previous tutoring, 59 passed the assessment.
  Construct a 95\% confidence interval for the difference in pass rates
  between students with and without previous tutoring.
\item
  \textbf{Skin Treatment Effectiveness Comparison} Recall Problem 3 from
  Section~\ref{sec-hyp-test-two-prop}. In a trial, 8 out of 25 patients
  receiving Treatment A showed improvement, while 12 out of 28 patients
  receiving Treatment B showed improvement. Construct a 95\% confidence
  interval for the difference in improvement rates between the two
  treatments.
\item
  \textbf{Coffee Shop Customer Satisfaction by Shift} Recall Problem 4
  from Section~\ref{sec-hyp-test-two-prop}. Of 45 morning customers
  surveyed, 38 reported being satisfied with their service. Of 52
  evening customers surveyed, 35 reported being satisfied. Construct a
  95\% confidence interval for the difference in satisfaction rates
  between morning and evening shifts.
\item
  \textbf{AP Calculus AB Exam by Gender} Recall Problem 5 from
  Section~\ref{sec-hyp-test-two-prop}. In 2007, of the 211,693 students
  who took the calculus AB exam, 102,598 were female and 109,095 were
  male. Construct a 95\% confidence interval for the difference in the
  proportion of female versus male students taking the calculus AB exam.
  (Note: For this problem, let \(p_1\) represent the proportion of all
  AP calculus AB test-takers who are female, and \(p_2\) represent the
  proportion who are male.)
\item
  \textbf{Autism Spectrum Disorder: Pennsylvania vs.~Utah} Recall
  Problem 6 from Section~\ref{sec-hyp-test-two-prop}. In Pennsylvania,
  245 eight-year-olds were diagnosed with ASD out of 18,440 evaluated.
  In Utah, 45 eight-year-olds were diagnosed with ASD out of 2,123
  evaluated. Construct a 99\% confidence interval for the difference in
  ASD diagnosis rates between Pennsylvania and Utah.
\item
  \textbf{Child Poisoning Deaths by Gender} Recall Problem 7 from
  Section~\ref{sec-hyp-test-two-prop}. Out of 1,830 children between the
  ages of one and four who died from poisoning, 1,031 were males and 799
  were females. Construct a 99\% confidence interval for the difference
  in the proportion of poisoning deaths between male and female
  children.
\item
  \textbf{AP Biology vs.~Calculus AB Exam by Gender} Recall Problem 8
  from Section~\ref{sec-hyp-test-two-prop}. In 2007, of the 144,796
  students who took the biology exam, 84,199 were female. Of the 211,693
  students who took the calculus AB exam, 102,598 were female. Construct
  a 95\% confidence interval for the difference in the proportion of
  female students between these two exams. (Note: For this problem, let
  \(p_1\) represent the proportion of biology test-takers who are
  female, and \(p_2\) represent the proportion of calculus AB
  test-takers who are female.)
\item
  \textbf{GSS 2024: Marijuana Legalization by Survey Mode} Recall
  Problem 9 from Section~\ref{sec-hyp-test-two-prop}. Using the GSS2024
  dataset, construct a 95\% confidence interval for the difference in

  between those surveyed in person and those surveyed by phone. The
  variable \Var{Mode} indicates the survey mode (In Person or Phone),

\end{enumerate}

\chapter{Statistical Inference for
Means}\label{statistical-inference-for-means}

\textbf{Before you begin, click to expand the box below to review the
process for importing a dataset.}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]
\begin{minipage}[t]{5.5mm}
\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{minipage}[t]{\textwidth - 5.5mm}

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{\includegraphics[width=0.22917in,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_Icons/R_circle_logo.pdf}
Importing Data to Rguroo}\vspace{3mm}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Open the \textbf{Data} toolbox in Rguroo.\\
\item
  From the \Dpd{Data Import} dropdown, select
  \Fun{Dataset Repository}.\\
\item
  In the top search box, type \TypeIn{kozak}, then select the
  \Repo{Statistics Using Technology – Kozak} repository.\\
\item

  name, and choose your desired dataset name that appears in the lower
  panel.\\
\item

  account.
\item

  \textbf{Data} toolbox list.

\end{minipage}%
\end{tcolorbox}

In this chapter we develop methods for drawing inferences about a
population mean \(\mu\) (read mu). Examples of population means abound
in practice: the mean SAT math score among incoming freshmen at a
particular university, the mean nightly sleep hours among college
students, the mean one-way commute time in a metropolitan area, and the
mean flipper length of Adélie penguins in the Palmer Archipelago. These
are four of the running examples we use throughout the chapter, and many
other applications follow the same pattern.

The framework established in the Foundations of Inference chapter
applies here unchanged. We still begin with a research question about a
population parameter --- now \(\mu.\) We collect a random sample,
compute a statistic from it, and study how that statistic varies from
sample to sample through its sampling distribution
(Section~\ref{sec-foundations-populations}). We test claims by examining
where our observed statistic falls within the null
distribution(Section~\ref{sec-foundations-hypotheses}), and make
decisions using p-values (Section~\ref{sec-foundations-pvalue}) or
critical regions (Section~\ref{sec-foundations-critical-region}).
Confidence intervals
(Section~\ref{sec-foundations-confidence-intervals}), significance
levels, Type I and Type II errors
(Section~\ref{sec-foundations-errors}), and confidence levels all retain
the meanings established in the foundations chapter.

How do we tell, in a real-world problem, whether the parameter of
interest is a mean or a proportion? As discussed in
Section~\ref{sec-foundations-mean-vs-prop}, the key is the variable
measured on each individual in the population. If the variable is
\textbf{numerical} --- a score, a quantity, a measurement --- the
parameter is a population \textbf{mean} \(\mu.\) All the examples in
this chapter are of this type: SAT scores in points, sleep duration in
hours, commute time in minutes, flipper length in millimeters. If
instead the variable is categorical (success/failure, yes/no), the
parameter is a population \textbf{proportion} \(p,\) and the methods
from the previous chapter apply.

For numerical data, the statistic we use to estimate the population mean
\(\mu\) is the sample mean, the arithmetic average of the numerical
measurements in the sample. As a random variable---that is, before we
collect data---we denote it by \(\bar{X}.\) Once we have collected the
data, we obtain a specific numerical value of this average, which we
denote by \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) and call the observed sample mean. To
make inferences about \(\mu,\) we determine where our observed statistic
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) lies within the sampling distribution of
\(\bar{X}.\)

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Notation for One-Sample Mean Inference}\vspace{3mm}

Throughout the one-sample mean sections, we use the following notation:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Symbol
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Meaning
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(\mu\) & Population mean, the parameter we want to make an inference
about \\
\(X\) & The numerical variable measured on each individual \\
\(n\) & Sample size \\
\(\bar{X}\) & Sample mean as a random variable, before the data are
collected \\
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) & Observed sample mean, the value computed from
the collected data \\
\(\sigma\) & Population standard deviation \\
\(s\) & Sample standard deviation \\
\(\mu_0\) & Boundary value specified by the null hypothesis \\
\end{longtable}

\end{tcolorbox}

We assume the variable under study has a normal distribution in the
population. In Section~\ref{sec-large-sample-mean}, we will see when the
sample size is large, many of the same methods remain valid even when
the population distribution is not normal. We will cover both
one-population and two-population settings. In the one-population
setting we draw inferences about a single population mean \(\mu.\) In
the two-population setting we compare two population means \(\mu_1\) and
\(\mu_2\) through their difference \(\mu_1 - \mu_2.\) We begin with the
one-population case.

\section{Basics of Hypothesis Testing for a Population
Mean}\label{sec-concept-setup-mean}

In this section we set up the elements common to all hypothesis tests
for a population mean: the form of the null and alternative hypotheses,
and the null distribution of \(\bar{X}.\) The specifics of this null
distribution depend on what we assume about the population, leading to
two cases that we develop in the subsections that follow.

\subsection{Null and Alternative
Hypotheses}\label{sec-null-alternative-mean}

As established in Section~\ref{sec-foundations-three-forms}, the null
and alternative hypotheses always come in one of three forms, depending
on the nature of the research question. For a population mean \(\mu,\)
with \(\mu_0\) denoting a specific value, the three cases are:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Case 1: } 
&\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu \leq \mu_0 \\
H_a: \mu > \mu_0
\end{cases}
\qquad
\text{Case 2: } 
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu \geq \mu_0 \\
H_a: \mu < \mu_0
\end{cases} \\
\\
\text{Case 3: } 
&\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu = \mu_0 \\
H_a: \mu \neq \mu_0
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]

The value \(\mu_0\) is the \textbf{boundary value} of \(H_0\) --- the
value at which the Type I error probability is maximized for one-sided
tests (Section~\ref{sec-foundations-boundary}).

Recall from Section~\ref{sec-foundations-three-forms} that in Cases 1
and 2, the alternative hypothesis claims that \(\mu\) is either greater
than \((>)\) or less than \((<)\) \(\mu_0,\) pointing in a single
direction. These are called \textbf{one-sided} (or \textbf{one-tailed})
hypotheses. In Case 3, the alternative hypothesis claims only that
\(\mu\) is different from \((\neq)\) \(\mu_0,\) without specifying a
direction. This is called a \textbf{two-sided} (or \textbf{two-tailed})
hypothesis. The form of the hypotheses determines how we set up our
decision rules.

Let's begin with a few examples.

\begin{example}[SAT Math Scores at
CSUF]\protect\hypertarget{exm-sat-csuf-mean}{}\label{exm-sat-csuf-mean}

According to the
\href{https://reports.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/2025-total-group-sat-suite-of-assessments-annual-report\%20ADA-v0.2_0.pdf}{College
Board}, the mean score on the math portion of the SAT for the high
school graduating class of 2025 was 508 points, with a standard
deviation of 113 points. These figures are computed from the more than 2
million high school students who took the exam that year.

We wish to investigate whether the mean math SAT score among incoming
freshmen in fall 2025 at California State University, Fullerton (CSUF)
is \emph{higher} than the national mean. Since CSUF does not require the
SAT for admission, the exact population mean for the CSUF students is
not available, so we take a random sample of \(n = 40\) incoming CSUF
freshmen and record their SAT math scores. The sample mean of these SAT
scores is \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\) points. Using this information,
answer the following questions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the population of interest?
\item
  Describe the parameter \(\mu\) in words.
\item
  Write the null and alternative hypotheses.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. The population of interest is all incoming freshmen in fall 2025 at
California State University, Fullerton (CSUF).

b. \(\mu\) is the mean math SAT score for all incoming freshmen in fall
2025 at CSUF.

c. The research question asks whether the mean math SAT score among
incoming CSUF freshmen is higher than the national mean of 508. Because
``higher than'' points in the greater-than direction, the alternative
hypothesis is \(H_a: \mu > 508.\) The null hypothesis includes the
opposite situation, together with equality, so it is
\(H_0: \mu \leq 508.\) The null and alternative hypotheses are
therefore: \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu \leq 508 \\
H_a: \mu > 508
\end{cases}
\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Sleep Hours Among University
Students]\protect\hypertarget{exm-sleep-university-mean}{}\label{exm-sleep-university-mean}

The
\href{https://www.thensf.org/how-many-hours-of-sleep-do-you-really-need/}{National
Sleep Foundation} and the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommend
that young adults sleep between 7 and 9 hours per night, with 7 hours
often cited as the minimum needed for healthy cognitive and physical
functioning. There is widespread concern, however, that college students
fall short of this recommendation.

We wish to investigate whether the mean nightly sleep among students at
our university is \emph{less than} 7 hours. We take a random sample of
\(n = 15\) students and ask each student how many hours they slept the
previous night. The resulting sample has a mean of
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 6.4\) hours and a standard deviation of
\(s=1.2\) hours. Using this information, answer the following questions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the population of interest?
\item
  Describe the parameter \(\mu\) in words.
\item
  Write the null and alternative hypotheses.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. The population of interest is all students at our university.

b. \(\mu\) is the mean nightly sleep, in hours, for all students at our
university.

c. For this example, the research question asks whether the mean nightly
sleep among students at our university is \textbf{less than} 7 hours.
Because ``less than'' points in the lower-than direction, the
alternative hypothesis is \(H_a: \mu < 7.\) The null hypothesis includes
the opposite situation, together with equality, so it is
\(H_0: \mu \geq 7.\)

The null and alternative hypotheses are therefore:

\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu \geq 7 \\
H_a: \mu < 7
\end{cases}
\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Commute Time in a Metropolitan
Area]\protect\hypertarget{exm-commute-metro-mean}{}\label{exm-commute-metro-mean}

According to the
\href{https://www.census.gov/topics/employment/commuting/guidance/acs-1yr.html}{U.S.
Census Bureau's American Community Survey}, the mean one-way commute
time for U.S. workers in 2023 was 26.8 minutes. Local commuting patterns
can differ substantially from the national average, however, because of
differences in population density, transportation infrastructure, and
the prevalence of remote work.

We wish to investigate whether the mean one-way commute time among
workers in our metropolitan area \emph{differs} from the national mean.
We take a random sample of \(n = 15\) commuters from the area and record
each person's one-way commute time. The sample has a mean of
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8\) minutes and a standard deviation of
\(s = 9.6\) minutes. Using this information, answer the following
questions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the population of interest?
\item
  Describe the parameter \(\mu\) in words.
\item
  Write the null and alternative hypotheses.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. The population of interest is all workers in our metropolitan area.

b. \(\mu\) is the mean one-way commute time, in minutes, for all workers
in our metropolitan area.

c. For this example, the research question asks whether the mean one-way
commute time among workers in our metropolitan area \textbf{differs
from} the national mean of 26.8 minutes. Because ``differs from'' does
not specify whether the local mean is higher or lower, the alternative
hypothesis is two-sided: \(H_a: \mu \neq 26.8.\) The null hypothesis
says there is no difference from the national mean, so it is
\(H_0: \mu = 26.8.\)

The null and alternative hypotheses are therefore:

\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu = 26.8 \\
H_a: \mu \neq 26.8
\end{cases}
\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Flipper Length of Adélie
Penguins]\protect\hypertarget{exm-penguin-flipper-mean}{}\label{exm-penguin-flipper-mean}

The \href{https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/}{Palmer

We wish to investigate whether the mean flipper length among Adélie

use the raw flipper length measurements of \(n = 151\) Adélie penguins
with recorded flipper lengths in the \Data{palmerpenguins_Adelie}

answer the following questions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the population of interest?
\item
  Describe the parameter \(\mu\) in words.
\item

\end{enumerate}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Homework for
Section~\ref{sec-concept-setup-mean}}{Homework for Section~}}\label{homework-for-sec-concept-setup-mean}

For each problem, answer the following questions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the population of interest?\\
\item
  Describe the parameter \(\mu\) in words.\\
\item
  Write the null and alternative hypotheses.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{CO2 Emissions} The Kyoto Protocol, signed in 1997, required
  participating countries to begin reducing their carbon emissions; it
  became enforceable in February 2005. In 2004, the mean CO2 emission
  was 4.87 metric tons per capita, computed by averaging each country's
  per-capita emission rate across countries. A researcher wants to
  determine whether the mean CO2 emission per capita across countries in
  2010 \emph{differs} from the 2004 mean.
\item
  \textbf{Mercury Concentration} The U.S. Food and Drug Administration
  (FDA) sets 1.0 mg/kg as the allowable amount of mercury in fish that
  is consumed. To assess whether fish in Florida lakes meet this
  standard, largemouth bass were collected from 53 different lakes and
  for each lake a standardized estimate of the mercury concentration in
  a three-year-old bass was computed from the fish sampled there. A
  researcher wants to determine whether the mean standardized mercury
  concentration across Florida lakes differs from the allowable amount
  of 1.0 mg/kg.
\item
  \textbf{Cereal Sugar} The amount of sugar in a Krispy Kreme glazed
  donut is 10 g. Many people feel that cereal is a healthier alternative
  to glazed donuts for children. A researcher wants to determine whether
  the mean amount of sugar in children's cereal \emph{differs} from the
  10 g found in a glazed donut.
\item
  \textbf{Pulse Rate} The mean pulse rate after running in place for one
  minute among females who do \emph{not} drink alcohol is 97 beats per
  minute. A researcher wants to determine whether the mean pulse rate
  after running, among females who \emph{do} drink alcohol, is
  \emph{higher} than this value.
\item
  \textbf{Economic Dynamism} Economic dynamism is an index of productive
  growth, measured on a scale from 0 (worst) to 100 (best). Countries
  that are considered high-income have a mean economic dynamism of
  60.29. A researcher wants to determine whether the mean economic
  dynamism of middle-income countries is \emph{less than} the
  high-income mean.
\item
  \textbf{Prenatal Care} In 1999, the mean percentage of women who
  received prenatal care per country was 80.1\%, computed by averaging
  each country's percentage across countries. A researcher wants to
  determine whether the mean percentage of women receiving prenatal care
  across countries in 2009 differs from the 1999 mean.
\item
  \textbf{Balance Study} Maintaining balance may become harder with age.
  In a study of steadiness, elderly subjects stood on a force platform
  and reacted to an unpredictable noise while the platform measured how
  much they swayed, in millimeters, in the forward/backward direction.
  The mean forward sway of younger people under the same conditions is
  18.125 mm. A researcher wants to determine whether the elderly sway
  \emph{more} than this value, on average.
\end{enumerate}

\section{The Null Distribution of the Sample
Mean}\label{sec-null-distribution-mean}

As we noted in Section~\ref{sec-foundations-populations}, to make
inferences about \(\mu,\) we use the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) as our
statistic, and we work with its sampling distribution.

To make this distribution concrete, we will \textbf{assume that the
variable under study has a normal distribution} in the population. Two
reasons motivate this assumption. First, the normal distribution
provides a reasonable model for many naturally occurring numerical
variables, including adult heights, weights, exam scores, and a wide
range of biological and physical measurements. Second, under this
assumption, the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) takes a clean,
exact form that allows us to focus on the main ideas of inference
without the distraction of approximations or special cases. In
Section~\ref{sec-QQ-Plot-mean} we discuss how to assess this assumption
graphically with a statistical test and normal probability plot, and in
Section~\ref{sec-large-sample-mean} we show that the methods developed
under the normality assumption remain approximately valid for large
samples even when the population is not normal.

The sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) depends on the unknown
population mean \(\mu\) --- the very quantity we want to make an
inference about. As in foundations
(Section~\ref{sec-foundations-boundary}), we proceed by evaluating the
sampling distribution at the boundary value of \(H_0\): the value
\(\mu_0\) where the Type I error probability is maximized. For two-sided
tests, \(H_0\) specifies \(\mu = \mu_0\) directly. For one-sided tests,
\(\mu_0\) is the boundary of the range of \(\mu\) values allowed by
\(H_0.\)

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{The Null Distribution}\vspace{3mm}

The \textbf{null distribution} of \(\bar{X}\) is the sampling
distribution of \(\bar{X}\) evaluated at \(\mu = \mu_0,\) the boundary
value of \(H_0.\) This is the distribution we use for hypothesis testing
--- to compute p-values and to determine critical regions.

\end{tcolorbox}

Under the normality assumption introduced above, the form of this null
distribution depends on whether the population standard deviation
\(\sigma\) is known. When \(\sigma\) is known, the null distribution is
exactly normal. When \(\sigma\) is unknown --- the typical situation in
practice --- we estimate it from the sample, and the resulting null
distribution is a Student \(t\) distribution. The subsections that
follow develop each case in turn.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{When \(\sigma\) Is
Known}{When \textbackslash sigma Is Known}}\label{sec-mean-inference-known-sigma}

In practice, the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is rarely
known exactly. There are, however, situations in which a value of
\(\sigma\) has been established from extensive prior data and can
reasonably be treated as known. The SAT example in
Example~\ref{exm-sat-csuf-mean} is one such case: the standard deviation
of \(\sigma = 113\) points is computed from the scores of more than 2
million students who took the exam in 2025, a population large enough
that we can reasonably treat this value as known when investigating the
mean score among a particular subgroup such as incoming CSUF freshmen.

Beyond examples of this kind, beginning with the known-\(\sigma\) case
is helpful pedagogically because it allows us to focus on the main ideas
of statistical inference while working with a simpler sampling
distribution. Once these ideas are established, we will turn to the more
realistic setting in which \(\sigma\) is unknown and must be estimated
from the sample data.

Let's pause to clarify a phrase that will appear repeatedly throughout
this chapter.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{A Convention on ``When \(H_0\) Is True''}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

For a two-sided test of a population mean, the null hypothesis is
\(H_0: \mu = \mu_0,\) so the phrase ``when \(H_0\) is true'' is
unambiguous: it means \(\mu = \mu_0.\)

For a one-sided test, however, the null hypothesis allows a range of
possible values. For example, if \(H_0: \mu \leq \mu_0,\) then any value
\(\mu \leq \mu_0\) is included in the null hypothesis; similarly, if
\(H_0: \mu \geq \mu_0,\) then any value \(\mu \geq \mu_0\) is included.
Thus, ``when \(H_0\) is true'' could in principle refer to any value in
that range. As established in Section~\ref{sec-foundations-boundary},
the \textbf{boundary value} \(\mu_0\) is the value within \(H_0\) at
which the Type I error probability is maximized; controlling the error
rate at \(\mu_0\) automatically controls it at every other value of
\(\mu\) allowed under \(H_0.\)

\textbf{Convention.} For the remainder of this chapter, whenever we say
\emph{``when \(H_0\) is true,''} \emph{``under \$H\_0,''} or
\emph{``assuming the null hypothesis,''} we mean \textbf{at the boundary
value \(\mu_0\)}.

\end{tcolorbox}

Under the assumptions introduced earlier, the sample mean \(\bar{X}\)
has a normal distribution when \(H_0\) is true. This distribution serves
as the null distribution for hypothesis testing about the population
mean \(\mu.\)

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{The Null Distribution}\vspace{3mm}

Under the assumptions that

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  the variable under study has a \textbf{normal distribution} in the
  population,
\item
  the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is known,
\item
  the sample size is \(n,\) and
\item
  the boundary value specified by \(H_0\) is \(\mu = \mu_0,\)
\end{itemize}

the null distribution of the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) is

\[
\bar{X} \sim N\left(\mu_0,\ \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right).
\]

\end{tcolorbox}

The result above tells us that, when \(H_0\) is true, the sample mean
\(\bar{X}\) is centered at \(\mu_0\) and varies around it with standard
deviation \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}.\) For instance, in the SAT example with
hypothesis \(H_0: \mu \leq 508,\) the random variable \(\bar{X}\) has a
normal distribution centered at 508 with standard deviation
\(113/\sqrt{40} \approx 17.87\) points.

Sometimes, the sample mean is standardized by subtracting its
null-hypothesis center \(\mu_0\) and dividing by its standard deviation
\(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\):

\[
Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}.
\]

When \(H_0\) is true, this standardized statistic has the standard
normal distribution,

\[
Z \sim N(0,1),
\]

and for this reason the procedure is commonly called the
\textbf{\(z\)-test}. Rguroo reports critical regions and p-values using
both the standardized statistic \(Z\) and the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) on
its original scale.

In this text, we will primarily use the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)
directly rather than its standardized version. Working on the original
scale of the data allows us to interpret critical regions and p-values
more naturally in the context of the problem and avoids the additional
step of converting observations to standardized scores. In the SAT
example, for instance, it is easier to reason about a sample mean of 542
points relative to a hypothesized population mean of 508 points than to
translate everything into the unitless \(z\) scale.

\begin{example}[SAT Math Scores at
CSUF]\protect\hypertarget{exm-sat-null-distribution-known}{}\label{exm-sat-null-distribution-known}

Recall the SAT Math Scores at CSUF example. The national mean math SAT
score for the high school graduating class of 2025 was 508 points, with
population standard deviation \(\sigma = 113\) points. We wish to
investigate whether the mean math SAT score among incoming CSUF freshmen
is higher than the national mean.

The hypotheses are

\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu \leq 508 \\
H_a: \mu > 508
\end{cases}
\]

Suppose we take a random sample of \(n = 40\) incoming CSUF freshmen.
Assume that SAT math scores are normally distributed in the population
and that the population standard deviation is known.

What is the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

Because \(H_0: \mu \leq 508,\) the boundary value is \(\mu_0 = 508.\)
Since the population standard deviation is known, we use the normal
distribution for the null distribution of \(\bar{X}.\)

Thus,

\[
\bar{X} \sim N\left(\mu_0,\ \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right).
\]

Substituting \(\mu_0 = 508,\) \(\sigma = 113,\) and \(n = 40,\) we get

\[
\bar{X} \sim N\left(508,\ \frac{113}{\sqrt{40}}\right).
\]

Since

\[
\frac{113}{\sqrt{40}} \approx 17.87,
\]

the null distribution is approximately

\[
\bar{X} \sim N(508,\ 17.87).
\]

So, when \(H_0\) is true at the boundary value \(\mu = 508,\) sample
means from samples of size 40 are normally distributed with center 508
and standard deviation approximately 17.87 points.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{When \(\sigma\) Is
Unknown}{When \textbackslash sigma Is Unknown}}\label{sec-mean-inference-unknown-sigma}

In practice, only in rare cases do we know the population standard
deviation \(\sigma.\) For example, in the sleep-hours example, we have
data from only a sample of students, not from all students at our
university, so we do not know the population standard deviation of
nightly sleep hours. Similarly, in the commute-time and Adélie penguin
examples, we have data from only samples, so the population standard
deviation must be estimated from the data.

The good news is that the sample standard deviation \(s\) gives us a way
to estimate the unknown population standard deviation \(\sigma.\) The
key point is that this estimate adds uncertainty: from sample to sample,
both the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) and the sample standard deviation \(s\)
can vary.

To handle this extra uncertainty, we use a closely related distribution
called the \textbf{Student \(t\) distribution} (or simply \(t\)
distribution). The assumption is still about the individual
measurements: we assume that the variable under study has a normal
distribution in the population. But because \(\sigma\) is unknown and
must be estimated by \(s,\) the sampling distribution we use for
\(\bar{X}\) is a \(t\) distribution rather than a normal distribution.

The name \emph{Student} was the pen name of William Sealy Gosset, a
statistician working for Guinness Brewery in Ireland in the early 1900s.
At the time, Guinness restricted employees from publishing research
under their own names in order to protect company information and trade
secrets. As a result, Gosset published his work under the pseudonym
\emph{Student}. His research led to the development of the \(t\)
distribution, which allows us to make reliable inferences about
population means when the population standard deviation is unknown.

The standard Student \(t\) distribution is similar in shape to the
standard normal distribution: both are symmetric, bell-shaped, and
centered at 0. Unlike the standard normal distribution, however, the
\(t\) distribution depends on a shape parameter called the
\textbf{degrees of freedom}, denoted \(\text{df},\) with different
values of \(\text{df}\) producing slightly different shapes. When the
degrees of freedom are small, the \(t\) distribution is more spread out
and has heavier tails; as the degrees of freedom increase, the \(t\)
distribution becomes closer and closer to the standard normal
distribution.

Figure~\ref{fig-three-t-distributions} shows three \(t\) distributions,
with 1, 3, and 10 degrees of freedom, compared with the standard normal
distribution (dashed gray). As the degrees of freedom increase, the
\(t\) distribution becomes taller at its center, its tails grow lighter,
and its shape approaches that of the standard normal.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Mean Inference/three_t_distributions_by_df.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-three-t-distributions}Compating t-distributions with
various degress of freeom to the normal distribution.}

\end{figure}%

The heavier tails of the \(t\) distribution are shown more clearly in
Figure~\ref{fig-normal-two-tail}, which compares the standard normal
distribution to a \(t\) distribution with 4 degrees of freedom. Notice
that the \(t\) distribution places more probability in the tails and
less probability near the center. This difference is important because,
when \(\sigma\) is unknown, we replace it with the sample standard
deviation \(s.\) Since \(s\) varies from sample to sample, additional
uncertainty is introduced into the inference procedure, and the heavier
tails of the \(t\) distribution account for this extra uncertainty.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Mean Inference/t4_vs_normal_tail_comparison.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-normal-two-tail}Comparison of the standard normal
distribution and the \(t\) distribution with 4 degrees of freedom.}

\end{figure}%

The amount of this additional uncertainty depends on the sample size.
Small samples provide less information about \(\sigma,\) so \(s\) is a
less reliable estimate and the \(t\) distribution has heavier tails;
larger samples make \(s\) more stable and bring the \(t\) distribution
closer to the standard normal. In mean inference, this relationship is
captured directly by the degrees of freedom, \(\text{df} = n - 1\): In
this way, the \(t\) distribution automatically adjusts the amount of
uncertainty in the inference to match the amount of information in the
sample.

Just as the standard normal distribution can be shifted and rescaled to
obtain a general normal distribution with any center and standard
deviation, the standard \(t\) distribution also has a more general form,
written as

\[
X \sim t_{\text{df}}(\text{location}, \text{scale}),
\]

where \(\text{df}\) denotes the degrees of freedom, the \emph{location}
parameter determines the center of the distribution, and the
\emph{scale} parameter controls its spread. In mean inference, the
degrees of freedom are \(n - 1,\) the location is the hypothesized
population mean \(\mu_0,\) and the scale is the estimated standard error
\(s/\sqrt{n},\) giving the null distribution of the sample mean stated
below.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{What has a \(t\) distribution?}\vspace{3mm}

It is important to be clear about \emph{what} is assumed to be normal
and \emph{what} follows a \(t\) distribution. The assumption is that the
\textbf{variable under study} has a normal distribution in the
population. Under this assumption, the \textbf{statistic} \(\bar{X}\)
follows a \(t\) distribution. In other words, the normality assumption
is about the individual measurements, while the \(t\) distribution
describes the behavior of the sample mean computed from those
measurements.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{The Null Distribution}\vspace{3mm}

Under the assumptions that

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  the variable under study has a \textbf{normal distribution} in the
  population,
\item
  the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown and is
  estimated by the sample standard deviation \(s,\)
\item
  the sample size is \(n,\) and
\item
  the boundary value specified by the null hypothesis is
  \(\mu = \mu_0,\)
\end{itemize}

the null distribution of the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) is

\[
\bar{X} \sim t_{n-1}\left(\mu_0,\ \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right),
\]

a \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom, centered at
\(\mu_0\) and with estimated standard error

\[
\hat\sigma_{\bar X} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]

\end{tcolorbox}

This result parallels the known-\(\sigma\) case, with two changes: the
normal distribution is replaced by a \(t\) distribution, and because
\(\sigma\) is no longer available, we replace it with the sample
standard deviation \(s,\) so the scale of the distribution is the
\textbf{estimated} standard error \(\hat\sigma_{\bar X} = s/\sqrt{n}\)
rather than the known standard error \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}.\)

As in the known-\(\sigma\) case, the distribution is centered at
\(\mu_0\) when the null hypothesis is true, and sample means far from
\(\mu_0\) constitute evidence against \(H_0.\)

For instance, in the sleep example, suppose the null hypothesis is
\(H_0: \mu \geq 7\) and we have a sample of size \(n = 15\) with sample
standard deviation \(s = 1.2\) hours. Then \(\bar{X}\) follows a \(t\)
distribution with \(n - 1 = 14\) degrees of freedom, centered at 7 hours
and with estimated standard error \(1.2/\sqrt{15} \approx 0.310\) hours.

We can also standardize the sample mean by subtracting its
null-hypothesis center \(\mu_0\) and dividing by its estimated standard
error \(s/\sqrt{n}\):

\[
T = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}.
\]

When \(H_0\) is true, this standardized statistic has a standard Student
\(t\) distribution with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom,

\[
T \sim t_{n-1}.
\]

This distribution, like the standard normal distribution, is centered at
zero, and its shape is determined by the degrees of freedom. Rguroo
reports critical regions and p-values using both the standardized
statistic \(T\) and the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) on its original scale.

As in the known-\(\sigma\) case, in this text we will primarily use the
null distribution of \(\bar{X}\) directly rather than its standardized
version. Working on the original scale of the data allows us to
interpret critical regions and p-values in the units of the problem. In
the sleep example, for instance, it is more natural to reason about a
sample mean of 6.4 hours relative to a hypothesized mean of 7 hours than
to translate everything into the unitless \(t\) scale.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{When the \(t\) and normal distributions agree}\vspace{3mm}

As we saw above, the \(t\) distribution becomes closer to the standard
normal distribution as the degrees of freedom increase. By the time the
degrees of freedom reach about 30 --- that is, a sample size of roughly
\(n = 30\) or more --- the two distributions are nearly
indistinguishable, and the critical values and p-values they produce are
essentially the same. For this reason, with large samples it makes
little practical difference whether one uses the \(t\) distribution or
the normal distribution, and the resulting inference is usually nearly
identical. We nonetheless recommend using the \(t\) distribution
whenever \(\sigma\) is unknown, regardless of sample size: it is always
at least as appropriate as the normal, and it requires no judgment about
whether the sample is ``large enough.''

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Adélie Flipper
Length]\protect\hypertarget{exm-adelie-null-distribution-unknown}{}\label{exm-adelie-null-distribution-unknown}

Recall the Adélie penguin flipper-length example. We wish to investigate
whether the mean flipper length among Adélie penguins in the Palmer
Archipelago differs from the reference value of 188 mm.

The hypotheses are

\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu = 188 \\
H_a: \mu \neq 188
\end{cases}
\]

Use the raw flipper-length data for Adélie penguins in the
\Data{PalmerPenguins} dataset. Assume that Adélie flipper lengths are
normally distributed in the population. Since the population standard
deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown, use Rguroo to obtain the sample size
\(n\) and sample standard deviation \(s.\)

What is the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

In this example, \(H_0: \mu = 188\) with the boundary value of
\(\mu_0 = 188.\) Since the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is
unknown, we estimate it using the sample standard deviation \(s,\) and
the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\) is a Student \(t\) distribution.

From Rguroo, the Adélie flipper-length data give

\[
n = 151
\]

and

\[
s = 6.539 \text{ mm}.
\]

Therefore, the degrees of freedom are

\[
n - 1 = 150,
\]

and the estimated standard error is

\[
\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{6.539}{\sqrt{151}} \approx 0.532.
\]

Thus, the null distribution is

\[
\bar{X} \sim t_{150}\left(188,\ \frac{6.539}{\sqrt{151}}\right).
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\bar{X} \sim t_{150}(188,\ 0.532).
\]

So, when \(H_0\) is true, sample means from samples of size 151 are
modeled by a Student \(t\) distribution centered at 188 mm, with
estimated standard error approximately 0.532 mm.

\end{tcolorbox}
