\section{The p-value Approach}\label{sec-pvalue-mean}

To measure how strongly the observed data provide evidence against
\(H_0\) and in favor of \(H_a,\) we use a quantity called the
\textbf{p-value}. This section develops the p-value approach to
hypothesis testing. An equivalent alternative, the critical region
approach, is developed in Section~\ref{sec-critical-region-mean}.

Conceptually, the p-value measures how strongly the evidence in our
observed sample favors the alternative hypothesis, assuming that the
null hypothesis is true. As in the proportion setting, we develop the
idea of the p-value through the \(H_a\) \textbf{support}: the set of
values of the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) that are at least as favorable to
the alternative hypothesis as the value we actually observed.

To make this concrete, recall that our observed sample mean is denoted
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}},\) and that we evaluate evidence using the null
distribution of \(\bar{X}.\) This null distribution is
\(N\!\left(\mu_0,\, \sigma/\sqrt{n}\right)\) when \(\sigma\) is known,
and \(t_{n-1}\!\left(\mu_0,\, s/\sqrt{n}\right)\) when \(\sigma\) is
unknown; in both cases, the probabilities below are computed under the
appropriate distribution. The \(H_a\) support depends on the form of the
alternative hypothesis. The callout that follows summarizes the \(H_a\)
support and the corresponding p-value for each type of alternative
hypothesis.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{p-value for the One-Sample Test of \(\mu\)}\vspace{3mm}

In each case, the p-value is computed under the null distribution of
\(\bar{X},\) which depends on whether \(\sigma\) is known:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  When \(\sigma\) is known:
  \(\bar{X} \sim N\!\left(\mu_0,\, \sigma/\sqrt{n}\right).\)
\item
  When \(\sigma\) is unknown:
  \(\bar{X} \sim t_{n-1}\!\left(\mu_0,\, s/\sqrt{n}\right).\)
\end{itemize}

All probabilities below are computed assuming the boundary value
\(\mu = \mu_0.\)

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Alternative Hypothesis
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\(H_a\) Support
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
p-value
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(H_a: \mu > \mu_0\) & \(\bar{X} \geq \bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) &
\(P\!\left(\bar{X} \geq \bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\right)\) \\
\(H_a: \mu < \mu_0\) & \(\bar{X} \leq \bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) &
\(P\!\left(\bar{X} \leq \bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\right)\) \\
\(H_a: \mu \neq \mu_0,\) with \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} < \mu_0\) & at
least as far below \(\mu_0\) as \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}},\) or equally far
above &
\(2 \times P\!\left(\bar{X} \leq \bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\right)\) \\
\(H_a: \mu \neq \mu_0,\) with \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} \geq \mu_0\) & at
least as far above \(\mu_0\) as \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}},\) or equally far
below &
\(2 \times P\!\left(\bar{X} \geq \bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\right)\) \\
\end{longtable}

\end{tcolorbox}

In each figure below, the curve shows the null distribution of
\(\bar{X},\) centered at \(\mu_0\) (dashed line), and the triangle marks
the observed sample mean \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\); the area of the
shaded region is the p-value. Figure~\ref{fig-pvalue-onesided} shows the
one-sided cases, where the shading is a single tail beyond
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}.\) Figure~\ref{fig-pvalue-twosided} shows the
two-sided case: shading appears in both tails, one beyond
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) itself and one an equal distance away on the
opposite side of \(\mu_0\) (marked with a lighter triangle) ---
together, these represent all sample means at least as far from
\(\mu_0\) as the one we observed. Panel (a) shows this when
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) falls below \(\mu_0,\) and panel (b) when it
falls at or above \(\mu_0,\) matching the two \(H_a: \mu \neq \mu_0\)
rows in the table above.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Mean Inference/pvalue_illustration_onesided.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-pvalue-onesided}The p-value for a one-sided
alternative hypothesis.}

\end{figure}%

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Mean Inference/pvalue_illustration_twosided.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-pvalue-twosided}The p-value for a two-sided
alternative hypothesis, depending on which side of \(\mu_0\) the
observed sample mean falls.}

\end{figure}%

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

In each case, the p-value is the probability, computed under the null
distribution, of observing a sample mean at least as favorable to
\(H_a\) as the one actually observed.

\end{tcolorbox}

Once the p-value has been computed, the decision rule is the same
regardless of the form of the alternative hypothesis: reject \(H_0\) if
the p-value is less than the significance level \(\alpha,\) and fail to
reject \(H_0\) otherwise.

Intuitively, a small p-value means that the observed sample mean would
be unusual under the null hypothesis, providing evidence against the
null hypothesis. A p-value larger than \(\alpha\) means that the
observed sample mean is reasonably consistent with the null hypothesis,
and we have insufficient evidence to reject it.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Worked Example: \(\sigma\)
Known}{Worked Example: \textbackslash sigma Known}}\label{sec-worked-examples-pvalue-known-sigma}

We now apply the p-value approach to the SAT example. As noted earlier,
the SAT setting is one of the rare cases in which the population
standard deviation \(\sigma\) can reasonably be treated as known (here,
\(\sigma = 113\) points, computed from the scores of more than 2 million
students). The remaining three running examples --- sleep, commute time,
and Adélie penguin flipper length --- are taken up in
Section~\ref{sec-worked-examples-pvalue-unknown-sigma}, where we treat
\(\sigma\) as unknown and use the Student \(t\) distribution.

\begin{example}[SAT Math Scores at
CSUF]\protect\hypertarget{exm-sat-csuf-mean-known}{}\label{exm-sat-csuf-mean-known}

We return to the SAT setting introduced in
Example~\ref{exm-sat-csuf-mean}. Recall that the national mean math SAT
score for the high school graduating class of 2025 was 508 points, with
a standard deviation of 113 points, and that we wished to investigate
whether the mean math SAT score among incoming CSUF freshmen in fall
2025 was higher than the national mean. A random sample of \(n = 40\)
incoming CSUF freshmen yielded a sample mean of
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\) points.

The hypotheses are \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu \leq 508 \\
H_a: \mu > 508
\end{cases}
\] where \(\mu\) denotes the mean math SAT score among incoming CSUF
freshmen in fall 2025. Assume that the population of math SAT scores is
normally distributed, and treat the population standard deviation as
known with \(\sigma = 113\) points. Perform a test of hypothesis at the
\(\alpha = 0.05\) significance level by answering the following
questions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
\item
  State a probability statement that defines the p-value for this test,
  and describe it in words.
\item
  Use Rguroo to obtain the p-value, interpret it in the context of the
  problem, and state whether you reject or fail to reject \(H_0\) at
  \(\alpha = 0.05\) significance level.
\item
  Give your decision.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. The null distribution is

\[\bar{X}\sim N\left(508, \frac{113}{\sqrt{40}}\right)\approx N\left(508,17.867 \right)
\]

b. The p-value is the probability of observing a sample mean greater
than or equal to our observed value of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\)
given that the true value of the population mean is \(\mu = 508.\) This
can be written mathematically as

\[\text{p-value} = P(\bar{X} \geq 542).\]

of 542 or larger is approximately 2.9\%. Because this probability is
small, and more specifically is less than 5\%, there is sufficient

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Worked Examples: \(\sigma\)
Unknown}{Worked Examples: \textbackslash sigma Unknown}}\label{sec-worked-examples-pvalue-unknown-sigma}

We now turn to the more realistic setting in which the population
standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown and is estimated from the
sample by \(s.\) The three running examples in this section --- sleep
hours, commute time, and Adélie penguin flipper length --- all use the
Student \(t\) distribution as the null distribution of \(\bar{X}.\) Each
example reuses the setup introduced earlier in the chapter; we now carry
out the p-value part of the hypothesis test. (The critical region part
of each of these same examples is taken up in
Section~\ref{sec-worked-examples-cr-unknown-sigma}.)

\begin{example}[Sleep Hours Among University
Students]\protect\hypertarget{exm-sleep-university-mean-unknown}{}\label{exm-sleep-university-mean-unknown}

We return to the sleep setting introduced in
Example~\ref{exm-sleep-university-mean}. Recall that the recommended
minimum nightly sleep for young adults is 7 hours, and that we wished to
investigate whether the mean nightly sleep among students at our
university is less than 7 hours. A random sample of \(n = 15\) students
yielded a sample mean of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 6.4\) hours and a
sample standard deviation of \(s = 1.2\) hours.

The hypotheses are \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu \geq 7 \\
H_a: \mu < 7
\end{cases}
\] where \(\mu\) denotes the mean nightly sleep, in hours, among
students at our university. Assume that the population of nightly sleep
hours is normally distributed. Because the population standard deviation
\(\sigma\) is unknown, we estimate it from the sample by \(s = 1.2\)
hours and use the Student \(t\) distribution. Perform a test of
hypothesis at the \(\alpha = 0.01\) significance level by answering the
following questions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
\item
  State a probability statement that defines the p-value for this test,
  and describe it in words.
\item
  Use Rguroo to obtain the p-value, interpret it in the context of the
  problem, and state whether you reject or fail to reject \(H_0\) at
  \(\alpha = 0.01\) level.
\item
  Give your decision.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. Because \(\sigma\) is unknown, the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)
is a Student \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1 = 14\) degrees of freedom,
centered at \(\mu_0 = 7\) with estimated standard error
\(s/\sqrt{n} = 1.2/\sqrt{15} \approx 0.3098\) hours:

\[
\bar{X}\sim t_{14}\left(7,\ \frac{1.2}{\sqrt{15}}\right)\approx t_{14}\!\left(7,\ 0.3098\right).
\]

b. The p-value is the probability of observing a sample mean less than
or equal to our observed value of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 6.4,\) given
that the true value of the population mean is \(\mu = 7.\) This can be
written mathematically as

\[
\text{p-value} = P(\bar{X} \leq 6.4),
\]

with the probability computed under the \(t_{14}(7,\ 0.3098)\) null
distribution.

c. Click to expand the box below to see how to use the
\Fun{Mean Inference} function in Rguroo to answer this question.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]
\begin{minipage}[t]{5.5mm}
\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{minipage}[t]{\textwidth - 5.5mm}

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{\includegraphics[width=0.22917in,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_Icons/R_circle_logo.pdf}
One-Population mean hypothesis test - Sleep example}\vspace{3mm}

The steps for using Rguroo's \Fun{Mean Inference} function are the same
as those in Example~\ref{exm-sat-csuf-mean-known}, with the following
differences in the \Dialog{One Population Mean Inference} dialog:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \Des{Sample Mean}: \TypeIn{6.4}, the value of
  \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}.\)
\item
  \Des{Sample S.d.}: \TypeIn{1.2}, the sample standard deviation \(s.\)
  (Leave \Des{Pop S.d.} empty since \(\sigma\) is unknown.)
\item
  \Des{Sample Size}: \TypeIn{15}, the size of the sample \(n.\)
\item
  In the text box \Des{\mu = Mean of} enter the label
  \TypeIn{Nightly Sleep}.
\item
  In the \Dpd{Alternative Hypothesis \mu} dropdown, select \TypeIn{<}
  and enter \TypeIn{7}, the value stated in \(H_a.\)
\item
  Select the \Des{t-statistic} checkbox (instead of z-statistic) to use
  the \(t\) distribution.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo One-Population Mean Inference dialog}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_dialogs/Mean Inference/sleep_dialog_mean.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-sleep-dialog}Rguroo setup for the Nightly Sleep
one-sample t-test.}

\end{figure}%

\end{tcolorbox}

\end{minipage}%
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo Output: Sleep example}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\end{tcolorbox}

Both the \textbf{\emph{Test of Hypothesis}} table and the
\textbf{\emph{P-value Graph}} in the Rguroo output show the p-value is
approximately \(0.0366 \approx 3.7\%.\) This means that if the true
population mean is in fact 7 hours, then the probability of having
observed a sample mean of 6.4 hours or less in a sample of size 15 is
approximately 3.7\%. Because this probability is larger than the
significance leve \(\alpha = 0.01,\) there is not sufficient evidence to
reject \(H_0\) at \(\alpha = 0.01\) significance level.

d. The decision is that, based on the observed sample mean of 6.4 hours,
there is not sufficient evidence at the \(\alpha = 0.01\) significance
level to conclude that the mean nightly sleep among students at our
university is less than the recommended 7 hours.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Commute Time in a Metropolitan
Area]\protect\hypertarget{exm-commute-metro-mean-unknown}{}\label{exm-commute-metro-mean-unknown}

We return to the commute setting introduced in
Example~\ref{exm-commute-metro-mean}. Recall that the national mean
one-way commute time for U.S. workers in 2023 was 26.8 minutes, and that
we wished to investigate whether the mean one-way commute time among
workers in our metropolitan area differs from the national mean. A
random sample of \(n = 15\) commuters yielded a sample mean of
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8\) minutes and a sample standard deviation
of \(s = 9.6\) minutes.

The hypotheses are \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu = 26.8 \\
H_a: \mu \neq 26.8
\end{cases}
\] where \(\mu\) denotes the mean one-way commute time, in minutes,
among workers in our metropolitan area. Assume that the population of
commute times is normally distributed. Perform a test of hypothesis at
the \(\alpha = 0.10\) significance level by answering the following
questions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
\item
  State a probability statement that defines the \(p\)-value for this
  test, and describe it in words.
\item
  Use Rguroo to obtain the \(p\)-value, interpret it in the context of
  the problem, and state whether you reject or fail to reject \(H_0\) at
  \(\alpha = 0.10\) significance level.
\item
  Give your decision.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. Because \(\sigma\) is unknown, the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)
is a Student \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1 = 14\) degrees of freedom,
centered at \(\mu_0 = 26.8\) with estimated standard error
\(s/\sqrt{n} = 9.6/\sqrt{15} \approx 2.4787\) minutes:

\[
\bar{X}\sim t_{14}\left(26.8,\ \frac{9.6}{\sqrt{15}}\right)\approx t_{14}\!\left(26.8,\ 2.4787\right).
\]

b. Because the test is two-sided, a sample mean that is far from 26.8 in
\emph{either} direction is evidence against \(H_0.\) The \(p\)-value is
therefore the probability, under the null distribution, of observing a
sample mean at least as far from 26.8 as our observed value of
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8.\) Since 24.8 is 2 units below 26.8, this
means a sample mean of 24.8 or less, or equally far above at 28.8 or
more. This can be written mathematically as

\[
\text{p-value} = P(\bar{X} \leq 24.8) + P(\bar{X} \geq 28.8).
\]

Because the null \(t\) distribution is symmetric about 26.8, this is
equal to

\[
\text{p-value} = 2 \times P(\bar{X} \leq 24.8),
\]

with the probability computed under the \(t_{14}(26.8,\ 2.4787)\) null
distribution.

c. The steps for using Rguroo's \Fun{Mean Inference} function are the
same as those in Example~\ref{exm-sat-csuf-mean-known}. To see the
differences in the \Dialog{One Population Mean Inference} dialog click
to open the box below:

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo One-Population Mean Inference dialog}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \Des{Sample Mean}: \TypeIn{24.8}, the value of
  \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}.\)
\item
  \Des{Sample S.d.}: \TypeIn{9.6}, the sample standard deviation \(s.\)
  (Leave \Des{Pop S.d.} empty since \(\sigma\) is unknown.)
\item
  \Des{Sample Size}: \TypeIn{15}, the size of the sample \(n.\)
\item
  In the text box \Des{\mu = Mean of} enter the label
  \TypeIn{Commute Times}.
\item
  In the \Dpd{Alternative Hypothesis \mu} dropdown, select \TypeIn{!=}
  and enter \TypeIn{26.8}, the value stated in \(H_a.\)
\item
  Select the \Des{t-statistic} checkbox (instead of z-statistic) to use
  the \(t\) distribution.
\end{itemize}

This is a two-sided test, so the \TypeIn{!=} option produces a p-value
computed from both tails of the null distribution.

Figure~\ref{fig-commute-dialog} shows the Rguroo dialog for the setup.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_dialogs/Mean Inference/commute_mean_dialog.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-commute-dialog}Rguroo setup for the Commute Times
one-sample t-test.}

\end{figure}%

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo Output: Commute Time in a Metropolitan Area}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\end{tcolorbox}

Both the \textbf{\emph{Test of Hypothesis}} table and the
\textbf{\emph{P-value Graph}} in the Rguroo output show the p-value is
approximately \(0.4332 \approx 43.3\%.\) This means that if the true
population mean is in fact 26.8 minutes, then the probability of
observing a sample mean at least as far from 26.8 as 24.8 is
approximately 43.3\%. Because this probability is large, and in
particular is greater than 10\%, there is insufficient evidence to
reject \(H_0.\)

d. The decision is that, based on the observed sample mean of 24.8
minutes, there is insufficient evidence at the \(\alpha = 0.10\)
significance level to conclude that the mean one-way commute time among
workers in our metropolitan area differs from the national mean of 26.8
minutes.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Flipper Length of Adélie
Penguins]\protect\hypertarget{exm-penguin-flipper-mean-unknown}{}\label{exm-penguin-flipper-mean-unknown}

We return to the penguin setting introduced in
Example~\ref{exm-penguin-flipper-mean}. Recall that the Palmer Penguins
dataset contains flipper length measurements for \(n = 151\) Adélie
penguins in the Palmer Archipelago, and that we wished to investigate
whether the mean flipper length among Adélie penguins differs from the
reference value of 188 mm. Computed from the raw data, the sample mean
is \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 189.95\) mm and the sample standard
deviation is \(s = 6.539\) mm.

The hypotheses are \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu = 188 \\
H_a: \mu \neq 188
\end{cases}
\] where \(\mu\) denotes the mean flipper length, in millimeters, of
Adélie penguins in the Palmer Archipelago. Assume that the population of
Adélie flipper lengths is normally distributed. Perform a test of
hypothesis at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) significance level by answering the
following questions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
\item
  State a probability statement that defines the p-value for this test,
  and describe it in words.
\item
  Use Rguroo to obtain the p-value, interpret it in the context of the
  problem, and state whether you reject or fail to reject \(H_0\) at
  \(\alpha = 0.05\) significane level.
\item
  Give your decision.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

See the codebook for the dataset
\hyperref[code-book-palmerpenguins]{here}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. Because \(\sigma\) is unknown, the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)
is a Student \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1 = 150\) degrees of freedom,
centered at \(\mu_0 = 188\) with estimated standard error
\(s/\sqrt{n} = 6.539/\sqrt{151} \approx 0.5321\) mm:

\[
\bar{X}\sim t_{150}\left(188,\ \frac{6.539}{\sqrt{151}}\right)\approx t_{150}\!\left(188,\ 0.5321\right).
\]

b. Because the test is two-sided, a sample mean that is far from 188 in
\emph{either} direction is evidence against \(H_0.\) The p-value is
therefore the probability, under the null distribution, of observing a
sample mean at least as far from 188 as our observed value of
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 189.95.\) Since 189.95 is 1.95 units above 188,
this means a sample mean of 189.95 or more, or equally far below at
186.05 or less. This can be written mathematically as

\[
\text{p-value} = P(\bar{X} \geq 189.95) + P(\bar{X} \leq 186.05).
\]

Because the null \(t\) distribution is symmetric about 188, this is
equal to

\[
\text{p-value} = 2 \times P(\bar{X} \geq 189.95),
\]

with the probability computed under the \(t_{150}(188,\ 0.5321)\) null
distribution.

c. Because this example uses raw data, the data entry differs from the
previous examples. Before using the \Fun{Mean Inference} function,
import the \TypeIn{palmerpenguins_Adélie} dataset from the book's Rguroo
dataset repository. This dataset was obtained by filtering the full
\TypeIn{palmerpenguins} dataset for the Adélie species.

The steps for using Rguroo's \Fun{Mean Inference} function are the same
as those in Example~\ref{exm-sat-csuf-mean-known}, with the differences
in the \Dialog{One Population Mean Inference} dialog shown in the box
below (click to open the box):

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo One-Population Mean Inference dialog}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  In the \Des{Dataset} dropdown, select \TypeIn{palmerpenguins_Adélie},
  and in the \Des{Variable} dropdown, select \TypeIn{flipper_length_mm}.
  Once the variable is selected, the \Des{Sample Mean},
  \Des{Sample S.d.}, and \Des{Sample Size} boxes are populated
  automatically from the data, showing
  \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 189.95,\) \(s = 6.539,\) and \(n = 151.\)
\item
  Leave the \Des{Pop S.d.} box empty since \(\sigma\) is unknown.
\item
  In the text box \Des{\mu = Mean of} enter the label
  \TypeIn{flipper_length_mm}.
\item
  In the \Dpd{Alternative Hypothesis \mu} dropdown, select \TypeIn{!=}
  and enter \TypeIn{188}, the value stated in \(H_a.\)
\item
  Select the \Des{t-statistic} checkbox (instead of z-statistic) to use
  the \(t\) distribution.
\end{itemize}

This is a two-sided test, so the \TypeIn{!=} option produces a p-value
computed from both tails of the null distribution.

Figure~\ref{fig-adelie-dialog} shows the Rguroo dialog for the setup.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_dialogs/Mean Inference/adelie_dialog.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-adelie-dialog}Rguroo setup for the Adélie flipper
length one-sample t-test.}

\end{figure}%

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo output: Adélie Flipper Length}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\end{tcolorbox}

Both the \textbf{\emph{Test of Hypothesis}} table and the right-hand
side plot of the \textbf{\emph{P-value Graph}} in the Rguroo output show
the p-value is approximately \(0.000343 \approx 0.034\%.\) This means
that if the true population mean is in fact 188 mm, then the probability
of observing a sample mean at least as far from 188 as 189.95 is
approximately 0.034\%. Because this probability is very small, and in
particular is less than 5\%, there is sufficient evidence to reject
\(H_0.\)

d. The decision is that, based on the observed sample mean of 189.95 mm,
there is sufficient evidence at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) significance level
to conclude that the mean flipper length of Adélie penguins in the
Palmer Archipelago differs from the reference value of 188 mm.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{The Critical Region Approach}\label{sec-critical-region-mean}

An equivalent way to decide between \(H_0\) and \(H_a\) --- alongside
the p-value approach of Section~\ref{sec-pvalue-mean} --- is the
\textbf{critical region} approach. Rather than summarizing the evidence
in a single probability, this approach identifies, in advance of seeing
the data, the set of values of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) that would lead
us to reject \(H_0.\)

To implement the critical region approach for testing hypotheses about
\(\mu,\) we need a rule that ensures the probability of a Type I error,
when \(\mu\) equals the boundary value \(\mu_0,\) is equal to a given
significance level \(\alpha.\) That is, the critical region must satisfy
\[
P(\text{Rejecting } H_0) = \alpha,\; \text{ assuming $\mu=\mu_0$}.
\] The form of the critical region depends on the alternative
hypothesis: large values of \(\bar{X}\) are evidence against \(H_0\)
when \(H_a\) points to large values of \(\mu,\) small values of
\(\bar{X}\) are evidence against \(H_0\) when \(H_a\) points to small
values of \(\mu,\) and values of \(\bar{X}\) far from \(\mu_0\) in
either direction are evidence against \(H_0\) when \(H_a\) allows
departure in either direction. As with the p-value, all critical values
are found using the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\):
\(N\!\left(\mu_0,\, \sigma/\sqrt{n}\right)\) when \(\sigma\) is known,
and \(t_{n-1}\!\left(\mu_0,\, s/\sqrt{n}\right)\) when \(\sigma\) is
unknown. The callout that follows summarizes the critical region in each
of these cases.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Critical Region for the One-Sample Test of \(\mu\)}\vspace{3mm}

All critical values are found using the null distribution of
\(\bar{X},\) which depends on whether \(\sigma\) is known:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  When \(\sigma\) is known:
  \(\bar{X} \sim N\!\left(\mu_0,\, \sigma/\sqrt{n}\right).\)
\item
  When \(\sigma\) is unknown:
  \(\bar{X} \sim t_{n-1}\!\left(\mu_0,\, s/\sqrt{n}\right).\)
\end{itemize}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Alternative Hypothesis
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Critical Region
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Critical Value Condition
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(H_a: \mu > \mu_0\) & \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} \geq c\) &
\(P(\bar{X} \geq c) = \alpha\) \\
\(H_a: \mu < \mu_0\) & \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} \leq c\) &
\(P(\bar{X} \leq c) = \alpha\) \\
\(H_a: \mu \neq \mu_0\) & \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} \leq c_1\) or
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} \geq c_2\) &
\(P(\bar{X} \leq c_1) = P(\bar{X} \geq c_2) = \alpha/2\) \\
\end{longtable}

\end{tcolorbox}

In each figure below, the curve is the null distribution of \(\bar{X},\)
centered at \(\mu_0\) (dashed line); the solid line marks the critical
value, and the shaded region is the critical (rejection) region --- if
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) falls there, we reject \(H_0.\)
Figure~\ref{fig-cr-onesided} shows the one-sided cases, where a single
critical value \(c\) marks off one tail. Figure~\ref{fig-cr-twosided}
shows the two-sided case: \(\alpha\) is split evenly between two
critical values, \(c_1\) and \(c_2,\) one in each tail.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Mean Inference/cr_illustration_onesided.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-cr-onesided}The critical region for a one-sided
alternative hypothesis.}

\end{figure}%

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.6\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Mean Inference/cr_illustration_twosided.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-cr-twosided}The critical region for a two-sided
alternative hypothesis.}

\end{figure}%

In the critical region approach, we reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_a\)
if the observed sample mean \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) falls in the
rejection region; otherwise, we fail to reject \(H_0.\)

Because both the p-value and the critical region approaches rely on the
same null distribution and answer the same underlying question --- how
unusual is the observed sample mean under \(H_0\)? --- they always lead
to the same decision: rejecting \(H_0\) using the critical region at
significance level \(\alpha\) is equivalent to obtaining a p-value less
than \(\alpha.\)

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Worked Example: \(\sigma\)
Known}{Worked Example: \textbackslash sigma Known}}\label{sec-worked-examples-cr-known-sigma}

We now apply the critical region approach to the SAT example. As noted
earlier, the SAT setting is one of the rare cases in which the
population standard deviation \(\sigma\) can reasonably be treated as
known (here, \(\sigma = 113\) points, computed from the scores of more
than 2 million students). The remaining three running examples ---
sleep, commute time, and Adélie penguin flipper length --- are taken up
in Section~\ref{sec-worked-examples-cr-unknown-sigma}, where we treat
\(\sigma\) as unknown and use the Student \(t\) distribution.

    Select the \Des{z-statistic} checkbox to use the normal
    distribution.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Click the \includegraphics{Rguroo_Icons/details.png} button to open
  the \Dialog{Advanced Features} dialog. In the \textbf{Test of
  Hypothesis} section select \Des{Critical Region Graph}. (Rguroo can
  also produce a p-value graph from this same setup; we use that output
  separately in Section~\ref{sec-pvalue-mean}.)
\item
  Click the preview icon
  \includegraphics{Rguroo_Icons/preview_inline.png} to view the output.
\item
  Click the \includegraphics{Rguroo_Icons/save_as.png} button and save
  the result as \TypeIn{CSUFSAT}.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{figure}[H]

{\centering \includegraphics[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_dialogs/Mean Inference/CSUFSAT.png}

}

\caption{Rguroo setup for the CSUF SAT Math one-sample mean hypothesis
test.}

\end{figure}%

\end{tcolorbox}

\end{minipage}%
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo Output: CSUF SAT example}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\end{tcolorbox}

The right-hand side plot of the \textbf{\emph{Critical Region Graph}} in
the Rguroo output displays the critical region in the observed data
scale. As shown, the critical value for a significance level of
\(\alpha =0.05\) is 537.39 and thus the critical region is
\(\bar{X} >537.39.\) Thus, if an observed sample mean is larger than
537.39, we would reject \(H_0.\)

Our observed sample mean is \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\) (shown by the
green triangle) falls in the rejection region since it is greater than
537.39. Therefore we reject \(H_0\) at 5\% level of significance.

c. The final decision is that based on the observed sample mean of 542,
there is sufficient evidence at 5\% significance level that the mean SAT
math scores of CSUF students is more than the national average.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Worked Examples: \(\sigma\)
Unknown}{Worked Examples: \textbackslash sigma Unknown}}\label{sec-worked-examples-cr-unknown-sigma}

We now turn to the more realistic setting in which the population
standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown and is estimated from the
sample by \(s.\) The three running examples in this section --- sleep
hours, commute time, and Adélie penguin flipper length --- all use the
Student \(t\) distribution as the null distribution of \(\bar{X}.\) Each
example reuses the setup introduced earlier in the chapter; we now carry
out the critical region part of the hypothesis test. (The p-value part
of each of these same examples was taken up in
Section~\ref{sec-worked-examples-pvalue-unknown-sigma}. To illustrate
the method at a variety of significance levels, this example uses
\(\alpha = 0.01\) instead of the \(\alpha = 0.05\) used in the p-value
version.)

\begin{example}[Sleep Hours Among University
Students]\protect\hypertarget{exm-sleep-university-mean-unknown-cr}{}\label{exm-sleep-university-mean-unknown-cr}

We return to the sleep setting introduced in
Example~\ref{exm-sleep-university-mean}. Recall that the recommended
minimum nightly sleep for young adults is 7 hours, and that we wished to
investigate whether the mean nightly sleep among students at our
university is less than 7 hours. A random sample of \(n = 15\) students
yielded a sample mean of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 6.4\) hours and a
sample standard deviation of \(s = 1.2\) hours.

The hypotheses are \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu \geq 7 \\
H_a: \mu < 7
\end{cases}
\] where \(\mu\) denotes the mean nightly sleep, in hours, among
students at our university. Assume that the population of nightly sleep
hours is normally distributed. Because the population standard deviation
\(\sigma\) is unknown, we estimate it from the sample by \(s = 1.2\)
hours and use the Student \(t\) distribution. Perform a test of
hypothesis at the \(\alpha = 0.01\) significance level by answering the
following questions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
\item
  Using a significance level of \(\alpha = 0.01,\) use Rguroo's
  \Fun{Mean Inference} function to obtain the critical region. Interpret
  the critical region in the context of the problem, and using the
  observed value, state whether you reject or fail to reject \(H_0.\)
\item
  Give your overall conclusion.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. Because \(\sigma\) is unknown, the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)
is a Student \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1 = 14\) degrees of freedom,
centered at \(\mu_0 = 7\) with estimated standard error
\(s/\sqrt{n} = 1.2/\sqrt{15} \approx 0.3098\) hours:

\[
\bar{X}\sim t_{14}\left(7,\ \frac{1.2}{\sqrt{15}}\right)\approx t_{14}\!\left(7,\ 0.3098\right).
\]

b. Click to expand the box below to see how to use the
\Fun{Mean Inference} function in Rguroo to answer this question.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]
\begin{minipage}[t]{5.5mm}
\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{minipage}[t]{\textwidth - 5.5mm}

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{\includegraphics[width=0.22917in,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_Icons/R_circle_logo.pdf}
One-Population mean hypothesis test - Sleep example}\vspace{3mm}

The steps for using Rguroo's \Fun{Mean Inference} function are the same
as those in Example~\ref{exm-sat-csuf-mean-known-cr}, with the following
differences in the \Dialog{One Population Mean Inference} dialog:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \Des{Sample Mean}: \TypeIn{6.4}, the value of
  \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}.\)
\item
  \Des{Sample S.d.}: \TypeIn{1.2}, the sample standard deviation \(s.\)
  (Leave \Des{Pop S.d.} empty since \(\sigma\) is unknown.)
\item
  \Des{Sample Size}: \TypeIn{15}, the size of the sample \(n.\)
\item
  In the text box \Des{\mu = Mean of} enter the label
  \TypeIn{Nightly Sleep}.
\item
  Change the \Des{Significance Level} textbox to \TypeIn{0.01}.
\item
  In the \Dpd{Alternative Hypothesis \mu} dropdown, select \TypeIn{<}
  and enter \TypeIn{7}, the value stated in \(H_a.\)
\item
  Select the \Des{t-statistic} checkbox (instead of z-statistic) to use
  the \(t\) distribution.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo One-Population Mean Inference dialog}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_dialogs/Mean Inference/sleep_dialog_mean.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-sleep-dialog-cr}Rguroo setup for the Nightly Sleep
one-sample t-test (α = 0.01).}

\end{figure}%

\end{tcolorbox}

\end{minipage}%
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo Output: Sleep example}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\end{tcolorbox}

The right-hand side plot of the \textbf{\emph{Critical Region Graph}} in
the Rguroo output displays the critical region in the observed data
scale. The critical value for a significance level of \(\alpha = 0.01\)
is 6.1868, and because the alternative hypothesis is of the form less
than (\(H_a: \mu < 7\)), the critical region is \(\bar{X} \leq 6.1868.\)
Thus, if an observed sample mean is less than 6.1868, we would reject
\(H_0.\)

Our observed sample mean is \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 6.4\) (shown by the
green triangle), which does \emph{not} fall in the rejection region
since it is greater than 6.1868. Therefore, we fail to reject \(H_0\) at
the \(\alpha = 0.01\) level of significance.

c. The final decision is that, based on the observed sample mean of 6.4
hours, there is insufficient evidence at the \(\alpha = 0.01\)
significance level to conclude that the mean nightly sleep among
students at our university is less than the recommended 7 hours.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Commute Time in a Metropolitan
Area]\protect\hypertarget{exm-commute-metro-mean-unknown-cr}{}\label{exm-commute-metro-mean-unknown-cr}

We return to the commute setting introduced in
Example~\ref{exm-commute-metro-mean}. Recall that the national mean
one-way commute time for U.S. workers in 2023 was 26.8 minutes, and that
we wished to investigate whether the mean one-way commute time among
workers in our metropolitan area differs from the national mean. A
random sample of \(n = 15\) commuters yielded a sample mean of
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8\) minutes and a sample standard deviation
of \(s = 9.6\) minutes.

The hypotheses are \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu = 26.8 \\
H_a: \mu \neq 26.8
\end{cases}
\] where \(\mu\) denotes the mean one-way commute time, in minutes,
among workers in our metropolitan area. Assume that the population of
commute times is normally distributed. Perform a test of hypothesis at
the \(\alpha = 0.10\) significance level by answering the following
questions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
\item
  Using a significance level of \(\alpha = 0.10,\) use Rguroo's
  \Fun{Mean Inference} function to obtain the critical region. Interpret
  the critical region in the context of the problem, and using the
  observed value, state whether you reject or fail to reject \(H_0.\)
\item
  Give your overall conclusion.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. Because \(\sigma\) is unknown, the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)
is a Student \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1 = 14\) degrees of freedom,
centered at \(\mu_0 = 26.8\) with estimated standard error
\(s/\sqrt{n} = 9.6/\sqrt{15} \approx 2.4787\) minutes:

\[
\bar{X}\sim t_{14}\left(26.8,\ \frac{9.6}{\sqrt{15}}\right)\approx t_{14}\!\left(26.8,\ 2.4787\right).
\]

b. The steps for using Rguroo's \Fun{Mean Inference} function are the
same as those in Example~\ref{exm-sat-csuf-mean-known-cr}. To see the
differences in the \Dialog{One Population Mean Inference} dialog click
to open the box below.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo One-Population Mean Inference dialog}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \Des{Sample Mean}: \TypeIn{24.8}, the value of
  \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}.\)
\item
  \Des{Sample S.d.}: \TypeIn{9.6}, the sample standard deviation \(s.\)
  (Leave \Des{Pop S.d.} empty since \(\sigma\) is unknown.)
\item
  \Des{Sample Size}: \TypeIn{15}, the size of the sample \(n.\)
\item
  In the text box \Des{\mu = Mean of} enter the label
  \TypeIn{Commute Times}.
\item
  Change the \Des{Significance Level} textbox to \TypeIn{0.10}.
\item
  In the \Dpd{Alternative Hypothesis \mu} dropdown, select \TypeIn{!=}
  and enter \TypeIn{26.8}, the value stated in \(H_a.\)
\item
  Select the \Des{t-statistic} checkbox (instead of z-statistic) to use
  the \(t\) distribution.
\end{itemize}

This is a two-sided test, so the \TypeIn{!=} option produces a critical
region with two parts, one in each tail of the null distribution.

Figure~\ref{fig-commute-dialog-cr} shows the Rguroo dialog for the
setup.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_dialogs/Mean Inference/commute_mean_dialog.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-commute-dialog-cr}Rguroo setup for the Commute Times
one-sample t-test (α = 0.10).}

\end{figure}%

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo Output: Commute Time in a Metropolitan Area}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\end{tcolorbox}

The right-hand side plot of the \textbf{\emph{Critical Region Graph}} in
the Rguroo output displays the critical region in the observed data
scale. Because the alternative hypothesis is two-sided,
\(H_a: \mu \neq 26.8,\) the significance level \(\alpha = 0.10\) is
split evenly between the two tails, with \(0.05\) in each. This produces
two critical values, approximately \(c_1 = 22.434\) and
\(c_2 = 31.166,\) and the critical region is \(\bar{X} \leq 22.434\) or
\(\bar{X} \geq 31.166.\) Thus, we would reject \(H_0\) if an observed
sample mean is less than 22.434 or greater than 31.166.

Our observed sample mean is \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8\) (shown by
the green triangle), which does not fall in either part of the rejection
region since it lies between 22.434 and 31.166. Therefore, we fail to
reject \(H_0\) at the \(\alpha = 0.10\) level of significance.

c. The final decision is that, based on the observed sample mean of 24.8
minutes, there is insufficient evidence at the \(\alpha = 0.10\)
significance level to conclude that the mean one-way commute time among
workers in our metropolitan area differs from the national mean of 26.8
minutes.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[Flipper Length of Adélie
Penguins]\protect\hypertarget{exm-penguin-flipper-mean-unknown-cr}{}\label{exm-penguin-flipper-mean-unknown-cr}

We return to the penguin setting introduced in

dataset contains flipper length measurements for \(n = 151\) Adélie
penguins in the Palmer Archipelago, and that we wished to investigate

reference value of 188 mm. Computed from the raw data, the sample mean
is \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 189.95\) mm and the sample standard
deviation is \(s = 6.539\) mm.

The hypotheses are \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu = 188 \\
H_a: \mu \neq 188
\end{cases}
\] where \(\mu\) denotes the mean flipper length, in millimeters, of
Adélie penguins in the Palmer Archipelago. Assume that the population of
Adélie flipper lengths is normally distributed. Perform a test of
hypothesis at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) significance level by answering the
following questions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
\item
  Using a significance level of \(\alpha = 0.05,\) use Rguroo's
  \Fun{Mean Inference} function to obtain the critical region. Interpret
  the critical region in the context of the problem, and using the
  observed value, state whether you reject or fail to reject \(H_0.\)
\item
  Give your overall conclusion.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

See the codebook for the dataset
\hyperref[code-book-palmerpenguins]{here}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

is a Student \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1 = 150\) degrees of freedom,
centered at \(\mu_0 = 188\) with estimated standard error

\[
\bar{X}\sim t_{150}\left(188,\ \frac{6.539}{\sqrt{151}}\right)\approx t_{150}\!\left(188,\ 0.5321\right).
\]

\(\bar{X} \geq 189.05.\) Thus, we would reject \(H_0\) if an observed

the green triangle), which falls in the upper part of the rejection

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Homework for
Section~\ref{sec-critical-region-mean}}{Homework for Section~}}\label{homework-for-sec-critical-region-mean}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  **CO2 Emissions* The Kyoto Protocol, signed in 1997, required
  participating countries to begin reducing their carbon emissions; it
  became enforceable in February 2005. In 2004, the mean CO2 emission
  was 4.87 metric tons per capita, computed by averaging each country's
  per-capita emission rate across countries. A researcher wants to
  determine whether the mean CO2 emission per capita across countries in
  2010 \emph{differs} from the 2004 mean. The hypotheses are \[
  \begin{cases}
  H_0: \mu = 4.87 \\
  H_a: \mu \neq 4.87
  \end{cases}
  \] where \(\mu\) denotes the mean CO2 emission, in metric tons per
  capita, across countries in 2010. Because the population standard
  deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown, import the \Data{Emission} dataset
  into Rguroo from the book's Rguroo dataset repository and use the
  variable \Var{y2010}. Perform a test of hypothesis at the
  \(\alpha = 0.05\) significance level by answering the following
  questions:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
\item
  Use Rguroo function to obtain the critical region. Interpret the
  critical region in the context of the problem, and using the observed
  value, state whether you reject or fail to reject \(H_0.\)
\item
  Give your overall conclusion.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Mercury Concentration} The U.S. Food and Drug Administration
  (FDA) sets 1.0 mg/kg as the allowable amount of mercury in fish that
  is consumed. To assess whether fish in Florida lakes meet this
  standard, largemouth bass were collected from 53 different lakes, and
  for each lake a standardized estimate of the mercury concentration in
  a three-year-old bass was computed from the fish sampled there. A
  researcher wants to determine whether the mean standardized mercury
  concentration across Florida lakes \emph{differs} from the allowable
  amount of 1.0 mg/kg. The hypotheses are \[
  \begin{cases}
  H_0: \mu = 1.0 \\
  H_a: \mu \neq 1.0
  \end{cases}

\section{Confidence Interval for a Population
Mean}\label{sec-confidence-interval-one-mean}

In the previous sections, the sample mean \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\)
played a central role: we used it to test a single candidate value
\(\mu_0\) for the population mean. The sample mean is also our best
single-number guess for the unknown population mean. This single-number
guess is called a \textbf{point estimate} of \(\mu.\) In the
commute-time setting of Example~\ref{exm-commute-metro-mean}, our sample
of \(n = 15\) commuters produced \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8\)
minutes. We offer 24.8 minutes as the point estimate of the mean one-way
commute time \(\mu\) among workers in our metropolitan area.

A point estimate has an obvious limitation. The sample mean \(\bar{X}\)
varies from sample to sample, so \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) will rarely
equal \(\mu\) exactly. The report ``our point estimate is 24.8 minutes''
leaves an important question unanswered: how close to \(\mu\) is 24.8
likely to be? Could \(\mu\) be 22? 28? 32? Reporting just
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8\) tells the reader nothing about the
accuracy of the estimate.

A more informative report is a range of plausible values for \(\mu,\)
constructed so that the long-run reliability of the construction is
known. This range is called a \textbf{confidence interval} for \(\mu.\)
As introduced in Section~\ref{sec-foundations-confidence-intervals} and
applied to proportions in Section~\ref{sec-confidence-interval-one-pop},
the construction rests on a single idea called \textbf{test inversion}.
We already know how to test, for any candidate value \(\mu_0,\) whether
the data are consistent with \(\mu = \mu_0.\) The confidence interval is
the collection of candidate values that survive the test --- the values
for which a two-sided test would fail to reject \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\) at
significance level \(\alpha.\)

To see what this means in numbers, consider the commute data in
Example~\ref{exm-commute-metro-mean}. Based on the observed sample mean
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8,\) a two-sided test of \(H_0: \mu = 26.8\)
at \(\alpha = 0.05\) would fail to reject the value 26.8, so 26.8 is a
plausible value for the population mean. On the other hand, a two-sided
test of \(H_0: \mu = 32\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\) is rejected since the
value 32 is too far from \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8,\) so 32 is not a
plausible value for the population mean. If we repeat this process for
many possible values of \(\mu,\) the values that are not rejected form
an interval. The endpoints of this interval are the two boundary values
where the test switches from ``fail to reject'' to ``reject.'' This is
illustrated graphically in Figure~\ref{fig-ci-inversion_commute}. As we
will formally define this shortly, the interval \((19.48, 30.12)\) is
called a 95\% confidence interval for the commute times, providing a set
of plausible values for the population mean commute time.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=1\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Mean Inference/ci-inversion-commute.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-ci-inversion_commute}A confidence interval as an
inverted test, illustrated for the mean of commute data.}

\end{figure}%

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Confidence Interval for \(\mu\) by Test Inversion}\vspace{3mm}

A \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu\) is the set
of values \(\mu_0\) for which a two-sided test of \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\)
at significance level \(\alpha\) fails to reject. The significance level
\(\alpha\) and the confidence level \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) are
complementary: \(\alpha = 0.05\) gives a 95\% confidence interval,
\(\alpha = 0.10\) gives a 90\% interval, and so on.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Confidence Intervals and Two-Sided Tests}\vspace{3mm}

A two-sided hypothesis test and a confidence interval at matching levels
lead to the same decision. For any candidate value \(\mu_0\):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  If \(\mu_0\) lies \textbf{outside} the \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\)
  confidence interval, a two-sided test of \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\) at
  significance level \(\alpha\) rejects \(H_0.\)
\item
  If \(\mu_0\) lies \textbf{inside} the \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\)
  confidence interval, a two-sided test of \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\) at
  significance level \(\alpha\) fails to reject \(H_0.\)
\end{itemize}

This equivalence is a direct consequence of the test-inversion
construction: the confidence interval is, by definition, the collection
of values \(\mu_0\) that the two-sided test does not reject. The
equivalence applies only to \textbf{two-sided} tests; a one-sided test
may reject a value that lies inside the corresponding two-sided
confidence interval.

\end{tcolorbox}

Every confidence interval for \(\mu\) that we construct in this chapter
has the same general form:

\[
\left(\text{point estimate} - \text{margin of error},\ 
\text{point estimate} + \text{margin of error}\right)\]

The \textbf{margin of error} is the largest plausible difference between
the point estimate and the true value of \(\mu,\) at the stated
confidence level. It is the product of a critical value and the standard
error of the point estimate:

\[
\text{margin of error} \;=\; (\text{critical value}) \times (\text{standard error}).
\]

The critical value depends on the desired confidence level and on the
sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\); the standard error measures how
much \(\bar{X}\) varies from sample to sample. Both depend on whether
\(\sigma\) is known, as we see in the next two subsections.

For the commute example, the margin of error becomes
\(t^*_{14} \cdot (9.6/\sqrt{15}).\) With 95\% confidence,
\(t^*_{14} = 2.145,\) giving margin of error
\(\approx 2.145 \times 2.479 \approx 5.32\) minutes, and the interval
\((24.8 - 5.32,\ 24.8 + 5.32),\) or \((19.48,\ 30.12).\) We work through
this example in detail below.

Figure~\ref{fig-ci-anatomy} shows the anatomy of this confidence
interval, using the commute example. The observed sample mean
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8\) sits at the center; the margin of error,
\(me \approx 5.32,\) extends equally to either side; subtracting and
adding it from \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) gives the endpoints 19.48 and
30.12 that bound the 95\% confidence interval.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Mean Inference/ci_anatomy.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-ci-anatomy}Anatomy of a confidence interval for the
population mean.}

\end{figure}%

The assumption from the hypothesis-testing sections continues to apply:
the variable under study has a normal distribution in the population.
The form of the resulting interval depends on whether the population
standard deviation \(\sigma\) is known. We treat the two cases
separately in the next two subsections. Conditions under which the
normality assumption can be relaxed are discussed in
Section~\ref{sec-large-sample-mean}.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Confidence Interval When \(\sigma\) Is
Known}{Confidence Interval When \textbackslash sigma Is Known}}\label{sec-ci-known-sigma}

When the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is known and the
variable under study has a normal distribution in the population, the
sample mean \(\bar{X}\) has a normal sampling distribution centered at
\(\mu\) with standard deviation \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}.\) The
\((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu\) takes the
form

\[
\left(\bar{X} - z^* \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},\ \ \bar{X} + z^* \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right),
\]

where \(z^*\) is the critical value from the standard normal
distribution corresponding to the desired confidence level.

The interval above is a \textbf{random} interval. Its endpoints depend
on the random variable \(\bar{X},\) so the whole interval shifts from
sample to sample. By construction, the probability that this random
interval contains \(\mu\) is \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\):

\[
P\!\left(\bar{X} - z^* \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \;\leq\; \mu \;\leq\; \bar{X} + z^* \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \;=\; 1 - \alpha.
\]

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Confidence Interval for \(\mu,\) \(\sigma\) Known}\vspace{3mm}

When the variable under study has a normal distribution in the
population and \(\sigma\) is known, the \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\)
confidence interval for \(\mu\) is

\[
\left(\bar{X} - z^* \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},\ \ \bar{X} + z^* \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right),
\]

where \(z^* \cdot \sigma/\sqrt{n}\) is the margin of error and \(z^*\)
is the critical value from the standard normal distribution
corresponding to the confidence level \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%.\) To
compute the interval from a specific sample, replace \(\bar{X}\) with
the observed value \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}.\)

\end{tcolorbox}

The critical values most commonly used for the standard normal
distribution are:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Confidence Level & \(\alpha\) & \(z^*\) \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
90\% & 0.10 & 1.645 \\
95\% & 0.05 & 1.960 \\
99\% & 0.01 & 2.576 \\
\end{longtable}

\begin{example}[SAT Math Scores at CSUF: Confidence
Interval]\protect\hypertarget{exm-sat-csuf-mean-ci-known}{}\label{exm-sat-csuf-mean-ci-known}

We return to the SAT setting introduced in
Example~\ref{exm-sat-csuf-mean}. Note that the hypothesis test in
Example~\ref{exm-sat-csuf-mean-known} was one-sided
(\(H_a: \mu > 508\)), but a confidence interval is always built from a
two-sided test (Section~\ref{sec-confidence-interval-one-mean}). So here
we set that alternative aside and construct a two-sided 95\% confidence
interval for \(\mu,\) which answers a different question --- a plausible
range of values for \(\mu\) --- than the one-sided test did.

The national mean math SAT score for the high school graduating class of
2025 was 508 points, with a standard deviation of \(\sigma = 113\)
points. A random sample of \(n = 40\) incoming CSUF freshmen in fall
2025 yielded a sample mean of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\) points.
Assume that the population of math SAT scores is normally distributed
and that \(\sigma = 113\) is known.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
\item
  Use Rguroo to construct a 95\% confidence interval for the mean math
  SAT score \(\mu\) among incoming CSUF freshmen in fall 2025. Report
  the margin of error and the interval.
\item
  Interpret the interval in the context of the problem.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\[
\bar{X} \sim N\!\left(\mu,\ \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = N\!\left(\mu,\ \frac{113}{\sqrt{40}}\right) \approx N(\mu,\ 17.867),
\]

centered at the unknown population mean \(\mu\) with standard error
\(113/\sqrt{40} \approx 17.867\) points.

b. The following box describes how to obtain the confidence interval
using Rguroo's \Fun{Mean Inference} function.

The \textbf{\emph{Normal-Based Confidence Interval}} table in the Rguroo
output contains all the information for answering this question:

The margin of error reported by Rguroo is approximately \(35.02\)
points, and the 95\% confidence interval for \(\mu\) is

\[
(506.98,\ 577.02) \text{ points}.
\]

c. \textbf{Interpretation:} We are 95\% confident that the true mean
math SAT score among incoming CSUF freshmen in fall 2025 is between
506.98 and 577.02 points.

\end{tcolorbox}

The confidence interval \((507,\ 577)\) computed above came from one
particular sample. The probability statement earlier in this section ---
that the random interval contains \(\mu\) with probability
\((1-\alpha)\times100\%\) --- is best understood through repeated
sampling.

Suppose we draw many independent samples of size \(n = 40\) from the
population of CSUF SAT scores, compute \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) for
each, and form the 95\% interval
\(\left(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} - 35,\ \bar{x}_{\text{obs}} + 35\right)\)
every time, where 35 is the margin of error. The intervals shift from
sample to sample because \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) does. Some intervals
capture the true mean \(\mu,\) others miss.
Figure~\ref{fig-ci-repeated-samples} shows the result of one such
simulation. Each of the twenty intervals is drawn as a horizontal
segment centered at its own \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\); the vertical line
marks the fixed (but unknown) true mean \(\mu.\) Intervals that capture
\(\mu\) are drawn in blue, and intervals that miss are drawn in red.
Roughly 1 in 20 --- that is, 5\% --- misses \(\mu,\) as we would expect
for a 95\% method; in this particular simulation, exactly 1 of the 20
intervals misses.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_outputs/Mean Inference/ci-repeated-samples.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-ci-repeated-samples}Twenty 95\% confidence intervals
from twenty independent samples of size \(n = 40.\)}

\end{figure}%

Before the data are collected, the interval is random: it is centered at
the random variable \(\bar{X},\) and the probability that it contains
\(\mu\) is 95\%. Once we collect the data and compute
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542,\) we plug it in for \(\bar{X}\) to obtain
the specific numerical interval \((507,\ 577).\) This specific interval
either contains the true \(\mu\) or it does not, and we cannot tell
which. The method that produced it captures \(\mu\) in 95\% of repeated
samples.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Confidence Interval When \(\sigma\) Is
Unknown}{Confidence Interval When \textbackslash sigma Is Unknown}}\label{sec-ci-unknown-sigma}

When the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown and the
variable under study has a normal distribution in the population, we
estimate \(\sigma\) by the sample standard deviation \(s\) and use the
Student \(t\) distribution in place of the normal
(Section~\ref{sec-mean-inference-unknown-sigma}). The form of the
confidence interval is the same as in the known-\(\sigma\) case, with
two substitutions: the sample standard deviation \(s\) replaces
\(\sigma,\) and the critical value \(t^*_{n-1}\) from the Student \(t\)
distribution with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom replaces \(z^*.\)

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Confidence Interval for \(\mu,\) \(\sigma\) Unknown}\vspace{3mm}

When the variable under study has a normal distribution in the
population and \(\sigma\) is unknown, the \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\)
confidence interval for \(\mu\) is

\[
\left(\bar{X} - t^*_{n-1} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}},\ \ \bar{X} + t^*_{n-1} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right),
\]

where \(t^*_{n-1} \cdot s/\sqrt{n}\) is the margin of error and
\(t^*_{n-1}\) is the critical value from the Student \(t\) distribution
with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom, corresponding to the confidence level
\((1-\alpha) \times 100\%.\) To compute the interval from a specific
sample, replace \(\bar{X}\) with the observed value
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}.\)

\end{tcolorbox}

The critical value \(z^*\) takes the same value regardless of sample
size. The critical value \(t^*_{n-1},\) by contrast, depends on the
degrees of freedom \(n - 1.\) The following table compares the 95\%
critical values for \(z^*\) and \(t^*_{n-1}\) at several common sample
sizes:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Sample size \(n\) & Degrees of freedom \(n-1\) & \(t^*_{n-1}\) at
95\% \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
5 & 4 & 2.776 \\
10 & 9 & 2.262 \\
15 & 14 & 2.145 \\
30 & 29 & 2.045 \\
100 & 99 & 1.984 \\
(large \(n,\) normal limit) & \(\infty\) & \(z^* = 1.960\) \\
\end{longtable}

The \(t\) critical value is noticeably larger than the normal value
\(z^* = 1.960\) for small samples, and the difference produces a wider
interval --- the extra width reflects the additional uncertainty
introduced by estimating \(\sigma\) from the data. The values approach
\(z^* = 1.960\) as \(n\) grows: by \(n = 30\) the difference is already
small, and by \(n = 100\) the two are essentially identical. This
reflects the broader fact, discussed in
Section~\ref{sec-mean-inference-unknown-sigma}, that the \(t\)
distribution approaches the standard normal as the degrees of freedom
increase. Rguroo computes \(t^*_{n-1}\) and reports the margin of error
automatically, so we do not look up these values by hand in practice.

\begin{example}[Commute Time in a Metropolitan Area: Confidence
Interval]\protect\hypertarget{exm-commute-metro-mean-ci}{}\label{exm-commute-metro-mean-ci}

We return to the commute setting introduced in
Example~\ref{exm-commute-metro-mean}. A random sample of \(n = 15\)
commuters yielded a sample mean of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8\)
minutes and a sample standard deviation of \(s = 9.6\) minutes. Assume
that the population of commute times is normally distributed.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
\item
  Use Rguroo to construct a 95\% confidence interval for the mean
  one-way commute time \(\mu\) among workers in our metropolitan area.
  Report the margin of error and the interval.
\item
  Interpret the interval in the context of the problem.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. The population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown and is
estimated by \(s = 9.6.\) The sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) is a
Student \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1 = 14\) degrees of freedom,
centered at \(\mu\) with estimated standard error
\(s/\sqrt{n} = 9.6/\sqrt{15} \approx 2.479\) minutes:

\[
\bar{X} \sim t_{14}\!\left(\mu,\ \frac{9.6}{\sqrt{15}}\right) \approx t_{14}(\mu,\ 2.479).
\]

b. The Rguroo steps follow those in

  (leave \Des{Pop S.d.} empty since \(\sigma\) is unknown),
  \Des{Sample Size}: \TypeIn{15}.
\item
  In the text box \Des{\mu = Mean of} enter the label
  \TypeIn{Commute Times}.
\item
  In the \textbf{Methods} section of the \Tab{Confidence Interval} tab,
  select the \Des{t-statistic} checkbox.
\end{itemize}

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_dialogs/Mean Inference/commute_dialog_ci.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-commute-ci-dialog}Rguroo setup for the Commute
one-population mean confidence interval.}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo Output: Commute Time in a Metropolitan Area}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

From the \textbf{\emph{t-Based Confidence Interval}} table in the Rguroo

(19.48,\ 30.12) \text{ minutes}.
\]

c. \textbf{Interpretation:} We are 95\% confident that the true mean
one-way commute time among workers in our metropolitan area is between

\textbf{Note.} The value 26.8 (the national mean) lies inside the 95\%
confidence interval \((19.48,\ 30.12).\) This is consistent with the

of Example~\ref{exm-commute-metro-mean-unknown}.
