\section{Checking the Normality Assumption}\label{sec-QQ-Plot-mean}

As we will see in Section~\ref{sec-large-sample-mean}, the role of the
normality assumption diminishes as the sample size increases. For larger
samples (often \(n > 30\)), the inferential procedures developed in this
chapter remain approximately valid under moderate departures from
normality, though severe skewness or outliers can still affect their
accuracy. For smaller samples, the assumption that the population
distribution is approximately normal plays a more central role in the
validity of both the normal and \(t\)-based procedures, and checking it
is important.

In some applications, the plausibility of the normality assumption is
supported by subject-matter knowledge and prior experience with the
variable being studied. When raw data are available, we can also assess
the assumption directly from the sample. In this section, we introduce
two commonly used approaches: a graphical method based on a
\textbf{normal probability plot} and a formal hypothesis test known as
the \textbf{Shapiro--Wilk test}. Both methods are available in Rguroo.

A \textbf{normal probability plot} (also called a \textbf{Q-Q plot},
short for \emph{quantile-quantile plot}) assesses normality by plotting
the ordered values from the sample against the values we would expect to
see if the data came from a normal distribution. If the population
distribution really is normal, the plotted points should fall close to a
straight line. Systematic departures from a straight line --- a curve,
an S-shape, or points that drift away in the tails --- indicate that the
data do not come from a normal distribution. Rguroo's normal probability
plot also displays a pair of dashed bands around the reference line;
these bands indicate the range in which the points would typically fall
if the data were normal. Points that stray outside the bands are
evidence of departure from normality.

The Shapiro--Wilk test assesses normality formally through a hypothesis
test. A large p-value, for example greater than 0.05, indicates that the
data are consistent with a normal distribution, whereas a small p-value
provides evidence against normality.

To assess normality in Rguroo, open the
\Dialog{One Population Mean Inference} as you did in the worked examples
earlier in the chapter, select your dataset and variable, and check the
boxes labeled \Des{Normal Probability Plot} and \Des{Test of Normality}.
As an example, Figure~\ref{fig-QQ-dialog} shows the dialog with the
\Data{palmerpenguins_Adelie} dataset and the variable
\Var{flipper_length_mm} selected, both normality assessment options
checked.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_dialogs/Mean Inference/QQ_dialog.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-QQ-dialog}Rguroo settings for generating a normal
probability plot and conducting a Shapiro--Wilk test of normality.}

\end{figure}%

The normal probability plot for these data is shown
Figure~\ref{fig-QQ-plot}. As you can see all data points follow a
straight line closely and they are all within the dashed band. This
indicates that the data for Adélie flipper lengths is normaly
distributed.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includesvg[width=0.6\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_html_output/Mean Inference/QQ_flipper_adelie_docx/G_NormalProbPlot1.svg}

}

\caption{\label{fig-QQ-plot}Normal probability plot indicating that the
flipper length data are approximately Adélie .}

\end{figure}%

A few points outside the bands does not necessarily indicate
non-normality, especially in larger samples where some scatter is
expected. When the plot is ambiguous --- most points on the line, but a
few outliers --- the Shapiro--Wilk test can supply a more formal
assessment.

Figure~\ref{fig-SW-test} shows the Rguroo output for the Shapiro-Wilk
test for the same data. The test reports a W-statistic of 0.993 and a
p-value of 0.720. The W-statistic is part of the test calculation, but
we do not need to interpret it directly here. The important value is the
p-value. Since 0.720 is large, the data do not give evidence against the
normality assumption. This agrees with the normal probability plot, so
it is reasonable to treat the Adélie flipper length data as
approximately normal.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_html_output/Mean Inference/QQ_flipper_adelie_docx/Shapiro_wilk_adellie.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-SW-test}Shapiro--Wilk test results indicating that
the flipper length data are consistent with a normal distribution.}

\end{figure}%

It is instructive to see an example of a normal probability plot and
Shapiro-Wilk test that indicate a departure from normality.
Figure~\ref{fig-QQ-plot-non-normal} shows the normal probability plot
for the variable \Var{flipper_length_mm} for all the species in the
\Data{palmerpenguins}. The points deviate from the straight reference
line, in both the lower and upper tails, and many points are outside the
dashed confidence bands. This suggests that the distribution of flipper
lengths for all penguins is not normal. The Shapiro-Wilk test for these
data, shown in Figure~\ref{fig-SW-test-non-normal}, reports a
W-statistic of 0.915 and a p-value of \(3.5\times 10^{-9}\) (3.5 times
10 to the power minus nine), providing strong evidence against the
assumption of normality for the all species combined flipper length
data.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includesvg[width=0.6\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_html_output/Mean Inference/QQ_flipper_palmerpenguins_docx/G_NormalProbPlot1.svg}

}

\caption{\label{fig-QQ-plot-non-normal}Normal probability plot
indicating that the flipper length data for all penguins are not Adélie
.}

\end{figure}%

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_html_output/Mean Inference/QQ_flipper_palmerpenguins_docx/Shapiro_wilk_palmerpenguins.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-SW-test-non-normal}Shapiro--Wilk test results
indicating that the flipper length data for all penguins are not
consistent with a normal distribution.}

\end{figure}%

Together, the normal probability plot and the Shapiro--Wilk test provide
complementary ways to check the normality assumption. The plot reveals
the shape of the departure (skewness, heavy tails, outliers); the test
offers a numerical summary. When both agree, the conclusion is clear.
When they disagree --- for instance, when a Shapiro--Wilk test rejects
normality but the plot shows only a few mild departures --- it is
reasonable to favor the visual evidence, since the test can be sensitive
to minor deviations in large samples. In small samples, the test may
have low power to detect real departures, so the plot remains essential.
The next section discusses situations when the normality assumption is
\emph{not} satisfied.

\section{Large-Sample Mean Inference: Dropping the Normality
Assumption}\label{sec-large-sample-mean}

Every method in this chapter so far has rested on one assumption: the
variable under study has a normal distribution in the population. For
small samples, this assumption matters, and we check it using the
methods of Section~\ref{sec-QQ-Plot-mean}.

For large samples, the normality assumption can be \textbf{dropped}, by
the \textbf{Central Limit Theorem}: when \(n\) is large, the sampling
distribution of \(\bar{X}\) is approximately normal whatever the shape
of the population. As a rule of thumb, \(n \geq 30\) is large enough;
strongly skewed populations or those with extreme outliers may need
more, and already-symmetric populations need less.

\textbf{This section matters only when you are unwilling to assume the
population is normal.} If the population can reasonably be assumed
normal, keep using the methods of the earlier sections --- \(z\) when
\(\sigma\) is known, \(t\) when \(\sigma\) is unknown --- regardless of
how large the sample is; those methods are already exact and there is
nothing to gain by switching. The normal approximation described here is
an alternative for when that assumption is not available.

When \(\sigma\) is known, the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) is
approximately \(N(\mu_0,\ \sigma/\sqrt{n}),\) and we proceed as in
Section~\ref{sec-ci-known-sigma}. When \(\sigma\) is unknown, we replace
it with \(s\); for a large sample \(s\) is a reliable estimate of
\(\sigma,\) and the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) is
approximately \(N(\mu_0,\ s/\sqrt{n}).\) In both cases we use the normal
distribution --- critical regions, p-values, and confidence intervals
are obtained exactly as in the known-\(\sigma\) sections, just with an
approximate rather than exact justification.

As shown in Section~\ref{sec-mean-inference-unknown-sigma}, the Student
\(t\) distribution approaches the standard normal as the degrees of
freedom increase. So even when the population is not assumed normal,
continuing to use \(t\) for a large sample gives essentially the same
answer as switching to \(z\) --- this is why it is common practice to
simply keep using \(t\) whenever \(\sigma\) is unknown, at any sample
size, and treat the normal approximation here as a good enough
alternative, not a required one.

The Adélie penguin example
(Example~\ref{exm-penguin-flipper-mean-unknown},
Example~\ref{exm-penguin-flipper-mean-ci}, \(n = 151\)) and the SAT
example (Example~\ref{exm-sat-csuf-mean-known},
Example~\ref{exm-sat-csuf-mean-ci-known}, \(n = 40\)) were both analyzed
assuming a normal population, so \(t\) and \(z\) respectively were the
right and exact choice there regardless of sample size. Their large
sample sizes do mean, however, that had we \emph{not} wanted to assume
normality, the normal-approximation method of this section would have
given nearly identical results.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]
\begin{minipage}[t]{5.5mm}
\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{minipage}[t]{\textwidth - 5.5mm}

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{\includegraphics[width=0.22917in,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_Icons/R_circle_logo.pdf}
Rguroo: Large-Sample Mean Inference}\vspace{3mm}

The large-sample analysis follows the same steps as the earlier mean
inference examples, with one change: in the \textbf{Methods} section of
the \Dialog{One Population Mean Inference} dialog, select the
\Des{z-statistic} checkbox instead of the \Des{t-statistic} checkbox.
\Des{Sample Mean}, \Des{Sample S.d.} (or \Des{Pop S.d.} when \(\sigma\)
is known), \Des{Sample Size}, the alternative hypothesis, and the
confidence level are all entered exactly as before. This single change
applies to both hypothesis tests and confidence intervals.

\end{minipage}%
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Large-Sample Mean Inference}\vspace{3mm}

When the sample is large (as a rule of thumb, \(n \geq 30\)) \textbf{and
we are not assuming the population is normal}, the Central Limit Theorem
makes the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) approximately normal
regardless of the population's shape:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{When \(\sigma\) is known}, \(\bar{X}\) is approximately
  \(N(\mu_0,\ \sigma/\sqrt{n}),\) and the confidence interval is
  \(\left(\bar{X} - z^* \cdot \sigma/\sqrt{n},\ \ \bar{X} + z^* \cdot \sigma/\sqrt{n}\right).\)
\item
  \textbf{When \(\sigma\) is unknown}, replace \(\sigma\) with \(s\):
  \(\bar{X}\) is approximately \(N(\mu_0,\ s/\sqrt{n}),\) and the
  confidence interval is
  \(\left(\bar{X} - z^* \cdot s/\sqrt{n},\ \ \bar{X} + z^* \cdot s/\sqrt{n}\right).\)
\end{itemize}

In both cases, use the standard normal critical value \(z^*\) (the
\Des{z-statistic} method in Rguroo). If the population can be assumed
normal, use \(z\) or \(t\) as in the earlier sections instead --- this
large-sample method is not needed.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Comparing Two Means with Paired
Measurements}\label{sec-mean-paired}

So far in this chapter we have drawn inferences about a single
population mean. We now turn to comparing \emph{two} means. Many
questions take this form: comparing the mean SAT Math scores of incoming
CSUF freshmen and incoming Cal Poly students, the mean blood pressure of
patients who receive a new drug and those who receive a placebo, the
mean flipper lengths of Adélie and Gentoo penguins, or the mean ages of
individuals who agree versus disagree with legalizing marijuana.

Although all of these involve comparing two means, the structure of the
data can differ. In some studies, the observations in one group are
unrelated to the observations in the other. A student's SAT score at
CSUF is not naturally linked to any particular student's score at Cal
Poly, and an Adélie penguin is not paired with a specific Gentoo
penguin. Data of this kind are called \textbf{independent groups}, and
we take them up in Section~\ref{sec-mean-independent}.

In other studies, each observation in one group is naturally linked to
an observation in the other. We might measure a person's blood pressure
before and after taking a drug, or compare the cholesterol levels of
identical twins when one twin receives a treatment and the other does
not. Here the observations come in pairs, and the two measurements
within a pair are related. Data of this kind are called \textbf{paired
measurements} (or \textbf{dependent samples}), and they are the subject
of this section.

Inference for paired data reduces to a one-mean problem: instead of
working with the two sets of measurements, we work with the difference
between each pair. We introduce the idea with a blood pressure example,
then state the general procedure.

A researcher wants to determine whether a 6-week exercise program lowers
systolic blood pressure. Ten participants are selected, and each
person's blood pressure is measured before the program and again after
completing the program. Because the same individuals are measured twice,
this is a matched-pairs design (See Chapter 1). The analysis is based on
the differences between the two measurements for each participant.

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}crrr@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Participant & Before & After & Difference (After − Before) \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
1 & 142 & 139 & -3 \\
2 & 138 & 140 & 2 \\
3 & 150 & 147 & -3 \\
4 & 147 & 145 & -2 \\
5 & 135 & 136 & 1 \\
6 & 144 & 142 & -2 \\
7 & 139 & 140 & 1 \\
8 & 152 & 149 & -3 \\
9 & 141 & 140 & -1 \\
10 & 146 & 146 & 0 \\
\textbf{Total} & \textbf{1434} & \textbf{1424} & \textbf{-10} \\
\end{longtable}

The matched-pairs analysis focuses on the differences rather than on the
two columns separately. Once the differences have been computed, the
original measurements play no further role in the analysis.

A negative difference indicates that the participant's blood pressure
decreased after completing the exercise program. Since the difference is
defined as

\[
\text{Difference} = \text{After} - \text{Before},
\]

we interpret the sign as follows:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{After} < \text{Before}
&\Rightarrow \text{negative difference} \\
&\Rightarrow \text{blood pressure decreased},\\[6pt]
\text{After} > \text{Before}
&\Rightarrow \text{positive difference} \\
&\Rightarrow \text{blood pressure increased},\\[6pt]
\text{After} = \text{Before}
&\Rightarrow \text{zero difference} \\
&\Rightarrow \text{no change}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For example, Participant 1 has

\[
139 - 142 = -3,
\]

so this person's blood pressure decreased by 3 units.

Let's denote the observed mean difference by \(\bar{d}_{\text{obs}}\).
In this example, there are \(n = 10\) paired observations, and the sum
of the differences is \(-10\) mmHg. Therefore,

\[
\bar{d}_{\text{obs}} = \frac{-10}{10} = -1 \text{ mmHg}.
\] This indicates that on average, participants experienced a decrease
of 1 mmHg in systolic blood pressure after the exercise program. To
determine whether this is statistically significant, we ask whether an
average difference of \(-1\) mmHg is large enough, relative to the
sample-to-sample variability, to provide evidence of a real decrease in
the population mean blood pressure. We answer this by performing a
hypothesis test or constructing a confidence interval for the mean
difference, using the same methods as for one mean but applied to the
differences.

Let \(D\) denote the difference for a randomly selected pair (for
example, After − Before), with population mean \(\mu_D.\) For a sample
of \(n\) pairs, let \(\bar{D}\) denote the sample mean of the
differences and \(\sigma_D\) the population standard deviation of the
differences. Assuming the pair differences are approximately normally
distributed, the sampling distribution of \(\bar{D}\) is

\[
\bar{D} \sim N\!\left(\mu_D,\ \frac{\sigma_D}{\sqrt{n}}\right).
\]

As in the one-mean case, if \(\sigma_D\) is unknown we estimate it with
the sample standard deviation \(s_D\) of the differences, and

\[
\bar{D} \sim t_{n-1}\!\left(\mu_D,\ \frac{s_D}{\sqrt{n}}\right).
\]

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{The Normality Assumption Applies to the Differences}\vspace{3mm}

In paired inference, the normality assumption is about the pair
differences \(D,\) not about the two sets of measurements separately. We
assume the \emph{differences} are approximately normally distributed in
the population. The before-measurements and after-measurements need not
be normal themselves, and we never analyze them separately once the
differences have been computed.

\end{tcolorbox}

Every method from the one-mean sections carries over to paired data by
substituting the paired-data quantities for their one-mean counterparts:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
One-mean quantity & Paired-data counterpart \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Variable \(X\) & Pair difference \(D\) \\
Population mean \(\mu\) & Mean difference \(\mu_D\) \\
Boundary value \(\mu_0\) & \(\mu_{D,0}\) (typically 0) \\
Sample mean \(\bar{X}\) & Mean of differences \(\bar{D}\) \\
Observed value \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) & \(\bar{d}_{\text{obs}}\) \\
Population SD \(\sigma\) & SD of differences \(\sigma_D\) \\
Sample SD \(s\) & SD of differences \(s_D\) \\
\end{longtable}

The general procedure --- the hypothesis forms, the null distribution,
and the confidence interval --- is summarized in the box below.

In a paired test, the boundary value is almost always 0, since the usual
question is whether there is \emph{any} mean difference between the
paired measurements. In symbols, this value is written as
\(\mu_{D,0} = 0\), where \(\mu_D\) represents the population mean
difference and the subscript 0 indicates the value specified by the null
hypothesis. In the blood pressure example, the researcher wants to know
whether the exercise program \emph{lowers} systolic blood pressure. With
the difference defined as After − Before, a decrease corresponds to a
negative difference, so this is a test of

\[
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_D \geq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_D < 0. \end{cases}
\]

The direction of the alternative depends on how the difference is
defined. Had we defined the difference as Before − After, a decrease in
blood pressure would correspond to a \emph{positive} difference, and the
same research question would give \(H_a: \mu_D > 0.\) Either convention
is correct, as long as the alternative hypothesis is stated to match it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Paired-Difference Inference}\vspace{3mm}

Let \(D\) denote the pair difference (for example, After − Before), with
population mean difference \(\mu_D.\) For a sample of \(n\) pairs, let
\(\bar{D}\) be the sample mean of the differences and \(s_D\) the sample
standard deviation of the differences. Assume the pair differences are
approximately normally distributed in the population. The boundary value
of the null hypothesis is taken to be \(\mu_{D,0} = 0,\) so the
hypotheses are one of

\[
\text{Case 1: } \begin{cases} H_0: \mu_D \leq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_D > 0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\text{Case 2: } \begin{cases} H_0: \mu_D \geq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_D < 0 \end{cases}
\]

\[
\text{Case 3: } \begin{cases} H_0: \mu_D = 0 \\ H_a: \mu_D \neq 0 \end{cases}
\]

\textbf{Null distribution of \(\bar{D}.\)}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  When \(\sigma_D\) is known: \[
  \bar{D} \sim N\!\left(0,\ \frac{\sigma_D}{\sqrt{n}}\right).
  \]
\item
  When \(\sigma_D\) is unknown, it is estimated by \(s_D\): \[
  \bar{D} \sim t_{n-1}\!\left(0,\ \frac{s_D}{\sqrt{n}}\right).
  \]
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Confidence interval for \(\mu_D.\)} The
\((1-\alpha)\times 100\%\) confidence interval is

\[
\left(\bar{D} - z^* \cdot \frac{\sigma_D}{\sqrt{n}},\ \ \bar{D} + z^* \cdot \frac{\sigma_D}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \quad (\sigma_D \text{ known}),
\]

\[
\left(\bar{D} - t^*_{n-1} \cdot \frac{s_D}{\sqrt{n}},\ \ \bar{D} + t^*_{n-1} \cdot \frac{s_D}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \quad (\sigma_D \text{ unknown}),
\]

where \(z^*\) and \(t^*_{n-1}\) are the critical values for confidence
level \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%.\) To compute the interval from a
specific sample, replace \(\bar{D}\) with its observed value
\(\bar{d}_{\text{obs}}.\)

\end{tcolorbox}

To analyze paired data in Rguroo, we can either provide the raw data and
let Rguroo compute the differences internally, or enter summary
statistics for the differences directly. When raw data are provided, the
two measurements are stored in separate columns --- for example, Before
and After --- with each row corresponding to a single pair.
Table~\ref{tbl-paired-wide} illustrates this format.

\toprule\noalign{}
Participant & Before & After \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endfirsthead
\toprule\noalign{}
Participant & Before & After \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot

\end{longtable}

\begin{example}[Blood Pressure and Exercise: Paired t-Test (P-Value
Approach)]\protect\hypertarget{exm-blood-pressure-paired-pvalue}{}\label{exm-blood-pressure-paired-pvalue}

A researcher wants to determine whether a 6-week exercise program lowers
systolic blood pressure. Ten participants are selected, and each
person's blood pressure is measured before the program and again after
completing the program. The dataset \Data{BP_Paired_wide} contains these
data in wide format, with the variables \Var{Before} and \Var{After}
recording the blood pressure measurements before and after the exercise
program, respectively. The first three rows of the dataset are shown in
Table~\ref{tbl-paired-wide}. The dataset is available in the book's
Rguroo dataset repository.

Define the difference for each participant as

\[
D=\text{After}-\text{Before}.
\]

Use Rguroo to conduct a paired \(t\)-test to determine whether the
exercise program lowers mean systolic blood pressure.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  State the null and alternative hypotheses in terms of the population
  mean difference \(\mu_D.\)
\item
  Obtain the observed mean difference \(\bar d_{\text{obs}}\) and the
  standard error of the mean difference from the Rguroo output.
\item
  State the sampling distribution of the test statistic under the null
  hypothesis.
\item
  Report the p-value from the Rguroo output and state whether you would
  reject \(H_0\) at the \(\alpha=0.05\) significance level.
\item
  Interpret the results in the context of the exercise program and blood
  pressure.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

To answer this question, import the \Data{BP_Paired_wide} dataset into
Rguroo from the book's Rguroo dataset repository.

from 10 participants before and after completing a 6-week exercise

The variables included in this dataset are described below.

\Var{Participant}: Participant identification number

\Var{Before}: Systolic blood pressure measured before the exercise

between the paired measurements, where \(D\) is defined as After −

\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu_D \geq 0 \\
H_a: \mu_D < 0
\end{cases}
\]

b. We begin by setting up the problem in Rguroo. Click to expand the box

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Open the \textbf{Analytics} toolbox in Rguroo.
\item
  From the \Dpd{Analysis} dropdown, select \Fun{Mean Inference}
  --\textgreater{} \Fun{One & Two Population}. This opens the

\item

  Once this box is checked, the summary statistics for the differences

}

\caption{Select the paired variables and verify the summary statistics.}

\end{figure}%%

}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo output: Blood Pressure Example}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\end{tcolorbox}

From the Rguroo output, the observed mean of the paired differences is
\(\bar{d}_{\text{obs}} = -1\) mmHg, and the standard error of the mean
difference is 0.596 mmHg.

c. Under the null hypothesis, the sampling distribution of the test
statistic \(\bar{D}\) is approximately a Student \(t\) distribution with
\(n - 1 = 9\) degrees of freedom, centered at 0, with standard error
\(s_D/\sqrt{n}\approx 0.596.\) That is, \[
\bar{D} \sim t_9\!\left(0,\ 0.596\right).
\] Recall from Section~\ref{sec-mean-inference-unknown-sigma} that when
the population standard deviation is unknown, we estimate it with the
sample standard deviation and we use the Student \(t\) distribution with
\(n-1\) degrees of freedom to account for the additional uncertainty in
the estimate.

d. The \textbf{\emph{P-value Graph: Paired t-Test}} in the Rguroo output
shows that the p-value for the test is 0.0639, which is greater than the
significance level of 0.05. Therefore, we do not reject the null
hypothesis.

e. Since the p-value of 0.0639 is greater than the significance level of
0.05, we do not have sufficient evidence to conclude that the exercise
program lowers mean systolic blood pressure.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. We use the same \Data{BP_Paired_wide} dataset and dialog as in

the dataset, the \Var{After}/\Var{Before} variables, and checking

and select the \Des{t-statistic} checkbox. Click the preview icon
\includegraphics{Rguroo_Icons/preview_inline.png} to view the output.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo Output: Blood Pressure and Exercise, Confidence Interval}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\end{tcolorbox}

The \textbf{\emph{t-Based Confidence Interval}} table in the Rguroo
output gives the 95\% confidence interval for the mean difference in
systolic blood pressure as approximately \((-2.348,\ 0.349)\) mmHg.

b. We are 95\% confident that the true mean difference in systolic blood
pressure (After − Before) in the population of participants lies between
\(-2.348\) mmHg and \(0.349\) mmHg. Based on this sample, the exercise
program may lower mean systolic blood pressure by as much as 2.348 mmHg,
or may increase it by as much as 0.349 mmHg.

c. Since the interval \((-2.348,\ 0.349)\) includes 0, we do not have
sufficient evidence to conclude that the exercise program significantly
changes mean systolic blood pressure.

Note that a confidence interval is used to test \textbf{two-sided}
hypothesis tests \(H_0: \mu_D = 0\) versus \(H_a: \mu_D \neq 0\),
whereas Example~\ref{exm-blood-pressure-paired-pvalue} and
Example~\ref{exm-blood-pressure-paired-critical} tested the
\textbf{one-sided} hypothesis \(H_0: \mu_D \geq 0\) versus
\(H_a: \mu_D < 0\) (whether the program \emph{lowers} blood pressure).
What the interval tells us is that, at the 95\% confidence level, a true
decrease of more than 2.348 mmHg or a true increase of more than 0.349
mmHg are not plausible values for \(\mu_D.\)

\end{tcolorbox}

Sometimes the raw paired data are not available --- only summary
statistics for the differences have been reported. Rguroo's
\Fun{Mean Inference –> One & Two Population} function can also be run
directly from summary statistics. Select the \Des{Paired Data} checkbox,
then, in the \textbf{Population Paired Difference} section of the
\Tab{Summary Statistics} tab, enter a label for the differences, the
observed mean difference, the sample standard deviation of the
differences, and the sample size. Note that these summary statistics
describe the \textbf{pair differences} themselves: the sample mean is
the mean of the differences, and the sample standard deviation is the
standard deviation of the differences, not the standard error. From
there, the hypothesis test or confidence interval is specified exactly
as in the previous examples.

\begin{example}[SAT Prep Course: Paired Inference from Summary
Statistics]\protect\hypertarget{exm-sat-prep-paired-summary}{}\label{exm-sat-prep-paired-summary}

A tutoring company offers a 4-week SAT prep course. To evaluate its
effectiveness, 20 students take the SAT once, complete the course, and
then retake the SAT. The company reports only the following summary
statistics for the score differences
\(D = \text{Score after course} - \text{Score before course}\): a sample
of \(n = 20\) students, a mean difference of
\(\bar d_{\text{obs}} = 35\) points, and a sample standard deviation of
the differences of \(s_D = 62\) points.

Use Rguroo, entering the summary statistics directly, to determine
whether the prep course increases mean SAT scores.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  State the null and alternative hypotheses in terms of the population
  mean difference \(\mu_D.\)
\item
  State the sampling distribution of the test statistic under the null
  hypothesis.
\item
  Use Rguroo to obtain the p-value and state your conclusion at the
  \(\alpha=0.05\) significance level.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. Since we want to know whether the course \emph{increases} mean SAT
scores, and \(D\) is defined as after minus before, an increase
corresponds to a positive difference. Therefore, the alternative
hypothesis uses \(>\): \(H_a: \mu_D > 0\). The hypotheses are

\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu_D \leq 0 \\
H_a: \mu_D > 0
\end{cases}
\]

b. We begin by setting up the problem in Rguroo. Click to expand the box
below to see how to enter the summary statistics for the pair
differences directly.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]
\begin{minipage}[t]{5.5mm}
\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{minipage}[t]{\textwidth - 5.5mm}

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{\includegraphics[width=0.22917in,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_Icons/R_circle_logo.pdf}
Rguroo: Paired t-test from Summary Statistics}\vspace{3mm}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Open the \textbf{Analytics} toolbox in Rguroo.
\item
  From the \Dpd{Analysis} dropdown, select \Fun{Mean Inference}
  --\textgreater{} \Fun{One & Two Population}. This opens the
  \Dialog{One & Two Population Mean Inference} dialog.
\item
  Select the \Des{Paired Data} checkbox in the \Tab{Summary} tab.
\item
  In the \textbf{Population Difference} section of the
  \Tab{Summary Statistics} tab, enter a label (for example,
  \TypeIn{SAT Difference}), the sample mean of the difference
  (\Des{Sample Mean} \TypeIn{35}), the standard deviation of the
  differences (\Des{Sample S.d.} \TypeIn{62}), and the \Des{Sample Size}
  \TypeIn{20}.
\item
  Select the \Tab{Population 1-2} tab and the \Tab{Test of Hypothesis}
  sub-tab. In the \Dpd{Alternative Hypothesis \mu_d} dropdown, select
  the option greater than (\Des{>}) and type in the value \TypeIn{0}.
\item
  Under the \Des{Methods} section, select the \Des{t-statistic}
  checkbox.
\item
  Click the preview icon
  \includegraphics{Rguroo_Icons/preview_inline.png} to view the output.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo One \& Two Population Mean Inference dialogs for paired data from
summary statistics}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\includegraphics{Rguroo_dialogs/Mean Inference/SA_Summary_HT.png}
\includegraphics{Rguroo_dialogs/Mean Inference/SA_test_HT.png}

\end{tcolorbox}

\end{minipage}%
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo Output: SAT Prep}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\end{tcolorbox}

Under the null hypothesis, the test statistic \(\bar D\) is
approximately a Student \(t\) distribution with \(n-1 = 19\) degrees of
freedom, centered at 0, with standard error
\(s_D/\sqrt{n} = 62/\sqrt{20} \approx 13.86.\) That is, \[
\bar{D} \sim t_{19}\!\left(0,\ 13.86\right).
\]

c. From the Rguroo output the p-value is approximately 0.010. Since this
is less than the significance level of 0.05, we reject \(H_0.\) There is
sufficient evidence that the prep course increases mean SAT scores.

\end{tcolorbox}

As in the one-mean case, the normality condition is less important when
the number of pairs is large. By the Central Limit Theorem, when there
are many pairs, the sampling distribution of \(\bar{D}\) is
approximately normal even if the individual differences are not
perfectly normal. In practice, the paired \(t\)-procedures are often
reasonably robust, especially when there are no strong outliers or
extreme skewness in the differences.

\begin{enumerate}

\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Cholesterol Test} The cholesterol level of patients who had
  heart attacks was measured multiple times after the heart attack.
  Researchers want to determine whether the mean cholesterol level
  changes as time since the heart attack increases. Each patient's
  cholesterol was measured on day 2 and again on day 4, so the two
  measurements form a matched pair. Define the difference for each
  patient as \(D = \text{day4} - \text{day2}.\) We wish to investigate
  whether the mean cholesterol level \emph{changes} from day 2 to day 4.
  Import the \Data{Cholesterol} dataset into Rguroo from the book's
  Rguroo dataset repository and use the variables \Var{day2} and
  \Var{day4}. The first rows of the dataset are shown in
  Table~\ref{tbl-Cholesterol}, and the
  \hyperref[code-book-cholesterol]{codebook is here}. Conduct a paired
  test at the \(\alpha=0.01\) significance level by answering the
  following questions:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  State the null and alternative hypotheses in terms of the population
  mean difference \(\mu_D.\)

  Use Rguroo to obtain the observed mean difference
  \(\bar{d}_{\text{obs}}\) and the standard error of the mean
  difference.
\item
  State the sampling distribution of the test statistic under the null
  hypothesis.
\item
  Use Rguroo to obtain the critical region, and determine whether the
  observed mean difference falls in the rejection region.
\item
  Report the p-value and state whether you reject \(H_0.\)
\item
  Interpret the results in the context of cholesterol levels and time
  since heart attack.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{7}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Reiki Pain Interval} Using the same Reiki data described in
  Problem 7, we now estimate the mean difference in VAS pain score from
  before to after treatment with a confidence interval. The difference
  for each volunteer is \(D = \text{vas\_after} - \text{vas\_before}.\)
  Import the \Data{Reiki} dataset into Rguroo from the book's Rguroo
  dataset repository and use the variables \Var{vas_before} and
  \Var{vas_after}. The first rows of the dataset are shown in
  Table~\ref{tbl-Reiki}, and the \hyperref[code-book-reiki]{codebook is
  here}.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Use Rguroo to construct a 90\% confidence interval for the mean
  difference \(\mu_D\) in VAS pain score. Report the margin of error and
  the interval.
\item
  Interpret the confidence interval in the context of Reiki treatment
  and pain.
\item
  Use the confidence interval to determine whether Reiki changes mean
  pain. Note that the test in Problem 7 was one-sided
  (\(H_a: \mu_D < 0\)), while the confidence interval corresponds to a
  two-sided test; comment on whether the two conclusions agree and why
  they may differ.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{8}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Labor Participation Test} The female labor force participation
  rate (FLFPR) is the percentage of the female population aged 15 and
  older that is in the labor force. For each country, this rate was
  recorded in 1990 and again in 2018, so the two rates form a matched
  pair linked by country. Define the difference for each country as
  \(D = \text{y2018} - \text{y1990}.\) We wish to investigate whether
  the mean female labor force participation rate \emph{differs} between
  1990 and 2018. Import the \Data{Labor} dataset into Rguroo from the
  book's Rguroo dataset repository and use the variables \Var{y1990} and
  \Var{y2018}. The first rows of the dataset are shown in
  Table~\ref{tbl-Labor}, and the \hyperref[code-book-labor]{codebook is
  here}. Conduct a paired test at the \(\alpha=0.05\) significance level
  by answering the following questions:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  State the null and alternative hypotheses in terms of the population
  mean difference \(\mu_D.\)
\item
  Use Rguroo to obtain the observed mean difference
  \(\bar{d}_{\text{obs}}\) and the standard error of the mean
  difference.
\item
  State the sampling distribution of the test statistic under the null
  hypothesis.
\item
  Use Rguroo to obtain the critical region, and determine whether the
  observed mean difference falls in the rejection region.
\item
  Report the p-value and state whether you reject \(H_0.\)
\item
  Interpret the results in the context of female labor force
  participation in 1990 versus 2018.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Comparing Two Means with Independent
Groups}\label{sec-mean-independent}

We now turn to the second setting introduced at the start of
Section~\ref{sec-mean-paired}: two \textbf{independent groups}, where
the observations in one group are unrelated to those in the other.
Unlike the paired case, the two samples need not even be the same size,
and there is no pairing of individual observations across groups. The
paired approach of reducing to a single sample of differences is
therefore unavailable, and we need a different approach.

As in the one-sample and paired cases, we begin by introducing the
notation and assumptions for inference about two means with independent
groups. We then describe the methods for hypothesis testing and
confidence interval construction, and illustrate them with examples and
Rguroo analyses.

Table~\ref{tbl-two-mean-notation} summarizes the notation used when
comparing two independent population means. The parameter of interest is
the difference in population means, \(\mu_1-\mu_2.\) We estimate this
parameter using the difference in sample means, \(\bar{X}_1-\bar{X}_2,\)
whose observed value is \(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2.\)

As in the one-sample case, we will have two versions of the methods for
comparing two means, depending on whether the population standard
deviations \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) are known or unknown. We also
begin with the assumption that the two populations are normally
distributed. We present the sampling distributions, hypothesis testing
procedures, and confidence interval formulas for each case in the
subsections that follow.

The parameter of interest throughout is the difference
\(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\) and the natural estimator is the difference in sample
means \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2.\) Because the two samples are
independent, the variance of the difference is the \emph{sum} of the two
individual variances. This single fact --- variances add for independent
samples --- is what distinguishes the standard error here from the
one-sample and paired cases, and it drives the formulas in the
subsections below.

\subsection{The Case When the Population Standard Deviations Are
Known}\label{sec-two-mean-known-sigma}

When both population standard deviations \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\)
are known and both populations are normally distributed, the difference
in sample means \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) has a normal sampling
distribution. It is centered at the true difference \(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\)
and its standard error combines the two population standard deviations:

\[
\text{SE}(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}.
\]

The two variances are added, not subtracted, because the samples are
independent. Under the null hypothesis, the boundary value of the
difference is typically \(\mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0,\) corresponding to equal
population means.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Two Independent Means, \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) Known}\vspace{3mm}

When both populations are normally distributed and \(\sigma_1\) and
\(\sigma_2\) are known, the difference in sample means has the sampling
distribution

\[
\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \sim N\!\left(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\ \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}\right).
\]

\textbf{Hypotheses.} The boundary value is typically
\(\mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0,\) giving one of the three forms

\[
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \leq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \geq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 < 0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq 0. \end{cases}
\]

\textbf{Confidence interval.} The \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%\) confidence
interval for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) is

\[
\left((\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - z^* \cdot \text{SE},\ \ (\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) + z^* \cdot \text{SE}\right),
\]

where \(z^*\) is the standard normal critical value for confidence level
\((1-\alpha)\times 100\%,\) and

\[
\text{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}.
\]

To compute the interval from a specific sample, replace
\(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) with its observed value
\(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2.\)

\end{tcolorbox}

As in the one-mean case, the known-\(\sigma\) setting is mostly of
conceptual value, since the population standard deviations are rarely
known in practice. The realistic case, in which \(\sigma_1\) and
\(\sigma_2\) are estimated from the data, is taken up next.

\subsection{The Case When the Population Standard Deviations Are
Unknown}\label{sec-two-mean-unknown-sigma}

When the population standard deviations are unknown, we estimate them
separately from the data using the sample standard deviations \(s_1\)
and \(s_2,\) making no assumption about whether the two population
variances are equal. The standard error of \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\)
becomes the \textbf{estimated standard error}

\[
\widehat{\text{SE}}(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}.
\]

As in the one-mean case, replacing the unknown standard deviations with
sample estimates introduces additional uncertainty, and the sampling
distribution of \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) is approximated by a Student
\(t\) distribution rather than a normal. The degrees of freedom are
computed from the two sample sizes and standard deviations by a formula
that statistical software evaluates automatically; the resulting value
need not be a whole number. We do not compute the degrees of freedom by
hand. Rguroo reports the degrees of freedom along with the critical
values and p-values.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Two Independent Means, \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) Unknown}\vspace{3mm}

When both populations are normally distributed and \(\sigma_1\) and
\(\sigma_2\) are unknown, the difference in sample means has the
approximate sampling distribution

\[
\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \sim t_{\text{df}}\!\left(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\ \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}\right),
\]

where the degrees of freedom \(\text{df}\) are computed from the data by
software.

\textbf{Hypotheses.} The boundary value is typically
\(\mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0,\) giving one of the three forms

\[
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \leq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \geq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 < 0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq 0. \end{cases}
\]

\textbf{Confidence interval.} The \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%\) confidence
interval for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) is

\[
\left((\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - t^*_{\text{df}} \cdot \widehat{\text{SE}},\ \ (\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) + t^*_{\text{df}} \cdot \widehat{\text{SE}}\right),
\]

where \(t^*_{\text{df}}\) is the Student \(t\) critical value for
confidence level \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%\) on the software-computed
degrees of freedom, and

\[
\widehat{\text{SE}} = \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}.
\]

To compute the interval from a specific sample, replace
\(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) with its observed value
\(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2.\)

\end{tcolorbox}

This is the version used in nearly all practical two-group comparisons.
The known-\(\sigma\) formulas of Section~\ref{sec-two-mean-known-sigma}
are the conceptual special case; the unknown-\(\sigma\) formulas here
are what we apply to real data.

\subsection{The Case of Equal Population
Variances}\label{sec-two-mean-equal-var}

The unknown-\(\sigma\) method of
Section~\ref{sec-two-mean-unknown-sigma} makes no assumption about how
the two population standard deviations compare: \(\sigma_1\) and
\(\sigma_2\) may be equal or unequal, and each is estimated separately
by its own sample standard deviation. In some studies, however, there is
good reason to believe the two populations have the \textbf{same}
standard deviation, even though its common value is unknown. For
example, when two groups differ only in the treatment they receive and
are otherwise drawn from similar populations, it is often reasonable to
assume their spreads are equal.

When the two population variances can be assumed equal,
\(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma,\) we no longer estimate two separate
standard deviations. Instead, we combine the information from both
samples into a single estimate of the common standard deviation, called
the \textbf{pooled standard deviation}:

\[
s_p = \sqrt{\frac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}}.
\]

The pooled standard deviation is a weighted average of the two sample
variances, with more weight given to the larger sample. Using \(s_p\) in
place of the two separate estimates, the estimated standard error of
\(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) becomes

\[
\widehat{\text{SE}}(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) = s_p \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}.
\]

Because the common variance is estimated from the data, the sampling
distribution of \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) is again a Student \(t\)
distribution. Unlike the unequal-variance case, however, the degrees of
freedom are now a simple whole number: \(n_1 + n_2 - 2.\)

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Two Independent Means, Equal Population Variances}\vspace{3mm}

When both populations are normally distributed with equal but unknown
variances, \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2,\) the difference in sample means has
the sampling distribution

\[
\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \sim t_{\,n_1 + n_2 - 2}\!\left(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\ s_p \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}\right),
\]

where the pooled standard deviation is

\[
s_p = \sqrt{\frac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}}.
\]

\textbf{Hypotheses.} The boundary value is typically
\(\mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0,\) giving one of the three forms

\[
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \leq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \geq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 < 0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq 0. \end{cases}
\]

\textbf{Confidence interval.} The \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%\) confidence
interval for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) is

\[
\left((\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - t^*_{\,n_1 + n_2 - 2} \cdot \widehat{\text{SE}},\ \ (\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) + t^*_{\,n_1 + n_2 - 2} \cdot \widehat{\text{SE}}\right),
\]

where \(t^*_{\,n_1 + n_2 - 2}\) is the Student \(t\) critical value for
confidence level \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%\) on \(n_1 + n_2 - 2\) degrees
of freedom, and

\[
\widehat{\text{SE}} = s_p \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}.
\]

To compute the interval from a specific sample, replace
\(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) with its observed value
\(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2.\)

\end{tcolorbox}

The equal-variance method and the unequal-variance method of
Section~\ref{sec-two-mean-unknown-sigma} answer the same question and
use the same hypotheses; they differ only in how the standard error and
degrees of freedom are computed. When the two population variances
really are equal, the equal-variance method is slightly more powerful,
since it uses a single pooled estimate and a larger degrees of freedom.
When the variances are not equal, however, the equal-variance method can
be misleading, while the unequal-variance method remains valid. We
return to the question of which method to use once both have been
illustrated with an example.

In Rguroo, the choice between the two methods is made with a single
checkbox. The unequal-variance method is obtained as described in
Section~\ref{sec-two-mean-unknown-sigma}; to use the equal-variance
method instead, select the \Des{Equal Variances} option in the
\Dialog{One & Two Population Mean Inference} dialog. All other steps ---
selecting the variables, specifying the hypotheses or confidence level,
and choosing the \Des{t-statistic} method --- are unchanged.

\begin{example}[Comparing Two Independent Means - Marijuana Legalization
and
Age]\protect\hypertarget{exm-two-mean-unknown-sigma}{}\label{exm-two-mean-unknown-sigma}

Recall the GSS2024 dataset, a subset of the 2024 General Social Survey
(GSS) conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago. After removing
observations with missing values, the dataset contains information on
\(n = 399\) individuals.

Although the dataset includes many variables, we focus on two variables:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \Var{age}, which records the respondent's age in years.
\item
  \Var{Grass}, which indicates whether the respondent supports
  legalizing marijuana (Yes) or does not support legalizing marijuana
  (No).
\end{itemize}

Our goal is to investigate whether respondents who support legalizing
marijuana tend to be younger, on average, than respondents who do not
support legalization.

a. Let \(\mu_1\) denote the mean age of respondents who do not support
legalizing marijuana (No), and let \(\mu_2\) denote the mean age of
respondents who support legalizing marijuana (Yes). State the null and
alternative hypotheses for testing whether the mean age of respondents
who support legalization is less than the mean age of respondents who do
not support legalization.

b. Set up the problem in Rguroo's \Fun{Mean Inference} function to
perform a hypothesis test comparing the mean ages of the two independent
groups using the GSS2024 dataset. From the output, obtain the mean age
for each group and the observed difference between the sample means.

c. From the output, obtain the standard error and degrees of freedom
used in the test. Then state the sampling distribution of the test
statistic under the null hypothesis.

d. Determine the critical value for the test in the scale of the data at
the \(\alpha=0.05\) significance level. Does the observed difference
between the sample means fall in the rejection region?

e. State the p-value and determine whether you should reject or fail to
reject the null hypothesis.

f. Interpret the results in the context of the relationship between age
and support for legalizing marijuana.

\includegraphics{Rguroo_Icons/Rguroo_repo_logo.png} The dataset for this
example is available in the Rguroo dataset repository \Repo{Kozak}, with
the dataset name \Data{GSS2024}.

\textbf{Code book for Dataset GSS2024 is given
\hyperref[code-book-gss2024]{here}.}

\end{example}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title={🔎 Solution}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

a. The null and alternative hypotheses for testing whether the mean age
of respondents who support legalization is less than the mean age of
respondents who do not support legalization are:

\[\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 \leq \mu_2 \\ H_a: \mu_1 > \mu_2 \end{cases}\]

where \(\mu_1\) is the mean age of respondents who do not support
legalizing marijuana (No), and \(\mu_2\) is the mean age of respondents
who support legalizing marijuana (Yes).

This can also be expressed as: \[
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \leq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0 \end{cases}
\]

b. Click to expand the box below to see how to set up the problem in
Rguroo's \Fun{Mean Inference} function.

Rguroo: Two Independent Means - Marijuana Legalization and Age}\vspace{3mm}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Open the \textbf{Analytics} toolbox in Rguroo.
\item
  From the \Dpd{Analysis} dropdown, select \Fun{Mean Inference}
  --\textgreater{} \Fun{One & Two Population}. This opens the
  \Dialog{One & Two Population Mean Inference} dialog.
\item
  In the \textbf{Data} section of the dialog, a. select the
  \Data{GSS2024} dataset from the dropdown menu b. select the
  \Des{Variable} radio button (second set of radio buttons), and from
  the dropdown, select the variable \Var{age}. c. From the
  \Des{BY Factor} dropdown, select the variable \Var{Grass}.
\item
  In the \Tab{Summary} tab, a. under the \textbf{Population 1} section,
  from the \Dpd{Level} dropdown, select the level \emph{No}. b. under
  the \textbf{Population 2} section, from the \Dpd{Level} dropdown,
  select the level \emph{Yes}.
\item
  Select the \Tab{Population 1-2} tab, and select the
  \Tab{Hypothesis Test} sub-tab to specify the hypothesis test settings.
  a. In the \Des{Alternative Hyp \mu_1-\mu_2} dropdown, select the
  option \TypeIn{>} and type in \TypeIn{0} in the corresponding textbox.
  b. In the \Des{Significance Level} field, enter \TypeIn{0.05} (this is
  the default). c. Select the \Des{t-statistic} checkbox to specify that

\item
  Under the \textbf{Assumptions} section, select {[}Unequal variances{]}

\item

  \Tab{Test of Hypothesis and Simulation Methods} section, select
  \Des{P-value Graph} and \Des{Critical Region Graph}. This will
  instruct Rguroo to give results for both critical regions and p-value.
\item
  Click the preview icon
  \includegraphics{Rguroo_Icons/preview_inline.png} to view the output.
\item
  Click the \includegraphics{Rguroo_Icons/save_as.png} button and save

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo One \& Two Population Mean Inference dialogs for two independent
means with GSS2024 dataset}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\includegraphics{Rguroo_dialogs/Mean Inference/GSS2024_Grass_Age_step1.png}
\includegraphics{Rguroo_dialogs/Mean Inference/GSS2024_Grass_Age_step2.png}

respondents who support and do not support legalizing marijuana using
the GSS2024 dataset.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Rguroo Output: Marijuana Legalization and Age}, colback=white, breakable, coltitle=black, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, left=2mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, bottomtitle=1mm, arc=.35mm, titlerule=0mm, toptitle=1mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0]

\end{tcolorbox}

Referring to the Rguroo output \textbf{\emph{Data Summary}} table, the
mean age for respondents who do not support legalizing marijuana (No) is
approximately 56.642 years, and the mean age for respondents who support
legalizing marijuana (Yes) is approximately 51.394 years. Therefore, the
observed difference between the sample means is approximately
\(56.642 - 51.394 = 5.248\) years.

c. From the Rguroo output \textbf{\emph{Test of Hypothesis - t-Test}}
table, the standard error of the difference in sample means is
approximately 2.076 years, and the degrees of freedom used in the test
is approximately 191.1. The sampling distribution of the test statistic
under the null hypothesis is approximately t-distributed with center at
0, standard error 2.076 and 191.1 degrees of freedom: \[
\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \sim t_{191.1}\!\left(0,\ 2.076\right).
\]

d. The left panel of the Rguroo output \textbf{\emph{Critical Region
Graph: t-Test}}, shows the critical value for the test in the scale of
the data. This value at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) significance level is
approximately 3.432. Since the observed difference between the sample
means (5.248) is greater than the critical value (3.432), it falls in
the rejection region, and we reject the null hypothesis.

e. The \textbf{\emph{Test of Hypothesis: t-test}} table and the
**\_\_P-value Graph: t-Test\_** in the Rguroo output show a p-value of
0.0061. Since this value is less than \(\alpha = 0.05\), we reject the
null hypothesis.

f. We reject the null hypothesis and conclude that there is sufficient
evidence at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) level of significance that the mean
age of those who do not support legalization of marijuana is greater
than that of those who support legalization.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  From the Rguroo output, the observed difference in sample means is
  \(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 = 56.642 - 51.394 = 5.248\) years. The margin
  of error is approximately 4.096 years, and the 95\% confidence
  interval for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) is approximately
\end{enumerate}

\[
(1.154,\ 9.343) \text{ years}.
\]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\item
  We are 95\% confident that the true difference in mean age between
  respondents who do not support legalizing marijuana and those who do
  is between approximately 1.15 and 9.34 years. Because the entire
  interval is positive, the respondents who do not support legalization
  are, on average, older than those who support it, by somewhere between
  about 1 and 9 years.
\item
  The value 0 lies outside the 95\% confidence interval
  \((1.153,\ 9.343).\) A two-sided test of \(H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0\) at
  \(\alpha = 0.05\) would therefore reject \(H_0,\) indicating that the
  mean ages of the two groups differ. This is consistent with the
  conclusion of Example~\ref{exm-two-mean-unknown-sigma}, where the
  one-sided test rejected \(H_0\) in favor of
  \(H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0.\) Both analyses point to the same finding:
  respondents who do not support legalization are older, on average,
  than those who do.
\end{enumerate}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Choosing a Method for Two Independent Means}\vspace{3mm}

Two questions determine which method to use.

\textbf{1. Are the population standard deviations known?}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Known} \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) (rare in practice): use
  the normal-based method of Section~\ref{sec-two-mean-known-sigma},
  with critical value \(z^*.\)
\item
  \textbf{Unknown} \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) (the usual case):
  estimate them from the data and use a \(t\)-based method. Proceed to
  question 2.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{2. Can the two population variances be assumed equal?}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{No, or unsure} (the safer default): use the unequal-variance
  method of Section~\ref{sec-two-mean-unknown-sigma}. The standard error
  is \(\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2},\) and software computes the degrees
  of freedom (generally not a whole number). This method performs almost
  as well as the equal-variance method even when the variances happen to
  be equal, which is why many statistical software packages, including
  Rguroo, use it by default.
\item
  \textbf{Yes, with good reason}: use the equal-variance method of
  Section~\ref{sec-two-mean-equal-var}. The standard error uses the
  pooled standard deviation \(s_p,\) and the degrees of freedom are
  \(n_1 + n_2 - 2.\) A common rule of thumb is that this assumption is
  reasonable when neither sample standard deviation is more than about
  twice the other.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Large samples.} When both samples are large (as a rule of thumb,
\(n_1 \geq 30\) and \(n_2 \geq 30\)), the normality assumption is not
needed, and the normal-based large-sample method of
Section~\ref{sec-two-mean-large-sample} applies, with critical value
\(z^*.\)

\textbf{When in doubt, use the unequal-variance \(t\) method.} It
requires no assumption about equal variances, performs almost as well as
the equal-variance method when the variances are in fact equal, and is
the default in most software, including Rguroo.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The NHANES dataset contains many variables measured on a sample of
  U.S. residents. One variable, \Var{hhincomemid}, records household
  income derived from the midpoint of income categories. We treat males
  and females as two independent groups and wish to investigate whether
  the mean household income \emph{differs} between them. Let \(\mu_1\)
  be the mean income for males and \(\mu_2\) the mean income for
  females. Import the \Data{NHANES} dataset into Rguroo from the book's
  Rguroo dataset repository, and use the variable \Var{hhincomemid} with
  the BY factor \Var{gender}. Set Population 1 to the level
  \TypeIn{male} and Population 2 to the level \TypeIn{female}. The first
  rows of the dataset are shown in Table~\ref{tbl-NHANES}, and the
  \hyperref[code-book-nhanes]{codebook is here}. Using the
  unequal-variance method, conduct a test at the \(\alpha = 0.01\)
  significance level by answering the following questions:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  State the null and alternative hypotheses in terms of
  \(\mu_1 - \mu_2.\)
\item
  Use Rguroo to obtain the mean income for each group and the observed
  difference in sample means.
\item
  From the output, obtain the standard error and degrees of freedom, and
  state the sampling distribution of the test statistic under the null
  hypothesis.
\item
  Use Rguroo to obtain the critical region, and determine whether the
  observed difference falls in the rejection region.
\item
  Report the p-value and state whether you reject \(H_0.\)
\item
  Interpret the results in the context of male and female household
  incomes.
\end{enumerate}

\item
  Use Rguroo with the equal-variance method to construct a 90\%
  confidence interval for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2.\)
\item
  Report the observed difference in sample means, the margin of error,
  and the interval.
\item
  Interpret the confidence interval in the context of infant crying time
  and handling method.
\item
  Note that the test in Problem 7 was one-sided
  (\(H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0\)), while the confidence interval
  corresponds to a two-sided test. Use the confidence interval to
  determine whether the mean crying times differ, and comment on whether
  this conclusion agrees with the test in Problem 7 and why they may
  differ.
\end{enumerate}

\section{The Large-Sample Case}\label{sec-two-mean-large-sample}

As in the one-mean case, the assumption that the two populations are
normally distributed can be relaxed when both samples are large. By the
Central Limit Theorem, when \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) are both large (as a
rule of thumb, each at least 30), the difference in sample means
\(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) is approximately normally distributed
regardless of the shape of the two population distributions. The methods
of this section then apply as approximations.

As before, this large-sample method is most useful when normality cannot
be assumed. If both populations can reasonably be assumed normal, the
\(t\)-based methods of Section~\ref{sec-two-mean-unknown-sigma} or
Section~\ref{sec-two-mean-equal-var} remain the correct choice
regardless of sample size --- a large \(n\) does not by itself justify
switching from \(t\) to \(z.\) The method of this section is for the
case where normality is in doubt but the samples are large enough for
the Central Limit Theorem to apply.

When the population standard deviations are unknown, we replace them
with the sample standard deviations \(s_1\) and \(s_2,\) just as in the
one-mean large-sample case. For large samples these are reliable
estimates, and the difference in sample means is approximately

\[
\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \sim N\!\left(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\ \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}\right).
\]

In Rguroo, the only change from the unknown-\(\sigma\) procedure is to
select the \Des{z-statistic} method rather than the \Des{t-statistic}
method, exactly as in the one-mean large-sample case
(Section~\ref{sec-large-sample-mean}). Because the \(t\) distribution is
nearly identical to the normal for large degrees of freedom, the two
methods give essentially the same critical regions, p-values, and
confidence intervals when normality does hold --- but when normality
cannot be assumed, the \(z\)-based method here is the one that remains
justified.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, toprule=.15mm, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, colback=white, breakable, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, left=2mm]

\vspace{-3mm}\textbf{Large-Sample Inference for Two Independent Means}\vspace{3mm}

When both samples are large (as a rule of thumb, \(n_1 \geq 30\) and
\(n_2 \geq 30\)), the Central Limit Theorem makes
\(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) approximately normal regardless of the shape
of the two populations, so the normality assumption is not needed. When
\(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) are unknown, replace them with \(s_1\) and
\(s_2.\) The difference in sample means then has the approximate
sampling distribution

\[
\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \sim N\!\left(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\ \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}\right).
\]

\textbf{Hypotheses.} The boundary value is typically
\(\mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0,\) giving one of the three forms

\[
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \leq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \geq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 < 0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq 0. \end{cases}
\]

\textbf{Confidence interval.} The \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%\) confidence
interval for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) is

\[
\left((\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - z^* \cdot \text{SE},\ \ (\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) + z^* \cdot \text{SE}\right),
\]

where \(z^*\) is the standard normal critical value for confidence level
\((1-\alpha)\times 100\%,\) and

\[
\text{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}.
\]

To compute the interval from a specific sample, replace
\(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) with its observed value
\(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2.\)

\end{tcolorbox}

The previous chapter focused on comparing populations to determine
whether there is a difference between them. In this chapter, we shift
our focus from comparing populations to examining \textbf{relationships
between variables}. The variables do not need to measure the same or
similar quantities. For example, we might investigate whether alcohol
content is related to the number of calories in a beer or whether the
value of a house is related to the rental income it generates.

We will use \textbf{regression} to model relationships between variables
and make predictions, and \textbf{correlation} to describe the strength
and direction of those relationships. In this book, we focus on
\textbf{linear relationships}, although other types of relationships can
also be used to describe and model data.

\section{Regression}\label{sec-Regression}

\subsection{Exploring Relationships Between
Variables}\label{exploring-relationships-between-variables}

Before we can study a relationship between two variables, we need to
identify the role that each variable plays. The \textbf{response
variable} is the variable whose variability we are trying to explain or
whose value we want to predict. The variable used to help explain or
predict the response variable is called the \textbf{explanatory
variable} or \textbf{predictor variable}. More generally, variables used
to explain changes in a response variable are also referred to as
\textbf{predictors} or \textbf{covariates}.

A useful first step in exploring the relationship between two
quantitative variables is to construct a \textbf{scatterplot}. A
scatterplot allows us to see whether the variables appear to be related
and, in particular, whether the relationship appears to follow a linear
pattern. We begin with an example involving the alcohol content and
number of calories in beer.

\begin{example}[Determining if There is a
Relationship]\protect\hypertarget{exm-determine-relationship}{}\label{exm-determine-relationship}

12-ounce beers, including alcohol content and number of calories for
each beer. The data were obtained from the
\href{https://www.beer100.com/beer-calories/}{Beer100} website.

\item

\subsection{Finding the Regression
Line}\label{finding-the-regression-line}

To describe the linear relationship between two quantitative variables,
we use a statistical method called \textbf{regression}. This method
finds the straight line that best fits the data points on a scatterplot.
The resulting line is called the \textbf{least squares line}. It is also
commonly referred to as the \textbf{regression line}, and in this text
we will use both terms. The equation of this line summarizes how the
response variable changes as the predictor variable changes.

To determine the least squares line, we imagine drawing a line through
the data and measuring the vertical distance from each point to the
line. These vertical distances are called \textbf{residuals}. The least
squares line is the line that makes the sum of the squares of these
residuals as small as possible. Figure~\ref{fig-Beer-point-line}
displays this line on the scatterplot of Number of Calories versus
Alcohol Content.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{index_files/mediabag/Rguroo_outputs/Regression/AlcoholCalorieScatterLS.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-Beer-point-line}Scatterplot of Beer Data with
Regression Line}

\end{figure}%

To add a regression (least squares) line to the scatterplot in Rguroo,
you simply select the checkbox \Des{LS Line} in the \textbf{Superimpose}
section of the \Dialog{Scatterplot} dialog, as shown in
Figure~\ref{fig-scatterplot_dialog_LS}.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth,height=\textheight]{Rguroo_dialogs/Regression/scatterplot_dialog_LS.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-scatterplot_dialog_LS}Rguroo Dialog Showing How to
Add a Regression Line}

\end{figure}%

Given a collection of paired sample data, the regression equation is

\[
\hat{y}=b+mx,
\]

where \(m\) is the \textbf{slope} of the line and the point \((0,b)\) is
the \textbf{\(y\)-intercept}. Using the terminology introduced earlier,
we let \(x\) represent the \textbf{predictor variable} and \(y\)
represent the \textbf{response variable}. The quantity \(\hat{y}\) (read
\emph{y-hat}) is called the \textbf{predicted value} or \textbf{fitted
value} of the response variable for a given value of \(x\).

In our beer example, alcohol content is the predictor variable (\(x\)),
and the number of calories is the response variable (\(y\)). Thus, the
regression equation will allow us to predict the number of calories in a
beer based on its alcohol content.

The \textbf{residuals} are the difference between the actual observed
values of the response and the corresponding estimated (predicted)
values, namely

\[\text{residual} = y - \hat{y} = \mbox{observed value} − \mbox{predicted value}.\]

As we will show, the \Fun{Linear Regression} function in the
\textbf{Analytics} toolbox is used in Rguroo to fit a linear model,
producing both the equation of the regression line and the associated
fitted values and residuals.

\subsection{The Regression Equation and
Prediction}\label{the-regression-equation-and-prediction}

In this section, we learn how to find the equation of the regression
line and use it to make predictions. The regression equation describes
the relationship between the predictor variable and the response
variable, allowing us to estimate the value of the response for a given
value of the predictor variable.

\begin{example}[Find the Equation of the Regression
Line]\protect\hypertarget{exm-find-regression-equation}{}\label{exm-find-regression-equation}

Is there a relationship between the alcohol content and the number of
calories in 12-ounce beer? To determine if there is one, we examine the
sample of beer's alcohol content and calories, a portion of which is
shown in Table~\ref{tbl-Beer}.

\item
  Interpret the slope and the y-intercept in the context of the problem.
\item
  Use the regression equation to find the number of calories when the
  alcohol content is 7\%. This is the predicted value or the fitted
  value at \(x=7\).
\item
  Use the regression equation to find the number of calories when the
  alcohol content is 14\%.This is the predicted value or the fitted
  value at \(x=14\).
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}
